metadata.title: teorth/equational_theories (Lean blueprint)

extraction_notes.note: Macros \Equaref/\Equareffull/\Equadef are not defined in the source and are not recognised as references; I resolved \Equaref{N} to the 'Equation N' definition by hand (basis named). Blueprint \uses/\lean annotations are absent.
metametatheorem/metatheorem environments are undeclared, so latex_facts did not report them; extracted as prose theorem nodes with the environment body as span.
A proof environment titled 'Note for category theorists' proves nothing; retyped as remark, its two questions extracted as nested open_problem nodes.
Long lists of (non-)implications and the tables of order-5 laws are summarised as one claim per list; the tables themselves (table1-3) are not extracted item by item.

OEIS sequence values, Lean/automation process descriptions (chapters 21-26), and short provenance remarks after each 'Equation N' definition (self-dual, Putnam origin) were not made into nodes, except explicit equivalence claims.
Obelix extension lemma uses an undefined family \mathscr{E} and multiplicative notation; the 477 confluence proof relies on an undefined notion of 'simple' term and external notes.
Theorem '14 implies 29' has an empty proof environment; no proof node emitted.
Sentences that give an example automorphism T (resp. assert the polynomial form P_{w,i}) also introduce symbols used later; typed as definitions rather than example/claim.
Prose proofs ending in a lead-in ('We can conclude', 'and proves', 'we conclude') without punctuation before the theorem environment.

nodes.statement: A \emph{magma} is a set $G$ equipped with a binary operation $\op: G \times G \to G$. A \emph{homomorphism} $\varphi : G \to H$ between two magmas is a map such that $\varphi(x \op y) = \varphi(x) \op \varphi(y)$ for all $x,y \in G$. An \emph{isomorphism} is an invertible homomorphism.
nodes.name: Magma
differentia: equipped with a binary operation $\op: G \times G \to G$
nodes.statement_short: Magma = set with a binary operation; homomorphisms preserve it; isomorphisms are invertible homomorphisms.
nodes.label: magma-def

nodes.statement: A magma is called \emph{empty} if it has cardinality zero, \emph{singleton} if it has cardinality one, and \emph{non-trivial} otherwise.
nodes.name: Empty, singleton and non-trivial magmas
Number of magma structures on an n-element set
conclusions: The number of magma structures on a set $G$ of cardinality $n$ is of course $n^{n^2}$

nodes.statement: As there are $n!$ ways to rearrange the elements of a set of cardinality $n$, the number of non-isomorphic magmas on a set of cardinality $n$ is at least $n^{n^2}/n!$; as it turns out, most magmas are idemprimal (which implies in particular that there are no non-trivial isomorphisms), so the number of non-isomorphic magmas is fairly close to this lower bound.
nodes.name: Lower bound on non-isomorphic magmas
conclusions: the number of non-isomorphic magmas on a set of cardinality $n$ is at least $n^{n^2}/n!$
nodes.statement_short: At least $n^{n^2}/n!$ non-isomorphic magmas of size $n$, close to the truth since most magmas are idemprimal.

nodes.statement: The \emph{free magma} $M_X$ generated by a set $X$ (which we call an \emph{alphabet}) is the set of all finite formal expressions built from elements of $X$ and the operation $\op$. An element of $M_X$ will be called a \emph{word} with alphabet $X$. The \emph{order} of a word is the number of $\op$ symbols needed to generate the word. Thus for instance $X$ is precisely the set of words of order $0$ in $M_X$.
nodes.name: Free magma
nodes.genus: set of all finite formal expressions
differentia: built from elements of $X$ and the operation $\op$
nodes.label: free-magma-def

nodes.statement: For sake of concreteness, we will take the alphabet $X$ to default to the natural numbers $\N$ if not otherwise specified.
nodes.name: Default alphabet

nodes.statement: For a finite alphabet $X$, the number of words of order $n$ is $C_n |X|^{n+1}$, where $C_n$ is the $n^{\mathrm{th}}$ Catalan number and $X$ is the cardinality of $X$.
nodes.name: Number of words of order n
assumptions: For a finite alphabet $X$
conclusions: the number of words of order $n$ is $C_n |X|^{n+1}$
nodes.statement_short: Words of order $n$ over a finite alphabet are counted by Catalan numbers times $|X|^{n+1}$.

nodes.statement: Follows from standard properties of Catalan numbers.
nodes.name: Proof of Number of words of order n
nodes.statement_short: Standard Catalan-number counting of binary bracketings.

nodes.statement: Given a function $f: X \to G$ from an alphabet $X$ to a magma $G$, the \emph{induced homomorphism} $\varphi_f: M_X \to G$ is the unique extension of $f$ to a magma homomorphism. Similarly, if $\pi \colon X \to Y$ is a function, we write $\pi_* \colon M_X \to M_Y$ for the unique extension of $\pi$ to a magma homomorphism.
nodes.name: Induced homomorphism
differentia: the unique extension of $f$ to a magma homomorphism
nodes.label: induced-def

nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a set. A \emph{law} with alphabet $X$ is a formal expression of the form $w \formaleq w'$, where $w, w' \in M_X$ are words with alphabet $X$ (thus one can identify laws with alphabet $X$ with elements of $M_X \times M_X$). A magma $G$ \emph{satisfies} the law $w \formaleq w'$ if we have $\varphi_f( w ) = \varphi_f ( w' )$ for all $f: X \to G$, in which case we write $G \models w \formaleq w'$.
nodes.name: Law
nodes.statement_short: A law is a formal equation $w \formaleq w'$ of words; a magma satisfies it if all evaluations agree.
nodes.label: law-def

nodes.statement: 0 \op 1 \formaleq 1 \op 0
nodes.name: Commutative law (formal)
nodes.label: comm-law

nodes.statement: x \op y = y \op x
nodes.name: Commutative equation
nodes.label: comm-law-2

nodes.statement: A \emph{theory} is a set $\Gamma$ of laws. Given a theory $\Gamma$, a magma $G$ is a \emph{model} of $\Gamma$ with the (overloaded) notation $G\models\Gamma$ if $G\models w\formaleq w'$ for every $w\formaleq w'$ in $\Gamma$; we also say that $G$ \emph{satisfies} $\Gamma$. Given a law $E$, we write $\Gamma \models E$ if every magma $G$ that models $\Gamma$, also models $E$.
nodes.name: Models
nodes.label: models-def

nodes.statement: Given a theory $\Gamma$ and a law $w\formaleq w'$ over a fixed alphabet $X$, we say that $\Gamma$ \emph{derives} $w\formaleq w'$, and write $\Gamma\vdash w\formaleq w'$, if the law can be obtained using a finite number of applications of the following rules: \begin{enumerate} \item if $w\formaleq w' \in \Gamma$, then $\Gamma\vdash w\formaleq w'$. \item $\Gamma\vdash w\formaleq w$ for any word $w$. \item if $\Gamma\vdash w\formaleq w'$, then $\Gamma\vdash w'\formaleq w$. \item if $\Gamma\vdash w\formaleq w'$ and $\Gamma\vdash w'\formaleq w''$, then $\Gamma\vdash w\formaleq w''$. \item if $\Gamma\vdash w\formaleq w'$, then $\Gamma\vdash \varphi_f(w) \formaleq \varphi_f(w')$ for every $f: X \to M_X$. \item if $\Gamma\vdash w_1\formaleq w_2$ and $\Gamma\vdash w_3\formaleq w_4$, then $\Gamma\vdash w_1 \op w_3\formaleq w_2\op w_4$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.name: Derivation
nodes.statement_short: $\Gamma \vdash$ law: obtainable by finitely many applications of axiom, reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity, substitution and congruence rules.
nodes.label: derivation-def

nodes.statement: For any theory $\Gamma$ and words $w, w'$ over a fixed alphabet $$ \Gamma\vdash w\formaleq w'\ \mathrm{iff}\ \Gamma\models w\formaleq w'.$$
nodes.name: Birkhoff's completeness theorem
assumptions: For any theory $\Gamma$ and words $w, w'$ over a fixed alphabet
conclusions: $$ \Gamma\vdash w\formaleq w'\ \mathrm{iff}\ \Gamma\models w\formaleq w'.$$
nodes.statement_short: Syntactic derivability and semantic entailment of laws coincide.
nodes.label: sound-complete

nodes.statement: (Sketch) The `only if' component is soundness, and follows from verifying that the rules of inference in \Cref{derivation-def} holds for $\models$. The `if' part is completeness, and is proven by constructing the magma of words, quotiented out by the relation $\Gamma \vdash w \formaleq w'$, which is easily seen to be an equivalence relation respecting the magma operation.
nodes.name: Proof of Birkhoff's completeness theorem
nodes.statement_short: Soundness by checking each inference rule; completeness via the term model quotiented by derivability.

nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ be a theory, and let $E$ be a law. Then $\Gamma \models E$ if and only if there exists a finite subset $\Gamma'$ of $\Gamma$ such that $\Gamma' \models E$.
nodes.name: Compactness theorem
assumptions: Let $\Gamma$ be a theory, and let $E$ be a law.
conclusions: $\Gamma \models E$ if and only if there exists a finite subset $\Gamma'$ of $\Gamma$ such that $\Gamma' \models E$.
equivalent_conditions: there exists a finite subset $\Gamma'$ of $\Gamma$ such that $\Gamma' \models E$
nodes.label: compactness-thm

nodes.statement: The claim is obvious for $\models$, and the claim then follows from \Cref{sound-complete}.
nodes.name: Proof of Compactness theorem
nodes.statement_short: Derivations are finite, so apply Birkhoff's completeness theorem.

nodes.statement: Let $w \formaleq w'$ be a law with some alphabet $X$, $G$ be a magma, and $\pi: X \to Y$ be a function. If $G \models w \formaleq w'$, then $G \models \pi_*(w) \formaleq \pi_*(w')$. In particular, if $\pi$ is a bijection, the statements $G \models w \formaleq w'$ and $G \models \pi_*(w) \formaleq \pi_*(w')$ are equivalent.

nodes.statement: Define the total order of a law $w \formaleq w'$ to be the sum of the orders of $w$ and $w'$.

nodes.statement: Up to relabeling, the number of laws $w \formaleq w'$ of total order $n$ is $C_{n+1} B_{n+2}$.

assumptions: Up to relabeling
conclusions: the number of laws $w \formaleq w'$ of total order $n$ is $C_{n+1} B_{n+2}$
nodes.statement_short: Laws of total order $n$ up to relabeling number $C_{n+1}B_{n+2}$ (Catalan times Bell).

nodes.statement: Follows from the properties of Catalan and Bell numbers.
nodes.name: Proof of Counting laws up to relabeling

nodes.statement: Up to relabeling and symmetry, the number of laws $w \formaleq w'$ of total order $n$ is $$ C_{n+1} B_{n+2}/2$$ when $n$ is odd, and $$ (C_{n+1} B_{n+2} + C_{n/2} (2D_{n+2} - B_{n+2}))/2$$ when $n$ is even, where $D_n$ is the number of partitions of $[n]$ up to reflection.
nodes.name: Counting laws up to relabeling and symmetry
assumptions: Up to relabeling and symmetry

nodes.statement: The number of such laws of total order $n$ is zero if $n$ is odd, and $C_{n/2} B_{n/2+1}$ if $n$ is even.

nodes.statement: For integers $0 \le a \le b$ let $E(a,b)$ be the number of magma equations $t_1 = t_2$ with $t_1$ of order $a$, $t_2$ of order $b$, counting up to relabelling, up to switching terms, and only allowing the equation $x=x$ of the form $t=t$.

Alternate formula for E(a,b)

The number of magma equations of order $n$ (under the given constraints) is then equal to
$$\sum_{0 \le a \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor } E(a,n-a) .

nodes.statement: (From \href{https://mathoverflow.net/a/450905/766}{MathOverflow}). By \Equaref{387}, one has the law \begin{equation} (x \op x) \op y = y \op x. \end{equation} Specializing to $y=x \op x$, we conclude $$(x \op x) \op (x \op x) = (x \op x) \op x$$ and hence by another application of \Equaref{387} we see that $x \op x$ is idempotent: \begin{equation} (x \op x) \op (x \op x) = x \op x. \end{equation} Now, replacing $x$ by $x \op x$ in \Cref{387-again} and then using \Cref{idem} we see that $$ (x \op x) \op y = y \op (x \op x)$$ so in particular $x \op x$ commutes with $y \op y$: \begin{equation} (x \op x) \op (y \op y) = (y \op y) \op (x \op x). \end{equation} Also, from two applications of \Cref{387-again} one has $$(x \op x) \op (y \op y) = (y \op y) \op x = x \op y.$$ Thus \Cref{op-idem} simplifies to $x \op y = y \op x$, which is \Equaref{43}.
nodes.name: Proof of 387 implies 43
nodes.statement_short: Specialize 387 to show squares are idempotent and central, then deduce commutativity.

nodes.statement: The implication of \Equaref{1689} from \Equaref{2} is trivial. The converse is a surprisingly long chain of implications; see pages 326--327 of \cite{Kisielewicz2}. With some computer assistance, we found the following human-readable proof. We denote $y^1=y$ and $y^{n+1}=y^n\op y$ for $n\geq 1$. We also introduce the notation \begin{equation} f(x,y) = (x \op y) \op y , \qquad g(x,y) = x\op f(x,y) = x \op ((x \op y) \op y) . \end{equation} The initial equation states $x = (y \op x) \op f(x,z)$. Our main step will be to prove that for all $t\in M$ there exists $w\in M$ such that $f(t,w) = t$. The rest of the proof is then straightforward. Indeed, the initial equation gives $t = (y \op t) \op f(t,w) = (y \op t) \op t = f(y,t)$ for any $t,y\in M$. With such a simple expression of $f$ the initial equation becomes $x = (y \op x) \op z$, which easily implies the singleton law, for instance by writing $x = ((y \op w) \op x) \op z = w \op z$ for any $w,x,y,z \in M$. There remains to prove $f(t,w) = t$ for a well-chosen $w \in M$, explicitly, $w=g(t,t^5)=t\op t^7$. For any $t,u,v \in M$, the combinations $x = f(t,u)$ and $y = v \op t$ satisfy $y \op x = t$. Inserting these values into the initial equation yields the identity \begin{equation} f(t,u) = t \op f(f(t,u),z) . \end{equation} Specialize to $z=f(u,v)$ and note that $f(t,u) \op z = (\cdots \op u) \op f(u,v) = u$ by the initial equation so that $f(f(t,u),z) = (f(t,u) \op z) \op z = u \op z = g(u,v)$. Inserting this into \eqref{Kisielewicz-tfftuz} yields \begin{equation} f(t,u) = t \op g(u,v) . \end{equation} On the one hand, \eqref{Kisielewicz-tfftuz} with $z=u=t$ states that $t^3 = t \op t^5$, so (using $f(t^n,t)=t^{n+2}$) \begin{equation} f(t,t^5) = (t \op t^5) \op t^5 = t^3 \op t^5 = t^3 \op f(t^3,t) = g(t^3,t) , \end{equation} and \eqref{Kisielewicz-ftg} with $(u,v)=(t^3,t)$ then implies $f(t,t^3) = t \op g(t^3,t) = t \op f(t,t^5) = g(t,t^5)$. On the other hand, \eqref{Kisielewicz-ftg} with $(u,v)=(t,t^5)$ implies $t^3 = t \op g(t,t^5)$. We deduce \begin{equation} f(t,g(t,t^5)) = (t \op g(t,t^5)) \op g(t,t^5) = t^3 \op f(t, t^3) = (\cdots \op t) \op f(t,\dots) = t . \end{equation}
nodes.name: Proof of 1689 is equivalent to 2
nodes.statement_short: Computer-assisted human-readable proof: show $f(t,w)=t$ for $w=t\op t^7$, after which 1689 collapses to the singleton law.

nodes.statement: Suppose that a magma $G$ satisfies \Equaref{1571}, thus \begin{equation} x = (y \op z) \op (y \op (x \op z)). \end{equation} $$ x = ((x \op y) \op (x \op y)) \op ((x \op y) \op (x \op (x \op y)))$$ and $$ x = (x \op y) \op (x \op (x \op y))$$ whence $$x = ((x \op y) \op (x \op y)) \op x$$ which is \Equaref{2662}. This gives $$y = ((y \op z) \op (y \op z)) \op y$$ while from \Cref{1571-again} one has $$ (y \op z) \op (y \op z) = (x \op y) \op (x \op ((y \op z) \op (y \op z) \op y))$$ whence $$ (x \op y) \op (x \op y) = (y \op z) \op (y \op z).$$ This implies that $(x \op y) \op (x \op y)$ does not depend on $x$, or on $y$, hence is equal to some constant $e$: $$ (x \op y) \op (x \op y) = e.$$ From \Cref{1571-again} the magma operation is surjective, hence \begin{equation} x \op x = e \end{equation} which gives \Equaref{40}. Applying \Cref{1571-again} with $x=y=z$ we conclude $$ x = e \op (x \op e)$$ while if we instead take $y=z=e$ we have $$ x = e \op (e \op (x \op e))$$ hence $$ x = e \op x$$ and then also $$ x = x \op e$$ from which we readily conclude \Equaref{23}, \Equaref{8}; thus $e$ is an identity element. From \Cref{1571-again} with $z=e$ we now have \begin{equation} x = y \op (y \op x) \end{equation} which is \Equaref{16}. If instead we take $y=e$ we have \begin{equation} x = z \op (x \op z) \end{equation} which is \Equaref{14}. So if we substitute $z = x \op y$ and use \Cref{16-again} we obtain $$ x = (x \op y) \op y$$ and hence $$ y \op x = y \op ((x \op y) \op y) = x \op y$$ thanks to \Cref{14-again}. This gives \Equaref{43}, thus $G$ is now commutative. From \Cref{1571-again} once more one has $$x \op (y \op z) = (y \op x) \op (z \op ((x \op (y \op z)) \op x))$$ which one can simplify using commutativity and \Cref{16-again} (or \Cref{14-again}) to eventually obtain $$x \op (y \op z) = (x \op y) \op z$$ which is \Equaref{4512}. $G$ is now commutative and associative, and every element is its own inverse and of exponent $2$, hence is an abelian group thanks to \Cref{xxe}, so $G$ is an abelian group of exponent $2$ as claimed. The converse is easily verified.
nodes.name: Proof of Consequences of 1571
nodes.statement_short: Chain of substitutions: derive 2662, a constant square $e$, identity element, 16 and 14, commutativity, associativity.

nodes.statement: x = (y \op z) \op (y \op (x \op z)).
nodes.name: Equation 1571 restated
nodes.label: 1571-again

nodes.statement: x \op x = e
nodes.name: All squares equal e

nodes.statement: x = y \op (y \op x)
nodes.name: Equation 16 derived
nodes.label: 16-again

nodes.statement: x = z \op (x \op z)
nodes.name: Equation 14 derived
nodes.label: 14-again

nodes.statement: \Equareffull{953} is equivalent to \Equaref{2}.
nodes.name: 953 is equivalent to 2
conclusions: \Equareffull{953} is equivalent to \Equaref{2}.
nodes.label: 953_equiv_2

nodes.statement: It suffices to show that \Equaref{953} implies \Equaref{2}. Pick an element $0$ of $G$ and define $1 = 0 \op 0$ and $2 = 1 \op 1$ (we do not require $0,1,2$ to be distinct). From \Equaref{953} with $x=z=0$ we have $$ 0 = y \op 2.$$ If we then apply \Equaref{953} with $z=1$ we conclude that $$ x = y \op 0$$ for all $x,y$, from which one concludes $x=x'$ for any $x,x' \in G$, giving \Equaref{2}.
nodes.name: Proof of 953 is equivalent to 2
nodes.statement_short: Specialize 953 at a chosen element to show every element equals a fixed product.

nodes.statement: Definition \Equareffull{345169} axiomatizes the Sheffer stroke operation $x \op y = \overline{xy}$ in a Boolean algebra.
nodes.name: Sheffer stroke axiom
conclusions: axiomatizes the Sheffer stroke operation $x \op y = \overline{xy}$ in a Boolean algebra
nodes.statement_short: Equation 345169 is a single axiom for the Sheffer stroke in Boolean algebras.
nodes.label: sheffer

nodes.statement: See \cite{mccune_et_al}. In fact this is the shortest law with this property. A sketch of proof follows. One can easily verify that the Sheffer stroke operation satisfies this law. Conversely, if this law holds, then automated theorem provers can show that the three Sheffer axioms $$ (x \op x) \op (x \op x) = x$$ $$ x \op (y \op (y \op y)) = x \op x$$ $$ (x \op (y \op z)) \op (x \op (y \op z)) = ((y \op y) \op x) \op ((z \op z) \op x)$$ are satisfied. A classical result of Sheffer \cite{sheffer} then allows one to conclude.
nodes.name: Proof of Sheffer stroke axiom
nodes.statement_short: Cited; sketch: automated provers derive Sheffer's three axioms, then apply Sheffer's classical result.

nodes.statement:
A \emph{natural central groupoid} is, up to isomorphism, a magma with carrier $S \times S$ for some set $S$ and operation
$$ (a,b) \op (c,d) = (b,c).$$
nodes.name: Natural central groupoid
differentia: with carrier $S \times S$ for some set $S$

nodes.statement: These are examples of central groupoids, \Equareffull{168}.
nodes.name: Natural central groupoids are central groupoids

nodes.statement: \Equareffull{26302} characterizes natural central groupoids.
nodes.name: Natural central groupoid axiom
conclusions: \Equareffull{26302} characterizes natural central groupoids.
nodes.label: natural-central-groupoid

nodes.statement: See \cite[Theorem 5]{knuth}. The proof is quite lengthy; a sketch is as follows. It is easy to see that natural central groupoids satisfy \Equaref{26302}. Conversely, if this law holds, then \begin{align*} (y \op z) \op (z \op w) &= (( x \op ((w \op (y \op z)) \op w)) \op ((y \op z) \op w)) \op (z \op w)\\ &= z \end{align*} so we have a central groupoid. Setting $y = (t \op t) \op t$, $z = t \op (t \op t)$, $w = t \op t$ in \Equaref{26302} we also obtain $$ (x \op t) \op t = (t \op t) \op t.$$ Using the notation $$ x^{(1)} := (x \op x) \op x, \quad x^{(2)} := x \op (x \op x)$$ we then have \begin{align*} x \op t &= ((x \op x) \op (x \op t)) \op ((x \op t) \op t) \\ &= x \op t^{(1)}. \end{align*} A lengthy computer-assisted argument then gave the dual identity $$ t^{(2)} \op x = t \op x$$ Together, these give $$ x^{(2)} \op y^{(1)} = x \op y.$$ Multiplying on the left by $x = x^{(1)}\op x^{(2)}$, one can conclude that $$ x^{(2)} = x \op (x \op y).$$ One then has \begin{align*} (x \op y)^{(1)} &= ((y \op x) \op (x \op y)) \op (x \op y) \\ &= x \op (x \op y) \\ &= x^{(2)} \end{align*} and a similar argument gives $$ (x \op y)^{(2)} = y^{(1)}.$$ Since $(x \op x)^{(1)} = x^{(2)}$ and $(x \op x)^{(2)} = x^{(1)}$, we conclude that $x^{(1)}$ and $x^{(2)}$ are idempotent. Since $x = x^{(1)} \op x^{(2)}$, we see that every $x$ is the product of two idempotents. One can show that this representation is unique, and gives a canonical identification with a natural central groupoid.
nodes.name: Proof of Natural central groupoid axiom
nodes.statement_short: Cited (Knuth); sketch: derive central groupoid identities, show each element is a unique product of two idempotents.

nodes.statement: An \emph{Austin law} is a law which admits infinite models, but no nontrivial finite models: the law is equivalent to \Equaref{2} for finite magmas.
nodes.name: Austin law
differentia: admits infinite models, but no nontrivial finite models
also_stated_at: As noted in \Cref{infinite-model-chapter}: an \emph{Austin law} is a law which admits infinite models, but no nontrivial finite models.

nodes.statement:
Austin \cite{austin} established the first such law, namely the order $9$ law
$$ (((1 \op 1) \op 1) \op 0) \op (((1 \op 1) \op ((1 \op 1) \op 1)) \op 2) \formaleq 0.$$
nodes.name: Austin's order 9 Austin law

nodes.statement: \Equareffull{374794} is an Austin law.
nodes.name: Kisielewicz's first Austin law
conclusions: \Equareffull{374794} is an Austin law.
nodes.label: kis-thm

nodes.statement:
First we show that every finite model of \Equaref{374794} is trivial. Write $y^2 := y \op y$ and $y^3 := y^2 \op y$. For any $y,z$, introduce the functions ${f_y: x \mapsto y^3 \op x}$ and ${g_{yz}: x \mapsto x \op (y^2 \op z)}$. \Equaref{374794} says that $g_{yz}(f_y(x))=x$, hence by finiteness $g_{yz}=f_y^{-1}$, showing that $g_{yz}$ does not depend on the value of $z$. Since $$ f_y(y^2 \op z) = g_{yz}(y^3),$$ it follows that $f_y(y^2 \op z)=f_y(y^3)$ which by injectivity of $f_y$ implies that $z\mapsto y^2 \op z$ is a constant function (with $y$ fixed). Substituting $y^2$ for $y$ shows that the same is true for $z\mapsto (y^2 \op y^2) \op z$, and since $$ f_y(z) = (y^2 \op y) \op z = (y^2 \op y^2) \op z$$ we conclude that $f_y$ is also a constant function. But this function is already known to be injective, thus there do not exist distinct elements in its domain, showing that the model must be trivial. To construct an infinite model, consider the magma of positive integers $\Z^+$ with the operation $x \op y$ defined by $$ x \op y =  egin{cases} 2^y, & x= y \ 3^y, & x= 1,\ y 
eq 1 \ z, & x=3^z,\ y 
eq x \ 1, & else \end{cases}. $$ Then $y \op y = 2^y$ and $(y \op y) \op y = 1$ for all $y$. If $x
eq 1$ we have that $$ ((y \op y) \op y) \op x = 3^x, $$ and since $(y \op y) \op z$ is a power of two for all $y, z$ it follows that $$ 3^x \op ((y \op y) \op z) = x. $$ The case $x=1$ requires a further argument: observe that $w = (y \op y) \op z$ evaluates to one unless $z = 2^y$, in which case it evaluates to $2^{2^y}$ (which is greater than or equal to four). In particular, $w$ never takes the value two. Thus $$ (((y \op y) \op y) \op 1) \op ((y \op y) \op z) = 2 \op w = 1, $$ concluding our proof that this magma is a model of \Equaref{374794}
nodes.name: Proof of Kisielewicz's first Austin law
nodes.statement_short: Finite models: injectivity of $f_y$ forces it constant, so trivial. Infinite model on $\Z^+$ via powers of 2 and 3.

nodes.statement: \Equareffull{28770} is an Austin law.
nodes.name: Kisielewicz's second Austin law
conclusions: \Equareffull{28770} is an Austin law.
nodes.label: kis-thm2

nodes.statement:
Using the $y^2$ and $y^3$ notation as before, the law reads  egin{equation} x = (y^3 \op x) \op (y \op z). \end{equation} In particular, for any $y$, the map $T_y \colon x \mapsto y^3 \op x$ is injective, hence bijective in a finite model $G$. In particular we can find a function $f : G 	o G$ such that $T_y f(y) = y^3$ for all $y$ Applying \Cref{kis2-law} with $x = f(y)$, we conclude $$ T_y(y \op z) = y^3 \op (y \op z) = f(y) $$ and thus $y \op z$ is independent of $z$ by injectivity of $T_y$. Thus, the right-hand side of \Cref{kis2-law} does not depend on $x$, and so the model is trivial. This shows there are no non-trivial finite models. To establish an infinite model, use $\N$ with $x \op y$ defined by requiring $$ y \op y = 2^y; \quad 2^y \op y = 3^y$$ and $$ 3^y \op x = 3^y 5^x$$ for $x 
eq 3^y$, and $$ (3^y 5^x) \op z = x$$ for $z 
eq 3^y 5^x$. Finally set $$ 2^{3^y} \op z = 3^y$$ for $z 
eq 3^y, 2^{3^y}$. All other assignments of $\op$ may be made almost arbitrarily, such as setting them to $1$. It is then a routine matter to establish \Cref{kis2-law}.
nodes.name: Proof of Kisielewicz's second Austin law
nodes.statement_short: Finite case: $T_y$ bijective makes $y\op z$ independent of $z$; infinite model on $\N$ by prime-power encoding.

nodes.statement: x = (y^3 \op x) \op (y \op z).
nodes.name: Equation 28770 in power notation
nodes.label: kis2-law

nodes.statement: In that paper a computer search was also used to show that no law of order four or less is an Austin law.
nodes.name: No Austin law of order at most four
conclusions: no law of order four or less is an Austin law
also_stated_at: Austin laws have order 5 or greater \cite{Kisielewicz2}.

nodes.statement: An open question is whether \Equareffull{5093} is an Austin law.
nodes.name: Is Equation 5093 an Austin law?

nodes.statement: \Equaref{5093} has no non-trivial finite models.
nodes.name: Equation 5093 has no non-trivial finite models
conclusions: \Equaref{5093} has no non-trivial finite models.
nodes.label: 5093-nontrivial

nodes.statement: From \Equaref{5093} we see that the map $w \mapsto y \op w$ is onto, hence injective in a finite model. Using this injectivity four times in \Equaref{5093}, we see that $z \op y$ does not depend on $z$, hence the expression $x \op (z \op y)$ does not depend on $x$. By \Equaref{5093} again, this means that $x$ does not depend on $x$, which is absurd in a non-trivial model.
nodes.name: Proof of Equation 5093 has no non-trivial finite models
nodes.statement_short: Left multiplication is onto, hence injective in finite models; peel off four times to get triviality.

nodes.statement: Any law with at most two variables has a non-trivial finite model.
nodes.name: Austin's finite model theorem
assumptions: Any law with at most two variables
conclusions: has a non-trivial finite model
nodes.label: austin-two

nodes.statement: If neither side of the law is a single variable then the zero law $x \op y = 0$ will work, so one can assume the law takes the form $x = f(x,y)$. Consider a finite field $F$ with the operation $x \op y := ax+by$ for some coefficients $a,b \in F$. Then the law becomes a pair of equations $P(a,b)=0$, $Q(a,b)=1$ in the coefficients for some polynomials $P,Q$ with integer coefficients, which one can verify to not divide each other (they have the same degree, and do not have the same set of non-zero monomials). From Bezout's theorem, this equation has a solution in some field, and hence by the Lefschetz principle it has a solution in a finite field.
nodes.name: Proof of Austin's finite model theorem
nodes.statement_short: Linear models $ax+by$ over a field; Bezout and the Lefschetz principle give a finite field solution.

nodes.statement: Many implications for finite magmas rely on the fact that if $f, g:X \to X$ are functions on a finite set $X$, then $f \circ g = I$ if and only if $g \circ f = I$.
nodes.name: Left inverse is right inverse on finite sets
assumptions: $f, g:X \to X$ are functions on a finite set $X$
conclusions: $f \circ g = I$ if and only if $g \circ f = I$

nodes.statement: Let $X$ be finite, and let $f, g: X \to X$ be such that $f = f \circ f \circ g$. Then $f = f \circ g \circ f$.
nodes.name: ffg lemma
assumptions: Let $X$ be finite, and let $f, g: X \to X$ be such that $f = f \circ f \circ g$.
conclusions: $f = f \circ g \circ f$
nodes.label: ffg

nodes.statement: Call a point $x \in X$ \emph{periodic} if $f^n(x) = x$ for some $n>0$. Because the forward orbit $x, f(x), f^2(x), \dots$ in a finite space $X$ must repeat, we see that for each $x$ there exists an $n$ such that $f^n(x)$ is periodic. Let $n_x$ be the first $n$ for which this occurs. If $n_x > 1$, then $g(x), f(g(x)), f(f(g(x))$ cannot be periodic (as this would imply $f(x)$ periodic), and then we can see that $n_{g(x)} = n_x + 1$. Hence the maximal value of $n_x$ is at most $1$, which implies that $f(x)$ is periodic for every $x$. Thus there is an $n > 1$ such that $f^n = f$. Since $f = f^2 \circ g$, we have $f^n = f^{n-2} \circ f \circ f = f^{n-2} \circ (f^2 \circ g) \circ f = f^n \circ g \circ f = f \circ g \circ f$, as desired.
nodes.name: Proof of ffg lemma
nodes.statement_short: Periodic points: every image point is periodic, so $f^n=f$ for some $n>1$, then rewrite.

nodes.statement: Let $X$ be finite, and let $f, g: X \to X$ be such that $f = g \circ f \circ f$. Then $f = f \circ g \circ f$.
nodes.name: gff lemma
assumptions: Let $X$ be finite, and let $f, g: X \to X$ be such that $f = g \circ f \circ f$.
conclusions: $f = f \circ g \circ f$
nodes.label: gff

nodes.statement: By hypothesis, $f^2(x)$ uniquely determines $f(x)$. This prevents $n_x = 2$ for any $x$ (because if $n>2$ is such that $f^{n+2}(x) = f^2(x)$, then $f^{n+1}(x) \neq f(x)$), and hence also prevents $n_x > 2$ for any $x$. So again we have $f(x)$ periodic for all $x$, so $f^n = f$ for some $n>1$. Then $f = f^n = f \circ (g \circ f^2) \circ f^{n-2} = f \circ g \circ f^n = f \circ g \circ f$ as required.
nodes.name: Proof of gff lemma
nodes.statement_short: As before: $f^2(x)$ determines $f(x)$, forcing all image points periodic, so $f^n=f$.

nodes.statement: Let $X$ be finite and $f: X \to X$. Then there exists $n \geq 1$ such that $f^{2n} = f^n$.
nodes.name: Eventual period
assumptions: Let $X$ be finite and $f: X \to X$.
conclusions: there exists $n \geq 1$ such that $f^{2n} = f^n$
nodes.label: period

nodes.statement: By the pigeonhole principle, there exists $n \geq 1$, $m \geq 0$ such that $f^{m+n} = f^m$, which implies on iteration that $f^{m+mn} = f^m$ and hence $f^{2mn} = f^{mn}$, giving the claim.
nodes.name: Proof of Eventual period

nodes.statement: All finite magmas which satisfy \Equareffull{3994} also satisfy \Equareffull{3588}.
nodes.name: 3994 implies 3588 for finite models
assumptions: All finite magmas which satisfy \Equareffull{3994}
conclusions: also satisfy \Equareffull{3588}
nodes.label: finite_imp_3994_3588_thm

nodes.statement: For a finite magma $M$, consider the set $S = \{x \op y | x, y \in M\}$. Now $f_z : x \mapsto z \op x$ and $g_z : x \mapsto x \op z$. They both map $S$ to $S$, and due to the hypothesis $g_z \op f_z$ is the identity on $S$, so because $S$ is finite $f_z$ and $g_z$ must be inverse bijections on it, and therefore they commute.
nodes.name: Proof of 3994 implies 3588 for finite models
nodes.statement_short: On the set of products, left and right multiplications are inverse bijections in finite magmas, so they commute.

nodes.statement: There exists a magma which satisfies \Equaref{3994} and not \Equaref{3588}.
nodes.name: 3994 does not imply 3588 for infinite models
conclusions: There exists a magma which satisfies \Equaref{3994} and not \Equaref{3588}.
nodes.label: non_imp_3994_3588_thm

nodes.statement: Consider $\mathbb{N}$, with $x \op y$ defined as $x \oplus y$ (bitwise XOR) if $x$ and $y$ are even, $y+2$ if only $y$ is even, $x \dot - 2$ if only $x$ is even, and $0$ if both are odd. Note that the range of the operation is the set of even naturals. \Equaref{3994} is satisfied, because for even $z$ we get $z \oplus (x \op y) \oplus z = x \op y$ and for odd $z$ we get $(x \op y) + 2 \dot - 2 = x \op y$. Setting $x = y = z = 1$, \Equaref{3588} isn't satisfied.
nodes.name: Proof of 3994 does not imply 3588 for infinite models
nodes.statement_short: Explicit model on $\N$ via bitwise XOR on evens.

nodes.statement: On a finite magma $M$, equation 3342, $x \op y= y \op (x \op (x \op x))$, implies equation 3522, $x \op y = x \op ((y \op y) \op y)$, as well as equation 4118, $x \op y = ((x \op x) \op x) \op y$.
nodes.name: 3342 implies 3522 and 4118 for finite magmas
assumptions: On a finite magma $M$, equation 3342, $x \op y= y \op (x \op (x \op x))$
conclusions: equation 3522, $x \op y = x \op ((y \op y) \op y)$
equation 4118, $x \op y = ((x \op x) \op x) \op y$

nodes.statement: Write $Sx := x \op$, $fx := x \op Sx$ and $Cx = Sx \op x$, then we have $x \op y= y \op fx$, and our task is to show $x \op y = Cx \op y$ and $x \op y = x \op Cy$ for finite magmas, giving the four open implications. Note that $x \op y= y \op fx = fx \op fy$, hence $f$ is a homomorphism. By \Cref{period}, there is $n \geq 1$ with $f^n = f^{2n}$. From 3342 we have $Sx = S fx$ and $Cx = Sx \op x = f^n Sx \op f^n x = f^n Sx \op f^{2n} x = f^{2n-1} x \op f^n Sx = f^{n-1} x \op S x = f(f^{n-1} x) = f^n x$. Then $$ Cx \op y = f^n x \op y = f^{2n} x \op f^n y = f^n x \op f^n y = x \op y$$ and a similar argument gives $x \op Cy = x \op y$.
nodes.name: Proof of 3342 implies 3522 and 4118 for finite magmas
nodes.statement_short: $f(x)=x\op Sx$ is a homomorphism; eventual period of $f$ gives $Cx=f^n x$ and hence the claims.

nodes.statement: For finite magmas, Equation 1167, $$ x = y \op ((z \op (y \op y)) \op x)$$ implies Equation 1096, $$ x = y \op ((x \op (z \op y)) \op x).$$
nodes.name: 1167 implies 1096 for finite magmas
assumptions: For finite magmas

Equation 1167,
  $$ x = y \op ((z \op (y \op y)) \op x)$$
conclusions:
implies Equation 1096,
$$ x = y \op ((x \op (z \op y)) \op x).$$

nodes.statement: We write 1167 as $$ L_y L_{z \op Sy} = I,$$ hence $L_y$ is invertible and $L_{z \op Sy} L_y = I$. In particular $L_{z \op Sy} Sy = y$, hence squaring is injective, hence surjective. So 1167 can be rewritten as $L_{S^{-1} y} L_{z \op y} = I$, hence $L_{z \op y}$ is independent of $z$. In particular $$ L_{x \op (z \op y)} = L_{S^{-2} z \op (z \op y)} = L_{L_{S^{-2} z} L_{S^{-1} z \op S S^{-2} z} y} = L_y$$ by 1167, hence the right-hand side of 1096 is independent of $z$. Replacing $z$ with $y$, the claim now follows from 1167.
nodes.name: Proof of 1167 implies 1096 for finite magmas
nodes.statement_short: Left-multiplication operator identities; finiteness makes squaring bijective.

nodes.statement: For finite magmas, Equation 1133, $$ x = y \op ((y \op (z \op y)) \op x)$$ implies Equation 1167, $$ x = y \op ((z \op (y \op y)) \op x).$$
nodes.name: 1133 implies 1167 for finite magmas
assumptions: For finite magmas

Equation 1133,
$$ x = y \op ((y \op (z \op y)) \op x)$$
conclusions:
implies Equation 1167,
  $$ x = y \op ((z \op (y \op y)) \op x).$$

nodes.statement: 1133 asserts that $L_y L_{y \op (z \op y)} = I$, hence $L_y$ is invertible and $L_{y \op (z \op y)} = L_y^{-1}$ does not depend on $z$. Setting $z = y \op Sy$ we see from 1133 that $y \op (z \op y) = y$ and hence we have left-involution: $L_y = L_y^{-1}$. Replacing $y$ with $L_z y$ in 1133 we now get $L_{L_z y} L_{L_z y \op y} = I$, which since $L_{L_z y}$ is its own inverse gives \begin{equation} L_{L_z y \op y} = L_{L_z y}. \end{equation} In particular $$ R_y^3 z = L_{L_z y \op y} y = L_{L_z y} y = R_y^2 z$$ hence as $L_{R_y^2 z}$ is its own inverse $$ y =L_{R_y^2 z} L_{R_y^2 z} y = L_{R_y^2 z} R_y^3 z = L_{R_y^2 z} R_y^3 z = S( R_y^2 z).$$ Thus squaring is surjective, hence invertible. Next, by \eqref{intermediate} we have $L_{z \op Sy} = L_w$ where $w = R_{Sy}^2 z$. By \eqref{intermediate} and the fact that $L_w$ is its own inverse, we have $$ L_w^2 w = w = L_{z \op Sy} Sy =L_w Sy,$$ hence $Sw = L_w w = Sy$. As $S$ is injective, we have $L_w = L_y$, and then $L_y L_{z \op Sy} = L_y^2 = I$, giving 1167.
nodes.name: Proof of 1133 implies 1167 for finite magmas
nodes.statement_short: Left multiplications are involutions; squaring is surjective hence invertible; conclude $L_w=L_y$.

nodes.statement: L_{L_z y \op y} = L_{L_z y}.
nodes.name: Intermediate identity for 1133
nodes.label: intermediate

nodes.statement: For finite magmas, Equation 1441, $$ x = (x \op y) \op (x \op (x \op x))$$ implies Equation 4067, $$ x \op x = ((x \op x) \op y) \op x,$$ and equation 1443, $$ x = (x \op y) \op (x \op (x \op z))$$ implies Equation 3055, $$ x = (((x \op x) \op y) \op x) \op x.$$
nodes.name: 1441 implies 4067, 1443 implies 3055 for finite magmas
assumptions: For finite magmas

Equation 1441,
$$ x = (x \op y) \op (x \op (x \op x))$$

equation 1443,
$$ x = (x \op y) \op (x \op (x \op z))$$
conclusions:
implies Equation 4067,
$$ x \op x = ((x \op x) \op y) \op x,$$

implies Equation 3055,
$$ x = (((x \op x) \op y) \op x) \op x.$$

assumptions:
Equation 1441,
$$ x = (x \op y) \op (x \op (x \op x))$$
conclusions:
implies Equation 4067,
$$ x \op x = ((x \op x) \op y) \op x,$$

assumptions:
equation 1443,
$$ x = (x \op y) \op (x \op (x \op z))$$
conclusions:
implies Equation 3055,
$$ x = (((x \op x) \op y) \op x) \op x.$$

nodes.statement: Write $\tilde C x = x \op Sx$, then 1441 asserts that $R_{\tilde Cx} R_y x = x$. Setting $$y=Sx$$ we get $x = S\tilde Cx$, so by finiteness $\tilde C Sx = x$. Replacing $x$ with $Sx$ in 1441 we conclude $R_x R_y Sx = Sx$ which is 4067. Clearly 1443 implies 1441, hence 4067 by the previous implication, so that 3055 simplifies to $x = Sx \op x$. Meanwhile, 1443 also implies $x = S(x \op (x \op z))$. On taking square roots and using $S \tilde C = x$, we obtain $x \op (x \op z) = \tilde Cx$. Applying this with $z = Sx$ we conclude $L_x \tilde Cx = \tilde Cx$, hence on replacing $x$ with $Sx$ we get $L_{Sx} x = x$ as required.
nodes.name: Proof of 1441 implies 4067, 1443 implies 3055 for finite magmas
nodes.statement_short: Right multiplication operator identities plus finiteness invert $\tilde C$ and $S$.

nodes.statement: For finite magmas, Equation 1681, $$ x = (y \op x) \op ((x \op x) \op x)$$ implies Equation 3877, $$ x \op x = (y \op (x \op x)) \op x,$$ and Equation 1701, $$ x = (y \op x) \op ((z \op x) \op x)$$ implies Equation 1035, $$ x = x \op ((y \op (x \op x)) \op x).$$
nodes.name: 1681 implies 3877, 1701 implies 1035 for finite magmas
assumptions: For finite magmas

Equation 1681,
$$ x = (y \op x) \op ((x \op x) \op x)$$

Equation 1701,
$$ x = (y \op x) \op ((z \op x) \op x)$$
conclusions:
implies Equation 3877,
$$ x \op x = (y \op (x \op x)) \op x,$$

implies Equation 1035,
$$ x = x \op ((y \op (x \op x)) \op x).$$

assumptions:
Equation 1681,
$$ x = (y \op x) \op ((x \op x) \op x)$$
conclusions:
implies Equation 3877,
$$ x \op x = (y \op (x \op x)) \op x,$$

assumptions:
Equation 1701,
$$ x = (y \op x) \op ((z \op x) \op x)$$
conclusions:
implies Equation 1035,
$$ x = x \op ((y \op (x \op x)) \op x).$$

nodes.statement: This is very similar to the previous proof. Write $Cx = Sx \op x$, then 1681 asserts $R_{Cx} L_y x = x$. Again setting $y=Sx$ yields $x=SCx$ hence $x = CSx$, and on replacing $x$ with $Sx$ in 1681 one obtains 3877. For the second part, we simplify to $x = x \op Sx$, while 1701 gives $x = S((z \op x) \op x)$ hence $(z \op x) \op x = Cx$, so $R_x Cx = Cx$, so $R_{Sx} x = x$ as required.
nodes.name: Proof of 1681 implies 3877, 1701 implies 1035 for finite magmas
nodes.statement_short: Same operator argument as the previous proposition with $Cx = Sx\op x$.

nodes.statement: Each magma can be used to establish anti-implications: if $\Gamma$ is the set of all laws satisfied by a magma $G$, then we have $\neg E \leq E'$ whenever $E \in \Gamma$ and $E' \not \in \Gamma$.
nodes.name: Magmas give anti-implications
assumptions: if $\Gamma$ is the set of all laws satisfied by a magma $G$
conclusions: we have $\neg E \leq E'$ whenever $E \in \Gamma$ and $E' \not \in \Gamma$

nodes.statement: A magma is a quasigroup if, for all $y$, the left/right multiplications $x\mapsto y\op x$ and $x\mapsto x\op y$ are bijective (equivalent to injective in a finite magma).
nodes.name: Quasigroup
differentia: the left/right multiplications $x\mapsto y\op x$ and $x\mapsto x\op y$ are bijective

nodes.statement: Knuth's construction \cite{knuth} of a central groupoid (\Equaref{168}) as follows.  Let $S$ be a (finite) set with a distinguished element $0$, and a binary operation $*$ such that $x*0=0$ and $0*x=x$   for all $x$, and for each $x,y$ there is a unique $z$ with $x*z=y$.  One can then define a central groupoid on $S \times S$ by defining $(a,b) \op (c,d)$ to equal $(b,c)$ if $c,d \neq 0$; $(b,e)$ if $b*e=c$ is non-zero and $d=0$; and $(a*b,0)$ if $c=0$.  One such example in \cite{knuth} is when $S = \{0,1,2\}$ with $1*1=2*1=2$ and $1*2=2*2=1$.
nodes.name: Knuth's construction of central groupoids
nodes.statement_short: Central groupoid on $S\times S$ built from a left-quasigroup-like operation $*$ on $S$ with distinguished $0$.

nodes.statement:
An Austin law admits infinite models but no nontrivial finite ones, while an Austin pair consists of
laws $P$ and $Q$ such that every finite model satisfying the law $P$ also satisfies $Q$, but some
infinite magma satisfies $P$ without also satisfying $Q$.
nodes.name: Austin pair
nodes.statement_short: Austin pair: $P$ implies $Q$ on finite magmas but not on all magmas.

nodes.statement:
A \emph{translation-invariant magma} is a magma whose carrier $G$ is an abelian group $(G,+,-,0)$, and whose magma operation takes the form
$$ y \op x = x + f(x-y)$$
for some function $f: G \to G$.
nodes.name: Translation-invariant magma

nodes.statement: A magma $G$ satisfying the left (\Equaref{4}) or right (\Equaref{5}) absorption laws is translation-invariant. Equip the carrier $G$ with an abelian group structure $(G,+,-,0)$ and define $f: G \to G$ as either $f(x) = -x$ or $f(x) = 0$.
nodes.name: Absorption magmas are translation-invariant
nodes.statement_short: Left/right absorption magmas are translation-invariant with $f(x)=-x$ or $f(x)=0$.

nodes.statement: Linear magmas $x\op y = ax+by$ on a field $(\mathbb{F},+,-,\cdot,0,1)$ are translation-invariant if $a + b = 1$, since $(\mathbb{F},+,-,0)$ forms an abelian group, and one can set $f(x) = -ax$.
nodes.name: Affine linear magmas are translation-invariant
nodes.statement_short: Linear magmas $ax+by$ with $a+b=1$ are translation-invariant with $f(x)=-ax$.

nodes.statement:
Note that if an example of the latter sort suffices to refute the implication between $P$ and $Q$ then
by the Lefschetz principle one can construct a counterexample where the field $\mathbb{F}$ is finite.
Consequently, $P$ and $Q$ cannot constitute an Austin pair.
nodes.name: Linear counterexamples are not Austin pairs
nodes.statement_short: Linear-field counterexamples transfer to finite fields by Lefschetz, so they never witness an Austin pair.

nodes.statement: Over translation-invariant magmas, equational laws simplify to univariate functional equations.
nodes.name: Translation-invariant reduction to functional equations

nodes.statement:
For instance, writing $x = y+h$, we have
$$ y \op x = x + f(h)$$
$$ x \op (y \op x) = x + f(h) + f^2(h)$$
$$ y \op (x \op (y \op x)) = x + f(h) + f^2(h) + f( h + f(h) + f^2(h) )$$
where $f^2 = f \circ f$, so the Asterix equation (\Equaref{65}) for such magmas simplifies to the univariant functional equation
\begin{equation} f(h) + f^2(h) + f( h + f(h) + f^2(h) ) = 0
\end{equation}
for $h \in G$.
nodes.name: Asterix law as a functional equation
assumptions: writing $x = y+h$
conclusions: the Asterix equation (\Equaref{65}) for such magmas simplifies to the univariant functional equation
nodes.statement_short: For translation-invariant magmas the Asterix law becomes $f(h)+f^2(h)+f(h+f(h)+f^2(h))=0$.

nodes.statement: This equation has some degenerate solutions, for instance we can take $f(h) = c$ for any constant $c$ of order $3$ in $G$.
nodes.name: Degenerate solutions of the Asterix functional equation
conclusions: we can take $f(h) = c$ for any constant $c$ of order $3$ in $G$

nodes.statement: A \emph{partial solution} $(E_0, E_1, E_2, f)$ to \Cref{fh} consists of nested finite sets $$ E_0 \subseteq E_1 \subseteq E_2 \subseteq \Z$$ together with a function $f: E_1 \to E_2$ with the following properties: \begin{description} \item[(a)] If $h \in E_0$, then $f(h) \in E_1$, so that $f^2(h)$ is well-defined as an element of $E_2$; furthermore, $h + f(h) + f^2(h)$ lies in $E_1$, so that the left-hand side of \Cref{fh} makes sense; and \Cref{fh} holds. \item[(b)] The function $f$ is a bijection from $E_1 \backslash E_0$ to $E_2 \backslash E_1$. \item[(c)] $f(0)=0$. \item[(d)] $h+f(h) \neq 0$ for all non-zero $h \in E_1$. \end{description} We partially order the space of partial solutions to \Cref{fh} by writing $(E_0, E_1, E_2, f) \leq (E'_0, E'_1, E'_2, f')$ if the following properties hold: \begin{itemize} \item $E_i \subseteq E'_i$ for $i=0,1,2$. \item $f$ agrees with $f'$ on $E_0$. \end{itemize} When this occurs we say that the partial solution $(E'_0, E'_1, E'_2, f')$ \emph{extends} the partial solution $(E_0, E_1, E_2, f)$. We define the \emph{trivial partial solution} $(E_0,E_1,E_2,f)$ by setting $E_0=E_1=E_2=\{0\}$ and $f(0)=0$; it is the minimal element of the above partial order.
nodes.name: Partial solution to the Asterix functional equation
nodes.statement_short: Nested finite sets $E_0\subseteq E_1\subseteq E_2\subseteq\Z$ with $f:E_1\to E_2$ satisfying (7.1) on $E_0$ plus bijectivity and non-degeneracy; ordered by extension.
nodes.label: partial-solution

nodes.statement: Let $(E_0, E_1, E_2, f)$ be a partial solution to \Cref{fh}, and let $h$ be an element of $\Z$ that does not lie in $E_0$. Then there exists a partial solution $(E'_0, E'_1, E'_2, f')$ to \Cref{fh} that extends $(E_0, E_1, E_2, f)$, such that $h \in E_0'$.
nodes.name: Enlarging a partial solution
assumptions: Let $(E_0, E_1, E_2, f)$ be a partial solution to \Cref{fh}, and let $h$ be an element of $\Z$ that does not lie in $E_0$.
conclusions: there exists a partial solution $(E'_0, E'_1, E'_2, f')$ to \Cref{fh} that extends $(E_0, E_1, E_2, f)$, such that $h \in E_0'$
nodes.label: iteration

nodes.statement:
Because $f$ maps $E_1  ackslash E_0$ bijectively to $E_2  ackslash E_1$, there are three cases:  egin{itemize} \item $h$ is equal to an element $h_0$ of $\Z  ackslash E_2$. \item $h$ is equal to an element $h_0$ of $E_1  ackslash E_0$. \item $h$ is equal to $h_1 = f(h_0)$ for some $h_0 \in E_1  ackslash E_0$, so that $h_1 \in E_2  ackslash E_1$. \end{itemize} We deal with these three cases in turn. First suppose that $h = h_0\in \Z  ackslash E_2$. We perform the following construction.  egin{itemize} \item Choose an element $h_1 \in \Z$ that does not lie in $E_2 \cup \{h_0, -h_0\}$; this is possible because $E_2$ is finite. \item Choose an element $h_2 \in \Z$ such that $h_2, h_0+h_1+h_2$, $-h_1$, and $-h_1-h_2$ are all distinct from each other and lie outside of $E_2 \cup \{h_0, h_1\}$; this is possible because $E_2$ is finite and $h_0+h_1 
eq 0$. \item Promote $h_0$ to $E_0$, promote $h_1, h_0+h_1+h_2$ to $E_1$, and promote $h_2, -h_1-h_2$ to $E_2$, creating new sets  egin{align*} E'_0 &:= E_0 \cup \{h_0\} \ E'_1 &:= E_1 \cup \{h_0, h_1, h_0+h_1+h_2\} \ E'_2 &:= E_2 \cup \{h_0, h_1, h_0+h_1+h_2, h_2, -h_1-h_2\}. \end{align*} Clearly we still have nested finite sets $E'_0 \subseteq E'_1 \subseteq E'_2$. \item Extend $f : E_1 	o E_2$ to a function $f': E'_1 	o E'_2$ by defining  egin{align*} f'(h_0) &:= h_1 \ f'(h_1) &:= h_2 \ f'(h_0+h_1+h_2) &:= -h_1-h_2 \end{align*} while keeping $f'(h)=f(h)$ for all $h \in E_1$. \end{itemize} It is then a routine matter to verify that $(E'_0,E'_1,E'_2,f')$ is a partial solution to \Cref{fh} extending $(E_0,E_1,E_2,f)$ and that $E'_0$ contains $h_0$, as required. Now suppose that $h = h_0 \in E_1  ackslash E_0$, then the quantity $h_1 := f(h_0)$ lies in $E_2  ackslash E_1$. We perform the following variant of the above construction:  egin{itemize} \item Choose an element $h_2 \in \Z$ such that $h_2, h_0+h_1+h_2$, and $-h_1-h_2$, $-h_1$ are all distinct and lie outside of $E_2$. This is possible because $E_2$ is finite and $h_0+h_1 = h_0+f(h_0) 
eq 0$. \item Promote $h_0$ to $E_0$, promote $h_1$ and $h_0+h_1+h_2$ to $E_1$, and promote $h_2, -h_1-h_2$ to $E_2$, thus creating new sets  egin{align*} E'_0 &:= E_0 \cup \{h_0\} \ E'_1 &:= E_1 \cup \{h_1, h_0+h_1+h_2\} \ E'_2 &:= E_2 \cup \{h_0+h_1+h_2, h_2, -h_1-h_2\}. \end{align*} Clearly we still have nested finite sets $E'_0 \subseteq E'_1 \subseteq E'_2$. \item Extend $f : E_1 	o E_2$ to a function $f': E'_1 	o E'_2$ by defining  egin{align*} f'(h_1) &:= h_2 \ f'(h_0+h_1+h_2) &:= -h_1-h_2 \end{align*} while keeping $f'(h)=f(h)$ for all $h \in E_1$. \end{itemize} It is then a routine matter to verify that $(E'_0,E'_1,E'_2,f')$ is a partial solution to \Cref{fh} extending $(E_0,E_1,E_2,f)$ and that $E'_0$ contains $h_0$, as required. Finally, suppose that $h = h_1 = f(h_0)$ for some $h_0 \in E_1  ackslash E_0$, so that $h_1 \in E_2  ackslash E_1$. Then we perform the following algorithm.  egin{itemize} \item Choose an element $h_2 \in \Z$ such that $h_2, h_0+h_1+h_2$, $-h_1$, and $-h_1-h_2$ are all distinct and lie outside of $E_2$. This is possible because $E_2$ is finite and $h_0+h_1 = h_0+f(h_0) 
eq 0$. \item Choose an element $h_3 \in \Z$ such that $h_3, h_1+h_2+h_3$, and $-h_2-h_3$ are all distinct and lie outside of $E_2 \cup \{h_2, h_0+h_1+h_2,-h_1-h_2\}$. This is possible because $E_2$ is finite. \item Promote $h_0, h_1$ to $E_0$, promote $h_2, h_0+h_1+h_2, h_1+h_2+h_3$ to $E_1$, and promote $h_3, -h_1-h_2,-h_2-h_3$ to $E_2$, creating new sets  egin{align*} E'_0 &:= E_0 \cup \{h_0, h_1 \}\ E'_1 &:= E_1 \cup \{h_1, h_2, h_0+h_1+h_2, h_1+h_2+h_3 \}\ E'_2 &:= E_2 \cup \{h_2, h_3, h_0+h_1+h_2, h_1+h_2+h_3, -h_1-h_2, -h_2-h_3\}. \end{align*} Clearly we still have nested finite sets $E'_0 \subseteq E'_1 \subseteq E'_2$. \item Extend $f : E_1 	o E_2$ to a function $f': E'_1 	o E'_2$ by defining  egin{align*} f'(h_1) &:= h_2 \ f'(h_0+h_1+h_2) &:= -h_1-h_2 \ f'(h_2) &:= h_3 \ f'(h_1+h_2+h_3) &:= -h_2-h_3 \end{align*} while keeping $f'(h)=f(h)$ for all $h \in E_1$. \end{itemize} It is then a routine matter to verify that $(E'_0,E'_1,E'_2,f')$ is a partial solution to \Cref{fh} extending $(E_0,E_1,E_2,f)$ and that $E'_0$ contains $h_0$, as required.
nodes.name: Proof of Enlarging a partial solution
nodes.statement_short: Three cases by where $h$ lies; in each, choose fresh integers and promote elements through $E_0,E_1,E_2$ defining $f'$ explicitly.

nodes.statement: Every partial solution $(E_0,E_1,E_2,f)$ to \Cref{fh} can be extended to a full solution $\tilde f: \Z \to \Z$.
nodes.name: Partial solutions extend to full solutions
assumptions: Every partial solution $(E_0,E_1,E_2,f)$ to \Cref{fh}
conclusions: can be extended to a full solution $\tilde f: \Z \to \Z$
nodes.label: extend

nodes.statement: If we arbitrarily well-order the integers, and iterate \Cref{iteration} to add the least element of $\Z \backslash E_0$ in this well-ordering to $E_0$, we obtain an increasing sequence $(E^{(n)}_0, E^{(n)}_1, E^{(n)}_2, f^{(n)})$ of partial solutions to \Cref{fh}, where the $E^{(n)}_0$ exhaust $\Z$: $\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty E^{(n)}_0 = \Z$. Taking limits, we obtain a full solution $\tilde f$.
nodes.name: Proof of Partial solutions extend to full solutions
nodes.statement_short: Well-order $\Z$ and iterate the enlarging lemma; take the limit.

nodes.statement: There exists a solution $f:\Z \to \Z$ to \Cref{fh} such that the map $h \mapsto h + f(h)$ is not injective.
nodes.name: Non-injective Asterix solution
conclusions: There exists a solution $f:\Z \to \Z$ to \Cref{fh} such that the map $h \mapsto h + f(h)$ is not injective.
nodes.label: no-inject

nodes.statement: Select integers $h_0,h_1,h_2,h'_0,h'_1,h'_2$ such that the quantities $$ 0, h_0, h_1, h_2, h_0+h_1+h_2, -h_1-h_2, h'_0, h'_1, h'_2, h'_0+h'_1+h'_2, -h'_1-h'_2$$ are all distinct, but such that $$ h_0 + h_1 = h'_0 + h'_1 \neq 0$$ (there are many assignments of variables that accomplish this). Then set \begin{align*} E_0 &:= \{0,h_0, h'_0\}\\ E_1 &:= E_0 \cup \{ h_1, h'_1, h_0+h_1+h_2, h'_0+h'_1+h'_2\}\\ E_2 &:= E_2 \cup \{ h_2, h'_2, -h_1-h_2, -h'_1-h'_2\} \end{align*} and define $f: E_1 \to E_2$ by the formulae \begin{align*} f(0) &:= 0 \\ f(h_0) &:= h_1 \\ f(h_1) &:= h_2 \\ f(h_0+h_1+h_2) &:= -h_1-h_2 \\ f(h'_0) &:= h'_1 \\ f(h'_1) &:= h'_2 \\ f(h'_0+h'_1+h'_2) &:= -h'_1-h'_2. \end{align*} One can then check that $(E_0, E_1, E_2, f)$ is a partial solution to \Cref{fh}, and by construction $h \mapsto h + f(h)$ is not injective on $E_1$. Using \Cref{iteration} to extend this partial solution to a full solution, we obtain the claim.
nodes.name: Proof of Non-injective Asterix solution
nodes.statement_short: Explicit finite partial solution with a collision $h_0+h_1=h'_0+h'_1$, extended by the enlarging lemma.

nodes.statement: There exists a magma satisfying the Asterix law (\Equaref{65}) with carrier $\Z$ such that the left-multiplication maps $L_y: x \mapsto y \op x$ are not injective for any $y \in \Z$. In particular, it does not satisfy the Obelix law (\Equareffull{1491}).
nodes.name: Asterix does not imply Obelix
conclusions: There exists a magma satisfying the Asterix law (\Equaref{65}) with carrier $\Z$ such that the left-multiplication maps $L_y: x \mapsto y \op x$ are not injective for any $y \in \Z$.
it does not satisfy the Obelix law (\Equareffull{1491})
nodes.label: asterix-obelix

nodes.statement: Note that $L_y (y+h) = y + h + f(h)$, so the injectivity of the left-multiplication maps is equivalent to the injectivity of the map $h \mapsto h + f(h)$. The non-injectivity then follows from \Cref{no-inject}. Note that the Obelix law clearly expresses $x$ as a function of $y$ and $L_y x = y \op x$, forcing injectivity of left-multiplication, so the Obelix law fails.
nodes.name: Proof of Asterix does not imply Obelix
nodes.statement_short: Left multiplications are injective iff $h\mapsto h+f(h)$ is; use the non-injective solution; Obelix forces injectivity.

nodes.statement: Any finite magma satisfying the Asterix law (\Equaref{65}) also is left-cancellative and satisfies the Obelix law (\Equaref{1491}).
nodes.name: Asterix implies Obelix for finite magmas
assumptions: Any finite magma satisfying the Asterix law (\Equaref{65})
conclusions: also is left-cancellative and satisfies the Obelix law (\Equaref{1491})
nodes.label: asterix-obelix-finite

nodes.statement: From \Equaref{65} we see the map $z \mapsto y \op z$ is surjective, hence injective on a finite magma; thus the magma is left-cancellative. Replacing $x$ by $y \op x$ in this law, we see that $$ y \op x = y \op ((y\op x) \op (y \op (y \op x)));$$ using injectivity, we conclude $$ x = (y\op x) \op (y \op (y \op x))$$ which is \Equaref{1491}.
nodes.name: Proof of Asterix implies Obelix for finite magmas
nodes.statement_short: Surjective left multiplication is injective in finite magmas; cancel in the substituted Asterix law.

nodes.statement: A very similar argument shows that a finite magma that satisfies the Obelix law has $z \mapsto y \op z$ injective, hence surjective, and then satisfies the Asterix law.
nodes.name: Obelix implies Asterix for finite magmas
assumptions: a finite magma that satisfies the Obelix law
conclusions: has $z \mapsto y \op z$ injective, hence surjective, and then satisfies the Asterix law

nodes.statement:
Obelix magmas are those satisfying equation 1491, \Equaref{1491}:
$$x = (y \op x) \op (y \op (y \op x))$$
nodes.name: Obelix magma
Obelix law as a functional equation
nodes.statement_short: For $x\op y = x+f(y-x)$ the Obelix law becomes $f(f^2(h)-f(h)) = h-f(h)$.

nodes.statement: A \emph{partial solution} for an Obelix is a partial function $f : G \to G$ with the properties: \begin{itemize} \item $f$ has finite domain. \item $f$ is injective. \item $f$ maps the identity (of $G$, so, 0) to the identity. \item If $x$ is in the domain of $f$, and $f(x)$ is in the domain, then so is $f^2(x) - f(x)$. \item If $x$ is in the domain of $f$, and $f(x)$ is in the domain, then $f(f^2(x) - f(x)) = f(x) - x$. This is well-defined by property (4). \item The function $x - f(x)$, which is defined on the same domain as $f$, is injective. \item If $x$ is in the domain of $f$ but $f(x)$ isn't in the domain, then $x - f(x)$ isn't in the domain or image of $f$. \end{itemize}
nodes.name: Partial solution for an Obelix
nodes.statement_short: Finite-domain injective partial $f$ fixing $0$, closed under $x\mapsto f^2(x)-f(x)$ where the Obelix equation holds, with injective $x-f(x)$ and a freshness condition.
nodes.label: partial-solution2

nodes.statement: Any partial solution can be extended to a complete solution.
nodes.name: Obelix partial solutions extend to complete solutions

nodes.statement: For any $E\in \mathscr{E}$ and any $a\in G$, there is an extension $E\subseteq E'\in \mathscr{E}$ where the functional equation holds for $a$.
nodes.name: Obelix extension lemma
assumptions: For any $E\in \mathscr{E}$ and any $a\in G$
conclusions: there is an extension $E\subseteq E'\in \mathscr{E}$ where the functional equation holds for $a$
nodes.label: obelix-extend

nodes.name: Proof of Obelix extension lemma
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on whether $a$ is in the domain; adjoin fresh generators and check the partial-solution conditions.

nodes.statement:
The actual mechanical proof requires checking roughly a few dozen statements of the form "the fresh
element is not related linearly to the existing elements". Each is individually obvious, and easily
discharged.
nodes.name: Mechanical proof of the Obelix extension

nodes.statement: There is an Obelix magma that is not Asterix (equation 65).
nodes.name: Obelix does not imply Asterix
conclusions: There is an Obelix magma that is not Asterix (equation 65).
also_stated_at: By picking an appropriate partial solution, we can then show that there are Obelix magmas that are not Asterix.

nodes.statement: This requires picking an initial set that still satisfies the correct initial closure properties. Letting $x_1$, $x_2$, $x_3$ and $x_4$ be independent elements, then taking the function $$\{(0,0), (x_1,x_2), (x_2-x_1, x_3), (x_1+x_3, x_4)\}$$ already has elements that contradict the Asterix equation, and it's a valid partial solution. By extending it, we can get an Obelix that does not satisfy the Asterix equation.
nodes.name: Proof of Obelix does not imply Asterix
nodes.statement_short: Seed partial solution violating Asterix, then extend.

nodes.name: Partially defined magma operation

nodes.statement: Such an operation is then associated (via a one-to-one correspondence) to a partially defined operation $\op : S \to G$ for some $S \subseteq G \times G$, with $R(x,y,z)$ holding if and only if $x \op y$ is well-defined (i.e., $(x,y) \in S$) and equal to $z$.
nodes.name: Partial operation associated to a relation

nodes.statement: Given a word $w(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ in variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$ (so $w$ is an element of the free magma on $n$ generators), we can say that $w(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ is \emph{well-defined} with respect to a partially defined magma operation $R$ if it can be fully evaluated using $R$.
nodes.name: Well-defined word

nodes.statement: We say that an expression $w(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ is \emph{almost well-defined} if all strict subexpressions of $w$ are well-defined.
nodes.name: Almost well-defined word

nodes.statement: An equational law $w_1 \formaleq w_2$ involving some variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$ is said to be \emph{locally satisfied} by $R$ if,  whenever $w_1(x_1,\dots,x_n)$, $w_2(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ are almost well-defined, and one of the two expressions is well-defined and evaluates to some output $y$, then the other expression is also well-defined and evaluates to the same output $y$.
nodes.name: Locally satisfied law

nodes.statement: Note that if the relation $R$ is associated to a genuine magma operation $\op$, then it locally satisfies a law $w_1 \formaleq w_2$ if and only if the magma operation $\op$ satisfies the law $w_1 \formaleq w_2$.
nodes.name: Local satisfaction agrees with satisfaction for total operations
assumptions: the relation $R$ is associated to a genuine magma operation $\op$
conclusions: it locally satisfies a law $w_1 \formaleq w_2$ if and only if the magma operation $\op$ satisfies the law $w_1 \formaleq w_2$

nodes.statement: If the carrier $G$ is infinite (e.g., if $G = \N$), one can then find another element $c$ which is \emph{novel}: it is not equal to $a, b$, or any of the $x,y,z$ for which $R(x,y,z)$ hold.
nodes.name: Novel element
Greedily extensible theory
nodes.statement_short: A theory is greedily extensible if any finite partial model can be extended to also define a prescribed undefined product as a novel element.

nodes.statement: Observe that if a theory $\Gamma$ containing (VLT) is greedily extensible, then any finitely supported ternary relation $R$ satisfying $\Gamma$ on a countably infinite carrier $G$ can be extended to a globally defined relation satisfying $\Gamma$, by iteratively selecting the first $(a,b)$ (in some fixed enumeration of $G \times G$) for which $a \op b$ is undefined, and then selecting a novel element $c$ to define as $a \op b$, and applying the greedily extensible property, and then taking a direct limit of the countable sequence of relations thus produced.
nodes.name: Greedy extensibility yields global models
assumptions: a theory $\Gamma$ containing (VLT) is greedily extensible
conclusions: any finitely supported ternary relation $R$ satisfying $\Gamma$ on a countably infinite carrier $G$ can be extended to a globally defined relation satisfying $\Gamma$
nodes.statement_short: Greedy extensibility plus an enumeration of $G\times G$ and a direct limit give a total magma model.

nodes.name: Proof that (VLT)+(65)+(65') is greedily extensible
nodes.statement_short: Find successive obstructions to the naive forcing extension and repair them by adding axiom (65'); then verify with an ATP.

nodes.statement: This shows that the theory $\Gamma$ is greedily extensible.
nodes.name: (VLT)+(65)+(65') is greedily extensible

nodes.statement:
Using this, one can for instance find a magma satisfying \Equaref{65} that fails the left-cancellative property
$$ y \op x = y \op x' \implies x=x'$$
or in terms of ternary relations
\begin{equation} R(y,x,z) \hbox{ and } R(y,x',z) \implies x=x'
\end{equation}
simply by starting with a partial solution, say on the natural numbers in which (e.g.) $R(1,2,0)$, $R(1,3,0)$ are the only situations in which $R$ holds.
nodes.name: Asterix magma that is not left-cancellative
conclusions: one can for instance find a magma satisfying \Equaref{65} that fails the left-cancellative property

nodes.statement: R(y,x,z) \hbox{ and } R(y,x',z) \implies x=x'
nodes.name: Left-cancellativity in relational form

nodes.statement: One can easily verify that this satisfies (VLT) and (65), (65'), but not \Cref{left-inject}, and so any magma constructed by the above greedy construction will not be left-cancellative.
nodes.name: Proof of Asterix magma that is not left-cancellative
nodes.statement_short: The seed relation satisfies the theory but not left-cancellativity, which survives the greedy construction.

nodes.statement: Since the Obelix law \Equaref{1491} forces left-cancellativity, this gives an alternate proof of \Cref{asterix-obelix}.
nodes.name: Alternate proof that Asterix does not imply Obelix
nodes.statement_short: Obelix forces left-cancellativity, which the greedy Asterix model lacks.

nodes.name: Equation 1722

nodes.statement: We abbreviate $Sy := y \op y$.
nodes.name: Squaring map S

nodes.statement:
Define a \emph{partial solution} to be a partial function $\op: E \to \N$ on some finite subset $E$ of $\N \times \N$ (which one can also think of as a finitely supported ternary relation $R(x,y,z)$ satisfying VLT) satisfying the following axioms:
\begin{itemize}
\item (Law 1) If $(x \op y) \op y$ is defined, then $Sy \op ((x \op y) \op y)$ is defined and equal to $x$.
\item (Law 2) If  If $x \op y$ and $z \op y$ are defined and equal to each other, then $x=z$.
\item (Law 3) If $Sx$ is defined, then $(Sx \op x) \op x$ is defined.
\item (Law 4) If there exists a $z$ such that $z \op x = x$ then $x \op x$ is defined.
nodes.name: Partial solution for 1722
nodes.statement_short: Finite partial operation satisfying four local axioms (Laws 1-4) for equation 1722.

nodes.statement: Suppose that $\op$ is a partial solution, and $a \op b$ is currently undefined. Then there exists an extension $\op'$ of $\op$ for which $a \op' b$ is defined.
nodes.name: 1722 extension
assumptions: Suppose that $\op$ is a partial solution, and $a \op b$ is currently undefined.
conclusions: there exists an extension $\op'$ of $\op$ for which $a \op' b$ is defined
nodes.label: 1722-extension

nodes.statement:
Suppose first that $b=a$, so $a \op a$ is undefined, then by Law 4 we have $d \op a 
eq a$ for all $d$ with $d \op a$ defined. Set $a_0=a$ and find nine distinct elements $a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4$ not previously appearing in the domain or range of $\op$. Extend the indices periodically by setting $a_{i+4} = a_i,b_{i+4} = b_i$ for $i \ge 1$, and define $a_i \op' a_i = a_{i+1}$ (so $a_i = S^i a$), $a_{i+1} \op' a_i = b_i$, $b_i \op' a_i = a_{i+2}$, $a_{i+3} \op' a_{i+1} = a_{i+1}$, $a_{i+1} \op' a_{i+2} = a_{i+1}$, $a_{i+1} \op' b_i = a_i$. We also define $x \op' y = x \op y$ whenever the right-hand side is defined. It is easy to see that laws 2,3,4 are preserved (though for law 2 note that we have not defined $a_2 \op' a_0$ due to the way indices are extended). Now we case check Law 1.  egin{itemize} \item Case 1. $y$ is fresh, that is $y \in \{a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4\}$. If $x \op' y$ is not defined, we are done, so assume this is so. In particular, $x \in \{a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4\}$. If $x,y \in \{a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4\}$ we are done by construction. If $x = b_i$ for some $i$, then $y = a_i$ and we are again done by construction. Finally, if $y = b_i$ for some $i$, then $x = a_{i+1}$ and $(x \op' y) \op' y$ is undefined. \item Case 2. $x$ is fresh, that is $x \in \{a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4\}$. If we are not in Case 1 and $x \op' y$ is defined, we must have $y = a_0$ and $x \in \{a_1, b_0\}$. The case $x = a_1$ holds by construction, and the case $x = b_0$ holds as $a_2 \op' a_0$ is not defined. \item Case 3. $x,y 
ot \in \{a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4\}$ and $x \op y$ was undefined. Then $x \op' y$ is undefined unless $x=y=a_0$, in which case Law 1 holds by construction. \item Case 4. $x,y 
ot \in \{a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4\}$, $x \op y$ was defined, and $(x \op y) \op y$ was not defined. Then $(x \op' y) \op' y$ is undefined unless $(x \op y) = a = y$, but this is impossible by Law $4$ as already observed. \item Case 5. $x,y 
ot \in \{a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4\}$ and $x \op y$ and $(x \op y) \op y$ were defined. Then the claim follows from Law 1 applied to $\op$. \end{itemize} Now suppose that $a \op b$ is undefined for some $a 
eq b$. By applying the previous construction, we may assume without loss of generality that $Sb$ is defined. We may assume that $a \op b$ remains undefined after doing so, since we are done otherwise. By Law 3, $a 
eq Sb \op b$. By Law 2, we have $d \op b = a$ for at most one $d$, which is necessarily different from $Sb$. Choose a $c$ not previously appearing in the domain or range of $\op$, and set $a \op' b = c$. If a $d$ exists as before, we additionally set $Sb \op' c = d$. Finally we define $x \op' y = x \op y$ whenever the right-hand side is defined. It is again routine to check that $\op'$ satisfies Laws 2,3,4. Now we case check Law 1.  egin{itemize} \item Case 1. $x=c$ or $x \op' y = c$. Not possible since no left multiplication by $c$ is defined. \item Case 2. $y=c$. This would force $x = Sb$ and $d = Sb$, but this is not possible since $d$ is different from $Sb$. \item Case 3: $(x \op' y) \op' y = c$. This forces $x=d$ and $y=b$, and the claim follows from construction. \item Case 4: None of the terms in $(x \op' y) \op' y$ are equal to $c$. Then the claim follows from Law 1 applied to $\op$. \end{itemize}
nodes.name: Proof of 1722 extension
nodes.statement_short: Two cases ($b=a$ and $b\ne a$): adjoin fresh elements with an explicit periodic table, then case-check Law 1.

nodes.statement: By the greedy algorithm, this implies that any partial solution can be extended to a 1722 magma on $\N$.
nodes.name: 1722 partial solutions extend to 1722 magmas

nodes.statement:
We can now refute the implication to equation 1832
$$ x = (x \op Sx) \op Sx,$$
equation 2644
$$ x = S^2 x \op x,$$
and equation 3050,
$$ x = ((Sx \op x) \op x) \op x$$
by using the partial solution
$$ 0 \op 0 = 1, 0 \op 1 = 2, 1 \op 0 = 2, 1 \op 1 = 3, 1 \op 2 = 0, 1 \op 3 = 1, 1 \op 4 = 2$$
$$ 2 \op 0 = 3, 2 \op 1 = 4, 3 \op 0 = 4, 3 \op 1 = 1, 3 \op 3 = 3, 3 \op 4 = 0$$
which violates all three equations at $x=0$.
nodes.name: 1722 does not imply 1832, 2644, 3050
nodes.statement_short: An explicit partial solution violating 1832, 2644 and 3050 at $x=0$ extends to a 1722 magma.

nodes.statement:
Here, the laws defining a partial solution are
\begin{itemize}
\item (Law 1) If $(y \op x) \op x$ is defined, then $y \op (y \op ((y \op x) \op x))$ is defined and equal to $x$.
\item (Law 2) $x \op y \neq y$ for all $x,y$.
\item (Law 3) If $Sx$ is defined, then so is $Sx \op x$.

conclusions: there exists an extension $\op'$ of $\op$ for which $a \op' b$ is defined

nodes.statement: First suppose that $a \op a$ is not defined. Set $a_0 := a$ and select three new elements $a_1,a_2,a_3$. Define $a_0 \op a_0 = a_1$, $a_1 \op a_0 = a_2$, $a_0 \op a_2 = a_3$, $a_0 \op a_1 = a_3$, $a_0 \op a_3 = a_0$. It is a routine but tedious matter to check that Laws 1,2,3 are preserved by these operations. (The trickiest case is the $x=a_0$ case of Law 1; here we need Law 2 to prevent $y \op a_0$ from equalling $a_0$.) Now suppose that $a \op b$ is undefined for some $a \neq b$. Let $d_1,d_2,\dots,d_n$ be all the elements with $d_i \op b = a$. Note from Law 3 that none of the $d_i$ can be equal to $b$. Choose a new element $c$, as well as $c_i$ for each $d_i$, and set $a \op b = c$, $d_i \op c = c_i$, and $d_i \op c_i = b$. It is easy to see that this preserves Laws 2,3. For Law 1 ,we do the usual case analysis: \begin{itemize} \item Case 1: $y = c$, $y = c_i$, $y \op x = c$, or $y \op x = c_i$. This case cannot occur because we have not defined left multiplication with $c$ or $c_i$. \item Case 2: $x = c$ or $x = c_i$. Because $d_i \neq b$, it is easy to see that $(y \op x) \op x$ is not defined for any $x$. \item Case 3: $(y \op x) \op x = c$ or $(y \op x) \op x = c_i$. This is only possible if $x=b$ and $y = d_j$ for some $j$, and the claim then follows from construction. \item Case 4: None of the terms in $(y \op x) \op x$ are equal to $c$ or $c_i$. This follows from the previous seed. \end{itemize}
nodes.name: Proof of 713 extension
nodes.statement_short: Case $a\op a$ undefined: adjoin three fresh elements; case $a\ne b$: adjoin $c$ and $c_i$ and case-check Law 1.

nodes.statement:
One can now refute the implications of the equations $x = x \op ((x \op x) \op (x \op x))$ (817), $x = (x \op x) \op (x \op (x \op x))$ (1426), $x \op x = (x \op (x \op x)) \op x$ (3862), $x \op x = ((x \op x) \op x) \op x$ (4065) by using the partial solution
$$ 0 \op 0 = 1, 0 \op 1 = 3, 0 \op 2 = 3, 0 \op 3 = 0$$
$$1\op 0 = 2, 1 \op 1 = 0, 1 \op 2 = 1, 1 \op 3 =2 , 1 \op 4 = 3$$
$$ 2 \op 0 = 2, 2 \op 2 = 4, 2 \op 4 = 0$$
$$ 4 \op 1 = 2, 4 \op 2 = 4, 4 \op 3 = 2, 4 \op 4 = 1.$$
which violates 3862 at $x=2$ and the other three laws at $x=0.$
nodes.name: 713 does not imply 817, 1426, 3862, 4065

nodes.statement:
For $x = y \op (((x \op y) \op y) \op y)$ (1289), one can similarly argue using the rules
\begin{itemize}
\item (Law 1) If $((x \op y) \op y) \op y$ is already defined, then $y \op (((x \op y) \op y) \op y)$ is also defined and equals $x$.
\item (Law 2) $R_x$ is injective for all $x$ currently in the table.

nodes.statement: Suppose that $\op$ is a partial solution, and $a \op b$ is currently undefined. Then there exists an extension $\op'$ of $\op$ for which $a \op' b$ is defined.
nodes.name: 1289 extension
assumptions: Suppose that $\op$ is a partial solution, and $a \op b$ is currently undefined.
conclusions: there exists an extension $\op'$ of $\op$ for which $a \op' b$ is defined
nodes.label: 1289-extension

nodes.statement:
If $a \op b$ is currently undefined, introduce a new element $c$ and define $a \op b = c$ and $ c \op c = c.$ If furthermore $a = (d \op b) \op b$ for some d, then also define $b \op c = d$ (This last step is well defined by injectivity of $R_b$). We now check that the three axioms still hold. Law 3 is obvious, law 2 follows since $d 
ot = c$. For law 1, we first make the observation that $a 
ot = b$, for otherwise $a \op b$ would have been defined. This has the consequence that if $d$ exists, then $d 
ot = b$, for otherwise $a = (b \op b) \op b = b.$ In particular, the product $d \op c$ remains undefined after running the algorithm once. We now work by cases on the values of the variables $x,y$ appearing in law 1:  egin{itemize} \item Case 1: $y=c$. In this case, for the product $x \op y$ to be defined, we require $x =b$ or $x = c$. In the former case either $b \op c$ or $(b \op c) \op c = d \op c$ is not defined. In the latter case, law 1 holds as $c$ is idempotent. \item Case 2: $y=b$. For $((x \op b) \op b) \op b$ to be defined now but not have been defined before, we require one of $x= a, (x \op b) = a, ((x \op b) \op b) = a.$ The first two cases are eliminated as $c \op b$ is not yet defined. The last case holds as then $d$ exists and equals $x$, so $b \op (((x \op b) \op b) \op b) = b \op (a \op b) = b \op c = x.$ \item Case 3: $y 
ot = c, y 
ot = b$. We have introduced no new products with a right-hand side other than $c$ or $b$, so if $((x \op y) \op y) \op y$ was undefined before it remains undefined now. \end{itemize}
nodes.name: Proof of 1289 extension
nodes.statement_short: Adjoin an idempotent fresh $c$ with $a\op b=c$ (and $b\op c=d$), then case-check Law 1 on $y$.

nodes.statement:
To refute $x \op (y \op x) = (x \op y) \op x$ (4435) and $x = (((y \op x) \op y) \op y) \op y$ (3316) we use the partial solution
$$ 0 \op 0 = 0; 0 \op 1 = 2; 0 \op 2 = 1; 0 \op 4 = 1$$
$$ 1 \op 0 = 2; 1 \op 1 = 1$$
$$ 2 \op 0 = 3; 2 \op 2 = 2$$
$$ 3 \op 0 = 4; 3 \op 3 = 3$$
$$ 4 \op 4 = 4$$
which violates 4435 at $(x,y)=(0,1)$ and 3116 at $(x,y)=(2,0).$
nodes.name: 1289 does not imply 4435, 3316

nodes.statement:
For $x = y \op (y \op (x \op y))$ (73), we argue similarly, now with laws
\begin{itemize}
\item Law 1.  If $y \op (x \op y)$ is defined, then $y \op (y \op (x \op y))$ is defined and equal to $x$.
\item Law 2.  $R_y$ is injective for all $y$ currently in the table.
\item Law 3.  $x \op y \neq y$ for all $x,y$ currently in the table.

nodes.statement:
If $a \op b$ is undefined, set it equal to a new element $c$. If we also have $b = d \op a$ for some $d$ (unique by Law 2, and only possible for $a 
eq b$ by Law 3), set $a \op c = d$. It is obvious that Laws 2, 3 are preserved. Now we case check Law 1:  egin{itemize} \item Case 1: $x=c$ or $y=c$. Not possible since no left multiplication with $c$ is defined. \item Case 2: $x \op y = c$. Only possible when $x = a$, $y = b$, but then $y \op (x \op y)$ is undefined since $y = b 
eq a$ if $d$ is defined. \item Case 3. $y \op (x \op y) = c$. Only possible when $y=a$ and $x=d$, and holds in this case. \item Case 4: $x, y, x \op y, y \op (x \op y) 
eq c$: this case is already covered by the previous seed. \end{itemize}
nodes.name: Proof of 73 extension
nodes.statement_short: Set $a\op b=c$ fresh (and $a\op c=d$), then case-check Law 1.

nodes.statement:
For $x = y \op (x \op (x \op y))$ (63), we argue similarly, now with laws
\begin{itemize}
  \item Law 1.  If $x \diamond (x \diamond y)$ is defined, then $y \diamond (x \diamond (x \diamond y))$ is defined and equal to $x$.
  \item Law 2.  If $x \diamond y = x \diamond z$ with $y,z$ distinct, then $y \diamond x$ (if defined) is not equal to $z$ or to $z \diamond x$ (if defined).
  \item Law 3: If $x \diamond x$ is defined, it is equal to $x$.
  \item Law 4: If $x \neq y$, then $x \diamond y$ is not equal to $x$.

nodes.label: 63-extension

nodes.statement:
If $a = b$, set $a \diamond' a = a$. This clearly does not destroy Laws 3 or 4, and because of Law 4, Law 2 will also be retained. Finally, using Law 4, we can check that this addition does not break Law 1. Now suppose $a 
eq b$. Let $d_1,d_2,..., d_n$ be all the elements with $b = a \diamond d_i$, and note from Law 3 and $a 
eq b $ that we have the crucial inequality $d_i 
eq a$ for all $i$. If $d_i \diamond a$ is defined, let $e_i = d_i \diamond a.$ From Law 4 and $d_i 
eq a$, we have $e_i 
eq d_i$. From Law 2 and $a \diamond d_i = a \diamond d_j$, we further have $e_i 
eq e_j$ and $e_i 
eq d_j$ for $i 
eq j$. For the algorithm, we set $a \diamond' b = c$ for some new $c$, $d_i \diamond' c = a$, and $c \diamond' e_i = d_i$ (This is well defined as we have just argued $e_i 
eq e_j$ for $i 
eq j$). This creates a new partial function. Law 2 is verified as follows: The case $x=c$ cannot occur because $c \diamond' e_i 
eq c \diamond' e_j$ for $i 
eq j$. If $y=c$, then $x = d_i$ for some $i$, but then $y \diamond' x = c \diamond' d_i$ is undefined as $d_i 
eq e_j$, so this case is vacuous. If $z=c$ and $x,y 
eq c$, then similarly $z \diamond' x$ is undefined, and $y \diamond' x$ is not equal to $c = z$, so we are ok in this case also. Law 3 is clearly unaffected, and it is also straightforward to check that Law 4 is also not invalidated (here it is essential that $d_i 
eq a$). Now we verify Law 1.  egin{itemize} \item Case 1: $x=c$. Then for $x \diamond' y$ to be defined we must have $y=e_i$ for some $i$, but then $x \diamond' (x \diamond' y) = c \op' d_i$ is undefined as $d_i 
eq e_j$ for all $j$. \item Case 2: $y=c$. Then for $x \diamond' y$ to be defined we must have $x = d_i$ for some $i$. Then $d_i \op' (d_i \op' c)$ is either undefined or is equal to $e_i$, in which case Law 1 holds as $c \op' e_i = d_i$. \item Case 3: $x \diamond' y = c$. Then $x=a$ and $y=b$. Since $d_i 
eq a$ for all $i$, $x \diamond (x \diamond y)$ is undefined. \item Case 4: $x \op' (x \op' y) = c$. Then $x = a$ and $y = d_i$ for some $i$, and Law 1 holds as $d_i \op' c = a$. \item Case 5: None of $x, y, x \diamond' y, x \op' (x \op' y)$ are equal to $c$. Then this case is covered by the previous seed. \end{itemize}
nodes.name: Proof of 63 extension
nodes.statement_short: Case $a=b$ set idempotent; case $a\ne b$ define $a\op b=c$, $d_i\op c=a$, $c\op e_i=d_i$ and verify Laws 1-4.

nodes.statement:
For $x = y \op ((x \op (x \op y)) \op y)$ (1076), we argue similarly. There are just two laws:
\begin{itemize}
    \item Law 1.  If $x \diamond (x \diamond y)$ is defined and equal to some $z$,
then $y \diamond (z \diamond y)$ is defined and equal to $x$.
    \item Law 2.  $x \diamond x$ is not equal to $x$.
