nodes.statement:
Set $a \diamond' b = c$ for some new element $c$. If $d_1,d_2,...,d_n$ are the elements for which $a \diamond d_i = b$, set $c \diamond' d_i = c'_i$ for some new element $c'_i$, and also set $d_i \diamond' c'_i = a$. If $d_i \diamond a$ is equal to some $e_i$, set $e_i \diamond' c'_i = c''_i$ and $c'_i \diamond' c''_i = d_i$, where $c''_i$ is equal to $a$ if $e_i = d_i$, or is some new element otherwise. One can verify that no collisions are caused by this construction (this is why we have to take $c''_i=a$ when $e_i=d_i$), and that Law 2 is preserved. We need to verify that these constructions preserve Law 1. There are several cases:  egin{itemize} \item $y=c$. Not possible since there are no right multiplications by $c$ defined. \item $x=c$. Not possible since it forces $y = d_i$, $x \diamond y = c'_i$ for some $i$. \item $y=c'_i$, $x = d_i$. True by construction. \item $y=c'_i$, $x 
eq d_i$. This forces $x = e_i 
eq d_i$ and $x \diamond' y = c''_i$, but then $x \diamond' (x \diamond' y)$ is undefined. \item $x=c'_i$. Not possible because this forces $x \diamond' y = d_i$, and $x \diamond' (x \diamond' y)$ will be undefined. (Here we use the fact that $e_i=d_i$ can only occur when $d_i 
eq a$, by Law 2.) \item $x = c''_i$ is new. Not possible as no left multiplications by $c''_i$ are defined. \item $y=c''_i$ is new. This forces $x = c'_i$ and $x \diamond' y = d_i$, but then $x \diamond' (x \diamond' y)$ is undefined. \item $x$ and $y$ are not new and $x \diamond y$ was undefined. This requires $x=a, y=b$, but then $x \diamond' (x \diamond' y)$ is undefined since right multiplication by $c$ is undefined. \item $x$, $y$ are not new and $x \diamond y$ was defined, but $x \diamond (x \diamond y)$ was undefined. This requires $x=a$, $x \diamond y = b$, and hence $y = d_i$ for some $i$. The claim now follows from construction. \item $x$, $y$, are not new and $x \diamond y$, $x \diamond (x \diamond y)$ were defined. This then follows from the previous seed. \end{itemize}
nodes.name: Proof of 1076 extension
nodes.statement_short: Define $a\op b=c$ and auxiliary fresh elements $c'_i, c''_i$, then check Law 1 in nine cases.

nodes.statement:
The implication between the laws \Equareffull{1648} and \Equareffull{206} can be refuted by a translation-invariant
magma on the integers. Define the function $f: \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ by
$$f(x) =
\begin{cases}
  -1  & \text{if } x > 0, \\
   0  & \text{if } x = 0, \\
   1  & \text{if } x < 0,
\end{cases}$$
and consider the translation-invariant magma on $\mathbb{Z}$ given by the operation $x \op y = x + f(y-x)$.

The resulting magma satisfies Equation 1648: one can show this by a case analysis on $f(y-x)$. If $f(y-x)=1$ we have $x \op y = x + f(y-x) = x + 1$, so
$$(x \op y) \op ((x \op y) \op y) = (x + 1) \op ((x + 1) \op y) = (x + 1) \op (x + 2) = (x + 1) - 1 = x.$$
Similar computations verify the other two cases.

However, setting $x=0$ and $y=-1$ in Equation 206, we get
$$(x \op (x \op y)) \op y = (x \op 1) \op y = (-1) \op y = -1 \neq x$$
so the magma does not satisfy \Equaref{206}. We can conclude
nodes.name: Proof that 1648 does not imply 206
nodes.statement_short: Translation-invariant magma on $\Z$ with $f=-\mathrm{sgn}$ satisfies 1648 by case analysis and violates 206 at $x=0,y=-1$.

nodes.statement: There exists a magma which satisfies \Equaref{1648} and not \Equaref{206}.
nodes.name: 1648 does not imply 206
conclusions: There exists a magma which satisfies \Equaref{1648} and not \Equaref{206}.
nodes.label: non_imp_1648_206_thm

nodes.statement:
For some pairs of laws $P$ and $Q$, it is possible to start with an infinite model $(M,\op)$ satisfying both $P$ and $Q$,
then modify the operation $\op$ in a limited way, resulting in a model $(M,\op')$ of $P$ that does not satisfy $Q$.
nodes.name: Modified base model construction

nodes.statement:
A model refuting the implication between the laws \Equareffull{1659} and \Equareffull{4315} can be constructed using
the modified base model technique. Start with the infinite model $(\mathbb{Z},\op)$ of \Equaref{1659} given by the following operation:
$$ x\op y = \begin{cases} x+1 & \text{if } x,y \text{ have the same parity} \\ x -1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$
A case analysis shows that the magma $(\mathbb{Z},\op)$  satisfies both \Equaref{1659} and \Equaref{4315}.
We will eventually \emph{modify} it by setting
$$x \op' y = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } x=0,\: x,y \text{ do not have the same parity} \\  x+1 & \text{if } x,y \text{ have the same parity} \\ x -1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$
and checking that $(\mathbb{N}, \op' )$ satisfies \Equaref{1659} but refutes \Equaref{4315}.

One finds these modifications using the following strategy:

First, choose some element (tuple) of the carrier $M$ that will constitute a counterexample to the
consequent in the modified model. In this specific case, the consequent, \Equaref{4315}, can be written as
$$ x \op (y \op x) = x \op (y \op z)$$
in equational form, which always holds when $x = z$. So let's choose the tuple $(0,0,1)$
to constitute the required counterexample. Computing $0 \op (0 \op 0) = 0 \op 1 = -1$ and similarly
$0 \op (0 \op 1) = -1$ suggest that we could force this tuple to be a counterexample by defining a new
operation $\op''$ and setting
$0 \op'' 1$ to something other than $-1$. One seemingly has many choices here: should we take
$0 \op'' 1 =0$, $0 \op'' 1 = 1$, $0 \op'' 1 = 2$, or perhaps even $0 \op'' 1 = -1$?

It's easy to rule out some of the possibilities. For instance, setting $0 \op'' 1 = 1$ would
yield $0 \op'' (0 \op'' 0) = 0 \op'' 1 = 0 \op'' (0 \op'' 1)$ again. The simplest possibility which results in
a counterexample to \Equaref{4315} sets $0 \op'' 1 = 0$ and $x \op'' y = x \op y$ for any $x \neq 0, y \neq 1$.

Unfortunately, the resulting $(M,\op'')$ would not then satisfy \Equaref{1659}. For any $z \in M$, one would have
$$ (0 \op'' 1) \op'' ((1 \op'' 1) \op'' z) = 0 \op'' (2 \op'' z)$$
which equals $0 \op'' 1 = 0$ as desired for even $z$, but equals $0 \op'' 3 = -1 \neq 0$ for odd $z$.

However, since $f$ takes finitely many values in the base model, the breakage is tightly controlled:
by considering what happens if $x \neq 0$ and $y \neq 1$, we see that all new counterexamples to \Equaref{4315}
have this form. The calculation now suggests defining yet another $\op'''$, where setting
$0 \op''' 3 = 0$ would eliminate
this counterexample. But doing that just moves the issue one level higher: one then has
$$ (0 \op''' 3) \op''' ((3 \op''' 3) \op''' z) = 0 \op''' (4 \op''' z)$$ which equals $0 \op''' 3 = 0$ as desired for even $z$, but equals $0 \op''' 5 = -1 \neq 0$ for odd $z$.

Instead, the infinitely many counterexamples arising from the iterated redefinition can be eliminated
all at once by setting:
$$x \op' y = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } x=0,\: x,y \text{ do not have the same parity} \\  x+1 & \text{if } x,y \text{ have the same parity} \\ x -1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$
and also truncating the model to $\mathbb{N}$ since the result of the $\op'$
operation is nonnegative whenever the operands are nonnegative. This finishes the construction without generating any further violations of \Equaref{1659} and proves
nodes.name: Proof that 1659 does not imply 4315
nodes.statement_short: Modified base model: start from the parity model on $\Z$, force a counterexample to 4315 at $(0,0,1)$, and repair 1659 by redefining infinitely many products at once.

nodes.statement: There exists a magma which satisfies \Equaref{1659} and not \Equaref{4315}.
nodes.name: 1659 does not imply 4315
conclusions: There exists a magma which satisfies \Equaref{1659} and not \Equaref{4315}.
nodes.label: non_imp_1659_4315_thm

nodes.statement:
If we adopt a translation-invariant model
$$ x \op y = x + f(y-x)$$
on some abelian group $G$, then with $y = x+h$, we have
$$ x \op y = x + f(h)$$
$$ x \op (x \op y) = x + f^2(h)$$
$$ y \op (x \op (x \op y)) = y + f(f^2(h)-h)$$
and so the Dupont law $x = y \op (x \op (x \op y))$ becomes the functional equation
\begin{equation} f(f^2(h)-h) = -h.
\end{equation}
nodes.name: Dupont law as a functional equation
nodes.statement_short: For $x\op y = x+f(y-x)$ the Dupont law becomes $f(f^2(h)-h)=-h$.

nodes.statement:
One way to solve this equation is to have an automorphism $T: G \to G$ that satisfies the identity
$$ T^3 - T = -I,$$
then one can just take $f(h) = T(h)$.
nodes.name: Automorphism solutions of the Dupont equation
assumptions:
an automorphism $T: G \to G$ that satisfies the identity
$$ T^3 - T = -I,$$
conclusions: one can just take $f(h) = T(h)$

nodes.statement:
For instance, if $G = \Z^3$, one can take the automorphism $T: \Z^3 \to \Z^3$ defined by
$$ T(x,y,z) := (-z,x+z,y).$$
nodes.name: Automorphism T of Z^3

nodes.statement:
Define a \emph{partial solution} $(E_1,E_2,f)$ to be a pair $\Z^3 \subseteq E_1 \subseteq E_2 \subseteq \Z^3 \times \Z$, and a function $f: E_2 \to E_1$ satisfying the following axioms.
\begin{description}
  \item[(a)] The set $E_2 \backslash \Z^3$ is finite.
  \item[(b)] For $h \in \Z^3$, $f(h) = Th$; in particular, $f$ is a bijection on $\Z^3$.
  \item[(c)] For $h \in E_1 \backslash \Z^3$, $f(h) \in E_1$.  Also, $-h + f^2(h) \in E_1$ and $f(-h + f^2(h)) = -h$. Note that this (and (b)) implies that $-h \in E_1$, thus $E_1$ is symmetric around the origin.
  \item[(d)] For $h \in E_2 \backslash E_1$, $f(h) \in E_1$.
  \item[(e)] The elements $-h$, $h - f^2(h)$, and $f^2(h) - h$ for $h \in E_2 \backslash E_1$ are all distinct from each other, and all lie outside of $E_2$.  In particular this forces $f^2(h) \neq 0$, hence $f(h) \neq 0$. It also forces $f^2(h) \neq h$, hence $f(h) \neq h$.
\end{description}
nodes.name: Partial solution for Dupont on Z^3 x Z
nodes.statement_short: $\Z^3\subseteq E_1\subseteq E_2$ with $f=T$ on $\Z^3$, the Dupont equation resolved on $E_1$, and freshness conditions (e) on $E_2\setminus E_1$.

nodes.statement: Thus for instance one can take $(\Z^3,\Z^3,T)$ as a partial solution.
nodes.name: Trivial Dupont partial solution

nodes.statement: We say that a partial solution $(E'_1, E'_2, f')$ is an \emph{extension} of $(E_1,E_2,f)$ if $E_1 \subseteq E'_1$, $E'_2 \subseteq E_2$, and $f'$ agrees with $f$ on $E_2$.
nodes.name: Extension of Dupont partial solutions

nodes.statement: If $(E_1,E_2,f)$ is a partial solution and $h \in E_2 \backslash E_1$, then there exists an extension $(E'_1,E'_2,f')$ of $(E_1,E_2,f)$ such that $h \in E'_1$.
nodes.name: Promoting to E1
assumptions: $(E_1,E_2,f)$ is a partial solution and $h \in E_2 \backslash E_1$
conclusions: there exists an extension $(E'_1,E'_2,f')$ of $(E_1,E_2,f)$ such that $h \in E'_1$
nodes.label: add-E1

nodes.statement: This will be a greedy construction, but we have to introduce a rather large number of additional elements to ensure that certain non-degeneracy conditions are maintained (in particular, the new elements $h'$ introduced have to be such that $f^2(h') - h'$ avoids $E_2$ and hence $\Z^3$, which requires a certain amount of complexity in the construction). Let $\tilde E_2$ denote the set $E_2$ together with all the elements of the form $-h'$, $h' - f^2(h')$, and $f^2(h') - h'$ for $h' \in E_2 \backslash E_1$; this is $\Z^3$ with a finite number of additional elements. Let $a$ be an element of $\Z^3$ such that the quantities $$ \pm Ta, \pm(Ta + a)$$ are distinct from each other and from $$0, \pm h, \pm (h - f(h)), \pm (f^2(h)-h);$$ this is possible since $T, T+1$ are invertible. Next, we pick an $x \in \Z^3 \times \Z$ such that the quantities $$ \pm x, \pm x + Ta, \pm x - Ta, \pm 2 x + Ta, \pm x + Ta + a, \pm (h + x), \pm (h - f(h) + x), \pm (f^2(h)-h + x + Ta)$$ are all distinct from each other and from $\tilde E_2$; indeed, from the choice of $a$ (and the non-zero nature of $h$, $f(h)$, $h-f(h)$, and $f^2(h)-h$) there are only finitely many $x$ for which a collision can occur between any pair of these expressions. We now promote $\pm h, \pm x, \pm x + Ta, \pm x - Ta$ to $E_1$, and also promote $h+x$, $h - f^2(h)$, $\pm 2x + Ta$, $\pm x + Ta + a$ to $E_2$. That is to say, we define $$ E'_1 := E_1 \cup \{\pm h, \pm x, \pm x + Ta, \pm x - Ta\}$$ and $$ E'_2 := E_2 \cup \{ -h, \pm x, \pm x + Ta, \pm x - Ta, h + x, h - f^2(h), \pm 2x + Ta \}.$$ We then define an extension $f'$ of $f$ to $E'_2$ by setting \begin{align*} f'(\pm x) &:= a \\ f'(\pm x + Ta) &:= \pm x \\ f'(\pm x - Ta) &:= \mp x + Ta \\ f'(\pm x + Ta + a) &:= \pm x - Ta \\ f'(\pm 2x + Ta) &:= \pm x + Ta \\ f'(\pm x + Ta + a) &:= \pm x - Ta \\ f'(-h) &:= x + Ta \\ f'(h+x) &:= h \\ f'(h - f^2(h)) &:= -h. \end{align*} It is easy to see that $(E'_1,E'_2,f')$ satisfies properties (a), (b), (d). By construction, we have $$ f'( (f')^2(h') - h') = -h'$$ for $$ h' = \pm h, \pm x, \pm x+Ta, \pm x-Ta$$ giving property (c). By construction, the quantities $$ -h', h' - f^2(h'), f^2(h') - h'$$ are distinct from each other and lie outside of $\tilde E_2 \cup E'_2$ for $$ h' = h+x, h - f^2(h), \pm 2x + Ta, \pm x + Ta + a$$ while these quantities are distinct from each other and lie in $\tilde E_2 \backslash E'_2$ for $h' \in E_2 \backslash E'_1$ (note that this forces $h' \neq \pm h$). This gives property (e).
nodes.name: Proof of Promoting to E1
nodes.statement_short: Greedy construction: choose $a\in\Z^3$ and a generic $x$, promote many elements and define $f'$ explicitly, then check axioms (a)-(e).

nodes.statement: If $(E_1,E_2,f)$ is a partial solution and $h \in (\Z^3 \times \Z) \backslash E_2$, then there exists an extension $(E'_1,E'_2,f')$ of $(E_1,E_2,f)$ such that $h \in E'_2$.
nodes.name: Promoting to E2
assumptions: $(E_1,E_2,f)$ is a partial solution and $h \in (\Z^3 \times \Z) \backslash E_2$
conclusions: there exists an extension $(E'_1,E'_2,f')$ of $(E_1,E_2,f)$ such that $h \in E'_2$
nodes.label: add-E2

nodes.statement: Let $\tilde E_2$ denote the set $E_2$ together with all elements of the form \begin{equation} -h', h' - f^2(h'), f^2(h') - h' \end{equation} for some $h' \in E_2 \backslash E_1$; this is $\Z^3$ with a finite number of elements attached, and is symmetric around the origin. First suppose that $h$ lies outside of $\tilde E_2$. Then we can find $a \in \Z^3$ such that the quantities $$ -h, \pm (h - Ta)$$ are distinct from each other, and lie outside of $\tilde E_2$. We now promote $h$ to $E_2$, thus setting $$ E'_1 := E_1$$ and $$ E'_2 := E_2 \cup \{h\}$$ and define an extension $f'$ of $f$ to $E'_2$ by setting $$ f'(h) := a.$$ It is then a routine matter to check that $(E'_1,E'_2,f')$ is an extension of $(E_1,E_2,f)$. Now suppose that $h$ lies in $\tilde E_2$. Then $h$ is of one of the forms \Cref{hp-form} for some $h' \in E_2 \backslash E_1$. Suppose it is of the form $-h'$ or $f^2(h') - h'$. We invoke \Cref{add-E1} to promote $h'$ to $E_1$ by using a suitable extension $(E'_1,E'_2,f')$; and now $h$ will lie in $E'_2$, giving the claim. If instead $h$ is of the form $h'-f^2(h')$, then this procedure might not place $h$ in $E'_2$; but if it does not, it will be of the form $-h''$ for $h'' = f^2(h')-h' \in E'_2 \backslash E'_1$. Applying \Cref{add-E1} one more time to now promote $h''$ to $E_1$, we will obtain a larger extension $(E''_1,E''_2,f'')$ with $h \in E''_2$, giving the claim.
nodes.name: Proof of Promoting to E2
nodes.statement_short: If $h$ is outside $\tilde E_2$ set $f'(h)=a$ generically; otherwise promote the relevant $h'$ to $E_1$ once or twice.

nodes.statement: Iterating these lemmas in the usual fashion, we can conclude that any partial solution can be completed to a global model of \Equaref{63}.
nodes.name: Dupont partial solutions complete to global models

nodes.statement: Among other things, this permits one to generate models in which the function $f$ is not injective.
nodes.name: Dupont models with non-injective f

nodes.statement:
To see this, let $a$ be a non-zero element of $\Z^3$, let $x$ be an element of $\Z^3 \times \Z$ outside of $\Z^3$, and consider the partial solution $(\Z^3, \Z^3 \cup \{x\}, f)$ where $f(h) = Th$ for $h \in \Z^3$ and $f(x) = a$.  One can check that this is a partial solution and is not injective, since $f(x) = f(T^{-1} a)$.  This non-injectivity implies in particular that the model is not left-cancellative, and hence does not satisfy the law
$$ x = (y \op x) \op ((y \op x) \op y)$$
(equation 1692).
nodes.name: Proof of Dupont models with non-injective f
nodes.statement_short: Seed partial solution with $f(x)=a=f(T^{-1}a)$; non-injectivity breaks left-cancellativity and 1692.

nodes.statement:
In this construction, we define a partial solution to be a function $f: E \to \Z$ defined on a finite subset of $E$ satisfying the following axioms:

\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] $E$ contains $E_0$, and $f$ agrees with $f_0$ on $E_0$.
\item[(ii)] If $h \in E$ and $f(h) \in E$, then $f^2(h)-h$ is also in $E$, and $f(f^2(h)-h) = -h$.
\item[(iii)] If $h \in E$ and $h \neq 3$, then $f(h) \neq 0$.
\item[(iv)]  If $a \neq a'$ are distinct elements of $E$ with $f(a)=f(a')$, and $-a \in E$, then $a' \neq a + f(-a)$.
\item[(v)]  If $a \neq a'$ are distinct elements of $E$ with $f(a)=f(a')$, and $-a, -a' \in E$, then $a' + f(-a') \neq a + f(-a)$.
\end{itemize}
nodes.name: Partial solution for Dupont on Z
nodes.statement_short: Finite partial $f$ on $\Z$ extending $f_0$, closed under the Dupont relation, with non-vanishing and anti-collision axioms (iii)-(v).

nodes.statement: We say that a partial solution $f': E' \to \Z$ \emph{extends} another $f: E \to \Z$ if $E'$ contains $E$ and $f'$ agrees with $f$ on $E$.
nodes.name: Extension of partial solutions on Z

nodes.statement: $f_0: E_0 \to \Z$ is a partial solution.
nodes.name: Seed solution
conclusions: $f_0: E_0 \to \Z$ is a partial solution.
nodes.label: finite-check

nodes.statement: Finite check.
nodes.name: Proof of Seed solution

nodes.statement: If $f: E \to \Z$ is a partial solution and $h_0 \in \Z$, then there exists an extension $f': E' \to \Z$ for which axiom (ii) applies, i.e., $h_0 \in E'$, $f'(h_0) \in E'$, $(f')^2(h_0)-h_0 \in E'$, and $f'((f')^2(h_0)-h_0) = -h_0$.
nodes.name: Dupont extension lemma
assumptions: $f: E \to \Z$ is a partial solution and $h_0 \in \Z$
conclusions: there exists an extension $f': E' \to \Z$ for which axiom (ii) applies, i.e., $h_0 \in E'$, $f'(h_0) \in E'$, $(f')^2(h_0)-h_0 \in E'$, and $f'((f')^2(h_0)-h_0) = -h_0$
nodes.label: extension-lemma

nodes.statement:
We divide into cases. { f Case 1:} $h_0 \in E$ and $f(h_0) \in E$. In this case we are already done thanks to axiom (ii). { f Case 2:} $h_0 \in E$ but $f(h_0) 
ot \in E$. This is the main case. Let $H$ be the set of all $h \in E$ such that $f(h) = f(h_0)$; this is a finite set containing $h_0$. Let $H' \subseteq H$ be the set of all $h' \in H$ such that $-h' \in E$. We make the following observations:  egin{itemize} \item[(a)] All elements $h$ of $H$ are non-zero. For if $h=0$ then $f(h_0)=f(h)=1 \in E$, contradicting the hypothesis $f(h_0) 
ot \in E$. \item[(b)] If $h' \in H'$ then $h' 
eq h'+f(-h')$. Otherwise we would have $f(-h')=0$, then by axiom (iii) we have $h' = -3$, hence $f(h_0) = f(h') = 4 \in E$ by axiom (i). But this again contradicts the hypothesis $f(h_0) 
ot \in E$. (This is the main reason we take $E_0$ to be so large.) \item[(c)] If $h_1 \in H$ and $h_2 \in H'$ are distinct then $h_1 
eq h_2+f(-h_2)$. This follows from axiom (iv). \item[(d)] If $h_1, h_2\in H'$ are distinct then $h_1+f(-h_1) 
eq h_2+f(-h_2)$. This follows from axiom (v). \end{itemize} From these observations, we see that if we take $c$ to be a sufficiently large integer, the following claims hold:  egin{itemize} \item[1.] The expressions $\pm c$, $\pm(c - h)$ for $h \in H$, and $\pm(c-h'-f(-h'))$ for $h \in H'$ are all distinct from each other. \item[2.] $c$ is not expressible as the sum of four or fewer elements of $\pm (E \cup f(E))$. \end{itemize} We select such a $c$. We then promote $f(h_0)$, $c - h$ for $h \in H$, and $-c+h'+f(-h')$ for $h' \in H'$, thus setting $$ E' := E \cup \{f(h_0)\} \cup \{ c-h: h \in H\} \cup \{ -c+h'+f(-h'): h' \in H'\}.$$ We then extend $f$ to $f': E' 	o \Z$ by setting  egin{align*} f(f(h_0)) &:= c \ f(c-h) &:= -h \ f(-c+h'+f(-h')) &:= h' - c \end{align*} for all $h \in H$ and $h' \in H'$. Axiom (i) is then obvious. Axiom (ii) needs to be verified for the new elements $h_0$ and $c-h'$, $h' \in H'$ of $E'$ (the other elements will not satisfy the hypotheses of this axiom), but this is routine. In particular $h_0$ satisfies the required conclusion of this lemma. We need to verify (iii) for the new elements of $E'$, but this is clear from property (a) and claim 2. Now we need to verify (iv). It suffices to do so when at least one of $a,a',-a$ are new elements of $E'$. If neither of $a$, $-a$ are new, then the only new elements $a'$ for which $f(a')$ could equal $f(a)$ take the form $c-h$ (thanks to claim 2), but then $a'$ cannot equal $a+f(-a)$, again thanks to claim 2. If instead one of $a, -a$ is new, then from claim 1 the new element must be $f(h_0)$. There is no old element $a'$ with $f(a') = c = f(f(h_0))$, so we must have $a = -f(h_0)$, but then $a + f(-a) = -f(h_0)+c$ will not equal $a'$, again thanks to claim 2. Finally, we need verify to (v). We may assume that at least one of $a,a',-a,-a'$ are new elements of $E'$. As before, this forces the new element to be $f(h_0)$, and this cannot be $a$ or $a'$, so without loss of generality we have $a = -f(h_0)$ and $a' \in E$. But then $a + f(-a) = -f(h_0)+c$ will not equal $a' + f(-a')$, again thanks to claim 2. { f Case 3:} $h_0 
ot \in E$ but $h_0 \in f(E)$. Here we can write $h_0 = f(h_1)$ where $h_1$ is of the form in Case 2. Applying the Case 2 construction, we can pass to an extension in which $f(h_1) = h_0$ lies in $E$, and so we are now in either Case 1 or Case 2, and so we can again conclude. { f Case 4:} $h_0 
ot \in E$ and $h_0 
ot \in f(E)$. We let $c$ be an integer so large that it is not expressible as the sum of four or fewer elements of $\pm (E \cup f(E))$. We then promote $h_0$ to $E$ by setting $$E' := E \cup \{h_0\}$$ and define an extension $f': E' 	o \Z$ by setting $f'(h_0) := c$. Axioms (i)-(iii) are obvious. For axiom (iv), since $f'(h_0)$ is not equal to any other value of $f'$, the only new case introduced is if $-a = h_0$, but then $a+f(-a) = -h_0+c$ is distinct from $a'$ by choice of $c$. A similar argument yields axiom (v). With this extension, we are now in Case 2, and so we repeat the previous analysis to conclude.
nodes.name: Proof of Dupont extension lemma
nodes.statement_short: Four cases by membership of $h_0$ and $f(h_0)$; main case adjoins elements built from a huge integer $c$ and checks axioms (i)-(v).

nodes.statement: Iterating this lemma, we conclude
nodes.name: Proof of greedy completion of Dupont

nodes.statement: Every partial solution $f: E \to \Z$ can be extended to a global solution $f': \Z \to\Z$ of \Cref{dupont-eq}.
nodes.name: Greedy completion of Dupont
assumptions: Every partial solution $f: E \to \Z$

nodes.statement: It suffices to find a partial solution that violates injectivity. This can be done for instance by adjoining $\{-13, 10\}$ to $E_0$ and defining $f(10)= 2 = f(6)$, $f(-13)=-10$, and performing a finite check to verify that this is still a partial solution.
nodes.name: Proof of Non-injective Dupont solution
nodes.statement_short: Exhibit a non-injective partial solution by adjoining two elements to $E_0$.

nodes.statement: There exists a magma which satisfies Equation 3342, $$ x \op y = y \op (x \op (x \op x)),$$ but such that none of the laws \begin{align*} x \op x &= x \op ((x \op x) \op x) \\ x \op y &= x \op ((y \op y) \op y) \\ x \op x &= ((x \op x) \op x) \op x \\ x \op y &= ((x \op x) \op x) \op y. \end{align*} hold.
nodes.name: 3342 ad hoc model
conclusions: There exists a magma which satisfies Equation 3342
nodes.statement_short: A magma on $\Z[t]$ satisfies 3342 but none of four related laws.

nodes.statement: We begin with some informal motivation. Writing \begin{equation} f(x) := x \op (x \op x), \end{equation} we conclude that \begin{equation} x \op y = y \op f(x) \end{equation} and hence on iteration $$ x \op y = f(x) \op f(y).$$ In particular, $x \op x = f(x) \op f(x)$, and $$ f(x) = x \op (x \op x) = (x \op x) \op f(x) = (f(x) \op f(x)) \op f(x).$$ If $f$ is surjective, this would imply $$ x = (x \op x) \op x$$ and hence the four laws stated above would hold in this case. This motivates the use of a non-surjective $f$. We will take $G$ to be the space of polynomials $\Z[t]$ of one variable with integer coefficients, and let $f: G \to G$ be the multiplication by $t$ map: $$ f(P) := tP.$$ This is of course non-surjective. The magma operation will be constructed as follows: \begin{itemize} \item If $P$ is a polynomial with $P(0) \neq 0$, then $t^n P \op t^n P = t^n P \op t^{n+1} P = 2P$ for all $n \geq 0$, and $t^{n+m} P \op 2t^n P = 2t^n P \op t^{n+m+1} P = t^{m+1} P$ for all $n, m \geq 0$. (This is well-defined since the $t^n P$, $2t^n P$ are all distinct polynomials.) \item We define $P \op Q = 0$ if not covered by the above laws. \end{itemize} It is a routine matter to verify \Cref{fdef} and \Cref{xop}, so that equation 3342 holds. However, one can check that the four laws in the conclusion fail with $x=y=1$.
nodes.name: Proof of 3342 ad hoc model
nodes.statement_short: Motivation shows $f(x)=x\op(x\op x)$ must be non-surjective; build a magma on $\Z[t]$ with $f$ = multiplication by $t$.

nodes.statement: f(x) := x \op (x \op x),
nodes.name: Definition of f(x)
nodes.label: fdef

nodes.statement: x \op y = y \op f(x)
nodes.name: x◇y = y◇f(x)
nodes.label: xop

nodes.statement: There exists a magma that satisfies Equation 1437, $$ x = (x \op x) \op (y \op (z \op x)),$$ but does not satisfy equation 4269, $$ x \op (x \op x) = x \op (y \op x).$$
nodes.name: 1437 does not imply 4269
conclusions: There exists a magma that satisfies Equation 1437
nodes.label: 1437-thm

nodes.statement: A first attempt would be the operation $i \op j := j+1$ on $\Z/3\Z$; this satisfies 1437, but unfortunately also satisfies 4269. However, an "extension" of this operation will work. Namely, we take the carrier $G = \N \times \Z/3\Z$ and define $(a,i) \op (b,j)$ to equal \begin{itemize} \item $(a-1,j+1)$ if $i=j+2$ and $a>0$; \item $(b,j+1)$ if $i=j+2$ and $a=0$; \item $(a+1,j+1)$ otherwise. \end{itemize} Note that $(a,i) \op (a,i) = (a+1,i+1)$, and that $(b,j) \op ((c,k) \op (a,i))$ will be of the form $(d,i+2)$ for some $d$. Hence $$ ((a,i) \op (a,i)) \op ((b,j) \op ((c,k) \op (a,i))) = (a+1-1, i+3) = (a,i),$$ giving 1437. On the other hand, $$ (0,i) \op ((b,i) \op (0,i)) = (0,i) \op (b+1,i+1) = (b+1,i+2)$$ and so equation 4269 fails.
nodes.name: Proof of 1437 does not imply 4269
nodes.statement_short: Extend the $\Z/3\Z$ operation $j+1$ to $\N\times\Z/3\Z$ with a counter.

nodes.section: 8 Equivalence with the constant and singleton laws
nodes.name: 85 laws equivalent to constant, 815 to singleton

nodes.statement: These are the laws up to 4 operations that follow from diagonalization of \Equaref{2} and \Equaref{46}.
nodes.section: 8 Equivalence with the constant and singleton laws
nodes.name: Constant/singleton equivalences come from diagonalization

nodes.statement: A \emph{metatheorem} is a general statement about implications; one can usually get many theorems from a single metatheorem.
nodes.name: Metatheorem

nodes.statement: Extending this idea, suppose we compute the set of all equations which are implied by $E$; we will call this set $\mathcal{Y}(E)$ (we use $\mathcal{Y}$ because this is an example of a \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoneda_lemma#The_Yoneda_embedding}{Yoneda embedding}).
nodes.name: Set of consequences Y(E)

nodes.statement: Then $\mathcal{Y}(E)$ is upwards closed, or closed under forward implication: no equation in $\mathcal{Y}(E)$ can imply an equation not in $\mathcal{Y}(E)$.
nodes.name: Y(E) is upwards closed

nodes.statement:
An \emph{invariant} for $E$ is some sort of data associated with expressions $w$ so that
\[
\mathcal{Y}(E) = \{w = w' \mid \text{Invariant}(w) = \text{Invariant}(w')\}
\]
nodes.name: Invariant

nodes.statement: Let $I$ be an invariant of $E$. If $w = w'$ implies $w'' = w'''$ and $I(w) = I(w')$ (that is, $E$ implies $w = w'$), then $I(w'') = I(w''')$.
nodes.name: Fundamental property of invariants
assumptions: Let $I$ be an invariant of $E$.
$w = w'$ implies $w'' = w'''$
also_stated_at: (w = w' \Rightarrow w'' = w''') \implies (I(w) = I(w') \Rightarrow I(w'') = I(w''')).

nodes.statement: Let $\Pi$ denote the preorder of magma equations ordered by implication. If $I$ is an invariant then define \[ I(w = w')\coloneqq \begin{cases} \texttt{true} & \text{ if }I(w) = I(w')\\ \texttt{false} & \text{ otherwise} \end{cases}. \] (In programming languages we would say $I(w = w') \coloneqq I(w) == I(w')$). Let $\textbf{Bool} = \{ \texttt{true}, \texttt{false}\}$ be the poset where $\texttt{false} \leq \texttt{true}$. Then $I$ becomes a function $\Pi \to \textbf{Bool}$, and the fundamental property of invariants just says that this function is monotone, i.e. functorial. Thus for every invariant $I$ we obtain a functor $\Pi \to \textbf{Bool}$. Question 1: Does every functor $\Pi \to \textbf{Bool}$ come from an invariant? Question 2: What can we say about the category of functors $\Pi \to \textbf{Bool}$? Give a nice interpretation of natural transformations between invariants.
nodes.name: Note for category theorists
nodes.statement_short: Invariants are exactly monotone maps (functors) from the implication preorder $\Pi$ to $\mathbf{Bool}$.

nodes.statement: Question 1: Does every functor $\Pi \to \textbf{Bool}$ come from an invariant?
nodes.name: Do all functors to Bool come from invariants?

nodes.statement: Question 2: What can we say about the category of functors $\Pi \to \textbf{Bool}$? Give a nice interpretation of natural transformations between invariants.
nodes.name: Category of functors from the implication preorder to Bool

nodes.statement:
Let $E$ be the equation $x \op y = x$. Intuitively, we must have
\[
\mathcal{Y}(E) = \{w = w' \mid \text{the leftmost variable is the same for $w$ and $w'$}\}.
\]
We will talk about proving statements like this one (say in Lean) later on; take it as given for now. The invariant is clear: we define $I(w)$ to be the leftmost variable of $w$. Instantiating this invariant in the fundamental property of invariants, we get the following metatheorem.
nodes.name: Invariant for the absorption law
nodes.statement_short: For $x\op y=x$ the invariant is the leftmost variable.

nodes.statement: Let $w = w'$ be an equation such that the leftmost variable of $w$ is the same as the leftmost variable of $w'$. Then $w = w'$ cannot imply an equation that does not have the property from the last sentence.
nodes.name: Leftmost-variable metatheorem
assumptions: Let $w = w'$ be an equation such that the leftmost variable of $w$ is the same as the leftmost variable of $w'$.
conclusions: $w = w'$ cannot imply an equation that does not have the property from the last sentence

nodes.statement:
For a more complicated example, let $E$ be the associativity equation $x \op (y \op z) = (x \op y) \op z$. Intuitively, we must have
\[
\mathcal{Y}(E) = \{\text{equations that, when we remove all parentheses, are of the form $w = w$}\}.
\]
There is an invariant lurking behind: it is the (ordered) list of variables appearing in an expression, counting repetitions. More formally, we define $I(w)$ to be the tuple of variables appearing in $w$, listed from left to right, say. Again, from the fundamental property of invariants we get the following.
nodes.name: Invariant for associativity
nodes.statement_short: For associativity the invariant is the ordered list of variables.

nodes.statement: Let $w = w'$ be an equation such that the variables appearing in $w$, taking into account order and repetitions, are the same ones that appear in $w'$. Then $w = w'$ cannot imply an equation that does not have the property from the last sentence.
nodes.name: Ordered-variables metatheorem
assumptions: Let $w = w'$ be an equation such that the variables appearing in $w$, taking into account order and repetitions, are the same ones that appear in $w'$.
conclusions: $w = w'$ cannot imply an equation that does not have the property from the last sentence

nodes.statement: Exercise: what is the invariant for commutativity? Answer: To compute $I(w)$ from $w$ replace all parentheses with curly braces and all symbols $\op$ with commas, and interpret the result as nested sets.
nodes.name: Invariant for commutativity

nodes.statement: Let $\Pi$ denote the preorder of equations (built from the language described) ordered by implication.
nodes.name: Implication preorder Pi

nodes.statement: Then we consider a bigger preorder $\Pi' \supseteq \Pi$ which includes equations and also conjunctions of equations.
nodes.name: Extended preorder Pi'

nodes.statement: If $\varphi$ is a formula, we can define $\mathcal{Y}(\varphi)$ to be the set of all formulae implied by $\varphi$; this agrees with our previous definition.
nodes.name: Y of a formula

nodes.statement:
Now define an invariant of $\varphi$ to be a function $I$ on terms such that
\[
\mathcal{Y}(\varphi) \cap \Pi = \{w = w' \mid I(w) = I(w')\}.
\]
nodes.name: Invariant of a formula

nodes.statement: Although $\mathcal{Y}(\varphi) \cap \Pi$ might not be upwards closed in $\Pi'$, it is upwards closed in $\Pi$, which is enough to get the fundamental property of invariants \emph{verbatim}.
nodes.name: Fundamental property for formulas

nodes.statement: Let $\varphi$ be the conjunction of the associative law and the idempotency law ($x \op x = x$). Again, we will rely on our intuition, which says that an invariant $I$ defined by taking $I(w)$ to be the set of all variables appearing in $w$, works. The corresponding metatheorem is the following
nodes.name: Invariant for associativity and idempotency

nodes.statement: Let $w = w'$ be an equation such that the set of variables appearing in $w$ is equal to the set of variables appearing on $w'$. Then $w = w'$ cannot imply an equation that does not have the property from the last sentence.
nodes.name: Variable-set metatheorem
assumptions: Let $w = w'$ be an equation such that the set of variables appearing in $w$ is equal to the set of variables appearing on $w'$.
conclusions: $w = w'$ cannot imply an equation that does not have the property from the last sentence

nodes.statement: For a similar example, we can let $\varphi$ be the conjunction of the associative and the commutative laws. Here we can define $I(w)$ to be the \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiset}{multiset} of variables appearing in $w$. We obtain the following metatheorem.
nodes.name: Invariant for associativity and commutativity

nodes.statement: Let $w = w'$ be an equation such that the variables appearing in $w$, taking into account multiplicity, are the same ones that appear in $w'$. Then $w = w'$ cannot imply an equation that does not have the property from the last sentence.
nodes.name: Multiset metatheorem
assumptions: Let $w = w'$ be an equation such that the variables appearing in $w$, taking into account multiplicity, are the same ones that appear in $w'$.
conclusions: $w = w'$ cannot imply an equation that does not have the property from the last sentence

nodes.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the conjunction of associativity, commutativity, the equations $1 \op x = x$, and
\[
\underbrace{x \op x \op \cdots \op x}_{m\text{ times}} = 1,
\]
for some fixed positive integer $m$. Pause to guess the invariant before we move on.

The invariant $I(w)$ is the multiset of variables appearing in $w$ but multiplicities are computed modulo $m$. Thus we have the pretty metatheorem:
nodes.section: Example: associativity and commutativity with a twist
nodes.name: Invariant for commutative monoids of exponent m
nodes.statement_short: For commutative monoids satisfying $x^m=1$ the invariant is the multiset of variables with multiplicities mod $m$.

nodes.statement: Fix some positive integer $m$. Let $w = w'$ be an equation such that every variable appearing in $w$ appears the same number of times in $w'$ modulo $m$. Then $w = w'$ cannot imply an equation that does not have the property from the last sentence.
nodes.section: Example: associativity and commutativity with a twist
nodes.name: Multiplicity mod m metatheorem
assumptions: Fix some positive integer $m$.
Let $w = w'$ be an equation such that every variable appearing in $w$ appears the same number of times in $w'$ modulo $m$.
conclusions: $w = w'$ cannot imply an equation that does not have the property from the last sentence

nodes.statement: A \emph{lifting magma family} is a family of magmas $\{G_\alpha\}$, one for each type $\alpha$, satisfying the following properties: \begin{itemize} \item For each type $\alpha$, there is a function $\iota_\alpha : \alpha \to G_\alpha$. \item Given a function $f : \alpha \to G_\alpha$, there is a magma homomorphism $\operatorname{lift}{f} : G_\alpha \to G_\alpha$ such that $\operatorname{lift}{f}(\iota_\alpha(x)) = f(x)$ for all $x$ in $\alpha$. \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 9.3 Proving metatheorems from invariants in Lean
nodes.name: Lifting magma family
nodes.genus: family of magmas $\{G_\alpha\}$, one for each type $\alpha$
differentia: For each type $\alpha$, there is a function $\iota_\alpha : \alpha \to G_\alpha$.

Given a function $f : \alpha \to G_\alpha$, there is a magma homomorphism $\operatorname{lift}{f} : G_\alpha \to G_\alpha$ such that $\operatorname{lift}{f}(\iota_\alpha(x)) = f(x)$ for all $x$ in $\alpha$.
nodes.label: lifting-magma-family

nodes.statement: The free abelian groups form a lifting magma family. When the underlying set is finite, the groups are isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}^n$.
nodes.section: 9.3 Proving metatheorems from invariants in Lean
nodes.name: Free abelian groups as a lifting magma family

nodes.statement: Lists form a lifting magma family.
nodes.section: 9.3 Proving metatheorems from invariants in Lean
nodes.name: Lists as a lifting magma family

nodes.statement: Suppose $E$ is an equation involving a set of variables $X$, and let $G$ be a lifting magma family. Determining whether $E$ is satisfied by $G_X$ is equivalent to checking that $E$ is true with the specific substitution $\iota_X$.
nodes.section: 9.3 Proving metatheorems from invariants in Lean
nodes.name: Evaluation theorem for lifting magma families
assumptions: Suppose $E$ is an equation involving a set of variables $X$, and let $G$ be a lifting magma family.
conclusions: Determining whether $E$ is satisfied by $G_X$ is equivalent to checking that $E$ is true with the specific substitution $\iota_X$.
equivalent_conditions: $E$ is true with the specific substitution $\iota_X$
nodes.label: lifting-magma-basis-evaluation

nodes.statement: For the forward direction, suppose $E$ is satisfied by $G_X$. Then, by definition, any substitution of the variables in $E$ with elements of $G_X$ will yield a true equation. In particular, substituting according to $\iota_X$ will yield a true equation. For the reverse direction, suppose that $E$ is true when evaluated with the substitution $\iota_X$. Now, consider an arbitrary substitution of variables $f : X \to G_X$. By the lifting magma family property, there is a magma homomorphism $\operatorname{lift}{f} : G_X \to G_X$ such that $\operatorname{lift}{f}(\iota_X(x)) = f(x)$ for all $x$ in $X$. In other words, applying the substitution $f$ is equivalent to first applying to substitution $\iota_X$ and then applying the homomorphism $\operatorname{lift}{f}$. Since $E$ is true when evaluated with the substitution $\iota_X$, it is also true after applying the homomorphism $\operatorname{lift}{f}$. Thus, $E$ is satisfied by $G_X$.
nodes.section: 9.3 Proving metatheorems from invariants in Lean
nodes.name: Proof of Evaluation theorem for lifting magma families
nodes.statement_short: Forward: specialize to $\iota_X$. Reverse: any substitution factors through $\iota_X$ via a lift homomorphism.

nodes.statement: Let $E$ and $E'$ be equations involving a set of variables $X$, and let $G$ be a lifting magma family. If $E$ is true with the substitution $\iota_X$, and $E$ implies $E'$, then so is $E'$.
nodes.section: 9.3 Proving metatheorems from invariants in Lean
nodes.name: The fundamental property of invariants
assumptions: Let $E$ and $E'$ be equations involving a set of variables $X$, and let $G$ be a lifting magma family.
$E$ is true with the substitution $\iota_X$
$E$ implies $E'$
conclusions: then so is $E'$
nodes.label: fundamental-property-of-invariants

nodes.statement: Applying the evaluation \Cref{lifting-magma-basis-evaluation}, we see that $E$ is satisfied by $G_X$. Since $E$ implies $E'$, $E'$ is also satisfied by $G_X$, and in particular, $E'$ is true with the substitution $\iota_X$.
nodes.section: 9.3 Proving metatheorems from invariants in Lean
nodes.name: Proof of The fundamental property of invariants
nodes.statement_short: Apply the evaluation theorem, then implication, then specialize to $\iota_X$.

nodes.statement: The result of evaluating an expression along the function $\iota_X : X \to G_X$ \emph{is} the invariant. In the case of abelian groups, the result of evaluation is the variables in the expression with multiplicity. In the case of lists, the result of evaluation is the variables in the expression in the order they appear. When the lifting magma family has good computational properties, calculating the invariant becomes easy.
nodes.section: 9.3 Proving metatheorems from invariants in Lean
nodes.name: Evaluation along iota is the invariant

nodes.statement: Given an equation $\phi$ in the language of magmas (possibly involving logical operations other than equality and universal quantification), the initial (i.e., most general) magmas satisfying $\phi$ (provided they exist) form a lifting magma family. However, for the purpose of generating invariants, we are interested in lifting magma families with convenient descriptions that are computationally tractable.
nodes.section: 9.3 Proving metatheorems from invariants in Lean
nodes.name: Initial magmas form lifting magma families

nodes.statement: Suppose $S$ is a finite set of equations in the language of magmas that is a confluent term rewriting system under a certain ordering of the terms (in the sense of the Knuth-Bendix algorithm). Then the initial magmas satisfying $S$ form a lifting magma family where equality of elements in the magma is decidable. This offers a way of generating examples of lifting magma families with good computational properties for computing invariants of expressions.
nodes.section: 9.3 Proving metatheorems from invariants in Lean
nodes.name: Confluent rewriting systems give computable lifting magma families

nodes.statement: Let $E$ be a magma law defined over $n$ variables and let $\tilde{E}$ be the same equation with variables ranging over the natural numbers (formally, $\tilde{E}$ is the image of $E$ under the canonical map from the finite set with $n$ elements to the natural numbers). Then any magma $M$ satisfies $E$ if and only if it satisfies $\tilde{E}$.
nodes.name: Compatibility between magma laws over finite sets and the natural numbers
assumptions: Let $E$ be a magma law defined over $n$ variables and let $\tilde{E}$ be the same equation with variables ranging over the natural numbers
conclusions: any magma $M$ satisfies $E$ if and only if it satisfies $\tilde{E}$
nodes.label: compatibility-between-magma-laws

nodes.statement: In the forward direction, suppose $\phi : \mathbb{N} \to M$ is a substitution. Then the restriction of $\phi$ to the first $n$ natural numbers is a substitution for the variables of $E$, and since $M$ satisfies $E$, the law $E$ is true in $M$ under this substitution. Since $\tilde{E}$ is the same as $E$ under the substitution $\phi$, $M$ satisfies $\tilde{E}$. In the reverse direction, suppose $\phi : \{0, 2, \ldots, n-1\} \to M$ is a substitution. Then $\phi$ can be extended to a substitution $\tilde{\phi} : \mathbb{N} \to M$ by setting $\tilde{\phi}(i) = \phi(i)$ for $i \leq n$ and $\tilde{\phi}(i) = 0$ for $i \geq n$. Since $M$ satisfies $\tilde{E}$ under the substitution $\tilde{\phi}$, it satisfies $E$ under the restriction of $\tilde{\phi}$ to the first $n$ natural numbers, which is precisely $\phi$. The special case where $n = 0$ is in fact impossible, since there cannot be an expression with no variables.
nodes.name: Proof of Compatibility between magma laws over finite sets and the natural numbers
nodes.statement_short: Restrict substitutions from $\N$ to the first $n$ numbers, and extend substitutions by zero.

nodes.statement: Q: If we were to define invariants as any functions satisfying the fundamental property, would anything change?
nodes.name: Invariants defined by the fundamental property

nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ be a theory with an alphabet $X$. A \emph{free magma} with alphabet $X$ subject to the theory $\Gamma$ is a magma $M_{X,\Gamma}$ together with a function $\iota_{X,\Gamma} : X \to M_{X,\Gamma}$, with the following properties: \begin{description} \item[(i)] $M_{X,\Gamma}$ satisfies the theory $\Gamma$: $M_{X,\Gamma} \models \Gamma$. \item[(ii)] For any magma $M$ satisfying the theory $\Gamma$ and any function $f: X \to M$, there exists a unique magma homomorphism $\tilde{f}: M_{X,\Gamma} \to M$ such that $\tilde{f} \circ \iota_{X,\Gamma} = f$. \end{description}
nodes.name: Free magma relative to a theory
nodes.definiendum: free magma with alphabet $X$ subject to the theory $\Gamma$
nodes.genus: magma $M_{X,\Gamma}$ together with a function $\iota_{X,\Gamma} : X \to M_{X,\Gamma}$
differentia: For any magma $M$ satisfying the theory $\Gamma$ and any function $f: X \to M$, there exists a unique magma homomorphism $\tilde{f}: M_{X,\Gamma} \to M$ such that $\tilde{f} \circ \iota_{X,\Gamma} = f$.
nodes.label: free-theory

nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ be a theory with alphabet $X$. \begin{description} \item[(i)] There exists a free magma $M_{X,\Gamma}$ with alphabet $X$ subject to the theory $\Gamma$. \item[(ii)] If $M_{X,\Gamma}$ and $M'_{X,\Gamma}$ are two free magmas with alphabet $X$ subject to the theory $\Gamma$, then there exists a unique magma isomorphism $\phi: M_{X,\Gamma} \to M'_{X,\Gamma}$ such that $\phi \circ \iota_{X,\Gamma} = \iota'_{X,\Gamma}$. \end{description}
nodes.name: Existence and uniqueness of free magmas
assumptions: Let $\Gamma$ be a theory with alphabet $X$.
If $M_{X,\Gamma}$ and $M'_{X,\Gamma}$ are two free magmas with alphabet $X$ subject to the theory $\Gamma$
conclusions: There exists a free magma $M_{X,\Gamma}$ with alphabet $X$ subject to the theory $\Gamma$.
there exists a unique magma isomorphism $\phi: M_{X,\Gamma} \to M'_{X,\Gamma}$ such that $\phi \circ \iota_{X,\Gamma} = \iota'_{X,\Gamma}$
There exists a free magma $M_{X,\Gamma}$ with alphabet $X$ subject to the theory $\Gamma$.

assumptions: If $M_{X,\Gamma}$ and $M'_{X,\Gamma}$ are two free magmas with alphabet $X$ subject to the theory $\Gamma$
conclusions: there exists a unique magma isomorphism $\phi: M_{X,\Gamma} \to M'_{X,\Gamma}$ such that $\phi \circ \iota_{X,\Gamma} = \iota'_{X,\Gamma}$

nodes.label: freemag-exist

nodes.statement: For (i), we define $M_{X,\Gamma} = M_X / \sim$, where the equivalence relation $\sim$ is defined by requiring $w \sim w'$ if and only if $\Gamma \models w \formaleq w'$; this is an equivalence relation thanks to \Cref{equiv}, and from \Cref{sound-complete} we see that this relation respects the magma operations, so that $M_{X,\Gamma}$ is a magma. The map $\iota_{X,\Gamma}: X \to M_{X,\Gamma}$ is defined by setting $\iota_{X,\Gamma}(x)$ to be the equivalence class of $x$ in $M_{X,\Gamma}$ for each $x \in X$. We first check that $M_{X,\Gamma}$ satisfies $\Gamma$. Let $w \formaleq w'$ be a law in $\Gamma$, and let $f: X \to M_{X,\Gamma}$ be a function. We may lift this function to a function $\tilde{f}: X \to M_X$. From \Cref{derivation-def}, we have $\Gamma \models w \formaleq w'$ and hence $\Gamma \models \varphi_{\tilde{f}}(w) \formaleq \varphi_{\tilde{f}}(w')$. By \Cref{sound-complete}, we conclude $\Gamma \models \varphi_{\tilde{f}}(w) \formaleq \varphi_{\tilde{f}}(w')$. Quotienting by $\sim$, we conclude that $\varphi_f(w) = \varphi(w')$, giving the claim by \Cref{models-def}. Now we check the universal property (ii). Let $M$ be a magma satisfying the theory $\Gamma$, and let $f: X \to M$ be a function, then we have a magma homomorphism $\varphi_f: M_X \to M$. If $w, w' \in M_X$ are such that $w \sim w'$, then $\Gamma \models w \formaleq w'$ and hence $\varphi_f(w) = \varphi_f(w')$. Hence $\varphi_f$ descends to a map $\tilde{f}: M_{X,\Gamma} \to M$, which one can check to be a magma homomorphism with $\tilde{f} \circ \iota_{X,\Gamma} = f$. By construction, $M_{X,\Gamma}$ is generated by $\iota_{X,\Gamma}(X)$, and so this homomorphism is unique.
nodes.name: Proof of Existence and uniqueness of free magmas
nodes.statement_short: Quotient the free magma by $\Gamma$-entailment; check it models $\Gamma$ and has the universal property.

nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ consist solely of the associative law, \Equaref{4512} (so $X$ contains $0,1,2$). Then one can take $M_{X,\Gamma}$ to be the set of nonempty strings with alphabet $X$, with magma operation given by concatenation, and $\iota_{X,\Gamma}(x)$ being the length one string $x$. It is a routine matter to verify that this satisfies the axioms of a free magma subject to $\Gamma$.
nodes.name: Free associative magma

nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ consist of the associative law (\Equaref{4512}) and the commutative law (\Equaref{43}). Then one can take $M_{X,\Gamma}$ to be the free abelian monoid $\N_0^X \backslash 0$ of tuples $(n_x)_{x \in X}$ with the $n_x$ natural numbers, not all zero, with all but finitely many of the $n_x$ vanishing, with the magma operation given by vector addition, and with $\iota_{X,\Gamma}(x)$ being the standard generator of $\N^X$ associated to $x \in X$; one can think of this space as the space of formal non-empty commuting associating sums of $X$. It is a routine matter to verify that this satisfies the axioms of a free magma subject to $\Gamma$.
nodes.name: Free associative commutative magma
nodes.label: facm

nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ consist of the left absorptive law (\Equaref{4}). Then one can take $M_{X,\Gamma}$ to be $X$ with the law $x \op y = x$, and $\iota_{X,\Gamma}$ to be the identity map. It is easy to see that this is indeed a free magma subject to $\Gamma$.
nodes.name: Free left absorptive magma
nodes.label: freeleft

nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ consist of the constant law (\Equaref{46}). Then one can take $M_{X,\Gamma}$ to be the disjoint union $X \uplus \{0\}$ of $X$ and another object $0$, with $\iota_{X,\Gamma}$ being the identity embedding, and with the zero magma law $x \op y = 0$ for all $x,y \in X \uplus \{0\}$.
nodes.name: Free constant magma
nodes.label: freeconst

nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ be a theory with some alphabet $X$, and let $M_{X,\Gamma}$ be a free magma with alphabet $X$ subject to $\Gamma$, with associated map $\iota_{X,\Gamma}: X \to M_{X,\Gamma}$. Then for any $w,w' \in M_X$, we have \[ \Gamma \models w \formaleq w' \text{ if and only if } \varphi_{\iota_{X,\Gamma}}(w) = \varphi_{\iota_{X,\Gamma}}(w'). \]
nodes.name: Canonical invariant
assumptions: Let $\Gamma$ be a theory with some alphabet $X$, and let $M_{X,\Gamma}$ be a free magma with alphabet $X$ subject to $\Gamma$, with associated map $\iota_{X,\Gamma}: X \to M_{X,\Gamma}$.
conclusions: \Gamma \models w \formaleq w' \text{ if and only if } \varphi_{\iota_{X,\Gamma}}(w) = \varphi_{\iota_{X,\Gamma}}(w').
nodes.label: canonical-invariant

nodes.statement: By \Cref{freemag-exist} we may take $M_{X,\Gamma}$ to be the canonical free magma constructed in the proof of that theorem. The claim is then clear from expanding out definitions.
nodes.name: Proof of Canonical invariant
nodes.statement_short: Use the canonical quotient construction and unfold definitions.

nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ be a theory with some alphabet $X$, and let $M_{X,\Gamma}$ be a free magma with alphabet $X$ subject to $\Gamma$, with associated map $\iota_{X,\Gamma}: X \to M_{X,\Gamma}$. Let $w \formaleq w'$ and $w'' \formaleq w'''$ be laws with alphabet $X$. If one has \[ \varphi_{\iota_{X,\Gamma}}(w) = \varphi_{\iota_{X,\Gamma}}(w') \] but \[ \varphi_{\iota_{X,\Gamma}}(w'') \neq \varphi_{\iota_{X,\Gamma}}(w'''), \] then the law $w \formaleq w'$ cannot imply the law $w'' \formaleq w'''$.
nodes.name: Criterion for anti-implication (free magmas)
assumptions: Let $\Gamma$ be a theory with some alphabet $X$, and let $M_{X,\Gamma}$ be a free magma with alphabet $X$ subject to $\Gamma$, with associated map $\iota_{X,\Gamma}: X \to M_{X,\Gamma}$.
\varphi_{\iota_{X,\Gamma}}(w) = \varphi_{\iota_{X,\Gamma}}(w')
\varphi_{\iota_{X,\Gamma}}(w'') \neq \varphi_{\iota_{X,\Gamma}}(w'''),
conclusions: the law $w \formaleq w'$ cannot imply the law $w'' \formaleq w'''$
nodes.label: anti-impl

nodes.statement: By \Cref{canonical-invariant}, the hypothesis $\iota_{X,\Gamma}(w) = \iota_{X,\Gamma}(w')$ is equivalent to $\Gamma \models w \formaleq w'$, and the hypothesis $\iota_{X,\Gamma}(w'') \neq \iota_{X,\Gamma}(w''')$ is equivalent to $\Gamma \not\models w'' \formaleq w'''$. The claim follows.
nodes.name: Proof of Criterion for anti-implication (free magmas)
nodes.statement_short: Translate both hypotheses via the canonical invariant.

nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ be the associative and commutative law, so that we can take $M_{X,\Gamma} = \N_0^X \backslash 0$ as in \Cref{facm}. One can then check that for any word $w \in M_X$, that $\varphi_{\iota_{X,\Gamma}}(w)$ is the tuple that assigns to each letter $x$ of the alphabet, the number of times $x$ appears in $w$. We conclude that if $w,w'$ have the same number of occurrences of each letter of the alphabet, but $w'', w'''$ do not, then $w \formaleq w'$ cannot imply $w'' \formaleq w'''$. This recovers \Cref{variable-impl}.
nodes.name: Multiplicity invariant from the free commutative semigroup

nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ consist of the left absorption law, so we can take $M_{X,\Gamma} = X$ as in \Cref{freeleft}. Then $\varphi_{\iota_{X,\Gamma}}(w)$ is the first letter of $w$. We conclude that if $w,w'$ have the same first letter, but $w'', w'''$ do not, then $w \formaleq w'$ cannot imply $w'' \formaleq w'''$.
nodes.name: First-letter invariant from left absorption

nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ consist of the constant law, so we can take $M_{X,\Gamma} = X \uplus \{0\}$ as in \Cref{freeconst}. Then $\varphi_{\iota_{X,\Gamma}}(w)$ is $x$ if $w$ is just a letter $x$ of the alphabet, and $0$ otherwise. We conclude that if $w,w', w'''$ have order at least one, but $w''$ has order zero, then $w \formaleq w'$ cannot imply $w'' \formaleq w'''$; this is basically \Cref{constant-impl}.
nodes.name: Constant-law invariant

nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ be the theory consisting of the commutative and associative laws, and an additional law $x^n \formaleq y^n$ for a fixed $n$, where $x^n$ denotes the magma operation applied to $n$ copies of $x$ (the order is irrelevant thanks to associativity), then one can check (for finite $X$) that the free magma $M_{X,\Gamma}$ can be taken to be $(\Z/n\Z)^X$ with the addition operation, and $\iota_{X,\Gamma}(x)$ being the standard generator associated to $x$. Then for any word $w$, $\varphi_{\iota_{X,\Gamma}}(w)$ corresponds to a tuple that assigns to each letter $x$ of the alphabet, the number of times $x$ occurs in $w$ modulo $n$. We conclude that if $w,w'$ have the same number of occurrences modulo $n$ of each letter of the alphabet, but $w'', w'''$ do not, then $w \formaleq w'$ cannot imply $w'' \formaleq w'''$. This is a stronger version of \Cref{variable-impl}.
nodes.name: Multiplicity mod n invariant

nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ be a theory. A word $w$ can be \emph{reduced} to another $w'$ if one can get from $w$ to $w'$ by a series of substitutions of laws in $\Gamma$, where no substitution increases the length of the word {\bf this is a working definition, might not be the best one to keep.}. A theory $\Gamma$ is \emph{confluent} if whenever a word $w$ can be reduced to both $w'$ and $w''$, then both $w'$ and $w''$ can be reduced further to a common reduction $\tilde w$. As such, each word $w \in M_X$ should have a \emph{unique simplification} to a reduced word $w_\Gamma$ in some normal form, for instance the shortest reduction that is minimal with respect to some suitable ordering such as lexicographical ordering.
nodes.name: Confluent theory
nodes.statement_short: Words reduce by length-nonincreasing substitutions; confluence means any two reductions have a common further reduction.
nodes.label: confluent-theory

nodes.statement: The associative law, \Equaref{4512}, appears to be confluent {\bf check this}.
nodes.name: Associative law appears confluent

nodes.statement: The theory consisting of both the associative and commutative laws, \Equaref{4512}, \Equaref{43}, appears to be confluent {\bf check this}.
nodes.name: Associative-commutative theory appears confluent

nodes.statement: The idempotent law, \Equaref{3}, appears to be confluent {\bf check this}.
nodes.name: Idempotent law appears confluent

nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ be a confluent theory. Then the free magma $M_{X,\Gamma}$ subject to this theory can be described as the space of reduced words in $M_X$ in normal form, where the operation $w \op_\Gamma w'$ on this magma is defined as the normal form reduction of $w \op w'$, and $\iota_{X,\Gamma}$ is the identity embedding (note that every single-letter word is already in normal form).
nodes.name: Free magma of a confluent theory
assumptions: Let $\Gamma$ be a confluent theory.
conclusions: the free magma $M_{X,\Gamma}$ subject to this theory can be described as the space of reduced words in $M_X$ in normal form
nodes.label: free-confluent

nodes.statement: Should just be a matter of expanding definitions properly.
nodes.name: Proof of Free magma of a confluent theory

nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ be a confluent theory. Then a law $w \formaleq w'$ is a consequence of $\Gamma$ if and only if $w,w'$ have the same normal form reduction. In particular, a law with this property cannot imply a law without this property.
nodes.name: Criterion for anti-implication (confluent theories)
assumptions: Let $\Gamma$ be a confluent theory.
conclusions: a law $w \formaleq w'$ is a consequence of $\Gamma$ if and only if $w,w'$ have the same normal form reduction
a law with this property cannot imply a law without this property
equivalent_conditions: a law $w \formaleq w'$ is a consequence of $\Gamma$
$w,w'$ have the same normal form reduction
nodes.label: confluent-anti-impl

nodes.statement: Follows from \Cref{anti-impl}.
nodes.name: Proof of Criterion for anti-implication (confluent theories)
nodes.statement_short: Follows from the free-magma anti-implication criterion.

nodes.statement: \Equareffull{477} is confluent.
nodes.name: 477 confluent
conclusions: \Equareffull{477} is confluent.
nodes.label: 477-confl

nodes.statement: See the notes \href{https://www.overleaf.com/project/66f847bb14d0d8f0b77f74e1}{here}. A sketch of proof is as follows. We induct on the length of the term. As before we consider terms of the form $XY$. Also, in both sequences if a simplification is applied to the whole term, then we can assume the sequence is simply final. By \Cref{477-lemma}, if any of the two sequences is final, then right before the last step, the two factors of the outermost product are both simple. This is also true for the result of the non-final sequence. By the induction hypothesis, they can be identified correspondingly, so the two sequences are either both final or both non-final, and in the first case, the same simplification is applied to give the same result.
nodes.name: Proof of 477 confluent
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: induction on term length, using the 477 lemma to compare final and non-final reduction sequences.

nodes.statement: If $Z$ and $W$ are simple, then $Z(W\cdots(WW))$ is simple.
nodes.name: 477 lemma
assumptions: If $Z$ and $W$ are simple
conclusions: $Z(W\cdots(WW))$ is simple
nodes.label: 477-lemma

nodes.statement: Assume the contrary. Then we have 2 cases. \textbf{Case 1: $W\cdots(WW)$ matches the pattern $y(x(y\cdots(yy)))$, with $k$ occurrences of $W$ ($k \le n$).} Since $|x(y\cdots(yy))| > n|y|$, but $|\cdots(WW)| \le (n-1)|W|$, this is impossible. \textbf{Case 2: $Z(W\cdots(WW))$ matches the pattern $y(x(y\cdots(yy)))$.} Since $n \ge 3$, we have $Z = y = W$, so $|W\cdots(WW)| = n|W| = n|Z|$, contradicting $|x(y\cdots(yy))| > n|y|$.
nodes.name: Proof of 477 lemma
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction by length comparison in two pattern-matching cases.

nodes.statement:
Group cohomology is a theory that constructs certain abelian groups $H^n(G,M)$ to a group $G$ acting as a module on an abelian group $M$, via a chain complex
$$ 0 \to C^0(G,M) \stackrel{d}{\to} C^1(G,M) \stackrel{d}{\to} C^2(G,M) \stackrel{d}{\to} C^3(G,M) \stackrel{d}{\to} \dots$$
where $C^n(G,M)$ is the space of functions $f: G^n \to M$, and the coboundary maps $d: C^n(G,M) \to C^{n+1}(G,M)$ are explicit maps satisfying the relation $d^2=0$.
nodes.name: Group cohomology

nodes.statement:
We let $M = (M,+)$ be an abelian group that also has a linear magma operation
$$ s \op t = as + bt$$
satisfying $E$ for some $a,b \in \mathrm{End}(M)$ in the endomorphism ring of $M$.
nodes.name: Linear magma M

nodes.statement:
Note that in such a linear magma, any word $w(s_1,\dots,s_n)$ takes the form
$$ w(s_1,\dots,s_n) = \sum_{i=1}^n P_{w,i}(a,b) s_i$$
for some (noncommutative) polynomials $P_{w,i}(a,b)$ in $a,b$ with natural number coefficients.
nodes.name: Polynomials P_{w,i}

nodes.statement:
The law $E$ is then satisfied when
$$ P_{w_{E,1},i}(a,b)= P_{w_{E,2},i}(a,b)$$
for $i=1,\dots,n$.
nodes.name: Linear magma satisfies E iff polynomial identities

nodes.statement:
For instance, the law 1110,
\begin{equation} x = y \op ((y \op (x \op x)) \op y)
\end{equation}
would be satisfied if one has
\begin{equation} baba+bab^2 = 1; \quad ba^2+b^2+a = 0.
\end{equation}
A solution here would be provided by $(a,b) = (\phi,-1)$, where $\phi$ solves the golden ratio equation $\phi^2 = \phi + 1$.
nodes.name: Linear model of equation 1110

nodes.statement: x = y \op ((y \op (x \op x)) \op y)
nodes.name: Equation 1110

nodes.statement: baba+bab^2 = 1; \quad ba^2+b^2+a = 0.
nodes.name: Linear conditions for 1110
nodes.label: baba

nodes.statement:
We consider \emph{extensions} of $G$ by $M$, which are magmas with carrier $G \times M$ with an operation of the form
\begin{equation} (x,s) \op (y,t) = (x \op y, as + bt + f(x,y))
\end{equation}
for some function $f: G \times G \to M$.
nodes.name: Extension of a magma by a linear magma

nodes.statement: (x,s) \op (y,t) = (x \op y, as + bt + f(x,y))
nodes.name: Extension operation
nodes.label: extension

nodes.statement:
An easy induction then shows that for any word $w(x_1,\dots,w_n)$, one has
$$ w((x_1,s_1),\dots,(x_n,s_n)) = (w(x_1,\dots,x_n), \sum_{i=1}^n P_{w,i}(a,b) x_i$$
$$ + \sum_{w_1 \op w_2 \leq w} Q_{w,w_1 \op w_2}(a,b) f(w_1(x_1,\dots,x_n), w_2(x_1,\dots,x_n)))$$
where $w_1 \op w_2$ ranges over all subterms of $w$ that are not single variables, and $Q_{w,w_1 \op w_2}(a,b)$ is a suitable (noncommutative) monomial in $a,b$.
nodes.name: Evaluation of words in extensions

nodes.statement:
Assuming \Cref{baba}, we conclude that this extension satisfies the law \Cref{1110} if and only if one has
\begin{equation} bab f(x,x) + ba f(y, x \op x) + bf(y \op (x \op x), y) + f( y, (y \op (x \op x)) \op y) = 0
\end{equation}
for all $x,y \in G$.
nodes.name: Cocycle condition for 1110

nodes.statement: bab f(x,x) + ba f(y, x \op x) + bf(y \op (x \op x), y) + f( y, (y \op (x \op x)) \op y) = 0
nodes.name: 1110 cocycle equation
nodes.label: cocycle-1110

nodes.statement:
More generally, an extension satisfies a law $E$ provided that
$$ \sum_{w_1 \op w_2 \leq w_{E,1}} Q_{w_{E,1},w_1 \op w_2}(a,b) f(w_1(x_1,\dots,x_n), w_2(x_1,\dots,x_n))$$
$$= \sum_{w_1 \op w_2 \leq w_{E,2}} Q_{w_{E,2},w_1 \op w_2}(a,b) f(w_1(x_1,\dots,x_n), w_2(x_1,\dots,x_n))$$
for all $x_1,\dots,x_n \in G$.
nodes.name: Extension satisfies E under the cocycle equation

nodes.statement: We call $f$ a \emph{$E$-cocycle} if this equation holds, and denote the space of such $E$-cocycles as $Z^2_E(G,M)$.
nodes.name: E-cocycle

nodes.statement: This is an abelian group, and each $E$-cocycle defines a magma on $G \times M$ satisfying $E$.
nodes.name: Cocycles form a group and define E-magmas

nodes.statement:
Given any function $g: G \to M$, one can define a bijection $(x,s) \mapsto (x,s+g(x))$ on $G \times M$, which conjugates the law \Cref{extension} to the law
$$ (x,s) \op (y,t) = (x \op y, as + bt + f(x,y) + g(x \op y) - ag(x) - bg(y)).$$
Being conjugate, this new operation will satisfy $E$ if and only if the original operation does.
nodes.name: Conjugation by g preserves E

nodes.statement: Thus if one defines a \emph{coboundary} to be a function $f: G \times G \to M$ of the form $f(x,y) =g(x \op y) - ag(x) - bg(y)$ for some $g: G \to M$, we can add a coboundary to an $E$-cocycle and still obtain a $E$-cocycle.
nodes.name: Coboundary

nodes.statement: So if we let $B^2(G,M)$ be the space of coboundaries, we see that $B^2(G,M)$ is a subgroup of $Z^2_E(G,M)$.
nodes.name: Space of coboundaries B^2

nodes.statement:
We define the \emph{$E$-cohomology} $H^2_E(G,M)$ to be the quotient
$$ H^2_E(G,M) := Z^2_E(G,M) / B^2(G,M).$$
nodes.name: E-cohomology

nodes.statement: Observe that if $E$ implies $E'$, then $H^2_E(G,M)$ is a subgroup of $H^2_{E'}(G,M)$.
nodes.name: Implication gives inclusion of cohomology
assumptions: $E$ implies $E'$
conclusions: $H^2_E(G,M)$ is a subgroup of $H^2_{E'}(G,M)$

nodes.name: Cohomological refutation criterion
nodes.statement_short: If $H^2_E(G,M)\not\subseteq H^2_{E'}(G,M)$ for some magma and linear magma satisfying both laws, then $E$ does not imply $E'$.

nodes.statement: H^2_E(G,M) \not\subseteq H^2_{E'}(G,M).
nodes.name: Cohomology non-inclusion
nodes.label: hgm

nodes.statement:
For instance, let us consider the law \Cref{1110} together with a putative consequence, equation 1629:
\begin{equation} x = (x \op x) \op ((x \op x) \op x).
\end{equation}
A simultaneous (linear) model for both \Cref{1110} and \Cref{1629} is given by carrier $G=M={\mathbb F}_5$ with $x \op y = 3x-y$.  Then the coboundaries $f: {\mathbb F}_5 \times {\mathbb F}_5 \to {\mathbb F}_5$ are of the form $f(x,y) = g(3x-y) - 3g(x) + g(y)$ for $g: {\mathbb F}_5 \to {\mathbb F}_5$, the $1110$-cocycles solve the equation
$$3 f(x,x) - 3 f(y, 2x) - f(3y - 2x, y) + f( y, 3y - x) = 0$$
for $x,y \in {\mathbb F}_5$, and the $1629$-cocycles solve the equation
$$ f(2x,0) - f(2x,x) = 0.$$
A function $g:{\mathbb F}_5 \to {\mathbb F}_5$ has vanishing derivative, $g(3x-y) - 3g(x) + g(y) = 0$, if and only if $g$ is linear, which is a one-dimensional space; so, by the rank-nullity theorem, the space $B^2(G,M)$ of coboundaries is four-dimensional.  One can check computationally that the space $Z^2_{1110}(G,M)$ is six-dimensional, so $H^2_{1110}(G,M)$ is two-dimensional.  One can check numerically that it contains an element not in $H^2_{1629}(G,M)$, leading to a finite counterexample on the 25-element carrier $G \times M$ to the implication of 1629 from 1110.
nodes.name: Cohomological refutation of 1110 implies 1629
nodes.statement_short: Over $\mathbb{F}_5$ with $x\op y=3x-y$, $H^2_{1110}$ is 2-dimensional and not inside $H^2_{1629}$, giving a 25-element counterexample.

nodes.statement: x = (x \op x) \op ((x \op x) \op x).
nodes.name: Equation 1629

nodes.statement: In the case the associative law (and taking $a=b=1$), the cocycle law becomes the familiar $$ f(x,y) + f(x \op y, z) = f(x, y \op z) + f(y,z)$$ and we recover the usual group cohomology (if $G$ is a group). The same occurs for Tarski's law 543 $x = y \op (z \op (x \op (y \op z)))$.
nodes.name: Associative case recovers group cohomology

nodes.statement: One can interpret the above cohomology group in terms of a partial chain complex $$ 0 \to C^0(G,M) \stackrel{d^0}{\to} C^1(G,M) \stackrel{d^1}{\to} C^2(G,M) \stackrel{d^2_E}{\to} C^n(G,M)$$ where the zeroth coboundary map $d^0: C^0(G,M) \to C^1(G,M)$ is the zero map, the first coboundary map $d: C^1(G,M) \to C^2(G,M)$ (which does not depend on the equation $E$) is defined by the formula $$ d^1 vf(x,y) := f(x \op y) - (f(x) \op f(y)) = f(x \op y) - af(x) - bf(y)$$ and the second coboundary map $d^2_E: C^2(G,M) \to C^n(G,M)$ (which does depend on $E$) is defined by the formula $$ d^2_E f(x_1,\dots,x_n) := \sum_{w_1 \op w_2 \leq w_{E,1}} Q_{w_{E,1},w_1 \op w_2}(a,b) f(w_1(x_1,\dots,x_n), w_2(x_1,\dots,x_n))$$ $$ - \sum_{w_1 \op w_2 \leq w_{E,2}} Q_{w_{E,2},w_1 \op w_2}(a,b) f(w_1(x_1,\dots,x_n), w_2(x_1,\dots,x_n)).$$ The fact that coboundaries are cocycles can then be rewritten as the chain complex relations $d^1 d^0=0$, $d^2_E d^1 = 0$. The group $H^2_E(G,M)$ is then just the second cohomology group of this chain complex. The first cohomology group $H^1_E(G,M)$ is the kernel of $d^1$, or equivalently the abelian group of magma homomorphisms from the magma $G$ to the linear magma $M$. When $E$ is the associative law, this partial chain complex can be extended to the usual group cohomology chain complex; however, it is not clear if any such extension exists for a general law $E$.
nodes.name: Partial chain complex interpretation

nodes.statement: Suppose that $G = M = \mathbb{F}_p$ is a field of prime size, and $a,b$ are coefficients in that field, with the magma operation on $G$ also given in a linear form $x \op y = a'x + b' y$. Then one can view a cocycle $f: \mathbb{F}_p \times \mathbb{F}_p \to \mathbb{F}_p$ as a bivariate polynomial of degree at most $2p-2$ with coefficients in $ \mathbb{F}_p$. The coboundary maps $d, d_E$ preserve degree, and so one can decompose (or ``grade'') the cohomology group $H^2_E(G,M)$ as $\bigoplus_{d=0}^{2p-2} H^2_E(G,M)_d$, where $H^2_E(G,M)_d$ are defined as with $H^2_E(G,M)$ but with the cocycles and coboundaries required to be homogeneous polynomials of degree at most $d$. To disprove an implication $E \implies E'$, it thus suffices to establish a non-inclusion $H^2_E(G,M)_d \not\subseteq H^2_{E'}(G,M)_d$ at a single degree $d$, which may be slightly easier computationally, and also provides for more compactly described counterexamples.
nodes.name: Graded cohomology over prime fields

nodes.statement: x = (y \op x) \op (x \op (z \op y)).
nodes.name: Weak central groupoid law (1485)

nodes.statement: \Equaref{1485} is equivalent to the dual law \begin{equation} x = ((y \op z) \op x) \op (x \op y) \end{equation} (equation 2162).
nodes.name: 1485 equivalent to 2162
conclusions: \Equaref{1485} is equivalent to the dual law
nodes.label: 1485-dual

nodes.statement: x = ((y \op z) \op x) \op (x \op y)
nodes.name: Equation 2162

nodes.statement: It suffices to prove that \Cref{1485} implies \Cref{2162}. Write $w = y \op z$, then from \Cref{1485} we can write $z = z_1 \op z_2$ with $z_1 = z \op z$ and $z_2 = z \op (z \op z)$, and then by \Cref{1485} $$ y = (z_2 \op y) \op (y \op (z_1 \op z_2)) = (z_2 \op y) \op w.$$ From another application of \Cref{1485} we have $$ x = (w \op x) \op (x \op ((z_2 \op y) \op w)) = ((y \op z) \op x) \op (x \op y)$$ as required.
nodes.name: Proof of 1485 equivalent to 2162
nodes.statement_short: Write $z$ as a product of its square and cube to rewrite $y$, then apply 1485 again.

nodes.statement: Given a weak central groupoid $G$, define a directed graph with vertices in $G$ by declaring $x \to y$ if and only if $y = x \op z$ for some $z$.
nodes.name: Directed graph of a weak central groupoid

nodes.statement: One has $x \to y$ if and only if $x = w \op y$ for some $w$.
nodes.name: Equivalent characterization of graph
conclusions: One has $x \to y$ if and only if $x = w \op y$ for some $w$.
nodes.label: graph-dual

nodes.statement: If $x \to y$ then $y = x \op z$, then writing $z = z_1 \op z_2$ as before we obtain $$ x = (z_2 \op x) \op (x \op (z_1 \op z_2)) = (z_2 \op x) \op y$$ giving the forward implication. The backwards implication follows by duality.
nodes.name: Proof of Equivalent characterization of graph
nodes.statement_short: Factor $z$ as before and apply 1485; backwards by duality.

nodes.statement: Define a \emph{good path} in $G$ to be a path of the form $$x \to x \op y \to y$$ for some $x,y \in G$ (we allow loops).
nodes.name: Good path

nodes.statement: The following claims are clear from definition and the above lemma:
nodes.name: Proof of Claims 1-3
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the definitions and the graph characterization.

nodes.statement: If $x,y \in G$ then there is exactly one good path $x \to z \to y$ from $x$ to $y$.
nodes.name: Claim 1 (unique good path)

nodes.statement: Any edge $x \to y$ in the directed graph is the initial segment of some good path $x \to y \to z$.
nodes.name: Claim 2 (edges extend forward)

nodes.statement: Any edge $x \to y$ in the directed graph is the final segment of some good path $w \to x \to y$.
nodes.name: Claim 3 (edges extend backward)

nodes.statement: If $a \to b \to c \to d \to e \to a$ is a 5-cycle in the directed graph, and $a \to b \to c$ and $c \to d \to e$ are good paths, then $b \to c \to d$ is also good.
nodes.name: Claim 4 (good 5-cycles)
assumptions: $a \to b \to c \to d \to e \to a$ is a 5-cycle in the directed graph
$a \to b \to c$ and $c \to d \to e$ are good paths
conclusions: $b \to c \to d$ is also good
nodes.label: claim-4

nodes.statement: If $a \to b \to c$ is good then $b = a \op c$; if $c \to d \to e$ is good then $d = c \op e$; and if $e \to a$ then $a = e \op z$ for some $z$ by definition. By \Cref{2162} we then have $$ c = ((e \op z) \op c) \op (c \op e) = b \op d$$ so $b \to c \to d$ is good.
nodes.name: Proof of Claim 4 (good 5-cycles)
nodes.statement_short: Unwind goodness and apply the dual law 2162.

nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a directed graph, with some paths of length two in the graph designated as ``good'', in such a way that Claims 1-4 hold. Then there is a weak central groupoid structure on the vertices of $G$ such that the good paths are precisely the paths of the form $x \to x \op y \to y$.
nodes.name: Reversing the claims
assumptions: Let $G$ be a directed graph, with some paths of length two in the graph designated as ``good'', in such a way that Claims 1-4 hold.
conclusions: there is a weak central groupoid structure on the vertices of $G$ such that the good paths are precisely the paths of the form $x \to x \op y \to y$
nodes.label: rev-claim

nodes.statement: Define an operation $\op: G \times G \to G$ by defining $x \op y$ to be the unique vertex $z$ for which one has a good path $x \to z \to y$; this is well-defined by Claim 1, and by Claims 2-3, the property $x \to y$ holds if and only if $y = x \op z$ for some $z$, and also if and only if $x = w \op y$ for some $w$. In particular, for all $x,y,z$, we have a $5$-cycle $$ y \to y \op x \to x \to x \op (z \op y) \to (z \op y) \to y$$ with $y \to y \op x \to x$ and $x \to x \op (z \op y) \to (z \op y)$ good, hence by Claim 4 we have \Cref{1485} as required.
nodes.name: Proof of Reversing the claims
nodes.statement_short: Define $x\op y$ as the middle of the unique good path; Claim 4 on a 5-cycle gives 1485.

nodes.name: Claim 1'

nodes.statement: Let us call a \emph{relaxed weak central groupoid} a directed graph with some paths of length 2 designated as ``good'' that satisfy Claims 1', 2, 3, 4.
nodes.name: Relaxed weak central groupoid
Partial weak central groupoid

nodes.statement: If we can upgrade Claim 1'' to Claim 1, and we also have Claim 2 and Claim 3, then we call this a \emph{complete weak central groupoid}, and by the previous proposition this is in correspondence with \Cref{1485}.
nodes.name: Complete weak central groupoid

nodes.statement: Let $G_0$ be a relaxed weak central groupoid. A \emph{partial extension} of $G_0$ is a partial weak central groupoid $G$ with a ``projection map'' $\pi: G \to G_0$, which is a homomorphism in the sense that the image $\pi(x) \to \pi(y)$ of any edge $x \to y$ in $G$ is an edge in $G_0$, the image $\pi(x) \to \pi(y) \to \pi(z)$ of any good path $x \to y \to z$ in $G$ is a good path in $G_0$, and the image $\pi(x) \to \pi(y) \to \pi(z)$ of any bad path $x \to y \to z$ in $G$ is a bad path in $G_0$.
nodes.name: Partial extension

nodes.statement: Note that Claim 4 for $G$ is then automatic from Claim 4 of the base $G_0$.
nodes.name: Claim 4 is inherited by partial extensions

nodes.statement: The extension is \emph{complete} if the partial weak central groupoid is complete.
nodes.name: Complete extension

nodes.statement: Let $G_0$ be a directed graph satisfying claims 1', 2, 3, 4. Then any finite partial extension of $G_0$ with carrier $G_0 \times \N$ (and projection map $\pi(a,n) = a$) can be completed to a complete extension.
nodes.name: Completion property
assumptions: Let $G_0$ be a directed graph satisfying claims 1', 2, 3, 4.
conclusions: any finite partial extension of $G_0$ with carrier $G_0 \times \N$ (and projection map $\pi(a,n) = a$) can be completed to a complete extension
nodes.label: greedy-prop

nodes.statement: By the previous comments, we can ignore Claim 4 as it is automatic, and focus on completing the partial weak central groupoid on $G$ to a complete weak central groupoid by ensuring Claims 1, 2, 3 hold. By the usual greedy algorithm, it suffices to show that any individual failure of Claim 1, 2 or 3 can be resolved by adding some finite number of edges to the graph. Suppose first that Claim 2 fails, that is to say the partial weak central groupoid contains an edge $(a,n) \to (b,m)$ that is not the initial segment of any good path. Since the base relaxed weak central groupoid $G_0$ satisfies Claim 2, we can find a good path $a \to b \to c$ in the base. We then pick a natural number $l$ not previously occurring in the partial weak central groupoid, and adjoin the edge $(b,m) \to (c,l)$ to that partial weak central groupoid. All new paths created in this way are declared good or bad depending on whether their images in $G_0$ are good or bad, in particular $(a,n) \to (b,m) \to (c,l)$ is good. This can be checked to still be a partial extension of $G_0$ (no violation of Claim 1'' is created), and now Claim 2 is resolved at for the edge $(a,n) \to (b,m)$. A similar argument permits one to resolve any violations of Claim 3. If Claim 1 is violated, then there is a pair $(a,n), (b,m)$ that currently has no good path of length two in the partial weak central groupoid. As the base relaxed weak central groupoid $G_0$ satisfies Claim 1', we can find a good path $a \to c \to b$ in $G_0$. We then pick a natural number $l$ not previously occurring, and adjoin the edges $(a,n) \to (c,l) \to (b,m)$. All new paths created in this way are declared good or bad depending on whether their images in $G_0$ are good or bad, in particular $(a,n) \to (c,l) \to (b,m) \to (c,l)$. One can check that this is still a partial extension of $G_0$ (no violation of Claim 1'' is created), and now Claim 1 is resolved at the pair $(a,n), (b,m)$.
nodes.name: Proof of Completion property
nodes.statement_short: Greedy algorithm: repair each failure of Claims 1-3 by adjoining fresh vertices lifted from good paths in the base.
