nodes.statement: \Equaref{1485} does not imply any of the following laws: \begin{itemize} \item Equation 3457: $x \op x = x \op ((x \op x) \op y)$. \item Equation 2087: $x = ((y \op x) \op x) \op (x \op x)$. \item Equation 2124: $x = ((y \op y) \op x) \op (x \op x)$. \item Equation 3511: $x \op y = x \op ((x \op y) \op x)$. \end{itemize}
nodes.name: 1485 does not imply 1483
conclusions: \Equaref{1485} does not imply any of the following laws:
nodes.statement_short: Weak central groupoid law does not imply equations 3457, 2087, 2124, 3511.
nodes.label: 1485-refutes

nodes.statement: Computer check reveals that the carrier $G_0=\{0,1,2,3 ,4\}$ with incidence matrix $$ \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ \end{pmatrix} $$ is a relaxed weak central groupoid if we declare the paths $0 \to 0 \to 0$, $0 \to 0 \to 1$, $0 \to 1 \to 1$, $1 \to 0 \to 0$, $1 \to 1 \to 0$, $1 \to 1 \to 1$ to be bad, and all other paths in the directed graph to be good. We can also check the following axioms: \begin{itemize} \item Anti-3457: There exist $x,y,z,w$ with $x \to z \to x$, $z \to w \to y$ both good, and $x \to z \to w$ bad. (One can take $x=1$, $y=4$, $z = 0$, $w = 0$.) \item Anti-2087: There exist $x,y,z,w,u$ with $y \to z \to x$, $z \to w \to x$, and $x \to u \to x$ good, and $w \to x \to u$ is bad. (One can take $x=1, y=2$, $z=4$, $w=1$, $u=0$.) \item Anti-2124: There exists $x,y,z,w,u$ with $y \to z \to y$, $z \to w \to x$ and $x \to u \to x$ good, and $w \to x \to u$ bad. (One can take $x=1$, $y=2$, $z=4$, $w = 1$, $u=0$.) \item Anti-3511: There exists $x,y,z,w$ with $x \to z \to y$ and $z \to w \to x$ good, and $x \to z \to w$ bad. (One can take $x=1$, $y=3$, $z = 1$, $w=0$.) \end{itemize} Let $G_*$ be a finite partial extension of $G_0$ to be chosen later. By \Cref{greedy-prop}, we can complete this to a complete weak central groupoid $G$ with carrier $G_0 \times \N$. Depending on how we choose $G_*$, we can ensure that this $G$ refutes one of the four laws 3457, 2087, 2124, 3511: \begin{itemize} \item Refuting 3457: Let $x,y,z,w$ be as in the claim Anti-3457, then select $G_*$ to be the directed graph with edges $(x,0) \to (z,2) \to (x,0) \to (z,2) \to (w,3) \to (y,1)$. One can check that this is a partial extension, and that $G$ will refute 3457 with $x,y$ replaced by $(x,0),(y,1)$. \item Refuting 2087: Let $x,y,z,w,u$ be as in the claim Anti-2087, then select $G_*$ to be the directed graph with edges $(y,1) \to (z,2) \to (x,0)$ and $(z,2) \to (w,3) \to (x,0) \to (u,4) \to (x,0)$. One can check that this is a partial extension, and that $G$ will refute 2087 with $x,y$ replaced by $(x,0),(y,1)$. \item Refuting 2124: Let $x,y,z,w,u$ be as in the claim Anti-2124, then select $G_*$ to be the directed graph with edges $(y,1) \to (z,2) \to (y,1)$ and $(z,2) \to (w,3) \to (x,0) \to (u,4) \to (x,0)$. One can check that this is a partial extension, and that $G$ will refute 2124 with $x,y$ replaced by $(x,0),(y,1)$. \item Refuting 3511: Let $x,y,z,w$ be as in the claim Anti-3511, then select $G_*$ to be the directed graph with edges $(x,0) \to (z,2) \to (y,1)$ and $(z,2) \to (w,3) \to (x,0)$. One can check that this is a partial extension, and that $G$ will refute 3511 with $x,y$ replaced by $(x,0),(y,1)$. \end{itemize}
nodes.name: Proof of 1485 does not imply 1483
nodes.statement_short: Computer-found 5-vertex relaxed weak central groupoid with anti-law witnesses, completed via the completion property.

nodes.statement: Occasionally, an equational law is preserved under a ``twist'' operation in which one replaces the magma operation $x \op y$ by $x \op' y := Tx \op Uy$ for some automorphisms $T,U$ of the magma $G$ that satisfy additional relations.
nodes.name: Twist of a magma operation

nodes.statement:
In the case of the weak central groupoid law \Cref{1485}, we see that
$$
(y \op' x) \op' (x \op' (z \op' y))= (T^2 y \op TUx) \op (UTx \op (UTUz \op U^3y))$$
so if $T$ is an automorphism of order $5$ and $U = T^{-1}$ (so that $T^2 = U^3$), we conclude that this twisted magma is also a weak central groupoid.
nodes.name: Twisting preserves weak central groupoids
assumptions: $T$ is an automorphism of order $5$ and $U = T^{-1}$
conclusions: this twisted magma is also a weak central groupoid

nodes.statement:
For instance, let $M_2$ be the order two weak central groupoid with carrier ${\mathbb F}_2$ and with the NAND operation $x \diamond y := 1 - xy$; this can easily be verified to be a weak central groupoid.  It does not have any nontrivial automorphisms, but its fifth power $M_2^{\otimes 5}$ has a cyclic shift $T$ of order $5$: $T( (x_i)_{i\in \Z/5\Z} ) = (x_{i+1})_{i \in \Z/5\Z}$.  If we twist $M_2^{\otimes 5}$ by $T$ and $T^{-1}$, we obtain a weak central groupoid $M$ with carrier ${\mathbb F}_2^5$ and magma operation
$$(x_i)_{i\in \Z/5\Z} \op (y_i)_{i\in \Z/5\Z} = (1 - x_{i+1} y_{i-1})_{i \in \Z/5\Z}.$$
In particular, if $x = (x_i)_{i\in \Z/5\Z}$, then
$$ x \op x = (1 - x_{i+1} x_{i-1})_{i \in \Z/5\Z}$$
and
$$ (x \op x) \op (x \op x) = (1 - (1 - x_{i+2} x_{i}) (1 - x_i x_{i-2}) )_{i \in \Z/5\Z}$$
which by the laws of boolean algebra simplify to
$$ (x \op x) \op (x \op x) = (x_i (x_{i-2} + x_i + x_{i+2}))_{i \in \Z/5\Z}$$
from which one can easily refute equation 151,
$$ x = (x \op x) \op (x \op x).$$
nodes.name: Twisted NAND magma refutes 151
nodes.statement_short: Twisting the fifth power of the NAND magma by a cyclic shift gives a weak central groupoid on $\mathbb{F}_2^5$ violating equation 151.

nodes.statement: x = y \op (x \op ((y \op x) \op y))
nodes.name: Equation 677

nodes.statement: x = ((x \op x) \op x) \op x.
nodes.name: Equation 255

nodes.statement:
Using the usual notation $L_y x = y \op x$, $R_y x = x \op y$, $Sx = x \op x$, we can rewrite equation 677 as
\begin{equation} x = L_y L_x L_{L_y x} y = L_y (x \op R_y L_y x)
\end{equation}
and 255 as
$$ x = (Sx \op x) \op x.$$
nodes.name: Left/right multiplication and squaring operators

nodes.statement: x = L_y L_x L_{L_y x} y = L_y (x \op R_y L_y x)
nodes.name: Equation 677 in operator form
nodes.label: 677-alt

nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a finite magma satisfying \eqref{677}. \begin{itemize} \item (i) The left multiplication operators $L_y: M \to M$ are all invertible, with $L_y^{-1} x = x \op R_y L_y x$. \item (ii) If $x,y \in M$ and $y \op x = x$, then $y = Sx \op x$. In particular, 255 holds if and only if the equation $y \op x = x$ is solvable for every $x$. \item (iii) For all $x,y \in M$, we have $x = L_y x \op R_y L_y^2 x$. \end{itemize}
nodes.name: Basic properties of 677 magma
assumptions: Let $M$ be a finite magma satisfying \eqref{677}.
conclusions: The left multiplication operators $L_y: M \to M$ are all invertible, with $L_y^{-1} x = x \op R_y L_y x$.
If $x,y \in M$ and $y \op x = x$, then $y = Sx \op x$.
For all $x,y \in M$, we have $x = L_y x \op R_y L_y^2 x$.
nodes.label: 677-basic

nodes.statement: From \eqref{677-alt} we see that $L_y$ is surjective, hence invertible on finite magmas, giving (i) (the formula for $L_y^{-1} x$ being immediate from \eqref{677-alt}). For (ii), using the fact that $L_y x = x$, (i) becomes $x = x \op R_y x = L_x L_x y$, then, using the invertibility of $L_x$ given by (i) we have \[y = L_x^{-1} L_x^{-1} x \stackrel{(i)}{=} L_x^{-1} (x \op R_x L_x x) = L_x^{-1} (L_x R_x L_x x) = R_x L_x x = Sx \op x.\] For (iii), we apply (i) with $x$ replaced by $L_y x$.
nodes.name: Proof of Basic properties of 677 magma
nodes.statement_short: Surjectivity of $L_y$ from the operator form gives invertibility; (ii),(iii) by substitution.

nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a finite magma satisfying \eqref{677}, and let $x \in M$. Then the following are equivalent: \begin{itemize} \item (i) 255 holds for $x$, that is to say $R_x (Sx \op x) = x$. \item (ii) The equation $R_x y = x$ has the unique solution $y = Sx \op x$. \item (iii) The equation $R_x y = x$ has a solution. \item (iv) The equation $R_x L_x z = x$ has a solution. \item (v) The equation $L_x R_x z = z$ has a solution. \item (vi) The equation $R_x L_x y = y$ has a solution. \item (vii) The equation $L_x S y = y$ has a solution. \end{itemize}
nodes.name: Equivalent characterizations of 255
assumptions: Let $M$ be a finite magma satisfying \eqref{677}, and let $x \in M$.
conclusions: the following are equivalent:
equivalent_conditions: 255 holds for $x$, that is to say $R_x (Sx \op x) = x$.
The equation $R_x y = x$ has the unique solution $y = Sx \op x$.
The equation $R_x y = x$ has a solution.
The equation $R_x L_x z = x$ has a solution.
The equation $L_x R_x z = z$ has a solution.
The equation $R_x L_x y = y$ has a solution.
The equation $L_x S y = y$ has a solution.
nodes.label: 255-equiv

nodes.statement: Clearly (ii) implies (i), which implies (iii). If (iii) holds, we apply \eqref{677-alt} to conclude that $$ y \op x = x = y \op (x \op (x \op y))$$ and hence by left invertibility $$ x = x \op (x \op y).$$ On the other hand, from \eqref{677} with $y$ replaced by $x$ we have $$ x = x \op (x \op (Sx \op x))$$ and hence by left invertibility $y = Sx \op x$, giving (ii). From left cancellativity we see that (v) and (vi) are equivalent, as are (iii) and (iv). If (vii) holds, then $L_x L_y y = y$, but from \eqref{677-alt} we have $y = L_x L_y R_x L_x y$, so (vi) follows from left-cancellativity; the converse implication follows by reversing the steps. If (v) holds, then we have $L_x L_z x = z$, but from \eqref{677-alt} one has $z = L_x L_z R_x L_x z$, giving the (iv) by left-cancellativity; the converse implication follows by reversing the steps.
nodes.name: Proof of Equivalent characterizations of 255
nodes.statement_short: Cycle of implications using left invertibility and the operator form of 677.

nodes.statement: Suppose we have a finite magma $M$ satisfying 677 which is linear in the sense that $M$ is an abelian group and $x \op y = \alpha x + \beta y + c$ for some endomorphisms $\alpha,\beta: M \to M$ and constant $c$. Then $M$ satisfies 255.
nodes.name: No linear counterexamples
assumptions: Suppose we have a finite magma $M$ satisfying 677 which is linear in the sense that $M$ is an abelian group and $x \op y = \alpha x + \beta y + c$ for some endomorphisms $\alpha,\beta: M \to M$ and constant $c$.
conclusions: $M$ satisfies 255
nodes.label: linear-obstruction

nodes.statement: By the previous lemma, it suffices to show that right multiplication $R_x$ is surjective, or equivalently injective by finiteness. If this is not the case, then we can find distinct $y,y'$ such that $R_x y = R_x y'$, hence $L_y x = L_{y'} x$. But in this linear model, $L_y$ and $L_{y'}$ differ by a constant, hence we have $L_y = L_{y'}$. Applying \eqref{677-alt} we have $$ L_y L_x L_{L_y x} y = x = L_y L_x L_{L_y x} y'$$ and hence by left-invertibility $y=y'$, a contradiction.
nodes.name: Proof of No linear counterexamples
nodes.statement_short: Show $R_x$ injective: in a linear model equal $L_y x$ forces equal $L_y$, contradicting left-invertibility.

nodes.statement: Suppose that we have a magma with carrier $G \times M$ satisfying 677, where $G$ already is a magma satisfying 677 and 255, $M$ is an abelian group, and the multiplication operation on $G \times M$ is of the form $$ (x,s) \op (y,t) = (x \op y, \alpha_{x,y} s + \beta_{x,y} t + c_{x,y})$$ for some endomorphisms $\alpha_{x,y},\beta_{x,y}: M \to M$ and constants $c_{x,y}$. Then $G \times M$ satisfies 255.
nodes.name: No counterexamples via linear extension
assumptions: $G$ already is a magma satisfying 677 and 255, $M$ is an abelian group, and the multiplication operation on $G \times M$ is of the form
conclusions: $G \times M$ satisfies 255
nodes.label: linear-2

nodes.statement: By \Cref{677-basic}, it suffices to show that for any $(y,t)$, the equation $(x,s) \op (y,t) = (y,t)$ is solvable. Since $G$ already satisfies 255, we know that we can find $x$ such that $x \op y = y$, so it suffices to show that the operation $s \mapsto \alpha_{x,y} s + \beta_{x,y} t + c_{x,y}$ is surjective, or equivalently injective. If this were not the case, then we could find $s,s'$ such that $\alpha_{x,y} s = \alpha_{x,y} s'$, and hence $L_{(x,s)} (y,t') = L_{(x,s')} (y,t')$ for all $t' \in M$. Since $$ x \op y = y = x \op (y \op ((x \op y) \op x))$$ from \eqref{677}, we have $y = y \op ((x \op y) \op x)$, and hence $L_{(y,t)} L_{L_{(x,s)} (y,t)} (x,s)$ is of the form $(y,t')$ for some $t'$, and similarly with $(x,s)$ replaced by $(x,s')$. We conclude that $$ L_{(x,s)} L_{(y,t)} L_{L_{(x,s)} (y,t)} (x,s) = (y,t) = L_{(x,s)} L_{(y,t)} L_{L_{(x,s)} (y,t)} (x,s')$$ and hence by left invertibility $s=s'$, a contradiction.
nodes.name: Proof of No counterexamples via linear extension
nodes.statement_short: Fibrewise version of the linear argument: injectivity of the affine fibre map via left-invertibility.

nodes.statement:
Linear models $x \op y = \alpha x + \beta y + c$ on the finite field $F_p$ turn out to be classified into two types:
\begin{itemize}
\item (Type 1) $\alpha=1-\beta$, $\beta$ is a primitive tenth root of unity, and $c=0$.  (These models are also translation-invariant.)
\item (Type 2) $\alpha$ is a primitive third root of unity, $c$ is arbitrary, and $\beta$ solves $\beta^3+\beta+1=-\alpha$ and $\beta^4+\beta^3+2\beta^2+2\beta+1=0$.
nodes.name: Classification of linear 677 models

nodes.statement:
Suppose $G$ is already a 677 magma, and to each pair $x,y \in G$ we assign a binary operation $\diamond_{x,y}: M \times M \to M$ such that one has the functional equation
\begin{equation} s = t \op_{y,L_y^{-1} x} (s \op_{x, (y \op x) \op y} ((t \op_{y,x} s) \op_{y \op x, y} t))
\end{equation}
for all $x,y \in G$, then the operation
$$ (x,s) \diamond (y,t) := (x \diamond y, s \diamond_{x,y} t)$$
is easily seen to be a 677 magma.
nodes.name: Twisted product extensions of 677 magmas

nodes.statement: s = t \op_{y,L_y^{-1} x} (s \op_{x, (y \op x) \op y} ((t \op_{y,x} s) \op_{y \op x, y} t))
nodes.name: Extension functional equation for 677
nodes.label: ext-eq

nodes.statement:
Suppose $M$ is a field that admits a primitive cube root of unity $\omega$ as well as a primitive fifth root of unity $\zeta$ (for instance, $M$ could be a field of size $16$).  Then the three operations
$$ s \op^0 t := s - \zeta(t-s)$$
$$ s \op^+ t := t$$
$$ s \op^- t := s - \omega(t-s)$$
can easily be seen to satisfy the identities
$$s = t \op^0 (s \op^0 ((t \op^0 s) \op^0 t))$$
$$s = t \op^+ (s \op^+ ((t \op^- s) \op^- t))$$
$$s = t \op^- (s \op^- ((t \op^+ s) \op^+ t))$$
for all $t,s$.
nodes.name: Three operations satisfying the 677 identities

nodes.statement: Now suppose that $G$ is also a field with a primitive fifth root of unity $\beta$ (so that $\beta = \left(\beta^{-2}\right)^2 = \beta^{-4}$ is a square), but $-1$ and $\beta+1$ are non-zero non-squares (for instance, $G$ could be the field of size $31$, with $\beta=2$).  If we define $x \op y = x - \beta(y-x)$, and then define $\op_{x,y}$ to be $\op^0$ when $y=x$, $\op^+$ when $y-x$ is a non-zero square, and $\op^-$ when $y-x$ is a non-zero non-square, one can then check that \eqref{ext-eq} holds.
nodes.name: Construction of a finite non-right-cancellative 677 magma
nodes.statement_short: Over $\mathbb{F}_{31}$ choose $\op_{x,y}$ by quadratic residuosity of $y-x$ so that (13.4) holds.

nodes.statement: Since $\op^0$ is not right-cancellative, this gives a finite 677 magma that is not right-cancellative.
nodes.name: Finite 677 magma that is not right-cancellative

nodes.statement: First let $M_X$ be the free magma generated $X$ with operation given by pairing $x,y \mapsto (x,y)$; one can think of elements of $M_X$ as finite trees with leaves in $X$.
nodes.name: Free magma as trees

nodes.statement: If $w = (x,y)$ we write $x = w_L$ and $y = w_R$ for the left and right components of $w$; we also define $w_{LL}$, $w_{LR}$, etc. iteratively if they are defined, for instance if $w = ((x,y),z)$ then $w_{LR} = y$.
nodes.name: Left and right components

nodes.statement: We define a partial order $<$ on $M_X$ by declaring $w < w'$ if $w$ is a subtree of $w'$, thus $w < w'$ if one of $w \leq w'_L$, $w \leq w'_R$ holds.
nodes.name: Subtree order
Free 677 operation

nodes.statement: Note that to define $x \diamond y$, one only needs to be able to compute $x' \diamond y'$ for $y' < y$.  Since there are no infinite descending chains in the partial order $<$, we see that $\diamond$ is well-defined.
nodes.name: The free 677 operation is well-defined

nodes.statement: By construction, we observe the following properties:
nodes.name: Proof of properties of operation

nodes.statement: Let $x,y \in M_X$ be such that $x \diamond y = z$. Then either $$ x, y < z = (x,y)$$ or $$ x, z < y = (z, (x \diamond z) \diamond x).$$ In particular, $x$ is strictly upper bounded by one of $y,z$.
nodes.name: Properties of operation
assumptions: Let $x,y \in M_X$ be such that $x \diamond y = z$.
conclusions: $x$ is strictly upper bounded by one of $y,z$
nodes.label: op-prop

nodes.statement: If $x,y \in M_X$, then $$ x \op ((y \op x) \op y) = (x, (y \op x) \op y).$$
nodes.name: Additional property
assumptions: If $x,y \in M_X$
conclusions: $$ x \op ((y \op x) \op y) = (x, (y \op x) \op y).$$
nodes.label: op-2-677

nodes.statement: Write $z := y \op x$, $u = z \op y$, $v = x \op u$. Our task is to show that $v = (x,u)$. From \Cref{op-prop} we know that $y$ is upper bounded by one of $z,x$, $z$ is upper bounded by one of $u,y$, and $x$ is upper bounded by one of $u,v$. So out of $x,y,z,u,v$, the only elements that can be maximal in this set are $u$ and $v$. If $v$ is maximal, then by \Cref{op-prop} we have $v = (x,u)$ as required, hence we may assume for contradiction that $u$ is maximal. From \Cref{op-prop}, this implies that $u = (z,y)$ and $u = (u_L, (x \op u_L) \op x)$, hence $u_L = z$ and $y = (x \op z) \op x$. From \Cref{op-prop}, $x$ is upper bounded by one of $x \op z$ and $z$, and $x \op z$ is upper bounded by one of $y$ and $x$. We also recall that $y$ was upper bounded by one of $z,x$. We conclude that out of $x,y,z,x \op z$, the only one that can be maximal is $z$. In particular $z$ is not bounded by $x$, hence by \Cref{op-prop} $z = (y,x)$. $z$ is also not bounded by $x \op z$, hence by \Cref{op-prop} $x \op z = z_L = y$, hence $y = y \op x = z$, contradicting the fact that $y$ was not maximal. This gives the required contradiction.
nodes.name: Proof of Additional property
nodes.statement_short: Maximality argument in the subtree order using the properties of the operation; contradiction if $u$ is maximal.

nodes.statement: The operation $\diamond$ satisfies \eqref{677}.
nodes.name: Free 677 operation satisfies 677
conclusions: The operation $\diamond$ satisfies \eqref{677}.
nodes.label: 677-satisfy

nodes.statement: By the previous lemma and definition of $\diamond$, it suffices to show that $y < (x, (y \op x) \op y)$. Defining $z,u,v$ as before, this amounts to showing that $y < v$. We already have $v = (x,u)$, hence by \Cref{op-prop} $x < v$. Also recall that $y$ is bounded by one of $x,z$, and $z$ is bounded by one of $y,u$. Since $u$ is also bounded by $v$, we obtain the claim.
nodes.name: Proof of Free 677 operation satisfies 677
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $y < v$ and chain the subtree bounds.

nodes.statement: Let $M_{X,677}$ be the magma generated by $X$ with operation $\diamond$. Then $M_{X,677}$ is the free magma for \eqref{677} generated by $X$.
nodes.name: Free 677 magma
assumptions: Let $M_{X,677}$ be the magma generated by $X$ with operation $\diamond$.
conclusions: $M_{X,677}$ is the free magma for \eqref{677} generated by $X$

nodes.statement: By the previous corollary, it suffices to show that every function $f: X \to M$ into a 677 magma $M$ can be extended to a unique homomorphism $\varphi_f: M_{X,677} \to X$. Uniqueness is clear since $M_{X,677}$ is generated by $X$. For existence, we define $\varphi_f$ by first extending $f$ to the unique homomorphism from $M_X$ to $X$ (using the pairing map) and then restricting to $M_{X,677}$. To verify the homomorphism property $\varphi_f(x \diamond y) = \varphi_f(x) \diamond \varphi_f(y)$, we are already done when $x \diamond y = (x,y)$. The only remaining case is when $x \diamond y = y_L$ and $x < y = (y_L, (x \diamond y_L) \diamond x)$. If we assume inductively that the homomorphism property $\varphi_f(x' \diamond y') = \varphi_f(x') \diamond \varphi_f(y')$ has already been verified for $y' < y$, then we have $$ \varphi_f(y) = \varphi_f(y_L) \diamond \varphi_f(y_R) = \varphi_f(y_L) \diamond (\varphi_f(x \diamond y_L) \diamond \varphi_f(x)) = \varphi_f(y_L) \diamond ((\varphi_f(x) \diamond \varphi_f(y_L)) \diamond \varphi_f(x))$$ and the claim now follows since $M$ satisfies 677.
nodes.name: Proof of Free 677 magma
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness from generation; existence by restricting the free homomorphism and verifying the homomorphism property inductively.

nodes.statement: By construction, we have $x \op y > y$ or $x \op y < y$ for any $x,y$.
nodes.name: Proof that the free 677 magma fails 255
nodes.statement_short: Products are always comparable but unequal to $y$.

nodes.statement: In particular, $M_{X,677}$ does not satisfy \eqref{255}.
nodes.name: Free 677 magma does not satisfy 255

nodes.statement: x = x \op ((y \op z) \op (x \op z))
nodes.name: Equation 854 (restated)

nodes.statement: x = x \op x^2.
nodes.name: Equation 8 as a consequence of 854

nodes.statement: (x \op y) \op y = x \op y
nodes.name: Equation 378 as a consequence of 854
Arrow relation for 854 magmas

nodes.statement: y \to x \iff x = x \op y.
nodes.name: Arrow characterization
nodes.label: yx

nodes.statement: (y \op z) \op (x \op z) \to x
nodes.name: 854 in arrow form
nodes.label: 854-alt

nodes.statement: We let $\Gamma$ be the theory consisting just of the law \Cref{854}, then as in \Cref{freemag-exist} we have the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $M_X$ defined by setting $w \sim w'$ iff $\Gamma \models w \formaleq w'$, then $M_X/\sim$ is a free magma for $\Gamma$.
nodes.name: 854 equivalence of words

nodes.statement: We can then also define a directed graph on $M_X$ by declaring $w' \to w$ if $w \sim w'' \op w'$ for some $w''$, or equivalently (by applying \Cref{yx} to $M_X/\sim$) that $w \sim w \op w'$.
nodes.name: Directed graph on words for 854

nodes.statement: Call a word $w$ \emph{irreducible} if it is not of the form $w = w_1 \op w_2$ with $w_2 \to w_1$, and \emph{reducible} otherwise.
nodes.name: Irreducible word

nodes.statement: Clearly if a word $w = w_1 \op w_2$ is reducible, then it is equivalent to the shorter word $w_1$.  Iterating, we conclude that every word is equivalent to an irreducible word.
nodes.name: Every word is equivalent to an irreducible word

nodes.statement: Let $w$ be an irreducible word, and let $w'$ be a word equivalent to $w$. \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] If $w$ is a product $w = w_1 \op w_2$, then $w'$ takes the form $$ w' = (((w'_1 \op w'_2) \op v_1) \op \dots \op v_n)$$ for some $w'_1 \sim w_1$, $w'_2 \sim w_2$, some $n \geq 0$, and some words $v_1, \dots, v_n$ such that for all $0 \leq i < n$, $v_{i+1}$ is of the form $$ v_{i+1} \sim (y_i \op z_i) \op (x_i \op z_i)$$ for some $x_i, y_i, z_i$ with $$ x_i \sim (((w'_1 \op w'_2) \op v_1) \op \dots \op v_i).$$ In particular, $v_{i+1} \to x_i$. \item[(ii)] Similarly, if $w$ is a generator, then $w'$ takes the form $$ w' = ((w \op v_1) \op \dots \op v_n)$$ for some $n \geq 0$, and some words $v_1, \dots, v_n$ such that for all $0 \leq i < n$, $v_{i+1}$ is of the form $$ v_{i+1} \sim (y_i \op z_i) \op (x_i \op z_i)$$ for some $x_i, y_i, z_i$ with $$ x_i \sim ((w \op v_1) \op \dots \op v_i).$$ In particular, $v_{i+1} \to x_i$. \end{itemize} Conversely, any word of the above forms is equivalent to $w$.
nodes.name: Description of equivalence
assumptions: Let $w$ be an irreducible word, and let $w'$ be a word equivalent to $w$.
conclusions: Conversely, any word of the above forms is equivalent to $w$.
nodes.statement_short: Words equivalent to an irreducible word are obtained from it by repeatedly right-multiplying by terms of the form $(y\op z)\op(x\op z)$.
nodes.label: irred-desc

nodes.statement: We just verify claim (i), as claim (ii) is similar. The converse direction is clear from \Cref{854-alt} (after quotienting down to $M_X/\sim$), so it suffices to prove the forward claim. By \Cref{sound-complete}, it suffices to prove that the class of words described by (i) is preserved by any term rewriting operation, in which a term in the word is replaced by an equivalent term using \Cref{854}. Clearly the term is in $w'_1$ or $w'_2$ then the form of the word is preserved, and similarly if the term is in one of the $v_i$. The only remaining case is if we are rewriting a term of the form $$ x_i = (((w'_1 \op w'_2) \op v_1) \op \dots \op v_i).$$ If $i>0$ we can rewrite this term down to $x_{i-1}$, and this still preserves the required form (decrementing $n$ by one). If $i=0$ then we cannot perform such a rewriting because of the irreducibility of $w_1 \op w_2$ and hence $w'_1 \op w'_2$. Finally, we can rewrite $x_i$ to $x_i \op v$ where $v$ is of the form $$ v_i = (y \op z) \op (x_i \op z),$$ and after some relabeling we are again of the required form (now incrementing $n$ by one).
nodes.name: Proof of Description of equivalence
nodes.statement_short: The described class is closed under single 854 rewrites (by completeness), using irreducibility at the base.

nodes.statement: Two irreducible words $w, w'$ are equivalent if and only if they are either the same generator of $X$, or are of the form $w = w_1 \op w_2$, $w' = w'_1 \op w'_2$ with $w_1 \sim w'_1$ and $w_2 \sim w'_2$.
nodes.name: Unique factorization
conclusions: Two irreducible words $w, w'$ are equivalent if and only if they are either the same generator of $X$, or are of the form $w = w_1 \op w_2$, $w' = w'_1 \op w'_2$ with $w_1 \sim w'_1$ and $w_2 \sim w'_2$.
equivalent_conditions: Two irreducible words $w, w'$ are equivalent
they are either the same generator of $X$, or are of the form $w = w_1 \op w_2$, $w' = w'_1 \op w'_2$ with $w_1 \sim w'_1$ and $w_2 \sim w'_2$
nodes.label: unique-factorization

nodes.statement: Immediate from \Cref{irred-desc}.
nodes.name: Proof of Unique factorization
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the description of equivalence.

nodes.statement: If $w,w'$ are words, then $w' \to w$ holds if and only if $w' \sim (Y \op Z) \op (w \op Z)$ for some words $Y,Z$.
nodes.name: Description of graph
assumptions: If $w,w'$ are words
conclusions: $w' \to w$ holds if and only if $w' \sim (Y \op Z) \op (w \op Z)$ for some words $Y,Z$
nodes.label: graph-desc

nodes.statement: By replacing $w,w'$ with irreducible equivalents, we may assume without loss of generality that $w,w'$ are irreducible. By hypothesis, $w$ is equivalent to $w \op w'$. The claim now follows from \Cref{irred-desc}.
nodes.name: Proof of Description of graph
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to irreducible words and apply the description of equivalence.

nodes.statement: The laws \begin{equation} x \op y = x \op (y \op (x \op y)) \end{equation} and \begin{equation} x \op y = (x \op (y \op x)) \op y \end{equation} are not implied by \Equaref{854}.
nodes.name: 854 does not imply 3316, 3925
conclusions: are not implied by \Equaref{854}
nodes.label: 854-anti

nodes.statement: x \op y = x \op (y \op (x \op y))
nodes.name: Equation 3316

nodes.statement: x \op y = (x \op (y \op x)) \op y
nodes.name: Equation 3925

nodes.statement: We work in the free group $M_X$ on two generators $X = \{x,y\}$. It suffices to show that $$ x \op y \not \sim x \op (y \op (x \op y))$$ and $$ x \op y \not \sim (x \op (y \op x)) \op y.$$ We begin with the first claim. Suppose this were not the case, then by \Cref{unique-factorization} one of the following statements must hold: \begin{itemize} \item (i) $$y \to x$$. \item (ii) $$(y \op (x \op y)) \to x$$. \item (iii) $$y \op (x \op y) \sim y.$$ \end{itemize} If (i) holds, then we have $x \op y = x$ (Equation 4) in $M_X/\sim$, hence in every magma satisfying \Equaref{854}. But we have examples of such magmas in which this fails. Similarly, if (iii) holds, then $y \op (x \op y) = y$ (Equation 10) holds in $M_X/\sim$, hence in every magma satisfying \Equaref{854}. But we have examples of such magmas in which this fails. Finally, if (ii) holds, then the claim $$ x \op y \sim x \op (y \op (x \op y))$$ to refute simplifies to $$ x \op y \sim x$$ and we are back to (i), which we already know not to be the case. For the latter equation, we similarly have the cases \begin{itemize} \item (iv) $$y \to x$$. \item (v) $$y \to x \op (y \op x)$$. \item (vi) $$x \sim x \op (y \op x).$$ \end{itemize} (iv) is (i), which was already ruled out, and (vi) is similarly a relabeled version of (iii). In case (v) holds, the claim to refute simplifies to $$ x \op y \sim x \op (y \op x)$$ and using \Cref{unique-factorization} we reduce to either $y \sim y \op x$, $y \to x$, or $y \op x \to x$, and each of these is already known to fail.
nodes.name: Proof of 854 does not imply 3316, 3925
nodes.statement_short: In the free 854 magma, unique factorization reduces each putative equivalence to cases refuted by known models.

nodes.statement: As in the previous section, we write $y \to x$ if $x = x \op y$.
nodes.name: Arrow relation for 854 magmas (restated)

nodes.statement: For $x, y$ in a 854 magma, the following are equivalent. \begin{itemize} \item (i) $y \to x$. \item (ii) $x = x \op y$. \item (iii) $x = z \op y$ for some $z$. \item (iv) $z, x \op z \to y$ for some $z$. \item (v) $x \op y^2 \to y$. \item (vi) $y \op (x \op y^2) = y$. \item (vii) $y = (w \op z) \op (x \op z)$ for some $w,z$. \item (viii) $y \to x \op y^2$. \end{itemize}
nodes.name: 854 equivalences, I
assumptions: For $x, y$ in a 854 magma
conclusions: the following are equivalent.
nodes.label: 854-equiv

nodes.statement: The equivalence of (i) and (ii), or (v) and (vi), is by definition. (iii) trivially implies (ii), and the converse comes from \Cref{378}. Using \Cref{8} we see that (v) implies (iv). If (iv) is true, then $y = (y \op z) \op (x \op z)$, giving (vii). From \Cref{854} we see that (vii) implies (ii). If (ii) is true, then $y \op (x \op y^2) = y \op ((x \op y) \op (y \op y)) = y$, giving (vi). Finally, to show the equivalence of (i) and (viii), use the already established equivalence of (i) and (v), together with \Cref{378} which gives $(x \op y^2) \op y^2 = x \op y^2$.
nodes.name: Proof of 854 equivalences, I
nodes.statement_short: Chain of implications using laws 8, 378 and 854.

nodes.statement: Introduce the notation $y \leq x$ for $x \op y \to x$.
nodes.name: Order relation for 854

nodes.statement: For $x,y$ in a 854 magma, the following are equivalent. \begin{itemize} \item (i) $y \leq x$. \item (ii) $x \op y \to x$. \item (iii) For all $z$, $y \to z$ implies $x \to z$. \item (iv) $x \to x \op y$. \end{itemize}
nodes.name: 854 equivalences, II
assumptions: For $x,y$ in a 854 magma
conclusions: the following are equivalent.
nodes.label: 854-equiv-2

nodes.statement: The equivalence of (i) and (ii) is by definition. If (ii) holds and $y \to z$, then by \Cref{854-equiv} we have $x = u \op (x \op y)$ and $z = v \op y$ for some $u,v$, hence $$ z \op x = z \op (x \op ((v \op y) \op (x \op y))) = z \op ((u \op (x \op y)) \op (z \op (x \op y))) = z,$$ giving the desired claim $x \to z$. Now if (iii) holds, note from \Cref{854-equiv} that $y \to x \op y$, hence $x \to x \op y$ by (iii), so that $(x \op y) \op x = x \op y$, giving (iv). Finally, if (iv) holds, note that \begin{align*} x \op ((x \op y) \op x) &= x \op ( ((x \op y) \op ((y \op y) \op ((x \op y) \op y))) \op x) \\ &= x \op (((x \op y) \op ((y \op y) \op (x \op y))) \op (x \op ((y \op y) \op (x \op y)))) \\ &= x \end{align*} and hence by (iv) $x \op (x \op y) = x$, giving (ii).
nodes.name: Proof of 854 equivalences, II
nodes.statement_short: Cycle (ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii)$\Rightarrow$(iv)$\Rightarrow$(ii) using the first equivalence lemma and 854.

nodes.statement: The relation $\leq$ is a pre-order, and for each $z$, the sets $\{ x: x \to z \}$ are upward closed in this preorder.
nodes.name: Preorder of 854 magma
conclusions: The relation $\leq$ is a pre-order, and for each $z$, the sets $\{ x: x \to z \}$ are upward closed in this preorder.

nodes.statement:
Define a \emph{partial 854 magma} to be a partial function $\op: \N \times \N \to \N$ satisfying the following axioms:

\begin{itemize}
  \item (Equation 854)  If $x,y,z \in \N$ are such that $(y \op z) \op (x \op z)$ is well-defined, then $x \op ((y \op z) \op (x \op z))$ is well-defined and equal to $x$.
  \item (Equation 8) If $x \in \N$ are such that $x \op x$ is well-defined, then $x \op (x \op x)$ is well-defined and equal to $x$.
  \item (Equation 101)  If $x,y \in \N$ are such that $(x \op y) \op x$ is well-defined, then $x \op ((x \op y) \op x)$ is well-defined and equal to $x$.
  \item (Equation 46155) If $x,y \in \N$ are such that $x \op (x \op y)$ is well-defined, then $(x \op y) \op (x \op (x \op y))$ is well-defined and equal to $x \op y$.
  \item (Equation 378) If $x,y \in \N$ is such that $x \op y$ is well-defined, then $(x \op y) \op y$ is well-defined and equal to $x \op y$.
  \item (No idempotence)  If $x \in \N$ is such that $x \op x$ is well-defined, then $x \op x \neq x$.
  \item (Auxiliary law)  If $x,y \in \N$ are such that $x \op (x \op y)$ is well-defined and equal to $x$, then $x=y$.
  \item (Unique factorization)  If $x,y,x',y' \in \N$ are such that $x \op y$, $x' \op y'$ are well-defined and equal to each other, then at least one of the assertions $x \op y = x$, $x' \op y' = x'$, or $(x,y) = (x',y')$ is true.
  \item (Monotonicity)  If $x,y \in \N$ is such that $x \op y$ is defined, then either $x \op y = x$ or $x \op y > x, y$.
nodes.name: Partial 854 magma
nodes.statement_short: Partial operation on $\N$ satisfying local versions of 854, 8, 101, 46155, 378, plus no idempotence, an auxiliary law, unique factorization and monotonicity.

nodes.statement: The first five laws are known consequences of 854.  The no idempotence law was known for the free magma $M_{854}$ because it maps to finite magmas without idempotents, such as $\Z/3\Z$ with law $x \op y = x - 1_{x=y}$.  The unique factorization law is also known for the free magma by \Cref{unique-factorization}.  The auxiliary law is a ``leap of faith'' that helped close the greedy argument, and the monotonicity property is a technical consequence of the greedy construction that will also help close the argument.
nodes.name: Justification of partial 854 axioms
nodes.statement_short: Explains which axioms are known consequences of 854 and which are heuristic additions.

nodes.statement: Suppose one has a partial 854 magma on $\N$ that is only finitely defined, and let $a,b \in G$ be such that $a \op b$ is currently undefined. Then it is possible to extend the magma to a larger partial 854 magma, such that $a \op b$ is now defined.
nodes.name: Greedy construction for 854
assumptions: Suppose one has a partial 854 magma on $\N$ that is only finitely defined, and let $a,b \in G$ be such that $a \op b$ is currently undefined.
conclusions: it is possible to extend the magma to a larger partial 854 magma, such that $a \op b$ is now defined
nodes.label: 854-extend

nodes.statement:
Define a directed graph by writing $x 	o y$ if $y \op x$ is defined and equal to $y$. By Equation 378, we see that $x 	o y$ if and only if $z \op x$ is well-defined and equal to $y$ for some $z$. From unique factorization, we see that $b$ has at most one representation of the form $b = b_1 \op b_2$ with $b_1 
eq b$, or equivalently $b_2 
ot 	o b_1$. We define $b_1, b_2$ accordingly if such a representation exists, otherwise we leave $b_1, b_2$ undefined. We say that $b_1$ is \emph{relevant} if $b_2 	o a$. Note that this forces $a 
eq b_1$ since $b_2 
ot 	o b_1$. Also, if $b_1,b_2$ exist, we see from monotonicity that $b = b_1 \op b_2 > b_1, b_2$. Let $c$ be a natural number that is larger than any number appearing in anywhere in the partial 854 magma multiplication table (in particular it is larger than $a,b$, as well as $b_1,b_2$ if they are defined). We then extend the multiplication table by defining $a \diamond b = c$, $b \diamond c = b$, and $c \diamond b = c$. If $b_1$ exists and is relevant, we also define $b_1 \diamond c = b_1$. Finally, if $b_1$ exists and is relevant, and additionally $b 	o b_1$, then we also define $c \diamond b_1 = c$. We remark that all new entries added are of the left absorptive form $x \diamond y = x$, except for $a \diamond b = c$. We now verify that all of the axioms of a partial 854 magma continue to hold. We begin with all the axioms except for 854:  egin{itemize} \item Monotonicity: Observe that all the new values $x \diamond y$ of the multiplication table introduced are either equal to $x$, or larger than both $x$ and $y$, so the monotonicity property is preserved. \item Unique factorization: the only way unique factorization breaks is if there is an element $z$ that has two distinct factorizations $z = x \op y = x' \op y'$ with neither $x \op y$ nor $x' \op y'$ a left absorptive product. Since the only non-left-absorptive product introduced is $a \op b = c$, and $c$ has no prior representation as a product, we see that the unique factorization property is preserved. \item No idempotence: The only possible product $x \op x$ that could be introduced here is $a \op b$ if $x=a=b$, but in that case $x \op x = a \op b = c$ is clearly not equal to $x$, so the no idempotence property is preserved. \item Equation 8: If $x \op x$ were already defined in the previous magma, the claim would already be established, so $x \op x$ must be one of the new products $a \op b$, $b \diamond c$, $c \diamond b$, $b_1 \diamond c$, or $c \diamond b_1$. As $c 
eq a,b,b_1$, the only option is $x = a = b$, but then $x \op (x \op x) = b \op c = b = x$, as required. \item Equation 101: By Equation 8, we may assume $x \op y 
eq x$, which implies $y 
eq c$ since $x \op c = x$ whenever the left-hand side is defined. We can also assume $x 
eq c$, since we have $c \op z = c$ whenever the left-hand side is defined. If $x \op y = c$, then $(x,y) = (a,b)$; as $(x \op y) \op x = c \op x$ is well-defined, $x=a$ is then either equal to $b$, or equal to $b_1$ if the latter exists and is relevant. But the second case cannot occur since $a 
eq b_1$, so we have $x = b$, and then $x \op ((x \op y) \op x) = b \op (c \op b) = b = x$, giving the claim. So we may assume $x \op y 
eq c$. If $(x \op y, x) 
eq (a,b)$, then $(x \op y) \op x$ was already defined in the original partial magma, and the claim follows from Equation 101; hence we may assume $(x \op y, x) = (a,b)$, then $x \op ((x \op y) \op x) = b \op c = b = x$, giving the claim. \item Equation 46155: By Equation 8, we may assume $x \op y 
eq x$ and hence $y 
eq c$ as before. The case $x=c$ is not possible, as this forces $x \op y = c$ and then $x \op (x \op y)$ is undefined. If $x \op y = c$, then $(x,y) = (a,b)$; in order for $x \op (x \op y) = a \op c$ to be defined, either $a=b$ or $a=b_1$ with $b_1$ relevant, but the latter is impossible since $a 
eq b_1$; thus $x=y=a=b$ and $(x \op y) \op (x \op (x \op y)) = c \op (b \op c) = c = (x \op y)$, giving the claim. Thus we may assume $x \op y 
eq c$. If $(x, x \op y) 
eq (a,b)$ then $x \op (x \op y)$ was already defined in the original partial magma, and the claim follows from Equation 46155; hence we may assume $(x, x \op y) = (a,b)$, and we have $(x \op y) \op (x \op (x \op y)) = b \op c = b = x \op y$, giving the claim. \item Equation 378: We can assume $x \op y 
eq x$, since the claim is trivial otherwise. This rules out the $y=c$ and $x=c$ cases. The only new case is then if $x \op y = c$, but forces $(x,y) = (a,b)$, and then $(x \op y) \op y = c \op b = c = x \op y$, giving the claim. \item Auxiliary law: if $x=c$, then the only possible value for $x \op y$ is $c$, and $c \op c$ is undefined, contradiction; thus $x 
eq c$. If $y = c$, then the only possible value for $x \op y$ is $x$, and then $x \op (x \op y)$ cannot equal $x$ by the no idempotence law. Thus $y 
eq c$. Since $x \op (x \op y) = x$ is not equal to $c$, $(x,x \op y)$ is not equal to $(a,b)$. If $(x,y) 
eq (a,b)$, then both $x \op y$ and $x \op (x \op y)$ were already defined in the original partial magma, and the claim follows from the auxiliary law for that magma. Thus we may assume $(x,y) = (a,b)$, in which case $a \op c = a$, hence by construction either $a=b$ or $a=b_1$. If $a=b$ then we are done. If $a = b_1$, then $b_1$ cannot be relevant, and then $a \op c = b_1 \op c$ remains undefined, a contradiction. \end{itemize} Now we tackle the most difficult verification, which is 854. This splits into a large number of cases.  egin{itemize} \item Case 1: $x=c$. Then $x \op z$ can only equal $c$, hence $z$ equals $b$ or $b_1$; and $y \op z$ can also only equal $b$ or $b_1$, and $(y \op z) \op (x \op z)$ is equal to $y \op z$. If $y \op z = b$, then we are done since $c \op b = c$. If $y \op z = b_1$, then $b_1 \op c$ needs to be defined, so $b_1$ is relevant. Furthermore, from equation 378 we have $b_1 \op z = b_1$, hence by the no idempotence property $z$ must equal $b$, so $b 	o b_1$, and hence $c \op b_1 = c$, giving the claim. \item Case 2: $x 
eq c$, $z = c$. This forces $x,y=b,b_1$ with $y \op z = y$ and $x \op z = x$, thus $y \op x$ is well-defined and we need $x \op (y \op x)$ well-defined and equal to $x$. If $x=y$, this follows from Equation 8; otherwise, either $x = b_1 \op b_2$ and $y = b_1$ or $x = b_1$ and $y = b_1 \op b_2$, and the claim follows from Equation 101 or Equation 46155 respectively. \item Case 3: $x, z 
eq c$, $y = c$. Then $z$ must equal $b$ or $b_1$, $y \op z$ must equal $c$, and $x \op z$ must equal $b$ or $b_1$, and $(y \op z) \op (x \op z)$ must equal $c$, with the $b_1$ options only available if $b_1$ is relevant. If $x \op z = z$ then by equation 378, $z \op z = z$, contradicting the no idempotence law. Thus we either have $z=b_1, x \op z = b$ or $z = b, x \op z = b_1$, and in either case $b_1$ must be relevant. If $z 	o x$, then either have $x=b$, or $x = b_1$ and $b_1$ is relevant, and in either case we have $x \op c = x$ as required. So we may assume $z 
ot 	o x$. In the case $z = b_1, x \op z = b = b_1 \op b_2$ we may then apply unique factorization to conclude that $z = b_2$ and $x = b_1$, thus $x \op c = x$ as required. In the opposite case $z = b$, $x \op z = b_1$ with $z 
ot 	o x$, we see from monotonicity that $b_1 = x \op z > z = b$; but from monotonicity again $b = b_1 \op b_2 > b_1$, a contradiction. \item Case 4: $x,y,z 
eq c$, $(y,z) = (a,b)$. Here, $y \op z$ and $(y \op z) \op (x \op z)$ must equal $c$, and $x \op z$ must then equal $b$ or $b_1$, with the latter an option only if $b_1$ is relevant. If $x \op z = b$, then by Equation 378, $b \op b = b$, contradicting idempotence, thus $x \op z = b_1$ and $b_1$ is relevant, and then $b 	o b_1$ by Equation 378 again. If $z 	o x$, then $x = b_1$, and the claim follows since $b_1 \op c = c$, so we may assume $z 
ot 	o x$. By monotonicity, this forces $b_1 = x \op z > z = b$ and $b = b_1 \op b_2 > b_1$, a contradiction. \item Case 5: $x,y,z 
eq c$, $(y,z) 
eq (a,b)$, $(x,z) = (a,b)$. Now $x \op z = c$, and $y \op z$ must equal $b$ or $b_1$. If $y \op z = b$, then by Equation 378, $b \op b = b$, contradicting idempotence, thus $y \op z = b_1$ and $b_1$ is relevant, and then $b 	o b_1$ by Equation 378 again, so $b_1 \op (b_1 \op b_2) = b_1$. By the auxiliary law, this forces $b_1 = b_2$, so $x = b_1$, and then we are done since $b_1 \op c = b_1$. \item Case 6: $x,y,z 
eq c$, $(y,z), (x,z) 
eq (a,b)$, $(y \op z, x \op z) = (a,b)$. Here $x \op z = b$ and $(y \op z) \op (x \op z) = c$. If $z 	o x$, then $x=b$ and we are done since $b \op c = b$. If $z 
ot 	o x$, then by unique factorization applied to $x \op z = b_1 \op b_2$ we have $(x,z) = (b_1,b_2)$. By Equation 378, we have $z 	o y \op z$, hence $b_2 	o a$, so $b_1$ is relevant. We are now done since $b_1 \op c = b_1$. \item Case 7: $x,y,z 
eq c$, $(y,z), (x,z) 
eq (a,b), (y \op z, x \op z) 
eq (a,b)$. In this case $x \op ((y \op z) \op (x \op z))$ would already have been defined and equal to $x$ in the previous partial magma, thanks to Equation 854. \end{itemize}
nodes.name: Proof of Greedy construction for 854
nodes.statement_short: Set $a\op b=c$ for a huge new $c$ plus a few left-absorptive entries, then verify each axiom and 854 by exhaustive case analysis.

nodes.statement: Suppose one has a partial 854 magma on $\N$ that is only finitely defined. Then it can be extended to a complete 854 magma that additionally satisfies the no idempotence law, the monotonicity law, the auxiliary law, and the unique factorization law.
nodes.name: 854 extension
assumptions: Suppose one has a partial 854 magma on $\N$ that is only finitely defined.
conclusions: it can be extended to a complete 854 magma that additionally satisfies the no idempotence law, the monotonicity law, the auxiliary law, and the unique factorization law
nodes.label: extend-854

nodes.statement: Apply the usual greedy algorithm.
nodes.name: Proof of 854 extension

nodes.statement: There is an 854 magma which does not satisfy the 413 law $x = x \op (x \op (x \op (y \op x)))$.
nodes.name: 854 does not imply 413
conclusions: There is an 854 magma which does not satisfy the 413 law $x = x \op (x \op (x \op (y \op x)))$.

nodes.statement: Create a partial magma by imposing the laws $1 \op 0 = 2$, $0 \op 2 = 3$, $2 \op 0 = 2$, $3 \op 2 = 3$. One can check that this is a partial magma. We then extend it to a global magma using \Cref{extend-854}. We claim that we have the 413 violation $$ 0 \op (0 \op (0 \op (1 \op 0))) = 0$$ or equivalently $$ 0 \op (0 \op 3) = 0.$$ Indeed this is immediate from the auxiliary law.
nodes.name: Proof of 854 does not imply 413
nodes.statement_short: Seed partial magma completed greedily; the auxiliary law forces the 413 violation.

nodes.statement: There is an 854 magma which does not satisfy the 1045 law $x = x \op ((y \op (y \op x)) \op x)$.
nodes.name: 854 does not imply 1045
conclusions: There is an 854 magma which does not satisfy the 1045 law $x = x \op ((y \op (y \op x)) \op x)$.

nodes.statement: Similar to previous, but start with the seed $$ 0 \op 0 = 2; 0 \op 1 = 0 \op 2 = 0; 1 \op 2 = 3; 2 \op 0 = 2 \op 1 = 2 \op 3 = 2; 3 \op 2 = 3$$ which already violates the law with $x=1,y=0$, and can be verified to be a partial 854 magma.
nodes.name: Proof of 854 does not imply 1045
nodes.statement_short: Same as previous with a seed already violating 1045.

nodes.statement: We recall the free magma $M_X$ from \Cref{free-magma-def}, though to avoid confusion we will denote the magma operation on $M_X$ by $*$ rather than $\op$.
nodes.name: Star operation on the free magma

nodes.statement: Recall that every word $w$ in $M_X$ has a length in $\N$, which is zero if $w$ is a generator in $X$, and is the sum of the lengths of $w_L$ and $w_R$ plus one if instead $w$ is of the form $w_L * w_R$ for the left and right components $w_L, w_R$ of $w$ (which are uniquely defined by $w$).
nodes.name: Length and components of words

nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $854$ magma, and let $\to$ be the associated operation, thus $x \to y$ if $y \op x = y$. Then $x \to y$ holds under any of the following assumptions: \begin{itemize} \item (i) $y = a \op x$ for some $a$. \item (ii) $x = a \op (y \op b)$ for some $a,b$ with $b \to a$. \item (iii) $y = a \op (x \op b)$ for some $a,b$ with $b \to a$ and $x \op b \to x$. \item (iv) $x = a \op y$ for some $a,z$ with $z \to a, y$. \item (v) $x = a \op y$ for some $a$, with either $a=y$, $a = y \op z$, or $y = a \op z$ for some $z$. \end{itemize}
nodes.name: The 854 relation
assumptions: Let $M$ be an $854$ magma, and let $\to$ be the associated operation, thus $x \to y$ if $y \op x = y$.
conclusions: $x \to y$ holds under any of the following assumptions:
nodes.label: 854-relation

nodes.statement: Case (i) follows from \Cref{378}. For (ii), we observe $$ y \op x = y \op ((a \op b) \op (y \op b)) = y$$ as required. For (iii), we see from (ii) that $y \to x$, and from (i) we have $x \op b \to y$, and then $$ y \op x = y \op ((x \op (x \op b)) \op (y \op (x \op b))) = y$$ as required. For (iv), we have $$ y \op x = y \op ((a \op z) \op (y \op z)) = y$$ as required. Finally, for (v), in the $a=y$ case we have from \Cref{8} that $$ y \op x = y \op ((y \op y^2) \op (y \op y^2)) = y,$$ in the $a = y \op z$ case we have from \Cref{8} that $$ y \op x = y \op (((y \op z) \op (y \op z)^2) \op (y \op (y \op z)^2)) = y,$$ and finally in the $y = a \op z$ case we have from \Cref{8} that $$ y \op x = y \op ( (a \op (a \op z)^2) \op ((a \op z) \op (a \op z)^2)) = y,$$ so the claim follows in all cases.
nodes.name: Proof of The 854 relation
nodes.statement_short: Each of the five sufficient conditions is checked by a direct 854 computation, using 8 and 378.

nodes.statement: For $x,y \in M_X$, we have $x \to y$ if and only if one of the following holds: \begin{itemize} \item (i) $x = y_R$. \item (ii) $y = x_{RL}$ and $x_{RR} \to x_L$. \item (iii) $x = y_{RL}$, $y_{RR} \to y_L$, and $y_R \to y_{RL}$. \item (iv) $y = x_R$, and there exists $z \in \{ x_{LR}, x_{LRL}, x_{RR}, x_{RRL} \}$ such that $z \to x_L$ and $z \to x_R$. \item (v) $y = x_R$, and one of the claims $x_L = x_R$, $x_L = x_{RL}$, or $x_R = x_{LL}$ holds. \end{itemize} Here we adopt the convention that a claim can only hold if all terms in it are well-defined, for instance claim (ii) can only hold if $x_{RL}$ is well-defined.
nodes.name: Relation on the free group
nodes.statement_short: Recursive definition of $x\to y$ on free-magma words by five structural clauses mirroring the 854 relation lemma.
nodes.label: free-relate

nodes.statement: If we define the ``max-length'' of a claim $x \to y$ to be the maximum of the length of $x$ and the length of $y$, we see that the verification of a claim $x \to y$ only involves claims $x' \to y'$ of strictly smaller max-length.  Thus this definition is well-defined.
nodes.name: The free 854 relation is well-defined
Arrows relate immediate subterms

nodes.statement: x=y_R, x=y_{RL}, y = x_R, y=x_{RL}
nodes.name: Four subterm options
nodes.label: one

nodes.statement: We then define a new operation $\diamond$ on $M_X$ by the rule $x \diamond y = x$ if $y \to x$, and $x \diamond y = x*y$ otherwise.
nodes.name: Free 854 operation

nodes.statement: We then define $M_{X,854}$ to be the magma generated by $X$ with the operation $\diamond$; thus, $w \in M_{X,854}$ if and only if either $w \in X$, or else $w_L, w_R \in M_{X,854}$ and $w_R \not \to w_L$.
nodes.name: Free 854 magma M_{X,854}

nodes.statement: The magma $M_{X,854}$ is a free 854 magma on $X$.
nodes.name: Free 854 magma
conclusions: The magma $M_{X,854}$ is a free 854 magma on $X$.
nodes.label: free-854

nodes.statement:
Let $f: X 	o M$ be a function from $X$ to an $854$ magma $M$, then $\varphi_f$ is a homomorphism from $M_X$ (with the operation $*$) to $M$. We claim that the restriction of $\varphi_f$ to $M_{X,854}$ is a homomorphism from $M_{X,854}$ (with operation $\diamond$) to $M$. Since $\varphi_f$ was already a homomorphism for $*$, it suffices to show that $\varphi_f$ preserves $	o$: that is to say, for any $x,y \in M_{X,854}$, that $x 	o y$ implies $\varphi_f(x) 	o \varphi_f(y)$. By definition, one of the five scenarios (i)-(v) in \Cref{free-relate} holds, and in each case one can establish the claim from the corresponding claim of \Cref{854-relation} and an induction on the max-length of the claim $x 	o y$. It remains to show that $M_{854}$ actually satisfies 854, that is to say that $$ (y \op z) \op (x \op z) 	o x$$ for all $x,y,z \in M_{854}$. Writing $w = y \op z$, we have $z 	o w$ by \Cref{free-relate}(i), and we need to show that $w \op (x \op z) 	o x$. We divide into four cases. Case 1: $x \op z 	o w$, $z 	o x$. Here we have $x \op z = x$ and $w \op (x \op z) = w$. We now have $z 	o x,w$ and $x 	o w$, and we need to show that $w 	o x$. From \Cref{one} we know that one of  egin{equation} z = x_R, z = x_{RL}, x = z_R, x = z_{RL} \end{equation} holds, one of  egin{equation} z = w_R, z = w_{RL}, w = z_R, w = z_{RL} \end{equation} holds, and one of  egin{equation} x = w_R, x = w_{RL}, w = x_R, w = x_{RL} \end{equation} holds. We split into subcases using \Cref{one-3}.  egin{itemize} \item If $x = w_R$ then the claim follows from \Cref{free-relate}(i). \item If $w = x_{RL}$ then from \Cref{free-relate}(iii) we have $x_{RR} 	o x_L$, and then the claim follows from \Cref{free-relate}(ii). \item If $x = w_{RL}$, then $w_{RR} 	o w_L$ by \Cref{free-relate}(ii) and from \Cref{free-relate}(iii) we will be done if we can show that $w_R 	o w_{RL}$. If $z = w_R$ then this follows from $z 	o x$. The claim $z = w_{RL}$ is not compatible with \Cref{one-1}, since $z=x$ in that case. If $w = z_R$ then $x = z_{RRL}$, and this is only compatible with \Cref{one-1} if $x = z_{RL}$, thus $z = a * (x * (x * b))$ and $w = x * (x * b)$ for some $a,b$. In order to have $x = w_{RL}$ in \Cref{one-3}, we must have $b 	o x$ by \Cref{free-relate}(iii), but then $x*b$ would not lie in $M_{854}$, a contradiction. \item If $w = x_R$, then we cannot then have $z = x_R$ as then $z=w$ which is incompatible with \Cref{one-2}. If $z = x_{RL} = w_L$ then $x_{RR} 	o x_L$ by \Cref{free-relate}(ii), and the only available options from \Cref{one-2} are $z = w_R$ and $z = w_{RL}$. For $z=w_R$ we have $w = z * z$ and $x = a * (z * z)$ for some $a$ with $z 	o a = x_L$. Since $z 	o z*z = x_R$ as well by \Cref{free-relate}(i), and $z = x_{RR}$, we obtain $w 	o x$ as required from \Cref{free-relate}(iv). \end{itemize} Case 2: $x \op z 	o w$, $z 
ot 	o x$. We now have $x * z, z 	o w$, and we need to show that $w 	o x$. From \Cref{one} we know that one of  egin{equation} w = (x * z)_R, w = (x * z)_{RL}, x * z = w_R, x * z = w_{RL} \end{equation} holds, and that one of  egin{equation} w = z_R, w = z_{RL}, z = w_R, z = w_{RL} \end{equation} holds. We split into cases depending on \Cref{wz-1}.  egin{itemize} \item If $w = (x*z)_R$ then $w=z$, which is incompatible with \Cref{wz}. \item If $w = (x*z)_{RL}$ then $w = z_L$ and $z_R 	o x$ by \Cref{free-relate}(ii). Only the first two possibilities of \Cref{wz} are compatible with $w=z_L$. In the first case we are done since $z_R 	o x$ and $w = z_R$. In the second case, we have $z = w * (w * a)$ for some $a$ with $a 	o w$ (from \Cref{free-relate}(ii) and $z 	o w$), but then $w * a$ will not lie in $M_{854}$, contradiction. \item If $x*z = w_R$ then $w$ is longer than $z$ and $z 
eq w_R$. Comparing this with \Cref{wz} we see that the only compatible option is $z = w_{RL}$, thus $x=z$, and then $w = a * (x * x)$ and $x 	o a$ by \Cref{free-relate}(iii), and the claim follows from \Cref{free-relate}(ii). \item If $x * z = w_{RL}$, then $w = a * ((x *z) * b)$ for some $a,b$. Then $w$, $w_R$, and $w_{RL}$ are all longer than $z$ and none of the options in \Cref{wz} can hold, a contradiction. \end{itemize} Case 3: $x \op z 
ot 	o w$, $z 	o x$. We now have $z 	o x, w$, and we need to show that $w * x 	o x$. If $z \in \{ w_R, w_{RL}, x_R, x_{RL} \}$, then the claim follows from \Cref{free-relate}(iv), so we may assume that this is not the case. By \Cref{one}, we then know that one of $$ x = z_R, x = z_{RL}$$ holds, and also one of $$ w = z_R, w = z_{RL}$$ holds. Thus, we either have one of $$ w = x, w = x_L, x = w_L.$$ But in any of these three cases the claim follows from \Cref{free-relate}(v). Case 4: $x \op z 
ot 	o w$, $z 
ot 	o x$. Then $x = (w \op (x \op z))_{RL}$ and $z 	o w$, so the claim follows from \Cref{free-relate}(ii).
nodes.name: Proof of Free 854 magma
nodes.statement_short: Homomorphism property via the 854 relation lemma by induction on max-length; then verify 854 in four cases using the subterm options.

nodes.name: Options for z and x
nodes.label: one-1

nodes.statement: z = w_R, z = w_{RL}, w = z_R, w = z_{RL}

nodes.statement:
Suppose for instance that $x,y$ are generators in $X$.  We cannot have $y 	o x$ (as none of \Cref{one} hold), so $y * x \in M_{X,854}$.  We also cannot have $y * x 	o x$ (by inspection of the cases in \Cref{free-relate}(iv), \Cref{free-relate}(v)), so $x * (y * x)$ lies in $M_{X,854}$.  Then $x * (y * x) 
ot 	o x$ (by \Cref{one}), so $x * (x * (y * x))$ lies in $M_{X,854}$; finally, $x * (x * (y * x)) 
ot 	o x$ (this follows from \Cref{free-relate}(ii) since $y * x 
ot 	o x$), so $x * (x * (x * (y * x)))$ lies in $M_{X,854}$.  This gives an alternate proof of \Cref{854-413}.
nodes.name: Alternate proof that 854 does not imply 413
nodes.statement_short: In the explicit free 854 magma, $x*(x*(x*(y*x)))$ is irreducible, so 413 fails.

nodes.statement: One can similarly establish \Cref{854-1045}.
nodes.name: Alternate proof that 854 does not imply 1045
nodes.statement_short: Similar computation in the free 854 magma.

nodes.statement: x = y \op ((y \op x) \op (x \op x))
nodes.name: Equation 906

nodes.statement: L_y (L_y x \op Sx) = x.
nodes.name: Equation 906 in operator form
nodes.label: 906-a

nodes.statement: L_y x \op Sx = L_y^{-1} x.
nodes.name: Inverse of left multiplication for 906
nodes.label: 906-b

nodes.statement: For any integer $n$, $$ L_y x = L_z x \implies L_y^{n} x = L_z^{n} x.$$
nodes.name: Edge disjointness of left cycles
assumptions: For any integer $n$
conclusions: $$ L_y x = L_z x \implies L_y^{n} x = L_z^{n} x.$$
nodes.label: edge-disjoint

nodes.statement: This is trivial for $n=0,1$, and $n=-1$ follows from \Cref{906-b}. Observe that if the claim holds for $n=0,-1,\dots,-m$ for any $m \geq 1$ then it also holds for $n=-m-1$. Finally, since there is a common period to all the $L_y$ by finiteness (or Legendre's theorem), the set of $n$ for which the claim holds is periodic. The claim follows.
nodes.name: Proof of Edge disjointness of left cycles
nodes.statement_short: Downward induction on $n$ from the inverse formula, then periodicity of the $L_y$.

nodes.statement: L_y x = L_z x \implies L_y^2 x = L_z^2 x.
nodes.name: Squares of left multiplications agree
nodes.label: lyzx

nodes.statement: For finite magmas, equation 906 implies equation 3862, \begin{equation} (x \op (x \op x)) \op x = x \op x. \end{equation}
nodes.name: 906 implies 3862 for finite magmas
assumptions: For finite magmas
conclusions:
equation 906 implies
equation 3862,

nodes.statement: (x \op (x \op x)) \op x = x \op x.
nodes.name: Equation 3862

nodes.statement: Observe from \Cref{906-a} that $$ L_x S^2 x = L_x (L_x x \op Sx) = x$$ while from \Cref{906-b} we have $$ L_{L_x Sx} S^2 x = L_x Sx \op S S x = L_x^{-1} Sx = x.$$ Thus $$ L_x S^2 x = L_{L_x Sx} S^2 x = x$$ and hence by the $n=2$ case of \Cref{edge-disjoint} $$ L_x x = L_{L_x Sx} x$$ giving the claim.

nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a countably infinite abelian torsion group of exponent $2$. Then there exists a bijection $\phi_a: G \to \Q^\times$ for each $a \in G \backslash \{0\}$ such that $\phi_a(0) = 1$ and $\phi_a(a+b) = -\phi_a(b)$ for all $b \in G$, so in particular $\phi_a(a)=-1$.
nodes.name: Bijections
assumptions: Let $G$ be a countably infinite abelian torsion group of exponent $2$.
conclusions:
there exists a bijection $\phi_a: G \to \Q^\times$ for each $a \in G \backslash \{0\}$ such that
 $\phi_a(0) = 1$ and $\phi_a(a+b) = -\phi_a(b)$ for all $b \in G$
nodes.label: bij

nodes.statement: Such a bijection can be easily constructed from the axiom of choice and a greedy algorithm, defining $\phi_a$ one pair $\{b,a+b\}$ at a time.
nodes.name: Proof of Bijections
nodes.statement_short: Axiom of choice and a greedy pairing construction.

nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a countably infinite abelian torsion group of exponent $2$, and let $\phi_a$ be as in the previous lemma. Let $N$ be the set of pairs $(x,a)$ with $x \in \Q^\times$ and $a \in G \backslash \{0\}$, and let $M = G \uplus N$ be the disjoint union of $G$ and $N$. Suppose that we have an operation $\op : M \times M \to M$ satisfying the following axioms: \begin{itemize} \item (i) We have \begin{equation} a \op b = a+b \end{equation} for $a,b \in G$. \item (ii) We have \begin{equation} (x,a) \op b = (\phi_a(b) x, a) \end{equation} \begin{equation} b \op (x,a) = (x / \phi_a(b), a) \end{equation} and \begin{equation} (\phi_a(b) x,a) \op (x,a) = a+b \end{equation} for $x \in \Q^\times$, $b \in G$, and $a \in G \backslash \{0\}$. \item (iii) If $a,b,0 \in G$ are distinct and $(x,a) \op (y,b) = (z,c)$ for some $x,y,z \in \Q^\times$ and $c \in G$, then $(y,b) \op (z,c) = (\phi_a(b) x,a)$. \end{itemize} Then \Cref{lr}, \Cref{lr-simp} and hence \Cref{1323} holds.
nodes.name: Building a magma
assumptions: Let $G$ be a countably infinite abelian torsion group of exponent $2$, and let $\phi_a$ be as in the previous lemma.
conclusions: Then \Cref{lr}, \Cref{lr-simp} and hence \Cref{1323} holds.
nodes.statement_short: Axioms (i)-(iii) on $M = G \uplus (\Q^\times\times G)$ give the two operator identities and hence 1323.
nodes.label: build-magma

nodes.statement: a \op b = a+b
nodes.name: Operation on G

nodes.name: Right action on N

nodes.statement: b \op (x,a) = (x / \phi_a(b), a)

nodes.statement: (\phi_a(b) x,a) \op (x,a) = a+b

nodes.label: op-3

nodes.statement: With these rules, $0$ is a unit, and the squaring operator is given by $Sa = 0$ and $S(x,a) = a$, so the set of squares is $G$. If $a \in G$ is a square number, we have $$ L_a b = R_a b = a+b$$ and $$ L_a (x,b) = (x/\phi_b(a), b); \quad R_a (x,b) = (x \phi_b(a), b)$$ so \Cref{lr} is satisfied. Now we verify \Cref{lr-simp}. If $y$ is a square, then the claim already follows from \Cref{lr} since $Sy=0$ is a unit. Otherwise, for $y \in \Q^\times$ and $b \in G \backslash \{0\}$, we have to show that $$ L_{(y,b)} R_{(y,b)} a = R_b a = a+b$$ for $a \in G$ and $$ L_{(y,b)} R_{(y,b)} (x,a) = R_b (x,a) = (\phi_a(b) x, a) $$ for $x \in \Q^\times$ and $a \in G \backslash \{0\}$. In the first case, we have from \Cref{op-2} that $$ R_{(y,b)} a = (y/\phi_a(b), b)$$ and then from \Cref{op-3} we have $$L_{(y,b)} R_{(y,b)} a = a+b$$ as required. In the second case, if $a=b$, then by the bijective nature of $\phi_a$, we can write $x = \phi_a(c) y$ for some $c \in G$, then from \Cref{op-3} we have $$ R_{(y,b)} (x,a) = a+c$$ and then by \Cref{op-1} $$ L_{(y,b)} R_{(y,b)} (x,a) = (\phi_a(a+c) y, a)$$ but from construction we have $\phi_a(a+c)=-\phi_a(c) = \phi_a(b)\phi_a(c)$ and hence $\phi_a(a+c) y = \phi_a(b) x$ as required. It remains to handle the case when $a,b$ are distinct elements of $G \backslash \{0\}$. But this follows from (iii).
nodes.name: Proof of Building a magma
nodes.statement_short: Compute squares and left/right multiplications by elements of $G$; verify the two identities case by case using axioms (ii),(iii).

nodes.statement: A \emph{partial solution} is a finite family ${\mathcal F}$ of tuples $(x,y,z,a,b,c) \in (\Q^\times)^3 \times G^6$ with $a,b,c,0$ distinct, such that the tuples $(\phi_a(b)^n x,a, \phi_b(c)^n y,b)$, $(\phi_b(c)^n y,b,\phi_c(a)^n z,c)$, $(\phi_c(a)^n z,c,\phi_a(b)^{n+1} x, a)$ for $(x,y,z,a,b,c) \in {\mathcal F}$ and $n \geq 0$ are all distinct.
nodes.name: Partial solution for 1323
nodes.genus: finite family ${\mathcal F}$ of tuples $(x,y,z,a,b,c) \in (\Q^\times)^3 \times G^6$
nodes.label: partial-1323

nodes.statement: Let ${\mathcal F}$ be a partial solution. Then if one defines a partial operation $\op$ on $M$ by requiring axioms (i), (ii), imposing the additional operations $$ (\phi_a(b)^n x,a) \op (\phi_b(c)^n y,b) = (\phi_c(a)^n z,c)$$ $$ (\phi_b(c)^n y,b) \op (\phi_c(a)^n z,c) = (\phi_a(b)^{n+1} x, a)$$ $$ (\phi_c(a)^n z,c) \op (\phi_a(b)^{n+1} x, a) = (\phi_b(c)^{n+1} y,b)$$ for all $n \geq 0$ and $(x,y,z,a,b,c) \in {\mathcal F}$, and no other operations, then this is a well-defined partial operation that satisfies axiom (iii) whenever it is defined.
nodes.name: Soundness
assumptions: Let ${\mathcal F}$ be a partial solution.
conclusions: this is a well-defined partial operation that satisfies axiom (iii) whenever it is defined
nodes.label: partial-1323-sound

nodes.statement: Routine.
nodes.name: Proof of Soundness

nodes.statement: If $\op$ is defined by a partial solution, and $(x,a) \op (y,b)$ is undefined for some $x,y \in \Q^\times$ and distinct $a,b \in G \backslash \{0\}$, then it is possible to extend the partial solution so that $(x,a) \op (y,b)$ is now defined.
nodes.name: Greedy extension for 1323
assumptions: If $\op$ is defined by a partial solution, and $(x,a) \op (y,b)$ is undefined for some $x,y \in \Q^\times$ and distinct $a,b \in G \backslash \{0\}$
conclusions: it is possible to extend the partial solution so that $(x,a) \op (y,b)$ is now defined
nodes.label: greedy-1323

nodes.statement: We select a $c \in G \backslash \{0\}$ that has not previously been used by the partial solution, let $z \in \Q^\times$ be arbitrary, (e.g., one could take $z=1$ if desired), and add $(x,y,z,a,b,c)$ to ${\mathcal F}$, thus we now also assign $$ (\phi_a(b)^n x,a) \op (\phi_b(c)^n y,b) = (\phi_c(a)^n z,c)$$ $$ (\phi_b(c)^n y,b) \op (\phi_c(a)^n z,c) = (\phi_a(b)^{n+1} x, a)$$ $$ (\phi_c(a)^n z,c) \op (\phi_a(b)^{n+1} x, a) = (\phi_b(c)^{n+1} y,b)$$ for all natural numbers $n$. As the $a,b,c$ are distinct, the $\phi_a(b), \phi_b(c), \phi_c(a)$ are not equal to $\pm 1$, and the members of this infinite sequence do not collide with each other. The second and third equations in this family cannot collide with previous assignments because $c$ is novel. If we arrange matters so that $\phi_b(c)$ involves primes in the numerator or denominator that do not appear in any previous $\phi_a(b), \phi_b(c), \phi_c(a), x, y, z$ used by the greedy algorithm, or the current $x,y,z$, then we also see that the first infinite sequence does not collide with any previously assigned value of $\op$ either.
nodes.name: Proof of Greedy extension for 1323
nodes.statement_short: Add a tuple with a novel $c$ and fresh primes in $\phi_b(c)$ so no collisions occur.

nodes.statement: Every partial solution can be extended to a complete solution that satisfies \Cref{lr} and \Cref{lr-simp}, and hence 1323.
nodes.name: Iterated greedy extension
conclusions: Every partial solution can be extended to a complete solution that satisfies \Cref{lr} and \Cref{lr-simp}, and hence 1323.
nodes.label: greedy-iterate

nodes.statement: Apply the usual greedy algorithm.
nodes.name: Proof of Iterated greedy extension

nodes.statement: There exists a 1323 magma which does not satisfy the 2744 equation $R_y L_{Sy} L_y x = x$.
nodes.name: 1323 does not imply 2744
conclusions: There exists a 1323 magma which does not satisfy the 2744 equation $R_y L_{Sy} L_y x = x$.
nodes.label: 1323-refute-2744

nodes.statement: It suffices to produce a partial solution in which $L_y$ is not injective. Pick distinct $a, b, b', c$ with $\phi_a(b)$, $\phi_a(b')$ having no prime factors in common in the numerator or denominator. We take the partial solution consisting of $(1,1,1,a,b,c)$ and $(1,1,1,a,b',c)$, that is to say we impose the conditions $$ (\phi_a(b)^n,a) \op (\phi_b(c)^n,b) = (\phi_c(a)^n,c)$$ $$ (\phi_b(c)^n,b) \op (\phi_c(a)^n,c) = (\phi_a(b)^{n+1}, a)$$ $$ (\phi_c(a)^n,c) \op (\phi_a(b)^{n+1}, a) = (\phi_b(c)^{n+1},b)$$ and $$ (\phi_a(b)^n,a) \op (\phi_{b'}(c)^n,b') = (\phi_c(a)^n,c)$$ $$ (\phi_{b'}(c)^n,b') \op (\phi_c(a)^n,c) = (\phi_a(b')^{n+1}, a)$$ $$ (\phi_c(a)^n,c) \op (\phi_{a}(b')^{n+1}, a) = (\phi_b(c)^{n+1},b').$$ One can check that no collisions occur; on the other hand, as $L_{(1,a)} (1,b) = L_{(1,a)} (1,b') = (1,c)$, we already have a violation of left injectivity. Completing this seed to a full magma using \Cref{greedy-iterate}, we obtain the claim.
nodes.name: Proof of 1323 does not imply 2744
nodes.statement_short: Seed partial solution with two tuples sharing $(a,c)$ breaks left injectivity; complete greedily.

Using the squaring operator $Sy := y \op y$ and the left and right multiplication operators $L_y x := y \op x$ and $R_y x = x \op y$, this law can be written as

nodes.name: Translation-invariant model on Z

nodes.statement: Thus, if we let $E = \{ (h, f(h))\}$ be the graph of $f$, then we have the following property: if $(a,b), (b,c) \in E$, then $(c-a,-a) \in E$.
nodes.name: Graph closure property for 1516
assumptions: if $(a,b), (b,c) \in E$
conclusions: $(c-a,-a) \in E$

nodes.statement:
A \emph{1516 seed} is a finite collection $E$ of pairs $(a,b)$ with $a,b \in \Z$ satisfying the following axioms:  egin{itemize} \item Axiom 1: $(0,0) \in E$. \item Axiom 2: If $(a,b) \in E$ and $a 
eq 0$, then $b 
eq 0, -a$. \item Axiom 3: If $(a,b), (a,b') \in E$, then $b=b'$. \item Axiom 4: If $(a,b), (b,c) \in E$, then $(c-a,-a) \in E$. \item Axiom 5: If $(b,a), (b',a), (-b, d), (-b',d') \in E$ with $b 
eq b'$, then $b+d 
eq d', b'+d'$. \end{itemize} An \emph{extension} of a 1516 seed $E$ is a 1516 seed $E'$ that contains $E$.
nodes.name: 1516 seed
nodes.statement_short: Finite partial graph of $f$ on $\Z$ containing $(0,0)$, functional, closed under the 1516 rule, with non-degeneracy axioms 2 and 5.
nodes.label: 1516-seed

nodes.statement: Let $E$ be a 1516 seed, and let $a_0 \in \Z$. Then there exists an extension $E'$ of $E$ that contains $(a_0,c_0)$ for some $c_0$.
nodes.name: 1516 extension
assumptions: Let $E$ be a 1516 seed, and let $a_0 \in \Z$.
conclusions: there exists an extension $E'$ of $E$ that contains $(a_0,c_0)$ for some $c_0$
nodes.label: 1516-ext

nodes.statement: We may assume that $E$ does not already contain any pair of the form $(a_0,c)$, since we are done otherwise. By Axiom 1 implies that $a_0 \neq 0$. Let $b_1,\dots,b_n$ denote all the integers $b_i$ such that $(b_i,a) \in E$, then $n \geq 0$ is finite, and by Axiom 2 all the $b_i$ are non-zero and not equal to $-a$. Let $c_0$ be a sufficiently large integer to be chosen later. We then add the pairs $(a_0,c_0)$ and $(c-b_i,-b_i)$ to $E$ for all $i$. Furthermore, if $i$ is such that $(-b_i,d_i) \in E$ for some (necessarily unique and non-zero) $d_i$, we also add $(d_i+b+i-c_0, b_i-c_0)$ to $E$. Let $E'$ be the resulting set of pairs. Axioms 4, 5 for $E$ ensure that (for $c_0$ large enough) the addition of these pairs do not cause a violation of Axioms 2 or 3 for $E'$, and of course Axiom 1 for $E'$ will also be retained. As for Axiom 4, one can check that the only new pairs of pairs $(',b), (b,c)$ that would trigger these axioms either take the form $(b_i,a_0), (a_0,c_0)$ or $(c_0-b_i,-b_i), (-b_i,d_i)$, and in either case we see from construction that Axiom 4 remains in effect for $E'$. Finally, the new quadruples of pairs $(b,a), (b',a), (-b, d), (-b',d') \in E'$ only arise when either $(-b,d)$, $(-b',d')$ is equal to $(a_0,c_0)$ and the other three pairs in the quadruple were already in $E$, and for $c_0$ large enough we see that Axiom 5 remains valid.
nodes.name: Proof of 1516 extension
nodes.statement_short: Add $(a_0,c_0)$ for a huge $c_0$ together with the pairs forced by Axiom 4, then check Axioms 1-5.

nodes.statement: Let $E$ be a 1516 seed, and let $h \in \Z$ be non-zero. Then there exists an extension $E'$ of $E$ that contains $(a_i,a_i+h)$ for $i=1, 2, 3, 4$, for some distinct $a_1, a_2, a_3, a_4$.
nodes.name: 1516 extension variant
assumptions: Let $E$ be a 1516 seed, and let $h \in \Z$ be non-zero.
conclusions: there exists an extension $E'$ of $E$ that contains $(a_i,a_i+h)$ for $i=1, 2, 3, 4$, for some distinct $a_1, a_2, a_3, a_4$
nodes.label: 1516-ext-var

nodes.statement: If we choose $a$ sufficiently large, and set $a_i = i a$ (say) for $i=1, 2, 3, 4$, the claim simply follows by adding $(a_i,a_i+h)$ to $E$ and verifying that none of the axioms are violated.
nodes.name: Proof of 1516 extension variant
nodes.statement_short: Add $(ia, ia+h)$ for a huge $a$ and check the axioms.

nodes.statement: There exists a 1516 magma with carrier $\Z$ with the properties that \begin{itemize} \item (i) $Sa=a$ for all $a$. \item (ii) For any distinct $a,b \in \Z$, the equation $R_a c = b$ has at least four solutions $c$. \item (iii) For each $a \in \Z$, there exist at least two $b \neq a$ such that $L_a R_a b = b$. \end{itemize}
nodes.name: Base magma for 1516
conclusions: There exists a 1516 magma with carrier $\Z$ with the properties that
nodes.statement_short: A translation-invariant 1516 magma on $\Z$ with idempotent squares, quadruple right-solvability and two fixed points of $L_aR_a$.
nodes.label: 1516-base

nodes.statement: Note from \Cref{1516} and the hypothesis $Sa=a$ that $R_a c = a$ if and only if $c=a$.
nodes.name: R_a c = a only for c = a

nodes.statement: By \Cref{1516-ext}, \Cref{1516-ext-var} and the greedy algorithm starting with the seed consisting of $(0,0)$, $(-1,2)$, $(3,1)$, $(-10,20)$, $(30,10)$, we obtain a graph $\{ (a,f(a)): a \in \Z \}$ of a function $f:\Z \to \Z$ with $f(0)=0$, $f(-1)=2$, $f(3)=1$, $f(-10) = 20$, $f(30)=10$ and the property that if $f(a)=b$ and $f(b)=c$, then $f(c-a)=-a$, and also with the property that for every non-zero $h$ there are distinct $a_{h,1}, a_{h,2}, a_{h,3}, a_{h,4}$ with $f(a_{h,i})=a_{h,i}+h$ for $i=1, 2, 3, 4$. We then have that \Cref{1516-f} holds. If we then define the magma operation $\op$ by \Cref{xy-1516}, we obtain \Cref{1516}, and since $f(0)=0$ we have (i). Also, from construction we see that $R_d (d - a_{h,i}) = d+h$ for any $d,h,i$, giving (ii). Finally, from construction we have $R_a (a+1) = a+1+f(-1) = a+3$, so $L_a R_a (a+1) = a + f(3) = a+1$, and similarly $L_a R_a (a+10) = a+10$, giving (iii).
nodes.name: Proof of Base magma for 1516
nodes.statement_short: Greedy completion of an explicit seed using both extension lemmas, then read off (i)-(iii).

nodes.statement:
Now we construct a more complex 1516 magma, whose carrier $G$ is $\Z \cup G'$, where
$$G' := \{ (a,c,n) \in \Z \times \Z \times \N : a \neq c\}.$$
nodes.name: Carrier G = Z union G'

nodes.statement: We extend the squaring map $S$ to all of $G$ by declaring $S(a,c,n) := a$, thus $S$ maps $G$ to $\Z$.
nodes.name: Extended squaring map

nodes.statement:
To create a 1516 magma structure on all of $G$, we need to extend the left multiplication operators $L_b$, $b \in \Z$ as maps from $G$ to $G$, and also introduce additional maps $L_x: G \to G$ for $x \in G'$, satisfying the following axioms:

\begin{itemize}
\item Axiom A: For any $x \in G'$, $L_x x = Sx$.
\item Axiom B: For any $x \in G'$ and $b \in \Z$, $L_{Sx} L_b L_b x = b$.
\item Axiom C: For any $x \in G$ and $y \in G'$, $L_{Sx} L_y L_y x = y$.
nodes.name: Axioms A, B, C

nodes.statement: One can assign $c_{y,b} \in \Z$ for each $y = (a,c,n) \in G'$ and $b \in \Z$ with the following properties: \begin{itemize} \item (i) For all $y = (a,c,n) \in G'$ and $b \in \Z$, $c_{y,b} \neq a,b,c$ and $L_a L_{c_{y,b}} b = c_{y,b}$. \item (ii) For all $y \in G'$, the map $b \mapsto c_{y,b}$ is injective. \end{itemize}
nodes.name: Useful elements
conclusions: One can assign $c_{y,b} \in \Z$ for each $y = (a,c,n) \in G'$ and $b \in \Z$ with the following properties:
nodes.label: aux

nodes.name: Proof of Useful elements
nodes.statement_short: Use properties (iii) and (ii) of the base magma to choose the $c_{y,b}$.

nodes.statement:
Define a \emph{partial solution} to be a partial assignment of $L_{c'} y \in G$ for $c' \in \Z$ and $y \in G$ that satisfies the following properties:
\begin{itemize}
\item (a) If $y \in \Z$, then $L_{c'} y$ agrees with the operation defined in \Cref{1516-base}.
\item (b) If $y = (a,c,0) \in G'$, then $L_a y = a$.
\item (c) If $y = (a,c,n) \in G'$ and $n \neq 0$, then $L_a y = (a,c,0)$.
\item (d) If $y = (a,c,n) \in G'$ and $b \in \Z$, then $L_{c_{y,b}} y = b$.
\item (e) For any $a,c$, $L_c (a,c,n)$ is only defined for finitely many $n$.
\item (f) If $y = (a,c,n) \in G'$ and $c' \in \Z$ are such that $L_{c'} y$ is defined, then $L_{c'} L_{c'} y$ and $L_a L_{c'} L_{c'} y$ are defined, with $L_a L_{c'} L_{c'} y$ equal to $c'$.
\item (g) If $y = (a,c,n) \in G'$ and $c' \in \Z$ are such that $c' \neq a$ and $L_{c'} y$ is defined, then $L_{c'} y \neq c'$.
nodes.name: Partial solution for 1516 (Axiom B)

nodes.statement: A partial solution exists.
nodes.name: Existence of partial solution (1516)
conclusions: A partial solution exists.
nodes.label: part-exist

nodes.statement: We define $L_{c'} y$ for $y = (a,c,n) \in G'$ as follows: \begin{itemize} \item (i) If $c' = a$ and $n=0$, then $L_{c'} y := a$. \item (ii) If $c' = a$ and $n \neq 0$, then $L_{c'} y := (a,c,0)$. \item (iii) If $c' = c_{y,b}$ for some $b$, then $L_{c'} y := b$. \item (iv) In all other cases, $L_{c'} y$ is undefined. \end{itemize} We of course also define $L_{c'} y$ for $y \in \Z$ using \Cref{1516-base}. From Lemma \ref{aux} we see that this is a well-defined operation, with $L_c y$ undefined for any $y = (a,c,n) \in G'$. So properties (a)-(e) and (g) are clear from construction. Property (e) is also clear from construction in each of the three cases (i), (ii), (iii) (for (i), (ii) we also use the fact that $L_a a = a$).
nodes.name: Proof of Existence of partial solution (1516)
nodes.statement_short: Explicit definition by cases using the useful elements.

nodes.statement: Suppose we have a partial solution for which $L_{c'} y$ is currently undefined for some $c' \in \Z$ and $y \in G$. Then one can extend this partial solution in such a manner that $L_{c'} y$ is now defined.
nodes.name: First extension
assumptions: Suppose we have a partial solution for which $L_{c'} y$ is currently undefined for some $c' \in \Z$ and $y \in G$.
conclusions: one can extend this partial solution in such a manner that $L_{c'} y$ is now defined
nodes.label: first-ext

nodes.statement: Write $y = (a,c,n)$. Because $L_a: \Z \to \Z$ and $L_{c'}: \Z \to \Z$ are surjective, we can find $b \in \Z$ such that $L_a L_{c'} b = c'$. If we had $b=c'$, then $L_a c' = c'$, which from \eqref{1516} (and $Sc' = c'$) implies that $a = c'$, which contradicts the undefined nature of $L_{c'} y$ thanks to properties (b), (c) of a partial solution. Hence, $b \neq c'$. We then set $L_{c'} y := b$. It is then clear that all the properties (a)-(g) of a partial solution are maintained.
nodes.name: Proof of First extension
nodes.statement_short: Surjectivity of $L_a, L_{c'}$ on $\Z$ gives $b$ with $L_aL_{c'}b=c'$, $b\ne c'$; set $L_{c'}y=b$.

nodes.statement: Suppose we have a partial solution, and let $c' \in \Z$ and $y = (a,c,n) \in G$. Then, unless one is in the case when $c'=a$ and $n=0$, then one can find $z \in G$ such that $L_{c'} z$ is currently undefined, but for which one can find an extension of the partial solution for which $L_{c'} z$ is now equal to $y$.

assumptions: Suppose we have a partial solution, and let $c' \in \Z$ and $y = (a,c,n) \in G$.

By Lemma ef{aux}, $c_{w,c'}$ is distinct from $c'$, and from property (d) of a partial solution, $L_{c_{w,c'}} w = c'$. By property (e) of a partial solution, we can find $z = (c_{w,c'}, c', n')$ such that $L_{c'} z$ is currently undefined. Then set $L_{c'} z := y$, so that we have $L_{c_{w,c'}} L_{c'} L_{c'} z = c'$. One then verifies that all the axioms (a)-(g) of a partial solution are valid in this case. \item Case 2: $c' 
eq a$ and $L_{c'} y = b$ for some $b \in \Z$. By property (g) of a partial solution, $c'

eq c'$. By property (e) of a partial solution, we can find $z = (a', c', n')$ such that $L_{c'} z$ is currently undefined. Then set $L_{c'} z = y$, so that we have $L_{a'} L_{c'} L_{c'} z = c'$. One then verifies that all the axioms (a)-(g) of a partial solution are valid in this case. \item Case 3: $c'
