nodes.statement: There exists a way to extend $L_b: \Z \to \Z$ to $L_b: G \to G$ for all $b \in \Z$, in such a way that Axiom B holds, and furthermore for each $b \in \Z$ and $x \in G'$, the set $\{ y \in G': L_b y = x \}$ is infinite. Also, we can ensure that $L_b x \neq x$ for any $b \in \Z$ and $x \in G'$.
nodes.name: Obtaining Axiom B
conclusions: There exists a way to extend $L_b: \Z \to \Z$ to $L_b: G \to G$ for all $b \in \Z$, in such a way that Axiom B holds
nodes.label: axiom-b

nodes.statement: By iterating \Cref{first-ext} and \Cref{second-ext} in alternation, we can find an increasing chain of partial solutions with the property that for any $y = (a,c,n) \in G'$ and $c' \in \Z$ and any natural number $k$, excluding the case where $c'=a$ and $n=0$, that one can find a partial solution on this chain for which $L_{c'} y$ is defined, and such that $L_{c'} z = y$ for at least $k$ distinct choices of $z \in G'$. Taking the limit of this chain, we can then find a fully defined operation $L_{c'} y$ for $c' \in \Z$ and $y \in G$ satisfying the properties (a)-(d), (f), (g) (but not (e)) of a partial solution, with the property that $y = (a,c,n) \in G'$ and $c' \in \Z$, excluding the case $c'=a$ and $n=0$, that there are infinitely many $z \in G'$ such that $L_{c'} z = y$. The excluded case $c'=a, n=0$ is also covered by property (b) of a partial solution. The claim follows.
nodes.name: Proof of Obtaining Axiom B
nodes.statement_short: Alternate the two extension lemmas along a chain and take the limit.

nodes.statement: One can find maps $L_x: G \to G$ for each ``non-square'' $x \in G'$, such that Axioms A, C hold.
nodes.name: Obtaining Axioms A, C
conclusions: One can find maps $L_x: G \to G$ for each ``non-square'' $x \in G'$, such that Axioms A, C hold.
nodes.label: axiom-c

nodes.statement: We can work with a single $x \in G'$. Our task is to find a function $L_x$ for which \begin{equation} L_x x = Sx \end{equation} and \begin{equation} L_{Sy} L_x L_x y = x \end{equation} for all $y \in G$ (note that $L_{Sy}$ is already fully constructed). Define a \emph{seed} to be an injective partial function $L_x$ defined on finitely many values and satisfying \Cref{axioma-again}, as well as \Cref{axiomb-again} whenever $L_x L_x y$ is defined. If there is a $y \in G$ for which $L_x y$ is currently undefined, then by hypothesis $y$ is equal to $L_x z$ for at most one $z$. If such a $z$ exists, we set $L_x y$ to be an element of $\{ w: L_{Sz} w = x \}$ different from $y$ that is not already in the domain or range of $L_x$; we are able to do so thanks to the infinite surjectivity (\Cref{1516-base} (ii)) and the fact that the domain and the range of $L_x$ are finite. If no such $z$ exists, we set $L_x y$ to be arbitrary element of $G$ not already in the domain or range. In either case, we see that the seed property is preserved. Starting from the seed in which $L_x$ is only defined on $x$ and maps it to $Sx$, we obtain the claim.
nodes.name: Proof of Obtaining Axioms A, C
nodes.statement_short: Greedy injective seed for each $L_x$, extended using infinite surjectivity.

nodes.statement: L_x x = Sx
nodes.name: Axiom A restated

nodes.statement: L_{Sy} L_x L_x y = x
nodes.name: Axiom C restated

nodes.statement: There exists a 1516 magma that does not satisfy the 255 equation $$x = ((x \op x) \op x) \op x.$$
nodes.name: 1516 does not imply 255
conclusions: There exists a 1516 magma that does not satisfy the 255 equation $$x = ((x \op x) \op x) \op x.$$

nodes.statement: Let us define the element $x_0 := (0, 1, 0) \in G'$. Since $S x_0 = 0$, we know that $0 \op x_0 = 0$ (see the first part of the proof of \Cref{axiom-b}). Therefore, $x_0$ does not satisfy the 255 equation, as we have $$((x_0 \op x_0) \op x_0) \op x_0 = (0 \op x_0) \op x_0 = 0 \op x_0 = 0 \neq x_0.$$
nodes.name: Proof of 1516 does not imply 255

nodes.statement: x = (y \op y) \op ((y \op x) \op y).
nodes.name: Equation 1729

nodes.statement:
Using the squaring operator $Sy := y \op y$ and the left and right multiplication operators $L_y x := y \op x$ and $R_y x = x \op y$, this law can be written as
$$ L_{Sy} R_y L_{y} x = x.$$
nodes.name: Operators S, L, R (1729 chapter)

nodes.statement: This implies that $L_y$ is injective and $L_{Sy}$ is surjective, hence $L_{Sy}$ is invertible.
nodes.name: Injectivity and invertibility for 1729

nodes.statement: If $y$ is a square (i.e., $y \in SM$), then $L_y$ and $L_{Sy}$ are both invertible, hence now $R_y$ is also invertible, with inverse $R_y^{-1} = L_y L_{Sy}$.
nodes.name: Right multiplication by squares is invertible

nodes.statement: Let $SM$ be a magma satisfying 1729, and let $N$ be another set disjoint from $SM$, and set $M := SM \uplus N$. Suppose that we have a squaring map $S': N \to SM$ (which will complement the existing squaring map $S: SM \to SM$), and bijections $L'_a, R'_a: N \to N$ for all $a \in SM$ (which will complement the existing bijections $L_a, R_a: SM \to SM$ coming from $SM$), satisfying the following axioms: \begin{itemize} \item (i) For all $a \in SM$, we have $L'_a = (R'_a)^{-1} (L'_{Sa})^{-1}$. \item (ii) For all $y \in N$, the elements $R'_a y \in N$ are distinct from each other and from $y$ as $a \in SM$ varies. \item (iii) If $R'_a x = y$ for some $a \in SM$ and some $x,y \in N$, then $L'_{S'y} L_{L_{S'x}^{-1} a} y = x$. \item (iv) For all $x \in N$, we have $(L'_{S'x})^2 x = x$. \end{itemize} Suppose also that we have an operation $\op': N \times N \to M$ satisfying the following axioms: \begin{itemize} \item (v) For all $x \in N$, we have $x \op' x = S'x$. \item (vi) For all $y \in N$ and $a \in SM$, we have $R'_a y \op' y = L_{S'y}^{-1} a$. \item (vii) For all $x,y \in N$ with $x \op' y$ not already covered by rules (v) or (vi), we have $x \op' y = z$ for some $z \in N$. Furthermore, $z \op' x = (L'_{S'x})^{-1} y$. \end{itemize} Then one can endow $M$ with an operation $\op'': M \times M \to M$ satisfying 1729 defined as follows: \begin{itemize} \item If $a,b \in SM$, then $a \op'' b = a \op b$. \item If $a \in SM$ and $x \in N$, then $a \op'' b := L'_a b$. \item If $x \in N$ and $a \in SM$, then $b \op'' a := R'_a b$. \item If $x,y \in N$, then $x \op'' y := x \op' y$. \end{itemize} Furthermore, the 817 law $x \op'' SS' x = x$ fails for any $x \in N$.
nodes.name: Extending a 1729 magma
assumptions: Let $SM$ be a magma satisfying 1729, and let $N$ be another set disjoint from $SM$, and set $M := SM \uplus N$.
conclusions: Then one can endow $M$ with an operation $\op'': M \times M \to M$ satisfying 1729 defined as follows:
Furthermore, the 817 law $x \op'' SS' x = x$ fails for any $x \in N$.
nodes.statement_short: Extending a 1729 magma by non-squares $N$ with maps satisfying axioms (i)-(vii) yields a 1729 magma failing 817.
nodes.label: mag

nodes.statement: We need to show that $\op''$ verifies the law \Cref{1729}. In the case when $x,y \in SM$, then the claim follows from the fact that $SM$ already satisfied this equation. If $x$ was equal to an element $a \in SM$ and $y \in N$, then by construction the law is equivalent to $L'_{Sa} R'_a L'_a y = y$, which follows from axiom (i). Now suppose that $x \in N$ and $y$ is equal to some element $a$ of $SM$. From axiom (v) we have $x \op'' x = S'x$, and then this case of \Cref{1729} becomes $$L_{S'x} ( R'_a x \op' x ) = a$$ which follows from axiom (vi). So the only remaining case is when $x,y \in N$. Using axiom (ii), we can divide into cases: \begin{itemize} \item Case 1: $x=y$. Then by (v) we need to show that $L'_{S'x} L'_{S'x} x = x$, which follows from axiom (iv). \item Case 2: $y = R'_a x$ for some $a \in SM$. Then by axiom (vi), we need to show that $L'_{S'y} L'_{L_{S'x}^{-1} a} y = x$, which follows from axiom (iii). \item Case 3: We are not in case 1 or case 2. Then by axiom (vii), we have $y \op'' x = z$ for some $z \in N$ with $z \op'' y = (L'_{S'y})^{-1} x$. But this implies $L'_{S'y} (z \op'' y) = x$, which is \Cref{1729}. \end{itemize} We have now verified that $\op''$ satisfies 1729. For any $x \in N$, we have $x \op'' SS' x = R'_{SS' x} x$, and so the final claim follows from axiom (ii).
nodes.name: Proof of Extending a 1729 magma
nodes.statement_short: Verify 1729 by cases on whether $x,y$ lie in $SM$ or $N$, using axioms (i)-(vii).

nodes.name: Reduction of 1729 not implying 817

nodes.statement: Take $SM$ to be a countably infinite abelian group of exponent $4$, generated by generators $E_n$ for $n \in \N$ subject to the relations $4E_n=0$.
nodes.name: Definition of SM
nodes.genus: countably infinite abelian group of exponent $4$
nodes.label: sm-def

nodes.statement: $SM$ is a 1729 magma, the squaring operation $S: SM \to SM$ is just the doubling map $Sa = 2a$, and the double squaring map $S^2: SM \to SM$ is constant: $S^2 a = 0$ for all $a \in SM$.
nodes.name: Basic properties of SM
conclusions: $SM$ is a 1729 magma, the squaring operation $S: SM \to SM$ is just the doubling map $Sa = 2a$, and the double squaring map $S^2: SM \to SM$ is constant: $S^2 a = 0$ for all $a \in SM$.
nodes.label: sm-1729

nodes.statement: Routine verification.
nodes.name: Proof of Basic properties of SM

nodes.statement: Take $N$ to be the free non-abelian group with a generator $e_a$ for each $a \in SM$, thus $N$ is the set of reduced words using the alphabet $e_a$, $e_a^{-1}$. Two elements $x,y \in SM$ are said to be \emph{adjacent} if $x = e_a y$ or $y = e_a x$ for some $a \in SM$; this defines a left Cayley graph on $N$. We make a partial ordering $\leq$ on $N$ by declaring $y \leq x$ if $y$ is a right subword of $x$ (or equivalently, $y$ is on the unique simple path from $1$ to $x$). For instance, if $a,b,c \in SM$ are distinct, then $$ 1 \leq e_c \leq e_b^{-1} e_c \leq e_a e_b^{-1} e_c.$$ If $x \in N$ is not the identity, we define the \emph{parent} of $x$ to be the unique element $y \in N$ adjacent to $x$ whose reduced word is shorter. For instance, the parent of $e_a e_b^{-1} e_c$ is $e_b^{-1} e_c$.
nodes.name: Definition of N
nodes.label: n-def

nodes.statement: $N$ is countable, and $\leq$ is a partial ordering.
nodes.name: Basic properties of N
conclusions: $N$ is countable, and $\leq$ is a partial ordering.
nodes.label: n-prop

nodes.statement: Routine verification.
nodes.name: Proof of Basic properties of N

nodes.statement: We set \begin{equation} R'_a x := e_a x \end{equation} for all $a \in SM$ and $x \in N$.
nodes.name: Definition of R'_a
nodes.label: ra-defn

nodes.statement: R'_a x := e_a x
nodes.name: R'_a as left translation
nodes.label: ra-def

nodes.statement: The operators $R'_a$ are bijective and satisfy axiom (ii).
nodes.name: Basic properties of R'_a
conclusions: The operators $R'_a$ are bijective and satisfy axiom (ii).
nodes.label: ra-prop

nodes.statement: Routine verification.
nodes.name: Proof of Basic properties of R'_a

nodes.statement:
From two applications of \Cref{lys} and the exponent 4 hypothesis we have
$$ L'_a = (R'_a)^{-1} (L'_{2a})^{-1} = (R'_a)^{-1} L'_0 R'_{2a}.$$
nodes.name: Left multiplications determined by L'_0
Definition of L'_a from L'_0
Axiom (i')

nodes.statement: Suppose we have a bijection $L'_0: N \to N$ that satisfies axiom (i'), and then define $L'_a$ for all $a \in SM$ by the formula \eqref{la0}. Then this recovers $L'_0$ when $a=0$ (to formalize this it may be convenient to give $L'_0$ and $L'_a$ distinct names), and the $L'_a$ are all bijections and satisfy axiom (i). Furthermore, we have \begin{equation} (L'_a)^{-1} := (R'_{2a})^{-1} L'_0 R'_0 R'_{a} \end{equation} for all $a \in SM$.
nodes.name: Using L'_0 to construct L'_a
assumptions: Suppose we have a bijection $L'_0: N \to N$ that satisfies axiom (i'), and then define $L'_a$ for all $a \in SM$ by the formula \eqref{la0}.
conclusions: this recovers $L'_0$ when $a=0$
the $L'_a$ are all bijections and satisfy axiom (i)
nodes.label: l0-la

nodes.statement: Routine verification.
nodes.name: Proof of Using L'_0 to construct L'_a

nodes.statement:
We now write the other remaining axioms in terms of $L'_0$ rather than $L'_a$ using \Cref{la0}, \Cref{la1}, \Cref{ra-def}, and the magma law on $SM$:
\begin{itemize}
\item (iii')  If $R'_a x = y$ for some $a \in SM$ and some $x,y \in N$, then $(R'_{S'y})^{-1} L'_0 R'_{2S'y} (R'_{a - S'x})^{-1} L'_0 R'_{2(a - S'x)} y = x$.
\item (iv')  For all $x \in N$, we have $(R'_{S'x})^{-1} L'_0 R'_{2S'x} (R'_{S'x})^{-1} L'_0 R'_{2S'x} x = x$.
\item (v)  For all $x \in N$, we have $x \op' x = S'x$.
\item (vi')  For all $y \in N$ and $a \in SM$, we have $e_a y \op' y = a - S'y$.
\item (vii')  For all $x,y \in N$ with $x \op' y$ not already covered by rules (v) or (v'), we have $x \op' y = z$ for some $z \in N$.  Furthermore, $z \op' x = (R'_{2S'x})^{-1} L'_0 e_0 e_{S'x} y$.
nodes.name: Axioms (iii')-(vii')

nodes.statement: Suppose we can find a function $S': N \to SM$, a bijection $L'_0: N \to N$, and an operation $\op': N \times N \to SM \uplus N$ satisfying axioms (i'), (iii'), (iv'), (v), (vi'), (vii'). Then there exists a magma satisfying 1729 but not 817.
nodes.name: Reduction to new axioms
assumptions: Suppose we can find a function $S': N \to SM$, a bijection $L'_0: N \to N$, and an operation $\op': N \times N \to SM \uplus N$ satisfying axioms (i'), (iii'), (iv'), (v), (vi'), (vii').
conclusions: there exists a magma satisfying 1729 but not 817
nodes.label: axiom-reduce

nodes.statement: Construct the $L'_a$ using \Cref{l0-la}. By \Cref{ra-prop} and direct verification we can noe verify axioms (i)-(vii), and then the claim follows from \Cref{mag}.
nodes.name: Proof of Reduction to new axioms
nodes.statement_short: Build $L'_a$ from $L'_0$, verify axioms (i)-(vii), apply the extension theorem.

nodes.statement:
Firstly, the axiom (i'), together with \eqref{ra-def} means that we cannot restrict $L'_0$ to be partially defined on just finitely many values: any relation of the form
$$ L'_0 x = y$$
for some $x,y \in N$ would automatically imply that
\begin{equation} L'_0 (R'_0)^n x = (R'_0)^n y
\end{equation}
and also
\begin{equation} L'_0 (R'_0)^n y = (R'_0)^{n-1} x
\end{equation}
for all $n \in \Z$.
nodes.name: L'_0 relations propagate along cosets

nodes.statement: So we will need to truncate this iteration by creating an addition category of ``pending'' identities $I[x,y,z]$ of the form ``$z \op' x = (R'_{2S'x})^{-1} L'_0 R'_0 e_{S'x} y$'' for some $x,y,z \in N$, which will be temporarily undefined because $S'x$ is undefined.
nodes.name: Pending identities

nodes.statement: A \emph{partial solution} $(L'_0, \op', S', {\mathcal I})$ is a collection of the following data: \begin{itemize} \item A partially defined function $L'_0: N \to N$, defined on a finite union of right cosets of $\langle e_0\rangle$; \item A partially defined operation $\op': N \times N \to M$, defined on a finite set; \item A partially defined function $S': N \to SM$, defined on a finite set; and \item A finite collection ${\mathcal I}$ of ``pending identities'' $I[x,y,z]$, which one can think of either as ordered triples of elements $x,y,z \in N$, or as formal strings of the form ``$z \op' x = (R'_{2S'x})^{-1} L'_0 R'_0 R'_{S'x} y$'' for some $x,y,z \in N$. \end{itemize} Furthermore, the following axioms are satisfied: \begin{itemize} \item (i'') $L'_0 x$ is defined and equal to $y$, then we have the identities \Cref{itero}, \Cref{itero-2} for all $n\in \Z$. \item (S) If $S'x$ is defined for some $x \in N$, then $S'y$ is defined for all $y \leq x$. \item (iii'') If $R'_a x = y$ for some $a \in SM$ and some $x,y \in N$, and $S'x, S'y$ are defined, then $(R'_{S'y})^{-1} L'_0 R'_{2S'y} (R'_{a-S'x})^{-1} L'_0 R'_{2(a-S'x)} y$ is defined and equal to $x$. \item (iv'') If $x \in N$ is such that $S'x$ is defined, then $(R'_{S'x})^{-1} L'_0 R'_{2S'x} (R'_{S'x})^{-1} L'_0 R'_{2S'x} x$ is defined and equal to $x$. \item (v'') If $x \in N$ and $x \op' x$ is defined, then $S'x$ is defined and equal to $x \op' x$. \item (vi'') For all $y \in N$ and $a \in SM$, if $R'_a y \op' y$ is defined, then $a - S'y$ is defined and equal to $R'_a y \op' y$. \item (vii'') For all $x,y \in N$ and $x$ is not equal to $y$ or $R'_a y$ for any $a \in SM$, and $x \op' y$ is defined, then it is equal to some $z \in N$. Furthermore, either $I[x,y,z]$ is a pending identity, or else $z \op' x$ and $(R'_{2S'x})^{-1} L'_0 R'_0 R'_{S'x} y$ are defined and equal to each other. \item (P) If $I[x,y,z]$ is a pending identity, then $x,y,z \in N$, and $Sx$ and $z \op' x$ are undefined. Furthermore, $z$ is not equal to $x$ or $R'_a x$ for any $a \in SM$, and $y$ is not of the form $(R'_0)^n x$ or $(R'_0)^n y_0$ for any $n$, where $y_0$ is the parent of $x$. \item (P') If $I[x,y,z]$ and $I[x,y',z]$ are pending identities, then $y=y'$. \item (P'') If $I[x,y,z]$ is a pending identity, then $x \op' y = z$. \item (L) If $y$ is the parent of $x$ with $x = R'_a y$, and $(R'_{a-S'y})^{-1} L'_0 R'_{2(a-S'y)} x$ is defined, then it is not equal to $x$. \end{itemize} We say that one partial solution $(\tilde L'_0, \tilde \op', \tilde S', \tilde {\mathcal I})$ \emph{extends} another if $(L'_0, \op', S', {\mathcal I})$ if $\tilde L'$ is an extension of $L'_0$, $\tilde \op'$ is an extension of $\op'$, and $\tilde S'$ is an extension of $S'$. (No constraint is imposed on the final components $\tilde {\mathcal I}, {\mathcal I}$.) This is a preordering.
nodes.name: Partial solution for 1729
nodes.statement_short: Partial $L'_0$ on finitely many cosets, partial $\op'$ and $S'$, and pending identities, subject to local versions of the axioms plus (S), (P), (P'), (P''), (L).
nodes.label: part-sol

nodes.statement: There exists a partial solution.
nodes.name: Existence of partial solution (1729)
conclusions: There exists a partial solution.
nodes.label: partial-exist

nodes.statement: Set $L'_0, \op', S'$ to be empty functions, and have the set of pending identities to also be empty. The verification of the required axioms is then routine.
nodes.name: Proof of Existence of partial solution (1729)

nodes.statement: Suppose that one has a sequence $(L'_{0,n}, \op'_{n}, S'_{n}, {\mathcal I}_n)$ of partial solutions, each one an extension of the previous, such that for any $x, y \in N$, $L'_{0,n} x$, $x \op'_{n} y$, and $S'_n x$ are defined for some $n$. Then there exists a 1729 magma that does not satisfy 817.
nodes.name: Chain of partial solutions
assumptions:
Suppose that one has a sequence
$(L'_{0,n}, \op'_{n}, S'_{n}, {\mathcal I}_n)$ of partial solutions, each one an extension of the previous, such that for any $x, y \in N$, $L'_{0,n} x$, $x \op'_{n} y$, and $S'_n x$ are defined for some $n$.
conclusions: there exists a 1729 magma that does not satisfy 817
nodes.label: chain

nodes.statement: Take the direct limit of the chain to obtain total functions $L'_0, \op', S'$. The axioms (i'), (iii'), (iv''), (v''), (vi''), (vii'') of the partial solutions then easily imply that the direct limit satisfies the axioms (i'), (iii'), (iv'), (v), (vi'), (vii') (one also uses axiom (P) to note that all pending identities disappear in the direct limit). The claim now follows from \Cref{axiom-reduce}.
nodes.name: Proof of Chain of partial solutions
nodes.statement_short: Direct limit satisfies the total axioms; apply the reduction lemma.

nodes.statement: Suppose one has a partial solution in which $L'_0 x$ is undefined for some $x \in N$. Then one can extend the partial solution so that $L'_0 x$ is now defined.
nodes.name: Enlarging L'_0
assumptions: Suppose one has a partial solution in which $L'_0 x$ is undefined for some $x \in N$.
conclusions: one can extend the partial solution so that $L'_0 x$ is now defined
nodes.label: enlarge-l0

nodes.statement: By axiom (i''), $L'_0 (R'_0)^n x$ is undefined for every integer $n$. Let $d = E_m$ be a generator of $SM$ that does not appear as a component of any index of any of the generators $e_a$ appearing anywhere in the partial solution; such a $d$ exists due to the finiteness hypotheses. We set $L'_0 x := e_d$, and then extend by \Cref{itero}, \Cref{itero-2}, thus $$L'_0 (R'_0)^n x := (R'_0)^n e_d$$ and $$L'_0 (R'_0)^n e_d := (R'_0)^{n-1} x.$$ Because of the new nature of $d$, no collisions in the partial function $L_0$ are created by this operation. It is then easy to check that axiom (i'') is preserved by this operation, whereas none of the other axioms (S), (iii''), (iv''), (v''), (vi''), (vii''), (P), (P'), (P'') are affected by this extension. With some effort, axiom (L) can also be verified.
nodes.name: Proof of Enlarging L'_0
nodes.statement_short: Define $L'_0 x$ as a fresh generator $e_d$ and propagate along cosets.

nodes.statement: Suppose one has a partial solution. Let $A$ be a finite subset of $N$. Then one can extend the partial solution so that $L'_0 x$ is now defined for all $x \in A$.
nodes.name: Enlarging L'_0 many times
assumptions: Suppose one has a partial solution.
Let $A$ be a finite subset of $N$.
conclusions: one can extend the partial solution so that $L'_0 x$ is now defined for all $x \in A$
nodes.label: enlarge-l0-many

nodes.statement: Iterate Proposition \ref{enlarge-l0} in the obvious fashion.
nodes.name: Proof of Enlarging L'_0 many times

nodes.statement: Suppose one has a partial solution in which $S'x$ is undefined for some $x \in N$, but $S'y$ is defined for all $y < x$. (This hypothesis is vacuous for $x=1$.) Let $y_0$ be the parent of $x$ (if $x \neq 1$), and assume the following additional axioms: \begin{itemize} \item (A) If $R'_a x = y_0$ for some $a \in SM$, then $L'_0 R'_{S' y_0} x$ is defined. \item (B) If $x = R'_a y_0$ for some $a \in SM$, then $L'_0 R'_{2(a-S'y_0)} x$ is defined. \item (C) If $I[x,y,z]$ for some $y,z \in N$, and $S'z$ is defined, then $L'_0 R'_0 R'_{S'z} x$ is defined. \end{itemize} Then one can extend the partial solution so that $S'x$ is now defined.
nodes.name: Enlarging S' with induction hypothesis and axioms
assumptions: Suppose one has a partial solution in which $S'x$ is undefined for some $x \in N$, but $S'y$ is defined for all $y < x$.
conclusions: one can extend the partial solution so that $S'x$ is now defined
nodes.label: enlarge-S-induct-axioms

nodes.statement: Let $d_0, d_1 \in SM$ be generators $E_{n_0}$ of $SM$ that do not appear in the index $a$ of any $e_a$ that currently appears in the partial solution (of which there are only finitely many). We also set some further distinct generators $d'_{y,z} \in SM$ for $y,z \in SM$ that are distinct from each other and all previous generators (this is possible as we have infinitely many generators). We set $S'x, x \op' x := d_0$; this preserves axiom (S) and (v''). We set $$ L'_0 R'_{2d_0} x := e_{d_1}$$ $$ L'_0 R'_{2d_0} (R'_{d_0})^{-1} e_{d_1} := R'_{d_0} x$$ and then extend these choices using \Cref{itero}, \Cref{itero-2} to recover axiom (i'), thus for instance $$ L'_0 (R'_0)^n R'_{2d_0} x := (R'_0)^n e_{d_1}$$ and $$ L'_0 (R'_0)^n e_{d_1} := (R'_0)^{n-1} R'_{2d_0} x$$ for all $n \in \Z$. To retain axiom (iii''), we perform the following actions: \begin{itemize} \item If $y_0$ is undefined, do nothing. \item If $R'_a x = y_0$ for some $a \in SM$ (so that $L'_0 R'_{S'y_0} x$ is defined, by hypothesis (A)), set $L'_0 R'_{2(a-d_0)} y_0 := R'_{a-d_0} (R'_{2S'y_0})^{-1} R'_0 L'_0 R'_{S'y_0} x$. Then extend using \Cref{itero}, \Cref{itero-2}. \item If $x = R'_a y_0$ for some $a \in SM$ (so that $L'_0 R'_{2(a-Sy_0)} x$ is already defined, by hypothesis (B)), set $L'_0 R'_{2d_0} (R'_{a-S'y_0})^{-1} L'_0 R'_{2(a-Sy_0)} x :=R'_{d_0} y_0$, and extend using \Cref{itero}, \Cref{itero-2}. \end{itemize} To retain axiom (P), we perform the following actions for each pending identity of the form $I[x,y,z]$ for some $y,z$, executed in some arbitrary order. \begin{itemize} \item Remove this identity $I[x,y,z]$ from the list of pending identities. \item Set $L'_0 R'_0 R'_{d_0} y := e_{d'_{y,z}}$, and $x' \op y' := z'$, where $(x',y',z') := (z, x, (R'_{2d_0})^{-1} e_{d'_{y,z}})$. Extend all the new definitions of $L'_0$ using \Cref{itero}, \Cref{itero-2}. \item If $S'x'$ is undefined, add $I[x',y',z']$ as a pending identity. \item If instead $S'x'$ is defined (which makes $L'_0 R'_0 R'_{S'x'} y'$ defined, by axiom (C)), set $x'' \op y'' = z''$, where $(x'',y'',z'') := (z', x', (R'_{2S'x'})^{-1} L'_0 R'_0 R'_{S'x'} y')$. Then add $I[x'',y'',z'']$ as a pending identity. \end{itemize} One can check that these definitions do not cause any collisions in the partial function $L'_0$, and that axioms (i'), (iii'), (iv''), (v''), (vii''), (P), (P'), (P'') are preserved; the remaining axiom (vi'') is unaffected by this extension. Axiom (L) can also be shown to be preserved after a tedious calculation.
nodes.name: Proof of Enlarging S' with induction hypothesis and axioms
nodes.statement_short: Set $S'x$ to a fresh generator, define new $L'_0$ values along cosets, repair axiom (iii'') and process pending identities.

nodes.statement: Suppose one has a partial solution in which $S'x$ is undefined for some $x \in N$, but $S'y$ is defined for all $y < x$. (This hypothesis is vacuous for $x=1$.) Then one can extend the partial solution so that $S'x$ is now defined.
nodes.name: Enlarging S' with induction hypothesis
assumptions: Suppose one has a partial solution in which $S'x$ is undefined for some $x \in N$, but $S'y$ is defined for all $y < x$.
conclusions: one can extend the partial solution so that $S'x$ is now defined
nodes.label: enlarge-S-induct

nodes.statement: Let $y_0$ be the parent of $x$, that is to say the unique neighbor of $x$ in the path to $1$ (this is only defined for $x \neq 1$), then by axiom (i'') $y_0$ is the unique neighbor for which $S'y_0$ is defined, and we either have $x = R'_a y_0$ or $R'_a x = y_0$ for some unique $a \in SM$. By using \Cref{enlarge-l0-many}, we may impose axioms (A), (B), (C) without loss of generality, as this only imposes a finite set of conditions. The claim now follows from \Cref{enlarge-S-induct-axioms}.
nodes.name: Proof of Enlarging S' with induction hypothesis
nodes.statement_short: Impose (A),(B),(C) by enlarging $L'_0$ finitely often, then apply the previous proposition.

nodes.statement: Suppose one has a partial solution in which $S'x$ is undefined for some $x \in N$. Then one can extend the partial solution so that $S'x$ is now defined.
nodes.name: Enlarging S'
assumptions: Suppose one has a partial solution in which $S'x$ is undefined for some $x \in N$.
conclusions: one can extend the partial solution so that $S'x$ is now defined
nodes.label: enlarge-S

nodes.statement: Obtained by induction from Proposition \ref{enlarge-S-induct}, using the fact that there are no infinite descending chains in $N$.
nodes.name: Proof of Enlarging S'
nodes.statement_short: Well-founded induction on $N$ using the previous proposition.

nodes.statement: Suppose one has a partial solution in which $x \op' y$ is undefined for some $x,y \in N$. Then one can extend the partial solution so that $x \op' y$ is now defined.
nodes.name: Enlarging the operation
assumptions: Suppose one has a partial solution in which $x \op' y$ is undefined for some $x,y \in N$.
conclusions: one can extend the partial solution so that $x \op' y$ is now defined
nodes.label: enlarge-op

nodes.statement: By applying \Cref{enlarge-S} as needed, we may assume without loss of generality that $S'x$ and $S'y$ are already defined (among other things, this removes the possibility that $x \op' y$ is part of a pending identity). If this makes $x \op' y$ defined, then we are done, so we may assume that this is not the case. Similarly, by using \Cref{enlarge-l0}, we may assume without loss of generality that $L'_0 R'_0 R'_{S'x} y$ is defined. We now divide into cases: Case 1: $x=y$. In this case we set $x \op' y := S'x$. It is clear that this preserves axiom (v''), and no other axiom is impacted. Case 2: If $x = R'_a y$ for some $a \in SM$, then we set $x \op' y := a - S'y$. This preserves axiom (vi''), and no other axiom is impacted. Case 3: If $x$ is not equal to $y$ or $R'_a y$ for any $a \in SM$. Let $d_0 \in SM$ be a generator that does not appear as a component of any index of any of the generators $e_a$ appearing anywhere in the partial solution. We set $x \op' y := z$ with $z := e^2_{d_0}$. This temporarily disrupts axiom (vii''). To recover it, we perform the following actions. \begin{itemize} \item Set $x' \op' y' = z'$, where $(x',y',z') := (z, x, (R'_{2S'x})^{-1} L_0 R'_0 R'_{Sx} y)$. \item Add $I[x',y',z']$ as a pending identity. \end{itemize} One can check that these definitions do not cause any collisions in the partial function $L'_0$, and that axioms (i'), (vii'), (P), (P') are preserved; the remaining axioms (S), (iii''), (iv''), (v''), (vi'') are unaffected by this extension.
nodes.name: Proof of Enlarging the operation
nodes.statement_short: Make $S'x,S'y$ and the needed $L'_0$ value defined, then three cases; in the generic case add a fresh product and a pending identity.

nodes.statement: We write $a \rightarrow b$ if $a\ R\ b$ holds in $A$, and say that $a$ \emph{rewrites to} (or \emph{reduces to}) $b$. We further define \begin{itemize} \item $\rightarrow^+$ as the transitive closure of $R$. \item $\rightarrow^*$ as the reflexive transitive closure of $R$. \item $\leftrightarrow^*$ as the reflexive transitive and symmetric closure of $R$. \end{itemize} We sometimes write $b\leftarrow a$, (resp. $b\ {}^*\leftarrow a$ etc) to mean $a\rightarrow b$ (resp. $a\rightarrow^*b$ etc), and chain notations, e.g. $b_1\leftarrow a\rightarrow b_2$.
nodes.name: Rewriting relations

nodes.statement: We say that $R$ is \emph{Church-Rosser} if whenever $a\leftrightarrow^* b$, there exists some $c$ such that \[a\rightarrow^* c\ {}^*\leftarrow b\] We say that $R$ is \emph{confluent} if whenever $b_1\ {}^*\leftarrow a\rightarrow^* b_2$ there exists some $c$ such that $b_1\rightarrow^* c\ {}^*\leftarrow b_2$. We say that $R$ is \emph{locally confluent} if whenever $b_1\leftarrow a\rightarrow b_2$ there exists some $c$ such that $b_1\rightarrow^* c\ {}^*\leftarrow b_2$. We say that (an arbitrary) $a$ is in \emph{normal form} (or $a$ is a normal form) if there is no $a' \neq a$ such that $a \rightarrow a'$, and that $R$ is \emph{weakly normalizing} if for every $a$, there is some $a'$ such that $a\rightarrow^*a'$ and $a'$ is in normal form. We say that $R$ is \emph{strongly normalizing} if there are no infinite rewrite sequences $a_1\rightarrow a_2\rightarrow \ldots$. In particular, a strongly normalizing $R$ is also weakly normalizing.
nodes.name: Church-Rosser, confluence and normalization

nodes.statement: If $R$ is Church-Rosser, then any normal form is \emph{unique}.
nodes.name: Uniqueness of normal forms
assumptions: If $R$ is Church-Rosser
conclusions: any normal form is \emph{unique}

nodes.statement: This means that, in this situation, $a$ and $b$ reduce to an identical normal form $c$ \emph{if and only if} $a\leftrightarrow^* b$!
nodes.name: Normal forms decide equivalence

nodes.statement:
This means that we have the following algorithm to decide $a\leftrightarrow^* b$ (and therefore $a\approx b$ if these relations coincide):
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Repeatedly apply $R$ to $a$ and $b$ until normal forms $a'$ and $b'$ are found for them (this is possible because $R$ is strongly normalizing).
  \item Compare $a'$ and $b'$ for exact equality (sometimes called ``syntactic equality'').
  \item If $a' = b'$, we can conclude $a\leftrightarrow^* b$.
  \item If $a' \neq b'$ can can conclude that they are \emph{not} equivalent due to the lemma.
nodes.name: Deciding equivalence by normal forms
nodes.statement_short: Reduce both terms to normal form and compare syntactically.

nodes.statement: We call such an $R$ \emph{complete for} $\approx$.
nodes.name: Complete rewrite system

nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item $R$ is Church-Rosser iff it is confluent. \item (Newman's lemma) if $R$ is strongly normalizing, then $R$ is confluent iff it is locally confluent. \end{enumerate}
nodes.name: Church-Rosser iff confluent; Newman's lemma
assumptions: if $R$ is strongly normalizing
conclusions: $R$ is Church-Rosser iff it is confluent.
$R$ is confluent iff it is locally confluent
$R$ is Church-Rosser iff it is confluent.

assumptions: if $R$ is strongly normalizing
conclusions: $R$ is confluent iff it is locally confluent

nodes.statement: A convenient way to represent this is via a \emph{rewrite system}: simply a set of pairs of words $(l, r) \in M_{X}$ (we typically write $l\rightarrow r$) which represents the smallest congruence, closed by substitutions that contains those pairs.
nodes.name: Rewrite system

nodes.statement:
Here is a non-confluent example:

\[ x \cdot (y \cdot z) \rightarrow y \]
We have $a\cdot (b \cdot (c \cdot d)) \rightarrow^* b$, but also $a\cdot (b\cdot (c\cdot d))\rightarrow^* a\cdot c$ for any $a, b, c, d$ (which are both in normal form).
nodes.name: A non-confluent rewrite rule

nodes.statement: The high-level idea is therefore to identify such pairs, and add them as an unoriented equation, to be oriented if possible, and repeating until no un-joinable pairs exist.
nodes.name: Knuth-Bendix completion
nodes.statement_short: Repeatedly compute critical pairs, add unjoinable ones as equations oriented if possible, until all are joinable.

nodes.statement: We denote by $w[w']_p$ the word $w$ with $w'$ inserted at position $p$.
nodes.name: Insertion at a position

nodes.statement: Given a rewrite system $R$ and two rules $\rho_1: l_1\rightarrow r_1$ and $\rho_2: l_2\rightarrow r_2$ in $R$, we say that $(t, u)$ is a \emph{critical pair} for $\rho_1$ and $\rho_2$ if there is some non-variable position $p$ in $l_1$ such that $l_2$ unifies with the term at that position. We denote by $\sigma$ the most general unifier thus obtained and have $t = r_1\sigma$ and $u = l_1\sigma[r_2\sigma]_p$
nodes.name: Critical pair

nodes.statement: Given a rewrite system $R$, if for every critical pair $(t, u)$ of $R$, there is a term $v$ such that $t\rightarrow^* v\ {}^*\leftarrow u$, then $R$ is locally confluent.
nodes.name: Critical pair lemma
assumptions: Given a rewrite system $R$, if for every critical pair $(t, u)$ of $R$, there is a term $v$ such that $t\rightarrow^* v\ {}^*\leftarrow u$
conclusions: $R$ is locally confluent

nodes.statement:
There are 57,882 equations of order 5 (not including the 4,694 equations of order $\le 4$).
\begin{itemize}
  \item 19,392 (33.5\%) admit only trivial models.
  \item 38,360 (66.2\%) have known satisfying finite models (and hence, also infinite models).
  \item 106 allow only trivial finite models. Of these, 10 are Austin laws, and it is unknown whether the remaining 96 admit infinite models.
  \item In 24 cases it is unknown whether they allow nontrivial finite models.
nodes.name: Classification of order 5 laws
nodes.statement_short: Of 57,882 order-5 laws: 19,392 only trivial models, 38,360 finite models, 106 only trivial finite models (10 Austin laws), 24 unknown.

nodes.statement: Of these, 10 are Austin laws, and it is unknown whether the remaining 96 admit infinite models.
nodes.name: Do the remaining 96 order-5 laws admit infinite models?

nodes.statement: In 24 cases it is unknown whether they allow nontrivial finite models.
nodes.name: Do 24 order-5 laws admit nontrivial finite models?

nodes.statement: Of the equations with known satisfying finite models, a few had a minimum satisfying model size of order 17 (the largest minimum satisfying model size in order $\le 4$ is 7.) One equation was found with a satisfying model of order 26, but the smaller orders were not exhaustively searched so it cannot be established that the order is minimal.
nodes.name: Minimum model sizes for order 5 laws

nodes.statement: 106 equations were found that admitted only trivial finite models. Of these, Vampire's decision procedure finished without finding an implication to Equation 2 for 10 equations, allowing us to establish that they are inequivalent, e.g. they allow non-trivial infinite models.
nodes.name: Proof that 10 order-5 laws are Austin laws
nodes.statement_short: Vampire's decision procedure finds no implication to the singleton law, so these laws have non-trivial infinite models.

nodes.statement: Hence, they must be Austin laws.
nodes.name: Ten order-5 Austin laws

nodes.statement: Note that Vampire's decision procedure also establishes that all 10 Austin laws are inequivalent to each other.
nodes.name: The ten Austin laws are pairwise inequivalent

nodes.statement: Using the graph of implications and refutations, it identifies equivalence classes/strongly-connected components in the implication graph and possible goals by subtracting out the refutation graph. Iterating through all equivalence classes, it can perform a meet-in-the-middle graph search where it searches outwards from both hypotheses and goals by performing equation substitutions. Depending on the number of hypotheses versus goals, it dynamically adjusts the search depth on both sides based on a configured branching factor.

\item \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?3342}{3342} does not imply 3456, 3522, 4065, 4118.
\item \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?3352}{3352} does not imply 4065.
\item \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?3475}{3475} does not imply 3659.
nodes.name: Final refutations: other two-variable equations

nodes.statement:
In the case of finite magmas, there are some non-trivial positive implications:
\begin{itemize}
\item \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?467}{467} implies 2847.
\item \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?906}{906} implies 3862.
\item \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?1516}{1516} implies 255.
\item \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?1441}{1441} implies 4067.
\item \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?1443}{1443} implies 3055.
\item \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?1681}{1681} implies 3877.
\item \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?1701}{1701} implies 1035.
\item \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?1113}{1113} implies 1167.
\item \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?1167}{1167} implies 1096.

There are also some tricky negative implications:
\begin{itemize}
\item \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?476}{476} does not imply 359, 4065.
\item \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?503}{503} does not imply 4065, 3862.
\item \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?854}{854} does not imply 107, 1248, 1251.
\item \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?1076}{1076} does not imply 2234, 2294, 4435.
\item \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?1518}{1518} does not imply 47, 817.
\item \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?3352}{3352} does not imply 4065.

nodes.name: Tricky finite non-implications

nodes.statement: Does \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?677}{677} imply 255?
nodes.name: Does 677 imply 255 for finite magmas?

nodes.statement: Does \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?13102}{13102} have a non-trivial finite model?
nodes.name: Does 13102 have a non-trivial finite model?
Restate Equation 387 in the form (4.1)
nodes.statement:
(From \href{https://mathoverflow.net/a/450905/766}{MathOverflow}).
  By \Equaref{387}, one has the law
\begin{equation} (x \op x) \op y = y \op x.
\end{equation}

nodes.name: Squares are idempotent
nodes.statement:
Specializing to $y=x \op x$, we conclude
$$(x \op x) \op (x \op x) = (x \op x) \op x$$
and hence by another application of \Equaref{387} we see that $x \op x$ is idempotent:
\begin{equation} (x \op x) \op (x \op x) = x \op x.
\end{equation}

nodes.name: Squares commute with squares
nodes.statement:
Now, replacing $x$ by $x \op x$ in \Cref{387-again} and then using \Cref{idem} we see that
$$ (x \op x) \op y = y \op (x \op x)$$
so in particular $x \op x$ commutes with $y \op y$:
\begin{equation} (x \op x) \op (y \op y) = (y \op y) \op (x \op x).
\end{equation}

nodes.name: Product of squares equals $x\op y$
nodes.statement:
Also, from two applications of \Cref{387-again} one has
$$(x \op x) \op (y \op y) = (y \op y) \op x = x \op y.$$

nodes.name: Conclude commutativity
nodes.statement: Thus \Cref{op-idem} simplifies to $x \op y = y \op x$, which is \Equaref{43}.

nodes.name: Restate 3744
nodes.statement:
By hypothesis, one has
$$x \op y = (x \op z) \op (w \op y)
  $$
for all $x,y,z,w$.

nodes.name: Three specializations
Deduce 3722 and 381
nodes.statement:
\Cref{381-2} gives \Equaref{3722}, while \Cref{381-1}, \Cref{381-2}, \Cref{381-3} gives
$$ x \op y = (x\op z) \op y$$
which is \Equaref{381}.

nodes.name: Trivial direction; cite Kisielewicz for the converse
nodes.statement: The implication of \Equaref{1689} from \Equaref{2} is trivial.  The converse is a surprisingly long chain of implications; see pages 326--327 of \cite{Kisielewicz2}.  With some computer assistance, we found the following human-readable proof.
nodes.statement_short: Trivial direction; cite Kisielewicz for the converse

nodes.name: Introduce powers and functions $f,g$
Reduce to finding $w$ with $f(t,w)=t$
nodes.statement:
The initial equation states $x = (y \op x) \op f(x,z)$.
Our main step will be to prove that for all $t\in M$ there exists $w\in M$ such that $f(t,w) = t$.

nodes.name: Main step implies the singleton law
nodes.statement:
The rest of the proof is then straightforward.
Indeed, the initial equation gives $t = (y \op t) \op f(t,w) = (y \op t) \op t = f(y,t)$ for any $t,y\in M$.
With such a simple expression of $f$ the initial equation becomes $x = (y \op x) \op z$, which easily implies the singleton law, for instance by writing $x = ((y \op w) \op x) \op z = w \op z$ for any $w,x,y,z \in M$.
nodes.statement_short: Main step implies the singleton law

nodes.name: Choose $w=t\op t^7$
nodes.statement: There remains to prove $f(t,w) = t$ for a well-chosen $w \in M$, explicitly, $w=g(t,t^5)=t\op t^7$.

nodes.name: Derive identity (4.8)
Derive identity (4.9)
Compute $f(t,t^3)=g(t,t^5)$
Compute $t^3 = t\op g(t,t^5)$
nodes.statement: On the other hand, \eqref{Kisielewicz-ftg} with $(u,v)=(t,t^5)$ implies $t^3 = t \op g(t,t^5)$.

nodes.name: Conclude $f(t,g(t,t^5))=t$
Assume 1571 and derive 2662
nodes.statement:
Suppose that a magma $G$ satisfies \Equaref{1571}, thus
\begin{equation} x = (y \op z) \op (y \op (x \op z)).
\end{equation}
$$ x = ((x \op y) \op (x \op y)) \op ((x \op y) \op (x \op (x \op y)))$$
and
$$ x = (x \op y) \op (x \op (x \op y))$$
whence
$$x = ((x \op y) \op (x \op y)) \op x$$
which is \Equaref{2662}.

nodes.name: Squares of products agree
nodes.statement:
This gives
$$y = ((y \op z) \op (y \op z)) \op y$$
while from \Cref{1571-again} one has
$$ (y \op z) \op (y \op z) = (x \op y) \op (x \op ((y \op z) \op (y \op z) \op y))$$
whence
$$ (x \op y) \op (x \op y) = (y \op z) \op (y \op z).$$

nodes.name: Squares of products are a constant $e$
nodes.statement:
This implies that $(x \op y) \op (x \op y)$ does not depend on $x$, or on $y$, hence is equal to some constant $e$:
$$ (x \op y) \op (x \op y) = e.$$
nodes.statement_short: Squares of products are a constant $e$

nodes.name: All squares equal $e$: Equation 40
nodes.statement:
From \Cref{1571-again} the magma operation is surjective, hence
\begin{equation} x \op x = e
\end{equation}
which gives \Equaref{40}.

nodes.name: $e$ is an identity element
nodes.statement:
Applying \Cref{1571-again} with $x=y=z$ we conclude
$$ x = e \op (x \op e)$$
while if we instead take $y=z=e$ we have
$$ x = e \op (e \op (x \op e))$$
hence
$$ x = e \op x$$
and then also
$$ x = x \op e$$
from which we readily conclude \Equaref{23}, \Equaref{8}; thus $e$ is an identity element.

nodes.name: Derive Equation 16
nodes.statement:
From \Cref{1571-again} with $z=e$ we now have
\begin{equation} x = y \op (y \op x)
\end{equation}
which is \Equaref{16}.

nodes.name: Derive Equation 14
nodes.statement:
If instead we take $y=e$ we have
\begin{equation} x = z \op (x \op z)
\end{equation}
which is \Equaref{14}.

nodes.name: Derive commutativity
nodes.statement:
So if we substitute $z = x \op y$ and use \Cref{16-again} we obtain
$$ x = (x \op y) \op y$$
and hence
$$ y \op x = y \op ((x \op y) \op y) = x \op y$$
thanks to \Cref{14-again}.  This gives \Equaref{43}, thus $G$ is now commutative.

nodes.name: Derive associativity
nodes.statement:
From \Cref{1571-again} once more one has
$$x \op (y \op z) = (y \op x) \op (z \op ((x \op (y \op z)) \op x))$$
which one can simplify using commutativity and \Cref{16-again} (or \Cref{14-again}) to eventually obtain
$$x \op (y \op z) = (x \op y) \op z$$
which is \Equaref{4512}.

nodes.name: Abelian group of exponent 2; converse easy
nodes.statement: $G$ is now commutative and associative, and every element is its own inverse and of exponent $2$, hence is an abelian group thanks to \Cref{xxe}, so $G$ is an abelian group of exponent $2$ as claimed.  The converse is easily verified.
nodes.statement_short: Abelian group of exponent 2; converse easy

nodes.name: Reduce to 953 implies 2
nodes.statement: It suffices to show that \Equaref{953} implies \Equaref{2}.

nodes.name: Specialize with $x=z=0$
nodes.statement:
Pick an element $0$ of $G$ and define $1 = 0 \op 0$ and $2 = 1 \op 1$ (we do not require $0,1,2$ to be distinct).
From \Equaref{953} with $x=z=0$ we have
$$ 0 = y \op 2.$$

nodes.name: Specialize with $z=1$ and conclude
nodes.statement:
If we then apply \Equaref{953} with $z=1$ we conclude that
$$ x = y \op 0$$
for all $x,y$, from which one concludes $x=x'$ for any $x,x' \in G$, giving \Equaref{2}.

nodes.name: Cite McCune et al.
nodes.statement: See \cite{mccune_et_al}.  In fact this is the shortest law with this property.

nodes.name: Sheffer stroke satisfies the law
nodes.statement: A sketch of proof follows.  One can easily verify that the Sheffer stroke operation satisfies this law.

nodes.name: ATP derives the three Sheffer axioms
nodes.statement:
Conversely, if this law holds, then automated theorem provers can show that the three Sheffer axioms
$$ (x \op x) \op (x \op x)  = x$$
$$ x \op (y \op (y \op y)) = x \op x$$
$$ (x \op (y \op z)) \op (x \op (y \op z)) = ((y \op y) \op x) \op ((z \op z) \op x)$$
are satisfied.
nodes.statement_short: ATP derives the three Sheffer axioms

nodes.name: Conclude by Sheffer's result
nodes.statement: A classical result of Sheffer \cite{sheffer} then allows one to conclude.

nodes.name: Cite Knuth; easy direction
nodes.statement: See \cite[Theorem 5]{knuth}.  The proof is quite lengthy; a sketch is as follows. It is easy to see that natural central groupoids satisfy \Equaref{26302}.

nodes.name: Derive the central groupoid law
Derive $(x\op t)\op t = (t\op t)\op t$
nodes.statement:
Setting $y = (t \op t) \op t$, $z = t \op (t \op t)$, $w = t \op t$ in \Equaref{26302} we also obtain
$$ (x \op t) \op t = (t \op t) \op t.$$

nodes.name: Introduce $x^{(1)},x^{(2)}$ and derive $x\op t = x\op t^{(1)}$
nodes.statement:
Using the notation
$$ x^{(1)} := (x \op x) \op x, \quad x^{(2)} := x \op (x \op x)$$
we then have
\begin{align*}
  x \op t &= ((x \op x) \op (x \op t)) \op ((x \op t) \op t) \\
  &= x \op t^{(1)}.
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $x^{(1)},x^{(2)}$ and derive $x\op t = x\op t^{(1)}$

nodes.name: Computer-assisted dual identity
nodes.statement:
A lengthy computer-assisted argument then gave the dual identity
$$ t^{(2)} \op x = t \op x$$

nodes.name: Combine identities
nodes.statement:
Together, these give
$$ x^{(2)} \op y^{(1)} = x \op y.$$

nodes.name: Derive $x^{(2)} = x\op(x\op y)$
nodes.statement:
Multiplying on the left by $x = x^{(1)}\op x^{(2)}$, one can conclude that
$$ x^{(2)} = x \op (x \op y).$$

nodes.name: Compute $(x\op y)^{(1)}$ and $(x\op y)^{(2)}$
Idempotent factorization gives natural central groupoid
nodes.statement: Since $(x \op x)^{(1)} = x^{(2)}$ and $(x \op x)^{(2)} = x^{(1)}$, we conclude that $x^{(1)}$ and $x^{(2)}$ are idempotent.  Since $x = x^{(1)} \op x^{(2)}$, we see that every $x$ is the product of two idempotents.  One can show that this representation is unique, and gives a canonical identification with a natural central groupoid.
nodes.statement_short: Idempotent factorization gives natural central groupoid

nodes.name: No non-trivial finite model
nodes.statement:
First we show that every finite model of \Equaref{374794} is trivial.  Write $y^2 := y \op y$ and $y^3 := y^2 \op y$.  For any $y,z$, introduce the functions ${f_y: x \mapsto y^3 \op x}$ and ${g_{yz}: x \mapsto x \op (y^2 \op z)}$.  \Equaref{374794} says that $g_{yz}(f_y(x))=x$, hence by finiteness $g_{yz}=f_y^{-1}$, showing that $g_{yz}$ does not depend on the value of $z$.  Since
$$ f_y(y^2 \op z) = g_{yz}(y^3),$$
it follows that $f_y(y^2 \op z)=f_y(y^3)$ which by injectivity of $f_y$ implies that $z\mapsto y^2 \op z$ is a constant function (with $y$ fixed).  Substituting $y^2$ for $y$ shows that the same is true for $z\mapsto (y^2 \op y^2) \op z$, and since
$$ f_y(z) = (y^2 \op y) \op z = (y^2 \op y^2) \op z$$
we conclude that $f_y$ is also a constant function.  But this function is already known to be injective, thus there do not exist distinct elements in its domain, showing that the model must be trivial.

nodes.name: Introduce $f_y$ and $g_{yz}$
nodes.statement: Write $y^2 := y \op y$ and $y^3 := y^2 \op y$.  For any $y,z$, introduce the functions ${f_y: x \mapsto y^3 \op x}$ and ${g_{yz}: x \mapsto x \op (y^2 \op z)}$.

nodes.name: By finiteness $g_{yz}=f_y^{-1}$
nodes.statement: \Equaref{374794} says that $g_{yz}(f_y(x))=x$, hence by finiteness $g_{yz}=f_y^{-1}$, showing that $g_{yz}$ does not depend on the value of $z$.

nodes.name: $z\mapsto y^2\op z$ is constant
nodes.statement:
Since
$$ f_y(y^2 \op z) = g_{yz}(y^3),$$
it follows that $f_y(y^2 \op z)=f_y(y^3)$ which by injectivity of $f_y$ implies that $z\mapsto y^2 \op z$ is a constant function (with $y$ fixed).

nodes.name: $f_y$ is constant
nodes.statement:
Substituting $y^2$ for $y$ shows that the same is true for $z\mapsto (y^2 \op y^2) \op z$, and since
$$ f_y(z) = (y^2 \op y) \op z = (y^2 \op y^2) \op z$$
we conclude that $f_y$ is also a constant function.  But this function is already known to be injective, thus there do not exist distinct elements in its domain, showing that the model must be trivial.

nodes.name: Define an operation on positive integers
nodes.statement:
To construct an infinite model, consider the magma of positive integers $\Z^+$ with the operation $x \op y$ defined by
$$
x \op y =
\begin{cases}
2^y, & x=  y            \\
3^y, & x=  1,\ y \neq 1 \\
  z, & x=3^z,\ y \neq x \\
  1, & else
\end{cases}.
$$
nodes.statement_short: Define an operation on positive integers

nodes.name: Compute squares and cubes
nodes.statement: Then $y \op y = 2^y$ and $(y \op y) \op y = 1$ for all $y$.

nodes.name: Case $x\neq 1$
nodes.statement:
If $x\neq 1$ we have that
$$ ((y \op y) \op y) \op x = 3^x, $$
and since $(y \op y) \op z$ is a power of two for all $y, z$ it follows that
$$ 3^x \op ((y \op y) \op z) = x. $$

nodes.name: Case $x=1$; model verified
Rewrite the law
$T_y$ is bijective in a finite model
nodes.statement: In particular, for any $y$, the map $T_y \colon x \mapsto y^3 \op x$ is injective, hence bijective in a finite model $G$.
nodes.statement_short: $T_y$ is bijective in a finite model

nodes.name: $y\op z$ is independent of $z$
nodes.statement:
In particular we can find a function $f : G \to G$ such that $T_y f(y) = y^3$ for all $y$  Applying \Cref{kis2-law} with $x = f(y)$, we conclude
$$ T_y(y \op z) = y^3 \op (y \op z) = f(y) $$
and thus $y \op z$ is independent of $z$ by injectivity of $T_y$.

nodes.name: Finite models are trivial
nodes.statement: Thus, the right-hand side of \Cref{kis2-law} does not depend on $x$, and so the model is trivial.  This shows there are no non-trivial finite models.

nodes.name: Define operation on $\N$
nodes.statement:
To establish an infinite model, use $\N$ with $x \op y$ defined by requiring
$$ y \op y = 2^y; \quad 2^y \op y = 3^y$$
and
$$ 3^y \op x = 3^y 5^x$$
for $x \neq 3^y$, and
$$ (3^y 5^x) \op z = x$$
for $z \neq 3^y 5^x$.

nodes.name: Complete the definition
nodes.statement:
Finally set
$$ 2^{3^y} \op z = 3^y$$
for $z \neq 3^y, 2^{3^y}$.  All other assignments of $\op$ may be made almost arbitrarily, such as setting them to $1$.

nodes.name: Verify the law
nodes.statement: It is then a routine matter to establish \Cref{kis2-law}.

nodes.name: Left multiplication is injective
nodes.statement: From \Equaref{5093} we see that the map $w \mapsto y \op w$ is onto, hence injective in a finite model.

nodes.name: $z\op y$ independent of $z$
nodes.statement:
Using this injectivity four times in \Equaref{5093}, we see that $z \op y$ does not depend on $z$, hence the expression
$x \op (z \op y)$ does not depend on $x$.

nodes.name: Contradiction in a non-trivial model
nodes.statement: By \Equaref{5093} again, this means that $x$ does not depend on $x$, which is absurd in a non-trivial model.

nodes.name: Reduce to laws $x=f(x,y)$
nodes.statement: If neither side of the law is a single variable then the zero law $x \op y = 0$ will work, so one can assume the law takes the form $x = f(x,y)$.

nodes.name: Use linear magmas
nodes.statement: Consider a finite field $F$ with the operation $x \op y := ax+by$ for some coefficients $a,b \in F$.  Then the law becomes a pair of equations $P(a,b)=0$, $Q(a,b)=1$ in the coefficients for some polynomials $P,Q$ with integer coefficients, which one can verify to not divide each other (they have the same degree, and do not have the same set of non-zero monomials).

nodes.name: Bezout and Lefschetz give finite field solution
nodes.statement: From Bezout's theorem, this equation has a solution in some field, and hence by the Lefschetz principle it has a solution in a finite field.
nodes.statement_short: Bezout and Lefschetz give finite field solution

nodes.name: Define periodic points; every orbit eventually periodic
nodes.statement: Call a point $x \in X$ \emph{periodic} if $f^n(x) = x$ for some $n>0$.  Because the forward orbit $x, f(x), f^2(x), \dots$ in a finite space $X$ must repeat, we see that for each $x$ there exists an $n$ such that $f^n(x)$ is periodic.
nodes.statement_short: Define periodic points; every orbit eventually periodic

nodes.name: If $n_x>1$ then $n_{g(x)}=n_x+1$
nodes.statement: Let $n_x$ be the first $n$ for which this occurs.  If $n_x > 1$, then $g(x), f(g(x)), f(f(g(x))$ cannot be periodic (as this would imply $f(x)$ periodic), and then we can see that $n_{g(x)} = n_x + 1$.

nodes.name: All $f(x)$ periodic, so $f^n=f$
nodes.statement: Hence the maximal value of $n_x$ is at most $1$, which implies that $f(x)$ is periodic for every $x$.  Thus there is an $n > 1$ such that $f^n = f$.

nodes.name: Rewrite $f^n$ to get $f\circ g\circ f$
nodes.statement: Since $f = f^2 \circ g$, we have $f^n = f^{n-2} \circ f \circ f = f^{n-2} \circ (f^2 \circ g) \circ f = f^n \circ g \circ f = f \circ g \circ f$, as desired.

nodes.name: $f^2(x)$ determines $f(x)$
nodes.statement: By hypothesis, $f^2(x)$ uniquely determines $f(x)$.

nodes.name: Rule out $n_x\ge 2$
nodes.statement: This prevents $n_x = 2$ for any $x$ (because if $n>2$ is such that $f^{n+2}(x) = f^2(x)$, then $f^{n+1}(x) \neq f(x)$), and hence also prevents $n_x > 2$ for any $x$.

nodes.name: $f^n=f$ for some $n>1$
nodes.statement: So again we have $f(x)$ periodic for all $x$, so $f^n = f$ for some $n>1$.

nodes.name: Rewrite to get $f\circ g\circ f$
nodes.statement: Then $f = f^n = f \circ (g \circ f^2) \circ f^{n-2} = f \circ g \circ f^n = f \circ g \circ f$ as required.

nodes.name: Introduce $S$, $f_z$, $g_z$
nodes.statement:
For a finite magma $M$, consider the set $S = \{x \op y | x, y \in M\}$.
  Now $f_z : x \mapsto z \op x$ and $g_z : x \mapsto x \op z$.

nodes.name: Inverse bijections commute
nodes.statement:
They both map $S$ to $S$, and due to the hypothesis $g_z \op f_z$ is the identity on $S$,
  so because $S$ is finite $f_z$ and $g_z$ must be inverse bijections on it, and therefore
  they commute.

nodes.name: Define the operation
nodes.statement:
Consider $\mathbb{N}$, with $x \op y$ defined as $x \oplus y$ (bitwise XOR) if $x$ and $y$ are even,
  $y+2$ if only $y$ is even, $x \dot - 2$ if only $x$ is even, and $0$ if both are odd.
  Note that the range of the operation is the set of even naturals.

nodes.name: Verify 3994
nodes.statement:
\Equaref{3994} is satisfied, because for even $z$ we get $z \oplus (x \op y) \oplus z = x \op y$
  and for odd $z$ we get $(x \op y) + 2 \dot - 2 = x \op y$.

nodes.name: 3588 fails
nodes.statement: Setting $x = y = z = 1$, \Equaref{3588} isn't satisfied.

nodes.name: Introduce $S$, $f$, $C$ and state the goal
nodes.statement: Write $Sx := x \op$, $fx := x \op Sx$ and $Cx = Sx \op x$, then we have $x \op y= y \op fx$, and our task is to show $x \op y = Cx \op y$ and $x \op y = x \op Cy$ for finite magmas, giving the four open implications.

nodes.name: $f$ is a homomorphism
nodes.statement: Note that $x \op y= y \op fx = fx \op fy$, hence $f$ is a homomorphism.

nodes.name: Eventual period of $f$
nodes.statement: By \Cref{period}, there is $n \geq 1$ with $f^n = f^{2n}$.

nodes.name: $Cx = f^n x$
nodes.statement: From 3342 we have $Sx = S fx$ and $Cx = Sx \op x = f^n Sx \op f^n x = f^n Sx \op f^{2n} x = f^{2n-1} x \op f^n Sx = f^{n-1} x \op S x = f(f^{n-1} x) = f^n x$.

nodes.name: Conclude both identities
nodes.statement:
Then
$$ Cx \op y = f^n x \op y = f^{2n} x \op f^n y = f^n x \op f^n y = x \op y$$
and a similar argument gives $x \op Cy = x \op y$.

nodes.name: Operator form of 1167
nodes.statement:
We write 1167 as
  $$ L_y L_{z \op Sy} = I,$$
hence $L_y$ is invertible and $L_{z \op Sy} L_y = I$.

nodes.name: Squaring is bijective
nodes.statement: In particular $L_{z \op Sy} Sy = y$, hence squaring is injective, hence surjective.

nodes.name: $L_{z\op y}$ independent of $z$
nodes.statement: So 1167 can be rewritten as $L_{S^{-1} y} L_{z \op y} = I$, hence $L_{z \op y}$ is independent of $z$.

nodes.name: RHS of 1096 independent of $z$
nodes.statement:
In particular
$$ L_{x \op (z \op y)} = L_{S^{-2} z \op (z \op y)} = L_{L_{S^{-2} z} L_{S^{-1} z \op S S^{-2} z} y} = L_y$$
by 1167, hence the right-hand side of 1096 is independent of $z$.

nodes.name: Conclude from 1167
nodes.statement: Replacing $z$ with $y$, the claim now follows from 1167.

nodes.name: Operator form of 1133
nodes.statement: 1133 asserts that $L_y L_{y \op (z \op y)} = I$, hence $L_y$ is invertible and $L_{y \op (z \op y)} = L_y^{-1}$ does not depend on $z$.

nodes.name: Left multiplications are involutions
nodes.statement: Setting $z = y \op Sy$ we see from 1133 that $y \op (z \op y) = y$ and hence we have left-involution: $L_y = L_y^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Derive (5.2)
Squaring is surjective, hence invertible
nodes.statement:
In particular
$$ R_y^3 z = L_{L_z y \op y} y = L_{L_z y} y = R_y^2 z$$
hence as $L_{R_y^2 z}$ is its own inverse
$$ y =L_{R_y^2 z} L_{R_y^2 z} y = L_{R_y^2 z} R_y^3 z =
L_{R_y^2 z} R_y^3 z = S( R_y^2 z).$$
Thus squaring is surjective, hence invertible.

nodes.name: Rewrite $L_{z\op Sy}=L_w$
nodes.statement: Next, by \eqref{intermediate} we have $L_{z \op Sy} = L_w$ where $w = R_{Sy}^2 z$.

nodes.name: $Sw = Sy$
nodes.statement:
By \eqref{intermediate} and the fact that $L_w$ is its own inverse, we have
$$ L_w^2 w = w = L_{z \op Sy} Sy =L_w Sy,$$
hence $Sw = L_w w = Sy$.

nodes.name: Conclude 1167
nodes.statement: As $S$ is injective, we have $L_w = L_y$, and then $L_y L_{z \op Sy} = L_y^2 = I$, giving 1167.

nodes.name: 1441 implies 4067
nodes.statement: Write $\tilde C x = x \op Sx$, then 1441 asserts that $R_{\tilde Cx} R_y x = x$.  Setting $$y=Sx$$ we get $x = S\tilde Cx$, so by finiteness $\tilde C Sx = x$.  Replacing $x$ with $Sx$ in 1441 we conclude $R_x R_y Sx = Sx$ which is 4067.

nodes.name: Operator form of 1441
nodes.statement: Write $\tilde C x = x \op Sx$, then 1441 asserts that $R_{\tilde Cx} R_y x = x$.

nodes.name: By finiteness $\tilde C S x = x$
nodes.statement: Setting $$y=Sx$$ we get $x = S\tilde Cx$, so by finiteness $\tilde C Sx = x$.
nodes.statement_short: By finiteness $\tilde C S x = x$

nodes.name: Obtain 4067
nodes.statement: Replacing $x$ with $Sx$ in 1441 we conclude $R_x R_y Sx = Sx$ which is 4067.

nodes.name: 1443 implies 3055
nodes.statement: Clearly 1443 implies 1441, hence 4067 by the previous implication, so that 3055 simplifies to $x = Sx \op x$.  Meanwhile, 1443 also implies $x = S(x \op (x \op z))$.  On taking square roots and using $S \tilde C = x$, we obtain $x \op (x \op z) = \tilde Cx$.  Applying this with $z = Sx$ we conclude $L_x \tilde Cx = \tilde Cx$, hence on replacing $x$ with $Sx$ we get $L_{Sx} x = x$ as required.

nodes.name: Reduce 3055 to $x = Sx\op x$
nodes.statement: Clearly 1443 implies 1441, hence 4067 by the previous implication, so that 3055 simplifies to $x = Sx \op x$.  Meanwhile, 1443 also implies $x = S(x \op (x \op z))$.

nodes.name: $x\op(x\op z) = \tilde Cx$
nodes.statement: On taking square roots and using $S \tilde C = x$, we obtain $x \op (x \op z) = \tilde Cx$.

nodes.name: Conclude $L_{Sx}x=x$
nodes.statement: Applying this with $z = Sx$ we conclude $L_x \tilde Cx = \tilde Cx$, hence on replacing $x$ with $Sx$ we get $L_{Sx} x = x$ as required.

nodes.name: Same method as before
nodes.statement: This is very similar to the previous proof.

nodes.name: Operator form of 1681
nodes.statement: Write $Cx = Sx \op x$, then 1681 asserts $R_{Cx} L_y x = x$.

nodes.name: Obtain 3877
nodes.statement: Again setting $y=Sx$ yields $x=SCx$ hence $x = CSx$, and on replacing $x$ with $Sx$ in 1681 one obtains 3877.

nodes.name: Obtain 1035 from 1701
nodes.statement: For the second part, we simplify to $x = x \op Sx$, while 1701 gives $x = S((z \op x) \op x)$ hence $(z \op x) \op x = Cx$, so $R_x Cx = Cx$, so $R_{Sx} x = x$ as required.

nodes.name: Split into three cases
nodes.statement:
Because $f$ maps $E_1 \backslash E_0$ bijectively to $E_2 \backslash E_1$, there are three cases:
\begin{itemize}
  \item $h$ is equal to an element $h_0$ of $\Z \backslash E_2$.
  \item $h$ is equal to an element $h_0$ of $E_1 \backslash E_0$.
  \item $h$ is equal to $h_1 = f(h_0)$ for some $h_0 \in E_1 \backslash E_0$, so that $h_1 \in E_2 \backslash E_1$.
\end{itemize}

We deal with these three cases in turn.

nodes.name: Case $h\notin E_2$
Choose fresh $h_1$
nodes.statement: Choose an element $h_1 \in \Z$ that does not lie in $E_2 \cup \{h_0, -h_0\}$; this is possible because $E_2$ is finite.

nodes.name: Choose fresh $h_2$
nodes.statement: Choose an element $h_2 \in \Z$ such that $h_2, h_0+h_1+h_2$, $-h_1$, and $-h_1-h_2$ are all distinct from each other and lie outside of $E_2 \cup \{h_0, h_1\}$; this is possible because $E_2$ is finite and $h_0+h_1 \neq 0$.

nodes.name: Promote elements
nodes.statement:
Promote $h_0$ to $E_0$, promote $h_1, h_0+h_1+h_2$ to $E_1$, and promote $h_2, -h_1-h_2$ to $E_2$, creating new sets
  \begin{align*}
    E'_0 &:= E_0 \cup \{h_0\} \\
    E'_1 &:= E_1 \cup \{h_0, h_1, h_0+h_1+h_2\} \\
    E'_2 &:= E_2 \cup \{h_0, h_1, h_0+h_1+h_2, h_2, -h_1-h_2\}.
  \end{align*}
  Clearly we still have nested finite sets $E'_0 \subseteq E'_1 \subseteq E'_2$.

nodes.name: Define $f'$
nodes.statement:
Extend $f : E_1 \to E_2$ to a function $f': E'_1 \to E'_2$ by defining
  \begin{align*}
    f'(h_0) &:= h_1 \\
    f'(h_1) &:= h_2 \\
    f'(h_0+h_1+h_2) &:= -h_1-h_2
  \end{align*}
  while keeping $f'(h)=f(h)$ for all $h \in E_1$.

nodes.name: Verify partial solution
nodes.statement: It is then a routine matter to verify that $(E'_0,E'_1,E'_2,f')$ is a partial solution to \Cref{fh} extending $(E_0,E_1,E_2,f)$ and that $E'_0$ contains $h_0$, as required.

nodes.name: Case $h\in E_1\setminus E_0$
Choose fresh $h_2$
nodes.statement: Choose an element $h_2 \in \Z$ such that $h_2, h_0+h_1+h_2$, and $-h_1-h_2$, $-h_1$ are all distinct and lie outside of $E_2$.  This is possible because $E_2$ is finite and $h_0+h_1 = h_0+f(h_0) \neq 0$.

nodes.name: Promote elements
nodes.statement:
Promote $h_0$ to $E_0$, promote $h_1$ and $h_0+h_1+h_2$ to $E_1$, and promote $h_2, -h_1-h_2$ to $E_2$, thus creating new sets
\begin{align*}
  E'_0 &:= E_0 \cup \{h_0\} \\
  E'_1 &:= E_1 \cup \{h_1, h_0+h_1+h_2\} \\
  E'_2 &:= E_2 \cup \{h_0+h_1+h_2, h_2, -h_1-h_2\}.
\end{align*}
Clearly we still have nested finite sets $E'_0 \subseteq E'_1 \subseteq E'_2$.

nodes.name: Define $f'$
Verify partial solution
nodes.statement: It is then a routine matter to verify that $(E'_0,E'_1,E'_2,f')$ is a partial solution to \Cref{fh} extending $(E_0,E_1,E_2,f)$ and that $E'_0$ contains $h_0$, as required.

nodes.name: Case $h\in E_2\setminus E_1$
nodes.statement:
Finally, suppose that $h = h_1 = f(h_0)$ for some $h_0 \in E_1 \backslash E_0$, so that $h_1 \in E_2 \backslash E_1$.  Then we perform the following algorithm.
\begin{itemize}
  \item Choose an element $h_2 \in \Z$ such that $h_2, h_0+h_1+h_2$, $-h_1$, and $-h_1-h_2$ are all distinct and lie outside of $E_2$.  This is possible because $E_2$ is finite and $h_0+h_1 = h_0+f(h_0) \neq 0$.
  \item Choose an element $h_3 \in \Z$ such that $h_3, h_1+h_2+h_3$, and $-h_2-h_3$ are all distinct and lie outside of $E_2 \cup \{h_2, h_0+h_1+h_2,-h_1-h_2\}$.  This is possible because $E_2$ is finite.
  \item Promote $h_0, h_1$ to $E_0$, promote $h_2, h_0+h_1+h_2, h_1+h_2+h_3$ to $E_1$, and promote $h_3, -h_1-h_2,-h_2-h_3$ to $E_2$, creating new sets
\begin{align*}
  E'_0 &:= E_0 \cup \{h_0, h_1 \}\\
  E'_1 &:= E_1 \cup \{h_1, h_2, h_0+h_1+h_2, h_1+h_2+h_3 \}\\
  E'_2 &:= E_2 \cup \{h_2, h_3, h_0+h_1+h_2, h_1+h_2+h_3, -h_1-h_2, -h_2-h_3\}.
\end{align*}
Clearly we still have nested finite sets $E'_0 \subseteq E'_1 \subseteq E'_2$.
\item Extend $f : E_1 \to E_2$ to a function $f': E'_1 \to E'_2$ by defining
\begin{align*}
  f'(h_1) &:= h_2 \\
  f'(h_0+h_1+h_2) &:= -h_1-h_2 \\
  f'(h_2) &:= h_3 \\
  f'(h_1+h_2+h_3) &:= -h_2-h_3
\end{align*}
while keeping $f'(h)=f(h)$ for all $h \in E_1$.
\end{itemize}
It is then a routine matter to verify that $(E'_0,E'_1,E'_2,f')$ is a partial solution to \Cref{fh} extending $(E_0,E_1,E_2,f)$ and that $E'_0$ contains $h_0$, as required.

nodes.name: Choose fresh $h_2$
nodes.statement: Choose an element $h_2 \in \Z$ such that $h_2, h_0+h_1+h_2$, $-h_1$, and $-h_1-h_2$ are all distinct and lie outside of $E_2$.  This is possible because $E_2$ is finite and $h_0+h_1 = h_0+f(h_0) \neq 0$.

nodes.name: Choose fresh $h_3$
nodes.statement: Choose an element $h_3 \in \Z$ such that $h_3, h_1+h_2+h_3$, and $-h_2-h_3$ are all distinct and lie outside of $E_2 \cup \{h_2, h_0+h_1+h_2,-h_1-h_2\}$.  This is possible because $E_2$ is finite.

nodes.name: Promote elements
nodes.statement:
Promote $h_0, h_1$ to $E_0$, promote $h_2, h_0+h_1+h_2, h_1+h_2+h_3$ to $E_1$, and promote $h_3, -h_1-h_2,-h_2-h_3$ to $E_2$, creating new sets
\begin{align*}
  E'_0 &:= E_0 \cup \{h_0, h_1 \}\\
  E'_1 &:= E_1 \cup \{h_1, h_2, h_0+h_1+h_2, h_1+h_2+h_3 \}\\
  E'_2 &:= E_2 \cup \{h_2, h_3, h_0+h_1+h_2, h_1+h_2+h_3, -h_1-h_2, -h_2-h_3\}.
\end{align*}
Clearly we still have nested finite sets $E'_0 \subseteq E'_1 \subseteq E'_2$.

nodes.name: Define $f'$
nodes.statement:
Extend $f : E_1 \to E_2$ to a function $f': E'_1 \to E'_2$ by defining
\begin{align*}
  f'(h_1) &:= h_2 \\
  f'(h_0+h_1+h_2) &:= -h_1-h_2 \\
  f'(h_2) &:= h_3 \\
  f'(h_1+h_2+h_3) &:= -h_2-h_3
\end{align*}
while keeping $f'(h)=f(h)$ for all $h \in E_1$.

nodes.name: Verify partial solution
nodes.statement: It is then a routine matter to verify that $(E'_0,E'_1,E'_2,f')$ is a partial solution to \Cref{fh} extending $(E_0,E_1,E_2,f)$ and that $E'_0$ contains $h_0$, as required.

nodes.name: Choose integers with a collision
nodes.statement:
Select integers $h_0,h_1,h_2,h'_0,h'_1,h'_2$ such that the quantities
  $$ 0, h_0, h_1, h_2, h_0+h_1+h_2, -h_1-h_2, h'_0, h'_1, h'_2, h'_0+h'_1+h'_2, -h'_1-h'_2$$
  are all distinct, but such that
  $$ h_0 + h_1 = h'_0 + h'_1 \neq 0$$
  (there are many assignments of variables that accomplish this).

nodes.name: It is a non-injective partial solution
nodes.statement: One can then check that $(E_0, E_1, E_2, f)$ is a partial solution to \Cref{fh}, and by construction $h \mapsto h + f(h)$ is not injective on $E_1$.
nodes.statement_short: It is a non-injective partial solution

nodes.name: Extend to a full solution
nodes.statement: Using \Cref{iteration} to extend this partial solution to a full solution, we obtain the claim.

nodes.name: Reduce to injectivity of $h\mapsto h+f(h)$
nodes.statement: Note that $L_y (y+h) = y + h + f(h)$, so the injectivity of the left-multiplication maps is equivalent to the injectivity of the map $h \mapsto h + f(h)$.

nodes.name: Apply the non-injective solution
nodes.statement: The non-injectivity then follows from \Cref{no-inject}. Note that the Obelix law clearly expresses $x$ as a function of $y$ and $L_y x = y \op x$, forcing injectivity of left-multiplication, so the Obelix law fails.

nodes.name: Case $(a,b)\in E$
Reduce to $b\notin\mathrm{dom}(E)$
nodes.statement: If $b\in {\rm dom}(E)$, then by condition (4) we are already done.  So reduce to the case when $b\notin {\rm dom}(E)$.

nodes.name: Consequences of conditions (2),(3),(6)
nodes.statement: In particular, by (2) and (3) we know $a,b\neq 1$, and also by (6) we know that $ab^{-1}\notin {\rm dom}(E)\cup{\rm im}(E)$ (and is not $1$).

nodes.name: Adjoin fresh generator $c$
Check condition (6)
nodes.statement:
Finally, for condition (6), a finite check works.  The main case is checking that $ca^{-1}
otin {m dom}(E')\cup {m im}(E')$.  This is clear since $a
eq 1$ and $a
eq b$ (by condition (5) for $E$).  One should also note that by condition (5) (and the fact that $E$ is a function), there is no pair $(x,y)\in E$ with $(x,y)
eq (a,b)$ and  $xy^{-1}=ab^{-1}$, so we don't ruin condition (6) for pairs already in $E$.

nodes.name: Case $a\notin\mathrm{dom}(E)$
nodes.statement:
{\bf Case 2}: Assume $a\notin {\rm dom}(E)$.  If $(x,a)\in E$ for some (unique by (2)) $x\in G$, then applying Case 1 to $x$, we reduce to the case when $a\in {\rm dom}(E)$.

Thus, we may consider the case when $a\notin {\rm dom}(E)\cup {\rm im}(E)$.  If $(x,y)\in E$ with $xy^{-1}=a$, then by applying Case 1 to $x$, we get $a\in {\rm im}(E)$, and reduce to a previously considered case.  So, we may assume there is no such pair $(x,y)$.  Fixing $b$ to be a generator of $G$ not appearing in the reduced forms for the entries in $E$, nor in $a$, then after passing to $E\cup\{(a,b)\}\in \mathscr{E}$ we again reduce to Case 1.

nodes.name: Reduce via Case 1 when $a$ is an image
nodes.statement: If $(x,a)\in E$ for some (unique by (2)) $x\in G$, then applying Case 1 to $x$, we reduce to the case when $a\in {\rm dom}(E)$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce via Case 1 when $a$ is an image

nodes.name: Case $a$ outside domain and image
nodes.statement: Thus, we may consider the case when $a\notin {\rm dom}(E)\cup {\rm im}(E)$.  If $(x,y)\in E$ with $xy^{-1}=a$, then by applying Case 1 to $x$, we get $a\in {\rm im}(E)$, and reduce to a previously considered case.  So, we may assume there is no such pair $(x,y)$.

nodes.name: Adjoin $(a,b)$ and reduce to Case 1
nodes.statement: Fixing $b$ to be a generator of $G$ not appearing in the reduced forms for the entries in $E$, nor in $a$, then after passing to $E\cup\{(a,b)\}\in \mathscr{E}$ we again reduce to Case 1.

nodes.name: Need a valid initial partial solution
nodes.statement: This requires picking an initial set that still satisfies the correct initial closure properties.
nodes.statement_short: Need a valid initial partial solution

nodes.name: Explicit seed violating Asterix
nodes.statement:
Letting
$x_1$, $x_2$, $x_3$ and $x_4$ be independent elements, then taking the function
$$\{(0,0), (x_1,x_2), (x_2-x_1, x_3), (x_1+x_3, x_4)\}$$
already has elements that contradict the Asterix equation, and it's a valid partial solution.

nodes.name: Extend to a full Obelix magma
nodes.statement:
By extending
it, we can get an Obelix that does not satisfy the Asterix equation.
nodes.statement_short: Extend to a full Obelix magma

nodes.name: Goal: greedy extension for Asterix
nodes.statement: Consider for instance the theory $\Gamma$ consisting of (VLT) and the Asterix law (65).  Given $a,b,c$ and a finitely supported $R$ satisfying $\Gamma$ as well as (novel-1), (novel-2), (undefined), we would like to construct a finitely supported  $R'$ satisfying $\Gamma$, (extend), (define).

nodes.name: Naive minimal extension
nodes.statement:
The naive guess would just be to take the minimal construction
$$ R'(x,y,z) \hbox{ iff } R(x,y,z) \hbox{ or } (x,y,z) = (a,b,c).$$

nodes.name: First obstruction and fix
nodes.statement:
This can work, but there is an obstruction: if $R(w,a,b)$ for some $w$, then (65) forces $R'(w,c,a)$.  So one would have to enlarge the definition of $R'(x,y,z)$, to hold true if one of the following statements holds:
\begin{itemize}
  \item $R(x,y,z)$ holds.
  \item $(x,y,z) = (a,b,c)$.
  \item $(x,y,z) = (w,c,a)$ for some $w$ with $R(w,a,b)$.

nodes.name: Second obstruction and fix
Add axiom (65')
Final definition of $R'$
nodes.statement:
With this modification to $\Gamma$, if we run the above analysis, we now see that if $R(b,a,b)$ hold (so that $R(a,a,b)$ also holds), then (65) will force $R'(a,c,a)$, $R'(b,c,a)$, and $R'(c,c,a)$.  So now the modified definition of $R'$ is that $R'(x,y,z)$ holds if one of the following statements holds:
\begin{itemize}
  \item $R(x,y,z)$ holds.
  \item $(x,y,z) = (a,b,c)$.
  \item $(x,y,z) = (w,c,a)$ for some $w$ with $R(w,a,b)$.
  \item $(x,y,z) = (a,c,a)$, $(b,c,a)$, or $(c,c,a)$, assuming $R(b,a,b)$ holds.

nodes.name: Verify with automated prover
nodes.statement: One can then finally (for instance, with the assistance of a automated theorem prover) verify that if $R$ is finitely supported and satisfies $\Gamma = (VLT) + (65) + (65')$ and $a,b,c$ satisfy (novel-1), (novel-2), (undefined), then the $R'$ defined above is also finitely supported and satisfies $\Gamma$, (extend), (define).

nodes.name: Case $b=a$
nodes.statement:
Suppose first that $b=a$, so $a \op a$ is undefined, then by Law 4 we have $d \op a \neq a$ for all $d$ with $d \op a$ defined. Set $a_0=a$ and find nine distinct elements $a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4$ not previously appearing in the domain or range of $\op$. Extend the indices periodically by setting $a_{i+4} = a_i,b_{i+4} = b_i$ for $i \ge 1$, and define $a_i \op' a_i = a_{i+1}$ (so $a_i = S^i a$), $a_{i+1} \op' a_i = b_i$, $b_i \op' a_i = a_{i+2}$, $a_{i+3} \op' a_{i+1} = a_{i+1}$, $a_{i+1} \op' a_{i+2} = a_{i+1}$, $a_{i+1} \op' b_i = a_i$.  We also define $x \op' y = x \op y$ whenever the right-hand side is defined. It is easy to see that laws 2,3,4 are preserved (though for law 2 note that we have not defined $a_2 \op' a_0$ due to the way indices are extended). Now we case check Law 1.  \begin{itemize}
    \item Case 1. $y$ is fresh, that is $y \in \{a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4\}$. If $x \op' y$ is not defined, we are done, so assume this is so. In particular, $x  \in \{a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4\}$. If $x,y \in \{a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4\}$ we are done by construction. If $x = b_i$ for some $i$, then $y = a_i$ and we are again done by construction. Finally, if $y = b_i$ for some $i$, then $x = a_{i+1}$ and $(x \op' y) \op' y$ is undefined.
    \item Case 2. $x$ is fresh, that is $x \in \{a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4\}$. If we are not in Case 1 and $x \op' y$ is defined, we must have $y = a_0$ and $x \in \{a_1, b_0\}$. The case $x = a_1$ holds by construction, and the case $x = b_0$ holds as $a_2 \op' a_0$ is not defined.
    \item Case 3. $x,y \not \in  \{a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4\}$ and $x \op y$ was undefined. Then $x \op' y$ is undefined unless $x=y=a_0$, in which case Law 1 holds by construction.
    \item Case 4. $x,y \not \in  \{a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4\}$, $x \op y$ was defined, and $(x \op y) \op y$ was not defined. Then $(x \op' y) \op' y$ is undefined unless $(x \op y) = a = y$, but this is impossible by Law $4$ as already observed.
    \item Case 5. $x,y \not \in  \{a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4\}$ and $x \op y$ and $(x \op y) \op y$ were defined. Then the claim follows from Law 1 applied to $\op$.

nodes.name: Adjoin nine fresh elements with periodic table
nodes.statement: Set $a_0=a$ and find nine distinct elements $a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4$ not previously appearing in the domain or range of $\op$. Extend the indices periodically by setting $a_{i+4} = a_i,b_{i+4} = b_i$ for $i \ge 1$, and define $a_i \op' a_i = a_{i+1}$ (so $a_i = S^i a$), $a_{i+1} \op' a_i = b_i$, $b_i \op' a_i = a_{i+2}$, $a_{i+3} \op' a_{i+1} = a_{i+1}$, $a_{i+1} \op' a_{i+2} = a_{i+1}$, $a_{i+1} \op' b_i = a_i$.  We also define $x \op' y = x \op y$ whenever the right-hand side is defined. It is easy to see that laws 2,3,4 are preserved (though for law 2 note that we have not defined $a_2 \op' a_0$ due to the way indices are extended).
nodes.statement_short: Adjoin nine fresh elements with periodic table

nodes.name: Check Law 1 by cases
nodes.statement: Now we case check Law 1.

nodes.name: Case: $y$ fresh
nodes.statement: Case 1. $y$ is fresh, that is $y \in \{a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4\}$. If $x \op' y$ is not defined, we are done, so assume this is so. In particular, $x  \in \{a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4\}$. If $x,y \in \{a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4\}$ we are done by construction. If $x = b_i$ for some $i$, then $y = a_i$ and we are again done by construction. Finally, if $y = b_i$ for some $i$, then $x = a_{i+1}$ and $(x \op' y) \op' y$ is undefined.

nodes.name: Case: $x$ fresh
nodes.statement: Case 2. $x$ is fresh, that is $x \in \{a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4\}$. If we are not in Case 1 and $x \op' y$ is defined, we must have $y = a_0$ and $x \in \{a_1, b_0\}$. The case $x = a_1$ holds by construction, and the case $x = b_0$ holds as $a_2 \op' a_0$ is not defined.

nodes.name: Case: $x\op y$ was undefined
nodes.statement: Case 3. $x,y \not \in  \{a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4\}$ and $x \op y$ was undefined. Then $x \op' y$ is undefined unless $x=y=a_0$, in which case Law 1 holds by construction.

nodes.name: Case: $(x\op y)\op y$ was undefined
nodes.statement: Case 4. $x,y \not \in  \{a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4\}$, $x \op y$ was defined, and $(x \op y) \op y$ was not defined. Then $(x \op' y) \op' y$ is undefined unless $(x \op y) = a = y$, but this is impossible by Law $4$ as already observed.

nodes.name: Case: all defined before
nodes.statement: Case 5. $x,y \not \in  \{a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4\}$ and $x \op y$ and $(x \op y) \op y$ were defined. Then the claim follows from Law 1 applied to $\op$.

nodes.name: Case $a\ne b$
nodes.statement:
Now suppose that $a \op b$ is undefined for some $a \neq b$.  By applying the previous construction, we may assume without loss of generality that $Sb$ is defined.  We may assume that $a \op b$ remains undefined after doing so, since we are done otherwise.  By Law 3, $a \neq Sb \op b$.  By Law 2, we have $d \op b = a$ for at most one $d$, which is necessarily different from $Sb$.  Choose a $c$ not previously appearing in the domain or range of $\op$, and set $a \op' b = c$.  If a $d$ exists as before, we additionally set $Sb \op' c = d$.  Finally we define $x \op' y = x \op y$ whenever the right-hand side is defined.
It is again routine to check that $\op'$ satisfies Laws 2,3,4.  Now we case check Law 1.

\begin{itemize}
