\item Case 1.  $x=c$ or $x \op' y = c$.  Not possible since no left multiplication by $c$ is defined.
\item Case 2.  $y=c$.  This would force $x = Sb$ and $d = Sb$, but this is not possible since $d$ is different from $Sb$.
\item Case 3: $(x \op' y) \op' y = c$. This forces $x=d$ and $y=b$, and the claim follows from construction.
\item Case 4: None of the terms in $(x \op' y) \op' y$ are equal to $c$.  Then the claim follows from Law 1 applied to $\op$.

nodes.name: WLOG $Sb$ defined
nodes.statement: By applying the previous construction, we may assume without loss of generality that $Sb$ is defined.  We may assume that $a \op b$ remains undefined after doing so, since we are done otherwise.

nodes.name: Consequences of Laws 2,3
nodes.statement: By Law 3, $a \neq Sb \op b$.  By Law 2, we have $d \op b = a$ for at most one $d$, which is necessarily different from $Sb$.

nodes.name: Define $a\op' b = c$ and $Sb\op' c = d$
nodes.statement: Choose a $c$ not previously appearing in the domain or range of $\op$, and set $a \op' b = c$.  If a $d$ exists as before, we additionally set $Sb \op' c = d$.  Finally we define $x \op' y = x \op y$ whenever the right-hand side is defined.
nodes.statement_short: Define $a\op' b = c$ and $Sb\op' c = d$

nodes.name: Laws 2-4 hold; check Law 1
nodes.statement: It is again routine to check that $\op'$ satisfies Laws 2,3,4.  Now we case check Law 1.

nodes.name: Case: $x=c$
nodes.statement: Case 1.  $x=c$ or $x \op' y = c$.  Not possible since no left multiplication by $c$ is defined.

nodes.name: Case: $y=c$
nodes.statement: Case 2.  $y=c$.  This would force $x = Sb$ and $d = Sb$, but this is not possible since $d$ is different from $Sb$.

nodes.name: Case: product equals $c$
nodes.statement: Case 3: $(x \op' y) \op' y = c$. This forces $x=d$ and $y=b$, and the claim follows from construction.

nodes.name: Case: no new terms
nodes.statement: Case 4: None of the terms in $(x \op' y) \op' y$ are equal to $c$.  Then the claim follows from Law 1 applied to $\op$.

nodes.name: Case $a\op a$ undefined
nodes.statement: First suppose that $a \op a$ is not defined.  Set $a_0 := a$ and select three new elements $a_1,a_2,a_3$.  Define $a_0 \op a_0 = a_1$, $a_1 \op a_0 = a_2$, $a_0 \op a_2 = a_3$, $a_0 \op a_1 = a_3$, $a_0 \op a_3 = a_0$.  It is a routine but tedious matter to check that Laws 1,2,3 are preserved by these operations.  (The trickiest case is the $x=a_0$ case of Law 1; here we need Law 2 to prevent $y \op a_0$ from equalling $a_0$.)

nodes.name: Adjoin three fresh elements
nodes.statement: Set $a_0 := a$ and select three new elements $a_1,a_2,a_3$.  Define $a_0 \op a_0 = a_1$, $a_1 \op a_0 = a_2$, $a_0 \op a_2 = a_3$, $a_0 \op a_1 = a_3$, $a_0 \op a_3 = a_0$.

nodes.name: Laws preserved
nodes.statement: It is a routine but tedious matter to check that Laws 1,2,3 are preserved by these operations.  (The trickiest case is the $x=a_0$ case of Law 1; here we need Law 2 to prevent $y \op a_0$ from equalling $a_0$.)

nodes.name: Case $a\ne b$
nodes.statement:
Now suppose that $a \op b$ is undefined for some $a \neq b$.  Let $d_1,d_2,\dots,d_n$ be all the elements with $d_i \op b = a$.  Note from Law 3 that none of the $d_i$ can be equal to $b$.  Choose a new element $c$, as well as $c_i$ for each $d_i$, and set $a \op b = c$, $d_i \op c = c_i$, and $d_i \op c_i = b$.  It is easy to see that this preserves Laws 2,3.  For Law 1 ,we do the usual case analysis:
\begin{itemize}
\item Case 1: $y = c$, $y = c_i$, $y \op x = c$, or $y \op x = c_i$.  This case cannot occur because we have not defined left multiplication with $c$ or $c_i$.
\item Case 2: $x = c$ or $x = c_i$.  Because $d_i \neq b$, it is easy to see that $(y \op x) \op x$ is not defined for any $x$.
\item Case 3: $(y \op x) \op x = c$ or $(y \op x) \op x = c_i$.  This is only possible if $x=b$ and $y = d_j$ for some $j$, and the claim then follows from construction.
\item Case 4: None of the terms in $(y \op x) \op x$ are equal to $c$ or $c_i$.  This follows from the previous seed.

nodes.name: Collect the $d_i$ with $d_i\op b=a$
nodes.statement: Let $d_1,d_2,\dots,d_n$ be all the elements with $d_i \op b = a$.  Note from Law 3 that none of the $d_i$ can be equal to $b$.

nodes.name: Define new products
nodes.statement: Choose a new element $c$, as well as $c_i$ for each $d_i$, and set $a \op b = c$, $d_i \op c = c_i$, and $d_i \op c_i = b$.  It is easy to see that this preserves Laws 2,3.

nodes.name: Check Law 1 by cases
nodes.statement: For Law 1 ,we do the usual case analysis:

nodes.name: Case: new left factors
nodes.statement: Case 1: $y = c$, $y = c_i$, $y \op x = c$, or $y \op x = c_i$.  This case cannot occur because we have not defined left multiplication with $c$ or $c_i$.

nodes.name: Case: $x$ new
nodes.statement: Case 2: $x = c$ or $x = c_i$.  Because $d_i \neq b$, it is easy to see that $(y \op x) \op x$ is not defined for any $x$.

nodes.name: Case: result is new
nodes.statement: Case 3: $(y \op x) \op x = c$ or $(y \op x) \op x = c_i$.  This is only possible if $x=b$ and $y = d_j$ for some $j$, and the claim then follows from construction.

nodes.name: Case: covered by previous seed
nodes.statement: Case 4: None of the terms in $(y \op x) \op x$ are equal to $c$ or $c_i$.  This follows from the previous seed.

nodes.name: Define new products
nodes.statement: If $a \op b$ is currently undefined, introduce a new element $c$ and define $a \op b = c$ and $ c \op c = c.$ If furthermore $a = (d \op b) \op b$ for some d, then also define $b \op c = d$ (This last step is well defined by injectivity of $R_b$).

nodes.name: Laws 2,3 preserved
nodes.statement: We now check that the three axioms still hold. Law 3 is obvious, law 2 follows since $d \not = c$.

nodes.name: Observations $a\ne b$, $d\ne b$
nodes.statement: For law 1, we first make the observation that $a \not = b$, for otherwise $a \op b$ would have been defined. This has the consequence that if $d$ exists, then $d \not = b$, for otherwise $a = (b \op b) \op b = b.$ In particular, the product $d \op c$ remains undefined after running the algorithm once.

nodes.name: Case analysis for Law 1
nodes.statement: We now work by cases on the values of the variables $x,y$ appearing in law 1:

nodes.name: Case $y=c$
nodes.statement: Case 1: $y=c$. In this case, for the product $x \op y$ to be defined, we require $x =b$ or $x = c$. In the former case either $b \op c$ or $(b \op c) \op c = d \op c$ is not defined. In the latter case, law 1 holds as $c$ is idempotent.

nodes.name: Case $y=b$
nodes.statement: Case 2: $y=b$. For $((x \op b) \op b) \op b$ to be defined now but not have been defined before, we require one of $x= a, (x \op b) = a, ((x \op b) \op b) = a.$ The first two cases are eliminated as $c \op b$ is not yet defined. The last case holds as then $d$ exists and equals $x$, so $b \op (((x \op b) \op b) \op b) = b \op (a \op b) = b \op c = x.$

nodes.name: Case $y\ne b,c$
nodes.statement: Case 3: $y \not = c, y \not = b$. We have introduced no new products with a right-hand side other than $c$ or $b$, so if $((x \op y) \op y) \op y$ was undefined before it remains undefined now.

nodes.name: Define new products
nodes.statement:
If $a \op b$ is undefined, set it equal to a new element $c$.  If we also have $b = d \op a$ for some $d$ (unique by Law 2, and only possible for $a \neq b$ by Law 3), set $a \op c = d$.

It is obvious that Laws 2, 3 are preserved.

nodes.name: Case analysis for Law 1
nodes.statement: Now we case check Law 1:

nodes.name: Case involving $c$ as factor
nodes.statement: Case 1: $x=c$ or $y=c$.  Not possible since no left multiplication with $c$ is defined.

nodes.name: Case $x\op y=c$
nodes.statement: Case 2: $x \op y = c$.  Only possible when $x = a$, $y = b$, but then $y \op (x \op y)$ is undefined since $y = b \neq a$ if $d$ is defined.

nodes.name: Case $y\op(x\op y)=c$
nodes.statement: Case 3. $y \op (x \op y) = c$.  Only possible when $y=a$ and $x=d$, and holds in this case.

nodes.name: Case covered by previous seed
nodes.statement: Case 4: $x, y, x \op y, y \op (x \op y) \neq c$: this case is already covered by the previous seed.

nodes.name: Case $a=b$
nodes.statement:
If $a = b$, set $a \diamond' a = a$.  This clearly does not destroy Laws 3 or 4, and because of Law 4, Law 2 will also be retained.
Finally, using Law 4, we can check that this addition does not break Law 1.

nodes.name: Case $a\ne b$
nodes.statement:
Now suppose $a \neq b$.
Let $d_1,d_2,..., d_n$ be all the elements with $b = a \diamond d_i$, and note from Law 3 and $a \neq b $ that we have the crucial inequality $d_i \neq a$ for all $i$.  If $d_i \diamond a$ is defined, let $e_i = d_i \diamond a.$ From Law 4 and $d_i \neq a$, we have $e_i \neq d_i$. From Law 2 and $a \diamond d_i = a \diamond d_j$, we further have $e_i \neq e_j$ and $e_i \neq d_j$ for $i \neq j$.

 For the algorithm, we set $a \diamond' b = c$ for some new $c$, $d_i \diamond' c = a$, and $c \diamond' e_i = d_i$ (This is well defined as we have just argued $e_i \neq e_j$ for $i \neq j$).

This creates a new partial function.  Law 2 is verified as follows:
The case $x=c$ cannot occur because $c \diamond' e_i \neq c \diamond' e_j$ for $i \neq j$.
If $y=c$, then $x = d_i$ for some $i$, but then $y \diamond' x = c \diamond' d_i$ is undefined as $d_i \neq e_j$, so this case is vacuous.
If $z=c$ and $x,y \neq c$, then similarly $z \diamond' x$ is undefined, and $y \diamond' x$ is not equal to
$c = z$, so we are ok in this case also.

Law 3 is clearly unaffected, and it is also straightforward to check that Law 4 is also not invalidated
(here it is essential that $d_i \neq a$).

Now we verify Law 1.
\begin{itemize}
  \item Case 1: $x=c$.  Then for $x \diamond' y$ to be defined we must have $y=e_i$ for some $i$, but then
$x \diamond' (x \diamond' y) = c \op' d_i$ is undefined as $d_i \neq e_j$ for all $j$.
\item Case 2: $y=c$. Then for $x \diamond' y$ to be defined we must have $x = d_i$ for some $i$. Then $d_i \op' (d_i \op' c)$ is either undefined or is equal to $e_i$, in which case Law 1 holds as $c \op' e_i = d_i$.
\item Case 3: $x \diamond' y = c$.  Then $x=a$ and $y=b$.  Since $d_i \neq a$ for all $i$, $x \diamond (x \diamond y)$ is undefined.
\item Case 4: $x \op' (x \op' y) = c$. Then $x = a$ and $y = d_i$ for some $i$, and Law 1 holds as $d_i \op' c = a$.
\item Case 5: None of $x, y, x \diamond' y, x \op' (x \op' y)$ are equal to $c$.  Then this case is covered by the previous seed.

nodes.name: Collect the $d_i$ and $e_i$
nodes.statement:
Let $d_1,d_2,..., d_n$ be all the elements with $b = a \diamond d_i$, and note from Law 3 and $a 
eq b $ that we have the crucial inequality $d_i 
eq a$ for all $i$.  If $d_i \diamond a$ is defined, let $e_i = d_i \diamond a.$ From Law 4 and $d_i 
eq a$, we have $e_i 
eq d_i$. From Law 2 and $a \diamond d_i = a \diamond d_j$, we further have $e_i 
eq e_j$ and $e_i 
eq d_j$ for $i 
eq j$.

nodes.name: Define new products
nodes.statement: For the algorithm, we set $a \diamond' b = c$ for some new $c$, $d_i \diamond' c = a$, and $c \diamond' e_i = d_i$ (This is well defined as we have just argued $e_i \neq e_j$ for $i \neq j$).

nodes.name: Verify Law 2
nodes.statement:
This creates a new partial function.  Law 2 is verified as follows:
The case $x=c$ cannot occur because $c \diamond' e_i \neq c \diamond' e_j$ for $i \neq j$.
If $y=c$, then $x = d_i$ for some $i$, but then $y \diamond' x = c \diamond' d_i$ is undefined as $d_i \neq e_j$, so this case is vacuous.
If $z=c$ and $x,y \neq c$, then similarly $z \diamond' x$ is undefined, and $y \diamond' x$ is not equal to
$c = z$, so we are ok in this case also.

Law 3 is clearly unaffected, and it is also straightforward to check that Law 4 is also not invalidated
(here it is essential that $d_i \neq a$).

nodes.name: Case analysis for Law 1
nodes.statement: Now we verify Law 1.

nodes.name: Case $x=c$
nodes.statement:
Case 1: $x=c$.  Then for $x \diamond' y$ to be defined we must have $y=e_i$ for some $i$, but then
$x \diamond' (x \diamond' y) = c \op' d_i$ is undefined as $d_i \neq e_j$ for all $j$.

nodes.name: Case $y=c$
nodes.statement: Case 2: $y=c$. Then for $x \diamond' y$ to be defined we must have $x = d_i$ for some $i$. Then $d_i \op' (d_i \op' c)$ is either undefined or is equal to $e_i$, in which case Law 1 holds as $c \op' e_i = d_i$.

nodes.name: Case $x\op y=c$
nodes.statement: Case 3: $x \diamond' y = c$.  Then $x=a$ and $y=b$.  Since $d_i \neq a$ for all $i$, $x \diamond (x \diamond y)$ is undefined.

nodes.name: Case $x\op(x\op y)=c$
nodes.statement: Case 4: $x \op' (x \op' y) = c$. Then $x = a$ and $y = d_i$ for some $i$, and Law 1 holds as $d_i \op' c = a$.

nodes.name: Case covered by previous seed
nodes.statement: Case 5: None of $x, y, x \diamond' y, x \op' (x \op' y)$ are equal to $c$.  Then this case is covered by the previous seed.

nodes.name: Define new products
nodes.statement:
Set $a \diamond' b = c$ for some new element $c$. If $d_1,d_2,...,d_n$ are the elements for which $a \diamond d_i = b$, set $c \diamond' d_i = c'_i$ for some new element $c'_i$, and also set
$d_i \diamond' c'_i = a$. If $d_i \diamond a$ is equal to some $e_i$, set $e_i \diamond' c'_i = c''_i$ and $c'_i \diamond' c''_i = d_i$,
where $c''_i$ is equal to $a$ if $e_i = d_i$, or is some new element otherwise.

nodes.name: No collisions; Law 2 preserved
nodes.statement:
One can verify that no collisions are caused by this construction (this is why we have to take $c''_i=a$ when $e_i=d_i$),
 and that Law 2 is preserved.

nodes.name: Case analysis for Law 1
nodes.statement: We need to verify that these constructions preserve Law 1.  There are several cases:

nodes.name: Case $y=c$
nodes.statement: $y=c$.  Not possible since there are no right multiplications by $c$ defined.

nodes.name: Case $x=c$
nodes.statement: $x=c$.  Not possible since it forces $y = d_i$, $x \diamond y = c'_i$ for some $i$.

nodes.name: Case $y=c'_i$, $x=d_i$
nodes.statement: $y=c'_i$, $x = d_i$.  True by construction.

nodes.name: Case $y=c'_i$, $x\ne d_i$
nodes.statement: $y=c'_i$, $x \neq d_i$.  This forces $x = e_i \neq d_i$ and $x \diamond' y = c''_i$, but then $x \diamond' (x \diamond' y)$ is undefined.

nodes.name: Case $x=c'_i$
nodes.statement:
$x=c'_i$.  Not possible because this forces $x \diamond' y = d_i$, and $x \diamond' (x \diamond' y)$ will be undefined.
 (Here we use the fact that $e_i=d_i$ can only occur when $d_i \neq a$, by Law 2.)

nodes.name: Case $x=c''_i$
nodes.statement: $x = c''_i$ is new.  Not possible as no left multiplications by $c''_i$ are defined.

nodes.name: Case $y=c''_i$
nodes.statement: $y=c''_i$ is new.  This forces $x = c'_i$ and $x \diamond' y = d_i$, but then $x \diamond' (x \diamond' y)$ is undefined.

nodes.name: Case old, product undefined
nodes.statement:
$x$ and $y$ are not new and $x \diamond y$ was undefined. This requires $x=a, y=b$, but then $x \diamond' (x \diamond' y)$
is undefined since right multiplication by $c$ is undefined.

nodes.name: Case old, outer product undefined
nodes.statement:
$x$, $y$ are not new and $x \diamond y$ was defined, but $x \diamond (x \diamond y)$ was undefined.
This requires $x=a$, $x \diamond y = b$, and hence $y = d_i$ for some $i$.  The claim now follows from construction.

nodes.name: Case covered by previous seed
nodes.statement: $x$, $y$, are not new and $x \diamond y$, $x \diamond (x \diamond y)$ were defined. This then follows from the previous seed.

nodes.name: Strategy: translation-invariant model
nodes.statement:
The implication between the laws \Equareffull{1648} and \Equareffull{206} can be refuted by a translation-invariant
magma on the integers.

nodes.name: Define $f$ and the magma
nodes.statement:
Define the function $f: \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ by
$$f(x) =
\begin{cases}
  -1  & \text{if } x > 0, \\
   0  & \text{if } x = 0, \\
   1  & \text{if } x < 0,
\end{cases}$$
and consider the translation-invariant magma on $\mathbb{Z}$ given by the operation $x \op y = x + f(y-x)$.

nodes.name: Verify 1648 by cases
nodes.statement:
The resulting magma satisfies Equation 1648: one can show this by a case analysis on $f(y-x)$. If $f(y-x)=1$ we have $x \op y = x + f(y-x) = x + 1$, so
$$(x \op y) \op ((x \op y) \op y) = (x + 1) \op ((x + 1) \op y) = (x + 1) \op (x + 2) = (x + 1) - 1 = x.$$
Similar computations verify the other two cases.

nodes.name: 206 fails
nodes.statement:
However, setting $x=0$ and $y=-1$ in Equation 206, we get
$$(x \op (x \op y)) \op y = (x \op 1) \op y = (-1) \op y = -1 \neq x$$
so the magma does not satisfy \Equaref{206}. We can conclude

nodes.name: Use the modified base model technique
nodes.statement:
A model refuting the implication between the laws \Equareffull{1659} and \Equareffull{4315} can be constructed using
the modified base model technique.
nodes.statement_short: Use the modified base model technique

nodes.name: Base model on $\Z$
nodes.statement:
Start with the infinite model $(\mathbb{Z},\op)$ of \Equaref{1659} given by the following operation:
$$ x\op y = \begin{cases} x+1 & \text{if } x,y \text{ have the same parity} \\ x -1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$

nodes.name: Base model satisfies both laws
nodes.statement: A case analysis shows that the magma $(\mathbb{Z},\op)$  satisfies both \Equaref{1659} and \Equaref{4315}.

nodes.name: State the modified operation
nodes.statement:
We will eventually \emph{modify} it by setting
$$x \op' y = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } x=0,\: x,y \text{ do not have the same parity} \\  x+1 & \text{if } x,y \text{ have the same parity} \\ x -1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$
and checking that $(\mathbb{N}, \op' )$ satisfies \Equaref{1659} but refutes \Equaref{4315}.

nodes.name: Strategy for finding modifications
nodes.statement: One finds these modifications using the following strategy:

nodes.name: Choose counterexample tuple $(0,0,1)$
nodes.statement:
First, choose some element (tuple) of the carrier $M$ that will constitute a counterexample to the
consequent in the modified model. In this specific case, the consequent, \Equaref{4315}, can be written as
$$ x \op (y \op x) = x \op (y \op z)$$
in equational form, which always holds when $x = z$. So let's choose the tuple $(0,0,1)$
to constitute the required counterexample. Computing $0 \op (0 \op 0) = 0 \op 1 = -1$ and similarly
$0 \op (0 \op 1) = -1$ suggest that we could force this tuple to be a counterexample by defining a new
operation $\op''$ and setting
$0 \op'' 1$ to something other than $-1$. One seemingly has many choices here: should we take
$0 \op'' 1 =0$, $0 \op'' 1 = 1$, $0 \op'' 1 = 2$, or perhaps even $0 \op'' 1 = -1$?

nodes.name: Choose $0\op'' 1 = 0$
nodes.statement:
It's easy to rule out some of the possibilities. For instance, setting $0 \op'' 1 = 1$ would
yield $0 \op'' (0 \op'' 0) = 0 \op'' 1 = 0 \op'' (0 \op'' 1)$ again. The simplest possibility which results in
a counterexample to \Equaref{4315} sets $0 \op'' 1 = 0$ and $x \op'' y = x \op y$ for any $x \neq 0, y \neq 1$.

nodes.name: New counterexamples to 1659
nodes.statement:
Unfortunately, the resulting $(M,\op'')$ would not then satisfy \Equaref{1659}. For any $z \in M$, one would have
$$ (0 \op'' 1) \op'' ((1 \op'' 1) \op'' z) = 0 \op'' (2 \op'' z)$$
which equals $0 \op'' 1 = 0$ as desired for even $z$, but equals $0 \op'' 3 = -1 \neq 0$ for odd $z$.

nodes.name: Breakage is controlled but propagates
nodes.statement:
However, since $f$ takes finitely many values in the base model, the breakage is tightly controlled:
by considering what happens if $x \neq 0$ and $y \neq 1$, we see that all new counterexamples to \Equaref{4315}
have this form. The calculation now suggests defining yet another $\op'''$, where setting
$0 \op''' 3 = 0$ would eliminate
this counterexample. But doing that just moves the issue one level higher: one then has
$$ (0 \op''' 3) \op''' ((3 \op''' 3) \op''' z) = 0 \op''' (4 \op''' z)$$ which equals $0 \op''' 3 = 0$ as desired for even $z$, but equals $0 \op''' 5 = -1 \neq 0$ for odd $z$.

nodes.name: Redefine all at once and truncate to $\N$
nodes.statement:
Instead, the infinitely many counterexamples arising from the iterated redefinition can be eliminated
all at once by setting:
$$x \op' y = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } x=0,\: x,y \text{ do not have the same parity} \\  x+1 & \text{if } x,y \text{ have the same parity} \\ x -1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$
and also truncating the model to $\mathbb{N}$ since the result of the $\op'$
operation is nonnegative whenever the operands are nonnegative. This finishes the construction without generating any further violations of \Equaref{1659} and proves
nodes.statement_short: Redefine all at once and truncate to $\N$

nodes.name: Overview of the greedy construction
nodes.statement: This will be a greedy construction, but we have to introduce a rather large number of additional elements to ensure that certain non-degeneracy conditions are maintained (in particular, the new elements $h'$ introduced have to be such that $f^2(h') - h'$ avoids $E_2$ and hence $\Z^3$, which requires a certain amount of complexity in the construction).

nodes.name: Define $\tilde E_2$
nodes.statement:
Let $\tilde E_2$ denote the set $E_2$ together with all the elements of the form $-h'$, $h' - f^2(h')$, and $f^2(h') - h'$ for $h' \in E_2 \backslash E_1$; this is $\Z^3$ with a finite number of additional elements.

Let $a$ be an element of $\Z^3$ such that the quantities
$$ \pm Ta, \pm(Ta + a)$$
are distinct from each other and from
$$0, \pm h, \pm (h - f(h)), \pm (f^2(h)-h);$$
this is possible since $T, T+1$ are invertible.

nodes.name: Choose $x$ generically
nodes.statement:
Next, we pick an $x \in \Z^3 \times \Z$ such that the quantities
$$ \pm x, \pm x + Ta, \pm x - Ta, \pm 2 x + Ta, \pm x + Ta + a, \pm (h + x), \pm (h - f(h) + x), \pm (f^2(h)-h + x + Ta)$$
are all distinct from each other and from $\tilde E_2$; indeed, from the choice of $a$ (and the non-zero nature of $h$, $f(h)$, $h-f(h)$, and $f^2(h)-h$) there are only finitely many $x$ for which a collision can occur between any pair of these expressions.

nodes.name: Define $E'_1, E'_2$
nodes.statement:
We now promote $\pm h, \pm x, \pm x + Ta, \pm x - Ta$ to $E_1$, and also promote $h+x$, $h - f^2(h)$, $\pm 2x + Ta$, $\pm x + Ta + a$ to $E_2$.  That is to say, we define
$$ E'_1 := E_1 \cup \{\pm h, \pm x, \pm x + Ta, \pm x - Ta\}$$
and
$$ E'_2 := E_2 \cup \{ -h, \pm x, \pm x + Ta, \pm x - Ta, h + x, h - f^2(h), \pm 2x + Ta \}.$$

nodes.name: Define $f'$; (a),(b),(d) hold
nodes.statement:
We then define an extension $f'$ of $f$ to $E'_2$ by setting
\begin{align*}
 f'(\pm x) &:= a \\
 f'(\pm x + Ta) &:= \pm x \\
 f'(\pm x - Ta) &:= \mp x + Ta \\
 f'(\pm x + Ta + a) &:= \pm x - Ta \\
 f'(\pm 2x + Ta) &:= \pm x + Ta \\
 f'(\pm x + Ta + a) &:= \pm x - Ta \\
 f'(-h) &:= x + Ta \\
 f'(h+x) &:= h \\
 f'(h - f^2(h)) &:= -h.
\end{align*}
It is easy to see that $(E'_1,E'_2,f')$ satisfies properties (a), (b), (d).

nodes.name: Property (c)
nodes.statement:
By construction, we have
$$ f'( (f')^2(h') - h') = -h'$$
for
$$ h' = \pm h, \pm x, \pm x+Ta, \pm x-Ta$$
giving property (c).

nodes.name: Property (e)
nodes.statement:
By construction, the quantities
$$ -h', h' - f^2(h'), f^2(h') - h'$$
are distinct from each other and lie outside of $\tilde E_2 \cup E'_2$ for
$$ h' = h+x, h - f^2(h), \pm 2x + Ta, \pm x + Ta + a$$
while these quantities are distinct from each other and lie in $\tilde E_2 \backslash E'_2$ for $h' \in E_2 \backslash E'_1$ (note that this forces $h' \neq \pm h$).  This gives property (e).

nodes.name: Define $\tilde E_2$
nodes.statement:
Let $\tilde E_2$ denote the set $E_2$ together with all elements of the form
\begin{equation} -h', h' - f^2(h'), f^2(h') - h'
\end{equation}
for some $h' \in E_2 \backslash E_1$; this is $\Z^3$ with a finite number of elements attached, and is symmetric around the origin.

nodes.name: Case $h\notin\tilde E_2$
nodes.statement:
First suppose that $h$ lies outside of $\tilde E_2$.  Then we can find $a \in \Z^3$ such that the quantities
$$ -h, \pm (h - Ta)$$
are distinct from each other, and lie outside of $\tilde E_2$.  We now promote $h$ to $E_2$, thus setting
$$ E'_1 := E_1$$
and
$$ E'_2 := E_2 \cup \{h\}$$
and define an extension $f'$ of $f$ to $E'_2$ by setting
$$ f'(h) := a.$$
It is then a routine matter to check that $(E'_1,E'_2,f')$ is an extension of $(E_1,E_2,f)$.

nodes.name: Choose $a$
nodes.statement:
Then we can find $a \in \Z^3$ such that the quantities
$$ -h, \pm (h - Ta)$$
are distinct from each other, and lie outside of $\tilde E_2$.

nodes.name: Define the extension
nodes.statement:
We now promote $h$ to $E_2$, thus setting
$$ E'_1 := E_1$$
and
$$ E'_2 := E_2 \cup \{h\}$$
and define an extension $f'$ of $f$ to $E'_2$ by setting
$$ f'(h) := a.$$

nodes.name: Routine check
nodes.statement: It is then a routine matter to check that $(E'_1,E'_2,f')$ is an extension of $(E_1,E_2,f)$.

nodes.name: Case $h\in\tilde E_2$
nodes.statement: Now suppose that $h$ lies in $\tilde E_2$.  Then $h$ is of one of the forms \Cref{hp-form} for some $h' \in E_2 \backslash E_1$.  Suppose it is of the form $-h'$ or $f^2(h') - h'$.  We invoke \Cref{add-E1} to promote $h'$ to $E_1$ by using a suitable extension $(E'_1,E'_2,f')$; and now $h$ will lie in $E'_2$, giving the claim.  If instead $h$ is of the form $h'-f^2(h')$, then this procedure might not place $h$ in $E'_2$; but if it does not, it will be of the form $-h''$ for $h'' = f^2(h')-h' \in E'_2 \backslash E'_1$.  Applying \Cref{add-E1} one more time to now promote $h''$ to $E_1$, we will obtain a larger extension $(E''_1,E''_2,f'')$ with $h \in E''_2$, giving the claim.

nodes.name: Identify $h'$
nodes.statement: Then $h$ is of one of the forms \Cref{hp-form} for some $h' \in E_2 \backslash E_1$.

nodes.name: Subcase: promote $h'$ via Lemma
nodes.statement: Suppose it is of the form $-h'$ or $f^2(h') - h'$.  We invoke \Cref{add-E1} to promote $h'$ to $E_1$ by using a suitable extension $(E'_1,E'_2,f')$; and now $h$ will lie in $E'_2$, giving the claim.

nodes.name: Subcase: apply Lemma twice
nodes.statement: If instead $h$ is of the form $h'-f^2(h')$, then this procedure might not place $h$ in $E'_2$; but if it does not, it will be of the form $-h''$ for $h'' = f^2(h')-h' \in E'_2 \backslash E'_1$.  Applying \Cref{add-E1} one more time to now promote $h''$ to $E_1$, we will obtain a larger extension $(E''_1,E''_2,f'')$ with $h \in E''_2$, giving the claim.

nodes.name: Seed partial solution
nodes.statement: To see this, let $a$ be a non-zero element of $\Z^3$, let $x$ be an element of $\Z^3 \times \Z$ outside of $\Z^3$, and consider the partial solution $(\Z^3, \Z^3 \cup \{x\}, f)$ where $f(h) = Th$ for $h \in \Z^3$ and $f(x) = a$.

nodes.name: It is non-injective
nodes.statement: One can check that this is a partial solution and is not injective, since $f(x) = f(T^{-1} a)$.

nodes.name: Fails 1692
nodes.statement:
This non-injectivity implies in particular that the model is not left-cancellative, and hence does not satisfy the law
$$ x = (y \op x) \op ((y \op x) \op y)$$
(equation 1692).

nodes.name: Case analysis
nodes.statement: We divide into cases.

nodes.name: Case 1: already done
nodes.statement: {\bf Case 1:} $h_0 \in E$ and $f(h_0) \in E$.  In this case we are already done thanks to axiom (ii).

nodes.name: Case 2: main case
nodes.statement:
{\bf Case 2:} $h_0 \in E$ but $f(h_0) \not \in E$.  This is the main case.  Let $H$ be the set of all $h \in E$ such that $f(h) = f(h_0)$; this is a finite set containing $h_0$.  Let $H' \subseteq H$ be the set of all $h' \in H$ such that $-h' \in E$.  We make the following observations:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item[(a)] All elements $h$ of $H$ are non-zero.  For if $h=0$ then $f(h_0)=f(h)=1 \in E$, contradicting the hypothesis $f(h_0) \not \in E$.
  \item[(b)]  If $h' \in H'$ then $h' \neq h'+f(-h')$.  Otherwise we would have $f(-h')=0$, then by axiom (iii) we have $h' = -3$, hence $f(h_0) = f(h') = 4 \in E$ by axiom (i).  But this again contradicts the hypothesis $f(h_0) \not \in E$. (This is the main reason we take $E_0$ to be so large.)
  \item[(c)]  If $h_1 \in H$ and $h_2 \in H'$ are distinct then $h_1 \neq h_2+f(-h_2)$.  This follows from axiom (iv).
  \item[(d)]  If $h_1, h_2\in H'$ are distinct then $h_1+f(-h_1) \neq h_2+f(-h_2)$. This follows from axiom (v).
  \end{itemize}

  From these observations, we see that if we take $c$ to be a sufficiently large integer, the following claims hold:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item[1.]  The expressions $\pm c$, $\pm(c - h)$ for $h \in H$, and $\pm(c-h'-f(-h'))$ for $h \in H'$ are all distinct from each other.
  \item[2.]  $c$ is not expressible as the sum of four or fewer elements of $\pm (E \cup f(E))$.
  \end{itemize}

  We select such a $c$.  We then promote $f(h_0)$, $c - h$ for $h \in H$, and $-c+h'+f(-h')$ for $h' \in H'$, thus setting
  $$ E' := E \cup \{f(h_0)\} \cup \{ c-h: h \in H\} \cup \{ -c+h'+f(-h'): h' \in H'\}.$$
We then extend $f$ to $f': E' \to \Z$ by setting
\begin{align*}
  f(f(h_0)) &:= c \\
  f(c-h) &:= -h \\
  f(-c+h'+f(-h')) &:= h' - c
\end{align*}
for all $h \in H$ and $h' \in H'$.  Axiom (i) is then obvious.  Axiom (ii) needs to be verified for the new elements $h_0$ and $c-h'$, $h' \in H'$ of $E'$ (the other elements will not satisfy the hypotheses of this axiom), but this is routine.  In particular $h_0$ satisfies the required conclusion of this lemma.

We need to verify (iii) for the new elements of $E'$, but this is clear from property (a) and claim 2.

Now we need to verify (iv).  It suffices to do so when at least one of $a,a',-a$ are new elements of $E'$.  If neither of $a$, $-a$ are new, then the only new elements $a'$ for which $f(a')$ could equal $f(a)$ take the form $c-h$ (thanks to claim 2), but then $a'$ cannot equal $a+f(-a)$, again thanks to claim 2.  If instead one of $a, -a$ is new, then from claim 1 the new element must be $f(h_0)$.  There is no old element $a'$ with $f(a') = c = f(f(h_0))$, so we must have $a = -f(h_0)$, but then $a + f(-a) = -f(h_0)+c$ will not equal $a'$, again thanks to claim 2.

Finally, we need verify to (v).  We may assume that at least one of $a,a',-a,-a'$ are new elements of $E'$.  As before, this forces the new element to be $f(h_0)$, and this cannot be $a$ or $a'$, so without loss of generality we have $a = -f(h_0)$ and $a' \in E$.  But then $a + f(-a) = -f(h_0)+c$ will not equal $a' + f(-a')$, again thanks to claim 2.

nodes.name: Define $H$ and $H'$
nodes.statement: This is the main case.  Let $H$ be the set of all $h \in E$ such that $f(h) = f(h_0)$; this is a finite set containing $h_0$.  Let $H' \subseteq H$ be the set of all $h' \in H$ such that $-h' \in E$.  We make the following observations:

nodes.name: Observation (a)
nodes.statement: [(a)] All elements $h$ of $H$ are non-zero.  For if $h=0$ then $f(h_0)=f(h)=1 \in E$, contradicting the hypothesis $f(h_0) \not \in E$.

nodes.name: Observation (b)
nodes.statement: [(b)]  If $h' \in H'$ then $h' \neq h'+f(-h')$.  Otherwise we would have $f(-h')=0$, then by axiom (iii) we have $h' = -3$, hence $f(h_0) = f(h') = 4 \in E$ by axiom (i).  But this again contradicts the hypothesis $f(h_0) \not \in E$. (This is the main reason we take $E_0$ to be so large.)

nodes.name: Observation (c)
nodes.statement: [(c)]  If $h_1 \in H$ and $h_2 \in H'$ are distinct then $h_1 \neq h_2+f(-h_2)$.  This follows from axiom (iv).

nodes.name: Observation (d)
nodes.statement: [(d)]  If $h_1, h_2\in H'$ are distinct then $h_1+f(-h_1) \neq h_2+f(-h_2)$. This follows from axiom (v).

nodes.name: Choose $c$ large
nodes.statement: From these observations, we see that if we take $c$ to be a sufficiently large integer, the following claims hold:

nodes.name: Claim 1
nodes.statement: [1.]  The expressions $\pm c$, $\pm(c - h)$ for $h \in H$, and $\pm(c-h'-f(-h'))$ for $h \in H'$ are all distinct from each other.

nodes.name: Claim 2
nodes.statement: [2.]  $c$ is not expressible as the sum of four or fewer elements of $\pm (E \cup f(E))$.

nodes.name: Promote elements and define $f'$; axioms (i),(ii)
nodes.statement:
We select such a $c$.  We then promote $f(h_0)$, $c - h$ for $h \in H$, and $-c+h'+f(-h')$ for $h' \in H'$, thus setting
  $$ E' := E \cup \{f(h_0)\} \cup \{ c-h: h \in H\} \cup \{ -c+h'+f(-h'): h' \in H'\}.$$
We then extend $f$ to $f': E' \to \Z$ by setting
\begin{align*}
  f(f(h_0)) &:= c \\
  f(c-h) &:= -h \\
  f(-c+h'+f(-h')) &:= h' - c
\end{align*}
for all $h \in H$ and $h' \in H'$.  Axiom (i) is then obvious.  Axiom (ii) needs to be verified for the new elements $h_0$ and $c-h'$, $h' \in H'$ of $E'$ (the other elements will not satisfy the hypotheses of this axiom), but this is routine.  In particular $h_0$ satisfies the required conclusion of this lemma.

We need to verify (iii) for the new elements of $E'$, but this is clear from property (a) and claim 2.

nodes.name: Axiom (iv)
nodes.statement: Now we need to verify (iv).  It suffices to do so when at least one of $a,a',-a$ are new elements of $E'$.  If neither of $a$, $-a$ are new, then the only new elements $a'$ for which $f(a')$ could equal $f(a)$ take the form $c-h$ (thanks to claim 2), but then $a'$ cannot equal $a+f(-a)$, again thanks to claim 2.  If instead one of $a, -a$ is new, then from claim 1 the new element must be $f(h_0)$.  There is no old element $a'$ with $f(a') = c = f(f(h_0))$, so we must have $a = -f(h_0)$, but then $a + f(-a) = -f(h_0)+c$ will not equal $a'$, again thanks to claim 2.

nodes.name: Axiom (v)
nodes.statement: Finally, we need verify to (v).  We may assume that at least one of $a,a',-a,-a'$ are new elements of $E'$.  As before, this forces the new element to be $f(h_0)$, and this cannot be $a$ or $a'$, so without loss of generality we have $a = -f(h_0)$ and $a' \in E$.  But then $a + f(-a) = -f(h_0)+c$ will not equal $a' + f(-a')$, again thanks to claim 2.

nodes.name: Case 3: reduce to Case 2
nodes.statement: {\bf Case 3:} $h_0 \not \in E$ but $h_0 \in f(E)$.  Here we can write $h_0 = f(h_1)$ where $h_1$ is of the form in Case 2.  Applying the Case 2 construction, we can pass to an extension in which $f(h_1) = h_0$ lies in $E$, and so we are now in either Case 1 or Case 2, and so we can again conclude.

nodes.name: Case 4: promote $h_0$ with large value
nodes.statement:
{\bf Case 4:} $h_0 \not \in E$ and $h_0 \not \in f(E)$.  We let $c$ be an integer so large that it is not expressible as the sum of four or fewer elements of $\pm (E \cup f(E))$.  We then promote $h_0$ to $E$ by setting
$$E' := E \cup \{h_0\}$$
and define an extension $f': E' \to \Z$ by setting $f'(h_0) := c$.  Axioms (i)-(iii) are obvious.  For axiom (iv), since $f'(h_0)$ is not equal to any other value of $f'$, the only new case introduced is if $-a = h_0$, but then $a+f(-a) = -h_0+c$ is distinct from $a'$ by choice of $c$.  A similar argument yields axiom (v).  With this extension, we are now in Case 2, and so we repeat the previous analysis to conclude.

nodes.name: Define $f'(h_0)=c$
nodes.statement:
We let $c$ be an integer so large that it is not expressible as the sum of four or fewer elements of $\pm (E \cup f(E))$.  We then promote $h_0$ to $E$ by setting
$$E' := E \cup \{h_0\}$$
and define an extension $f': E' \to \Z$ by setting $f'(h_0) := c$.  Axioms (i)-(iii) are obvious.

nodes.name: Axioms (iv), (v)
nodes.statement: For axiom (iv), since $f'(h_0)$ is not equal to any other value of $f'$, the only new case introduced is if $-a = h_0$, but then $a+f(-a) = -h_0+c$ is distinct from $a'$ by choice of $c$.  A similar argument yields axiom (v).

nodes.name: Reduce to Case 2
nodes.statement: With this extension, we are now in Case 2, and so we repeat the previous analysis to conclude.

nodes.name: Motivation: derive $x\op y = f(x)\op f(y)$
nodes.statement:
We begin with some informal motivation. Writing
\begin{equation} f(x) := x \op (x \op x),
\end{equation}
we conclude that
\begin{equation} x \op y = y \op f(x)
\end{equation}
and hence on iteration
$$ x \op y = f(x) \op f(y).$$

nodes.name: Identity for $f(x)$
nodes.statement:
In particular, $x \op x = f(x) \op f(x)$, and
$$ f(x) = x \op (x \op x) = (x \op x) \op f(x) = (f(x) \op f(x)) \op f(x).$$

nodes.name: Surjective $f$ would force the four laws
nodes.statement:
If $f$ is surjective, this would imply
$$ x = (x \op x) \op x$$
and hence the four laws stated above would hold in this case.
nodes.statement_short: Surjective $f$ would force the four laws

nodes.name: Take $G=\Z[t]$, $f(P)=tP$
nodes.statement:
This motivates the use of a non-surjective $f$.  We will take $G$ to be the space of polynomials $\Z[t]$ of one variable with integer coefficients, and let $f: G \to G$ be the multiplication by $t$ map:
$$ f(P) := tP.$$
This is of course non-surjective.

nodes.name: Define the operation
nodes.statement: The magma operation will be constructed as follows:

nodes.name: Products on multiples of $P$
nodes.statement: If $P$ is a polynomial with $P(0) \neq 0$, then $t^n P \op t^n P = t^n P \op t^{n+1} P = 2P$ for all $n \geq 0$, and $t^{n+m} P \op 2t^n P = 2t^n P \op t^{n+m+1} P = t^{m+1} P$ for all $n, m \geq 0$.  (This is well-defined since the $t^n P$, $2t^n P$ are all distinct polynomials.)

nodes.name: All other products are 0
nodes.statement: We define $P \op Q = 0$ if not covered by the above laws.

nodes.name: 3342 holds
nodes.statement: It is a routine matter to verify \Cref{fdef} and \Cref{xop}, so that equation 3342 holds.

nodes.name: The four laws fail at $x=y=1$
nodes.statement: However, one can check that the four laws in the conclusion fail with $x=y=1$.

nodes.name: First attempt on $\Z/3\Z$
nodes.statement: A first attempt would be the operation $i \op j := j+1$ on $\Z/3\Z$; this satisfies 1437, but unfortunately also satisfies 4269.

nodes.name: Define the operation on $\N\times\Z/3\Z$
Verify 1437
nodes.statement:
Note that $(a,i) \op (a,i) = (a+1,i+1)$, and that $(b,j) \op ((c,k) \op (a,i))$ will be of the form $(d,i+2)$ for some $d$.  Hence
$$ ((a,i) \op (a,i)) \op ((b,j) \op ((c,k) \op (a,i))) = (a+1-1, i+3) = (a,i),$$
giving 1437.

nodes.name: 4269 fails
nodes.statement:
On the other hand,
$$ (0,i) \op ((b,i) \op (0,i)) = (0,i) \op (b+1,i+1) = (b+1,i+2)$$
and so equation 4269 fails.

nodes.name: Forward direction
nodes.statement: For the forward direction, suppose $E$ is satisfied by $G_X$. Then, by definition, any substitution of the variables in $E$ with elements of $G_X$ will yield a true equation. In particular, substituting according to $\iota_X$ will yield a true equation.
nodes.section: 9.3 Proving metatheorems from invariants in Lean

nodes.name: Reverse direction via lift homomorphism
nodes.statement: For the reverse direction, suppose that $E$ is true when evaluated with the substitution $\iota_X$. Now, consider an arbitrary substitution of variables $f : X \to G_X$. By the lifting magma family property, there is a magma homomorphism $\operatorname{lift}{f} : G_X \to G_X$ such that $\operatorname{lift}{f}(\iota_X(x)) = f(x)$ for all $x$ in $X$. In other words, applying the substitution $f$ is equivalent to first applying to substitution $\iota_X$ and then applying the homomorphism $\operatorname{lift}{f}$. Since $E$ is true when evaluated with the substitution $\iota_X$, it is also true after applying the homomorphism $\operatorname{lift}{f}$. Thus, $E$ is satisfied by $G_X$.
nodes.section: 9.3 Proving metatheorems from invariants in Lean

nodes.name: Forward: restrict substitution
nodes.statement: In the forward direction, suppose $\phi : \mathbb{N} \to M$ is a substitution. Then the restriction of $\phi$ to the first $n$ natural numbers is a substitution for the variables of $E$, and since $M$ satisfies $E$, the law $E$ is true in $M$ under this substitution. Since $\tilde{E}$ is the same as $E$ under the substitution $\phi$, $M$ satisfies $\tilde{E}$.

nodes.name: Reverse: extend substitution by 0
nodes.statement: In the reverse direction, suppose $\phi : \{0, 2, \ldots, n-1\} \to M$ is a substitution. Then $\phi$ can be extended to a substitution $\tilde{\phi} : \mathbb{N} \to M$ by setting $\tilde{\phi}(i) = \phi(i)$ for $i \leq n$ and $\tilde{\phi}(i) = 0$ for $i \geq n$. Since $M$ satisfies $\tilde{E}$ under the substitution $\tilde{\phi}$, it satisfies $E$ under the restriction of $\tilde{\phi}$ to the first $n$ natural numbers, which is precisely $\phi$. The special case where $n = 0$ is in fact impossible, since there cannot be an expression with no variables.

nodes.name: Construct $M_X/\sim$
nodes.statement: For (i), we define $M_{X,\Gamma} = M_X / \sim$, where the equivalence relation $\sim$ is defined by requiring $w \sim w'$ if and only if $\Gamma \models w \formaleq w'$; this is an equivalence relation thanks to \Cref{equiv}, and from \Cref{sound-complete} we see that this relation respects the magma operations, so that $M_{X,\Gamma}$ is a magma. The map $\iota_{X,\Gamma}: X \to M_{X,\Gamma}$ is defined by setting $\iota_{X,\Gamma}(x)$ to be the equivalence class of $x$ in $M_{X,\Gamma}$ for each $x \in X$.

nodes.name: The quotient satisfies $\Gamma$
nodes.statement: We first check that $M_{X,\Gamma}$ satisfies $\Gamma$. Let $w \formaleq w'$ be a law in $\Gamma$, and let $f: X \to M_{X,\Gamma}$ be a function. We may lift this function to a function $\tilde{f}: X \to M_X$. From \Cref{derivation-def}, we have $\Gamma \models w \formaleq w'$ and hence $\Gamma \models \varphi_{\tilde{f}}(w) \formaleq \varphi_{\tilde{f}}(w')$. By \Cref{sound-complete}, we conclude $\Gamma \models \varphi_{\tilde{f}}(w) \formaleq \varphi_{\tilde{f}}(w')$. Quotienting by $\sim$, we conclude that $\varphi_f(w) = \varphi(w')$, giving the claim by \Cref{models-def}.

nodes.name: Lift a substitution
nodes.statement: Let $w \formaleq w'$ be a law in $\Gamma$, and let $f: X \to M_{X,\Gamma}$ be a function. We may lift this function to a function $\tilde{f}: X \to M_X$.

nodes.name: Entailment of the substituted law
nodes.statement: From \Cref{derivation-def}, we have $\Gamma \models w \formaleq w'$ and hence $\Gamma \models \varphi_{\tilde{f}}(w) \formaleq \varphi_{\tilde{f}}(w')$.

nodes.name: Apply completeness
nodes.statement: By \Cref{sound-complete}, we conclude $\Gamma \models \varphi_{\tilde{f}}(w) \formaleq \varphi_{\tilde{f}}(w')$.

nodes.name: Pass to the quotient
nodes.statement: Quotienting by $\sim$, we conclude that $\varphi_f(w) = \varphi(w')$, giving the claim by \Cref{models-def}.

nodes.name: Universal property
nodes.statement: Now we check the universal property (ii). Let $M$ be a magma satisfying the theory $\Gamma$, and let $f: X \to M$ be a function, then we have a magma homomorphism $\varphi_f: M_X \to M$. If $w, w' \in M_X$ are such that $w \sim w'$, then $\Gamma \models w \formaleq w'$ and hence $\varphi_f(w) = \varphi_f(w')$. Hence $\varphi_f$ descends to a map $\tilde{f}: M_{X,\Gamma} \to M$, which one can check to be a magma homomorphism with $\tilde{f} \circ \iota_{X,\Gamma} = f$. By construction, $M_{X,\Gamma}$ is generated by $\iota_{X,\Gamma}(X)$, and so this homomorphism is unique.

nodes.name: Take the induced homomorphism
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a magma satisfying the theory $\Gamma$, and let $f: X \to M$ be a function, then we have a magma homomorphism $\varphi_f: M_X \to M$.

nodes.name: It respects $\sim$
nodes.statement: If $w, w' \in M_X$ are such that $w \sim w'$, then $\Gamma \models w \formaleq w'$ and hence $\varphi_f(w) = \varphi_f(w')$.

nodes.name: Descend to the quotient
nodes.statement: Hence $\varphi_f$ descends to a map $\tilde{f}: M_{X,\Gamma} \to M$, which one can check to be a magma homomorphism with $\tilde{f} \circ \iota_{X,\Gamma} = f$.

nodes.name: Uniqueness from generation
nodes.statement: By construction, $M_{X,\Gamma}$ is generated by $\iota_{X,\Gamma}(X)$, and so this homomorphism is unique.

nodes.name: Refer to external notes; sketch follows
nodes.statement:
See the notes \href{https://www.overleaf.com/project/66f847bb14d0d8f0b77f74e1}{here}.
  A sketch of proof is as follows.
nodes.statement_short: Refer to external notes; sketch follows

nodes.name: Set up induction on terms $XY$
nodes.statement:
We induct on the length of the term.
  As before we consider terms of the form $XY$.
  Also, in both sequences if a simplification is applied to the whole term,
  then we can assume the sequence is simply final.

nodes.name: Apply the 477 lemma
nodes.statement:
By \Cref{477-lemma}, if any of the two sequences is final,
  then right before the last step, the two factors of the outermost product are both simple.

nodes.name: Same for the non-final sequence
nodes.statement: This is also true for the result of the non-final sequence.

nodes.name: Conclude by induction
nodes.statement:
By the induction hypothesis,
  they can be identified correspondingly, so the two sequences are either both final or both
  non-final, and in the first case, the same simplification is applied to give the same result.

nodes.name: Assume not simple; two cases
nodes.statement: Assume the contrary. Then we have 2 cases.

nodes.name: Case 1: length bound violated
Case 2: forces $Z=y=W$, contradiction
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Case 2: $Z(W\cdots(WW))$ matches the pattern
    $y(x(y\cdots(yy)))$.} Since $n \ge 3$, we have $Z = y = W$,
    so $|W\cdots(WW)| = n|W| = n|Z|$,
    contradicting $|x(y\cdots(yy))| > n|y|$.

nodes.name: Reduce to one direction; factor $z$
nodes.statement:
It suffices to prove that \Cref{1485} implies \Cref{2162}. Write $w = y \op z$, then from \Cref{1485} we can write $z = z_1 \op z_2$ with $z_1 = z \op z$ and $z_2 = z \op (z \op z)$, and then by \Cref{1485}
  $$ y = (z_2 \op y) \op (y \op (z_1 \op z_2)) = (z_2 \op y) \op w.$$

nodes.name: Apply 1485 again
nodes.statement:
From another application of \Cref{1485} we have
  $$ x = (w \op x) \op (x \op ((z_2 \op y) \op w)) = ((y \op z) \op x) \op (x \op y)$$
  as required.

nodes.name: Claim 4 automatic; reduce to Claims 1-3
nodes.statement: By the previous comments, we can ignore Claim 4 as it is automatic, and focus on completing the partial weak central groupoid on $G$ to a complete weak central groupoid by ensuring Claims 1, 2, 3 hold.

nodes.name: Suffices to repair single failures
nodes.statement: By the usual greedy algorithm, it suffices to show that any individual failure of Claim 1, 2 or 3 can be resolved by adding some finite number of edges to the graph.

nodes.name: Repair a failure of Claim 2 (and 3)
nodes.statement: Suppose first that Claim 2 fails, that is to say the partial weak central groupoid contains an edge $(a,n) \to (b,m)$ that is not the initial segment of any good path. Since the base relaxed weak central groupoid $G_0$ satisfies Claim 2, we can find a good path $a \to b \to c$ in the base. We then pick a natural number $l$ not previously occurring in the partial weak central groupoid, and adjoin the edge $(b,m) \to (c,l)$ to that partial weak central groupoid. All new paths created in this way are declared good or bad depending on whether their images in $G_0$ are good or bad, in particular $(a,n) \to (b,m) \to (c,l)$ is good. This can be checked to still be a partial extension of $G_0$ (no violation of Claim 1'' is created), and now Claim 2 is resolved at for the edge $(a,n) \to (b,m)$. A similar argument permits one to resolve any violations of Claim 3.

nodes.name: Lift a good path from $G_0$
nodes.statement: Since the base relaxed weak central groupoid $G_0$ satisfies Claim 2, we can find a good path $a \to b \to c$ in the base.

nodes.name: Adjoin a fresh edge
nodes.statement: We then pick a natural number $l$ not previously occurring in the partial weak central groupoid, and adjoin the edge $(b,m) \to (c,l)$ to that partial weak central groupoid.

nodes.name: Declare goodness by projection
nodes.statement: All new paths created in this way are declared good or bad depending on whether their images in $G_0$ are good or bad, in particular $(a,n) \to (b,m) \to (c,l)$ is good.

nodes.name: Still a partial extension
nodes.statement: This can be checked to still be a partial extension of $G_0$ (no violation of Claim 1'' is created), and now Claim 2 is resolved at for the edge $(a,n) \to (b,m)$. A similar argument permits one to resolve any violations of Claim 3.

nodes.name: Repair a failure of Claim 1
nodes.statement: If Claim 1 is violated, then there is a pair $(a,n), (b,m)$ that currently has no good path of length two in the partial weak central groupoid. As the base relaxed weak central groupoid $G_0$ satisfies Claim 1', we can find a good path $a \to c \to b$ in $G_0$. We then pick a natural number $l$ not previously occurring, and adjoin the edges $(a,n) \to (c,l) \to (b,m)$. All new paths created in this way are declared good or bad depending on whether their images in $G_0$ are good or bad, in particular $(a,n) \to (c,l) \to (b,m) \to (c,l)$. One can check that this is still a partial extension of $G_0$ (no violation of Claim 1'' is created), and now Claim 1 is resolved at the pair $(a,n), (b,m)$.

nodes.name: Use Claim 1' in $G_0$
nodes.statement: As the base relaxed weak central groupoid $G_0$ satisfies Claim 1', we can find a good path $a \to c \to b$ in $G_0$.

nodes.name: Adjoin fresh edges
nodes.statement: We then pick a natural number $l$ not previously occurring, and adjoin the edges $(a,n) \to (c,l) \to (b,m)$.

nodes.name: Declare goodness by projection
nodes.statement: All new paths created in this way are declared good or bad depending on whether their images in $G_0$ are good or bad, in particular $(a,n) \to (c,l) \to (b,m) \to (c,l)$.

nodes.name: Still a partial extension
nodes.statement: One can check that this is still a partial extension of $G_0$ (no violation of Claim 1'' is created), and now Claim 1 is resolved at the pair $(a,n), (b,m)$.

nodes.name: A 5-vertex relaxed weak central groupoid
nodes.statement:
Computer check reveals that the carrier $G_0=\{0,1,2,3 ,4\}$ with incidence matrix
  $$
  \begin{pmatrix}
   1 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\
   1 & 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\
   0 & 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\
   1 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\
   0 & 1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\
  \end{pmatrix}
  $$
  is a relaxed weak central groupoid if we declare the paths $0 \to 0 \to 0$, $0 \to 0 \to 1$, $0 \to 1 \to 1$, $1 \to 0 \to 0$, $1 \to 1 \to 0$, $1 \to 1 \to 1$ to be bad, and all other paths in the directed graph to be good.

nodes.name: Witness axioms
nodes.statement: We can also check the following axioms:

nodes.name: Anti-3457 witness
nodes.statement: Anti-3457: There exist $x,y,z,w$ with $x \to z \to x$,  $z \to w \to y$ both good, and $x \to z \to w$ bad. (One can take $x=1$, $y=4$, $z = 0$, $w = 0$.)

nodes.name: Anti-2087 witness
nodes.statement: Anti-2087: There exist $x,y,z,w,u$ with $y \to z \to x$, $z \to w \to x$, and $x \to u \to x$ good, and $w \to x \to u$ is bad. (One can take $x=1, y=2$, $z=4$, $w=1$, $u=0$.)

nodes.name: Anti-2124 witness
nodes.statement: Anti-2124: There exists $x,y,z,w,u$ with $y \to z \to y$, $z \to w \to x$ and $x \to u \to x$ good, and $w \to x \to u$  bad. (One can take $x=1$, $y=2$, $z=4$, $w = 1$, $u=0$.)

nodes.name: Anti-3511 witness
nodes.statement: Anti-3511: There exists $x,y,z,w$ with $x \to z \to y$ and $z \to w \to x$ good, and $x \to z \to w$ bad. (One can take $x=1$, $y=3$, $z = 1$, $w=0$.)

nodes.name: Complete a chosen finite partial extension
nodes.statement: Let $G_*$ be a finite partial extension of $G_0$ to be chosen later. By \Cref{greedy-prop}, we can complete this to a complete weak central groupoid $G$ with carrier $G_0 \times \N$. Depending on how we choose $G_*$, we can ensure that this $G$ refutes one of the four laws 3457, 2087, 2124, 3511:
nodes.statement_short: Complete a chosen finite partial extension

nodes.name: Refute 3457
nodes.statement: Refuting 3457: Let $x,y,z,w$ be as in the claim Anti-3457, then select $G_*$ to be the directed graph with edges $(x,0) \to (z,2) \to (x,0) \to (z,2) \to (w,3) \to (y,1)$. One can check that this is a partial extension, and that $G$ will refute 3457 with $x,y$ replaced by $(x,0),(y,1)$.

nodes.name: Refute 2087
nodes.statement: Refuting 2087: Let $x,y,z,w,u$ be as in the claim Anti-2087, then select $G_*$ to be the directed graph with edges $(y,1) \to (z,2) \to (x,0)$ and $(z,2) \to (w,3) \to (x,0) \to (u,4) \to (x,0)$. One can check that this is a partial extension, and that $G$ will refute 2087 with $x,y$ replaced by $(x,0),(y,1)$.

nodes.name: Refute 2124
nodes.statement: Refuting 2124: Let $x,y,z,w,u$ be as in the claim Anti-2124, then select $G_*$ to be the directed graph with edges $(y,1) \to (z,2) \to (y,1)$ and $(z,2) \to (w,3) \to (x,0) \to (u,4) \to (x,0)$. One can check that this is a partial extension, and that $G$ will refute 2124 with $x,y$ replaced by $(x,0),(y,1)$.

nodes.name: Refute 3511
nodes.statement: Refuting 3511: Let $x,y,z,w$ be as in the claim Anti-3511, then select $G_*$ to be the directed graph with edges $(x,0) \to (z,2) \to (y,1)$ and $(z,2) \to (w,3) \to (x,0)$. One can check that this is a partial extension, and that $G$ will refute 3511 with $x,y$ replaced by $(x,0),(y,1)$.

nodes.name: Part (i): $L_y$ invertible
nodes.statement: From \eqref{677-alt} we see that $L_y$ is surjective, hence invertible on finite magmas, giving (i) (the formula for $L_y^{-1} x$ being immediate from \eqref{677-alt}).

nodes.name: Part (ii)
nodes.statement:
For (ii), using the fact that $L_y x = x$, (i) becomes $x = x \op R_y x = L_x L_x y$, then, using the invertibility of $L_x$ given by (i) we have
  \[y = L_x^{-1} L_x^{-1} x \stackrel{(i)}{=} L_x^{-1} (x \op R_x L_x x) = L_x^{-1} (L_x R_x L_x x) =
  R_x L_x x = Sx \op x.\]

nodes.name: Part (iii)
nodes.statement: For (iii), we apply (i) with $x$ replaced by $L_y x$.

nodes.name: (i), (ii), (iii) equivalent
nodes.statement:
Clearly (ii) implies (i), which implies (iii).  If (iii) holds,
  we apply \eqref{677-alt} to conclude that
  $$ y \op x = x = y \op (x \op (x \op y))$$
  and hence by left invertibility
  $$ x = x \op (x \op y).$$
  On the other hand, from \eqref{677} with $y$ replaced by $x$ we have
  $$ x = x \op (x \op (Sx \op x))$$
 and hence by left invertibility $y = Sx \op x$, giving (ii).

nodes.name: (iii)$\Leftrightarrow$(iv), (v)$\Leftrightarrow$(vi)
nodes.statement: From left cancellativity we see that (v) and (vi) are equivalent, as are (iii) and (iv).

nodes.name: (vi)$\Leftrightarrow$(vii)
nodes.statement: If (vii) holds, then $L_x L_y y = y$, but from \eqref{677-alt} we have $y = L_x L_y R_x L_x y$, so (vi) follows from left-cancellativity; the converse implication follows by reversing the steps.

nodes.name: (iv)$\Leftrightarrow$(v)
nodes.statement: If (v) holds, then we have $L_x L_z x = z$, but from \eqref{677-alt} one has $z = L_x L_z R_x L_x z$, giving the (iv) by left-cancellativity; the converse implication follows by reversing the steps.

nodes.name: Reduce to injectivity of $R_x$
nodes.statement: By the previous lemma, it suffices to show that right multiplication $R_x$ is surjective, or equivalently injective by finiteness.

nodes.name: Suppose $R_x y = R_x y'$
nodes.statement: If this is not the case, then we can find distinct $y,y'$ such that $R_x y = R_x y'$, hence $L_y x = L_{y'} x$.

nodes.name: $L_y = L_{y'}$
nodes.statement: But in this linear model, $L_y$ and $L_{y'}$ differ by a constant, hence we have $L_y = L_{y'}$.

nodes.name: Left-invertibility gives $y=y'$
nodes.statement:
Applying \eqref{677-alt} we have
$$  L_y L_x L_{L_y x} y = x =  L_y L_x L_{L_y x} y'$$
and hence by left-invertibility $y=y'$, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Reduce to solvability
nodes.statement: By \Cref{677-basic}, it suffices to show that for any $(y,t)$, the equation $(x,s) \op (y,t) = (y,t)$ is solvable.

nodes.name: Reduce to fibre injectivity
nodes.statement: Since $G$ already satisfies 255, we know that we can find $x$ such that $x \op y = y$, so it suffices to show that the operation $s \mapsto \alpha_{x,y} s + \beta_{x,y} t + c_{x,y}$ is surjective, or equivalently injective.

nodes.name: Suppose non-injective
nodes.statement: If this were not the case, then we could find $s,s'$ such that $\alpha_{x,y} s = \alpha_{x,y} s'$, and hence $L_{(x,s)} (y,t') = L_{(x,s')} (y,t')$ for all $t' \in M$.

nodes.name: Compute with 677
nodes.statement:
Since
  $$ x \op y = y = x \op (y \op ((x \op y) \op x))$$
  from \eqref{677}, we have $y = y \op ((x \op y) \op x)$, and hence $L_{(y,t)} L_{L_{(x,s)} (y,t)} (x,s)$ is of the form $(y,t')$ for some $t'$, and similarly with $(x,s)$ replaced by $(x,s')$.

nodes.name: Left-invertibility gives $s=s'$
nodes.statement:
We conclude that
$$ L_{(x,s)} L_{(y,t)} L_{L_{(x,s)} (y,t)} (x,s) = (y,t) =
L_{(x,s)} L_{(y,t)} L_{L_{(x,s)} (y,t)} (x,s')$$
and hence by left invertibility $s=s'$, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Introduce $z,u,v$; goal $v=(x,u)$
nodes.statement: Write $z := y \op x$, $u = z \op y$, $v = x \op u$.  Our task is to show that $v = (x,u)$.

nodes.name: Only $u,v$ can be maximal
nodes.statement: From \Cref{op-prop} we know that $y$ is upper bounded by one of $z,x$, $z$ is upper bounded by one of $u,y$, and $x$ is upper bounded by one of $u,v$.  So out of $x,y,z,u,v$, the only elements that can be maximal in this set are $u$ and $v$.

nodes.name: If $v$ maximal done; assume $u$ maximal
nodes.statement: If $v$ is maximal, then by \Cref{op-prop} we have $v = (x,u)$ as required, hence we may assume for contradiction that $u$ is maximal.

nodes.name: Structure of $u$
nodes.statement: From \Cref{op-prop}, this implies that $u = (z,y)$ and $u = (u_L, (x \op u_L) \op x)$, hence $u_L = z$ and $y = (x \op z) \op x$.

nodes.name: More upper bounds
nodes.statement: From \Cref{op-prop}, $x$ is upper bounded by one of $x \op z$ and $z$, and $x \op z$ is upper bounded by one of $y$ and $x$.  We also recall that $y$ was upper bounded by one of $z,x$.

nodes.name: Only $z$ can be maximal
nodes.statement: We conclude that out of $x,y,z,x \op z$, the only one that can be maximal is $z$.

nodes.name: $z=(y,x)$
nodes.statement: In particular $z$ is not bounded by $x$, hence by \Cref{op-prop} $z = (y,x)$.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: $z$ is also not bounded by $x \op z$, hence by \Cref{op-prop} $x \op z = z_L = y$, hence $y = y \op x = z$, contradicting the fact that $y$ was not maximal. This gives the required contradiction.

nodes.name: Reduce to $y<v$
nodes.statement: By the previous lemma and definition of $\diamond$, it suffices to show that $y < (x, (y \op x) \op y)$.  Defining $z,u,v$ as before, this amounts to showing that $y < v$.

nodes.name: $x<v$
nodes.statement: We already have $v = (x,u)$, hence by \Cref{op-prop} $x < v$.

nodes.name: Chain bounds to get $y<v$
nodes.statement: Also recall that $y$ is bounded by one of $x,z$, and $z$ is bounded by one of $y,u$.  Since $u$ is also bounded by $v$, we obtain the claim.

nodes.name: Reduce to the universal property
nodes.statement: By the previous corollary, it suffices to show that every function $f: X \to M$ into a 677 magma $M$ can be extended to a unique homomorphism $\varphi_f: M_{X,677} \to X$. Uniqueness is clear since $M_{X,677}$ is generated by $X$.

nodes.name: Define $\varphi_f$
nodes.statement: For existence, we define $\varphi_f$ by first extending $f$ to the unique homomorphism from $M_X$ to $X$ (using the pairing map) and then restricting to $M_{X,677}$.

nodes.name: Remaining case
nodes.statement: To verify the homomorphism property $\varphi_f(x \diamond y) = \varphi_f(x) \diamond \varphi_f(y)$, we are already done when $x \diamond y = (x,y)$. The only remaining case is when $x \diamond y = y_L$ and $x < y = (y_L,  (x \diamond y_L) \diamond x)$.

nodes.name: Inductive verification
nodes.statement:
If we assume inductively that the homomorphism property $\varphi_f(x' \diamond y') = \varphi_f(x') \diamond \varphi_f(y')$ has already been verified for $y' < y$, then we have
  $$ \varphi_f(y) = \varphi_f(y_L) \diamond \varphi_f(y_R) = \varphi_f(y_L) \diamond (\varphi_f(x \diamond y_L) \diamond \varphi_f(x)) =  \varphi_f(y_L) \diamond ((\varphi_f(x) \diamond \varphi_f(y_L)) \diamond \varphi_f(x))$$
  and the claim now follows since $M$ satisfies 677.

nodes.name: Reduce to (i)
nodes.statement: We just verify claim (i), as claim (ii) is similar.

nodes.name: Converse is clear; prove forward
nodes.statement: The converse direction is clear from \Cref{854-alt} (after quotienting down to $M_X/\sim$), so it suffices to prove the forward claim.

nodes.name: Reduce to invariance under rewrites
nodes.statement: By \Cref{sound-complete}, it suffices to prove that the class of words described by (i) is preserved by any term rewriting operation, in which a term in the word is replaced by an equivalent term using \Cref{854}.  Clearly the term is in $w'_1$ or $w'_2$ then the form of the word is preserved, and similarly if the term is in one of the $v_i$.

nodes.name: Rewriting a prefix term
nodes.statement:
The only remaining case is if we are rewriting a term of the form
$$ x_i = (((w'_1 \op w'_2) \op v_1) \op \dots \op v_i).$$

nodes.name: Case $i>0$
nodes.statement: If $i>0$ we can rewrite this term down to $x_{i-1}$, and this still preserves the required form (decrementing $n$ by one).

nodes.name: Case $i=0$
nodes.statement: If $i=0$ then we cannot perform such a rewriting because of the irreducibility of $w_1 \op w_2$ and hence $w'_1 \op w'_2$.

nodes.name: Rewriting by expansion
nodes.statement:
Finally, we can rewrite $x_i$ to $x_i \op v$ where $v$ is of the form
$$ v_i = (y \op z) \op (x_i \op z),$$
and after some relabeling we are again of the required form (now incrementing $n$ by one).

nodes.name: WLOG irreducible
nodes.statement: By replacing $w,w'$ with irreducible equivalents, we may assume without loss of generality that $w,w'$ are irreducible.

nodes.name: $w \sim w\op w'$
nodes.statement: By hypothesis, $w$ is equivalent to $w \op w'$.

nodes.name: Apply the description
nodes.statement: The claim now follows from \Cref{irred-desc}.

nodes.name: Reduce to non-equivalence in the free magma
nodes.statement:
We work in the free group $M_X$ on two generators $X = \{x,y\}$.  It suffices to show that
$$  x \op y \not \sim x \op (y \op (x \op y))$$
and
$$
x \op y \not \sim (x \op (y \op x)) \op y.$$
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to non-equivalence in the free magma

nodes.name: Three cases via unique factorization
nodes.statement: We begin with the first claim.  Suppose this were not the case, then by \Cref{unique-factorization} one of the following statements must hold:

nodes.name: Case (ii)
nodes.statement: (ii) $$(y \op (x \op y)) \to x$$.

nodes.name: Case (iii)
nodes.statement: (iii) $$y \op (x \op y) \sim y.$$

nodes.name: Refute (i) via a model
nodes.statement: If (i) holds, then we have $x \op y = x$ (Equation 4) in $M_X/\sim$, hence in every magma satisfying \Equaref{854}.  But we have examples of such magmas in which this fails.

nodes.name: Refute (iii) via a model
nodes.statement: Similarly, if (iii) holds, then $y \op (x \op y) = y$ (Equation 10) holds in $M_X/\sim$, hence in every magma satisfying \Equaref{854}.  But we have examples of such magmas in which this fails.

nodes.name: Case (ii) reduces to (i)
nodes.statement:
Finally, if (ii) holds, then the claim
$$  x \op y \sim x \op (y \op (x \op y))$$
to refute simplifies to
$$  x \op y \sim x$$
and we are back to (i), which we already know not to be the case.

For the latter equation, we similarly have the cases

nodes.name: Case (iv)
nodes.statement: (iv) $$y \to x$$.

nodes.name: Case (v)
nodes.statement: (v) $$y \to x \op (y \op x)$$.

nodes.name: Case (vi)
nodes.statement: (vi) $$x \sim x \op (y \op x).$$

nodes.name: All cases already refuted
nodes.statement:
(iv) is (i), which was already ruled out, and (vi) is similarly a relabeled version of (iii). In case (v) holds, the claim to refute simplifies to
$$
x \op y \sim x \op (y \op x)$$
and using \Cref{unique-factorization} we reduce to either $y \sim y \op x$, $y \to x$, or $y \op x \to x$, and each of these is already known to fail.

nodes.name: (i)-(ii), (v)-(vi) by definition
nodes.statement: The equivalence of (i) and (ii), or (v) and (vi), is by definition.

nodes.name: (ii)$\Leftrightarrow$(iii) via 378
nodes.statement: (iii) trivially implies (ii), and the converse comes from \Cref{378}.

nodes.name: (v) implies (iv)
nodes.statement: Using \Cref{8} we see that (v) implies (iv).

nodes.name: (iv) implies (vii)
nodes.statement: If (iv) is true, then $y = (y \op z) \op (x \op z)$, giving (vii).

nodes.name: (vii) implies (ii)
nodes.statement: From \Cref{854} we see that (vii) implies (ii).

nodes.name: (ii) implies (vi)
nodes.statement: If (ii) is true, then $y \op (x \op y^2) = y \op ((x \op y) \op (y \op y)) = y$, giving (vi).

nodes.name: (i)$\Leftrightarrow$(viii)
nodes.statement: Finally, to show the equivalence of (i) and (viii), use the already established equivalence of (i) and (v), together with \Cref{378} which gives $(x \op y^2) \op y^2 = x \op y^2$.

nodes.name: (i)$\Leftrightarrow$(ii)
nodes.statement: The equivalence of (i) and (ii) is by definition.

nodes.name: (ii) implies (iii)
nodes.statement:
If (ii) holds and $y \to z$, then by \Cref{854-equiv} we have $x = u \op (x \op y)$ and $z = v \op y$ for some $u,v$, hence
  $$ z \op x = z \op (x \op ((v \op y) \op (x \op y))) = z \op ((u \op (x \op y)) \op (z \op (x \op y))) = z,$$
giving the desired claim $x \to z$.

nodes.name: (iii) implies (iv)
nodes.statement: Now if (iii) holds, note from \Cref{854-equiv} that $y \to x \op y$, hence $x \to x \op y$ by (iii), so that $(x \op y) \op x = x \op y$, giving (iv).

nodes.name: (iv) implies (ii)
nodes.statement:
Finally, if (iv) holds, note that
\begin{align*}
  x \op ((x \op y) \op x) &= x \op ( ((x \op y) \op ((y \op y) \op ((x \op y) \op y))) \op x) \\
  &= x \op (((x \op y) \op ((y \op y) \op (x \op y))) \op (x \op ((y \op y) \op (x \op y)))) \\
  &= x
\end{align*}
and hence by (iv) $x \op (x \op y) = x$, giving (ii).

nodes.name: Arrow relation on the partial magma
nodes.statement: Define a directed graph by writing $x \to y$ if $y \op x$ is defined and equal to $y$.  By Equation 378, we see that $x \to y$ if and only if $z \op x$ is well-defined and equal to $y$ for some $z$.
nodes.statement_short: Arrow relation on the partial magma

nodes.name: Factor $b$ and define relevance
nodes.statement:
From unique factorization, we see that $b$ has at most one representation of the form $b = b_1 \op b_2$ with $b_1 
eq b$, or equivalently $b_2 
ot 	o b_1$.  We define $b_1, b_2$ accordingly if such a representation exists, otherwise we leave $b_1, b_2$ undefined.  We say that $b_1$ is \emph{relevant} if $b_2 	o a$. Note that this forces $a 
eq b_1$ since $b_2 
ot 	o b_1$.  Also, if $b_1,b_2$ exist, we see from monotonicity that $b = b_1 \op b_2 > b_1, b_2$.

nodes.name: Define new table entries
nodes.statement: Let $c$ be a natural number that is larger than any number appearing in anywhere in the partial 854 magma multiplication table (in particular it is larger than $a,b$, as well as $b_1,b_2$ if they are defined).  We then extend the multiplication table by  defining $a \diamond b = c$, $b \diamond c = b$, and $c \diamond b = c$.  If $b_1$ exists and is relevant, we also define $b_1 \diamond c = b_1$.  Finally, if $b_1$ exists and is relevant, and additionally $b \to b_1$, then we also define $c \diamond b_1 = c$.  We remark that all new entries added are of the left absorptive form $x \diamond y = x$, except for $a \diamond b = c$.

nodes.name: Verify axioms other than 854
nodes.statement:
We now verify that all of the axioms of a partial 854 magma continue to hold.  We begin with all the axioms except for 854:

 egin{itemize}
  \item Monotonicity: Observe that all the new values $x \diamond y$ of the multiplication table introduced are either equal to $x$, or larger than both $x$ and $y$, so the monotonicity property is preserved.
  \item Unique factorization: the only way unique factorization breaks is if there is an element $z$ that has two distinct factorizations $z = x \op y = x' \op y'$ with neither $x \op y$ nor $x' \op y'$ a left absorptive product.  Since the only non-left-absorptive product introduced is $a \op b = c$, and $c$ has no prior representation as a product, we see that the unique factorization property is preserved.
  \item No idempotence: The only possible product $x \op x$ that could be introduced here is $a \op b$ if $x=a=b$, but in that case $x \op x = a \op b = c$ is clearly not equal to $x$, so the no idempotence property is preserved.
  \item Equation 8: If $x \op x$ were already defined in the previous magma, the claim would already be established, so $x \op x$ must be one of the new products $a \op b$, $b \diamond c$, $c \diamond b$, $b_1 \diamond c$, or $c \diamond b_1$.  As $c 
eq a,b,b_1$, the only option is $x = a = b$, but then $x \op (x \op x) = b \op c = b = x$, as required.
  \item Equation 101: By Equation 8, we may assume $x \op y 
eq x$, which implies $y 
eq c$ since $x \op c = x$ whenever the left-hand side is defined.  We can also assume $x 
eq c$, since we have $c \op z = c$ whenever the left-hand side is defined.  If $x \op y = c$, then $(x,y) = (a,b)$; as $(x \op y) \op x = c \op x$ is well-defined, $x=a$ is then either equal to $b$, or equal to $b_1$ if the latter exists and is relevant.  But the second case cannot occur since $a 
eq b_1$, so we have $x = b$, and then $x \op ((x \op y) \op x) = b \op (c \op b) = b = x$, giving the claim.  So we may assume $x \op y 
eq c$.  If $(x \op y, x) 
eq (a,b)$, then $(x \op y) \op x$ was already defined in the original partial magma, and the claim follows from Equation 101; hence we may assume $(x \op y, x) = (a,b)$, then $x \op ((x \op y) \op x) = b \op c = b = x$, giving the claim.
  \item Equation 46155: By Equation 8, we may assume $x \op y 
eq x$ and hence $y 
eq c$ as before.  The case $x=c$ is not possible, as this forces $x \op y = c$ and then $x \op (x \op y)$ is undefined.  If $x \op y = c$, then $(x,y) = (a,b)$; in order for $x \op (x \op y) = a \op c$ to be defined, either $a=b$ or $a=b_1$ with $b_1$ relevant, but the latter is impossible since $a 
eq b_1$; thus $x=y=a=b$ and $(x \op y) \op (x \op (x \op y)) = c \op (b \op c) = c = (x \op y)$, giving the claim.  Thus we may assume $x \op y 
eq c$.  If $(x, x \op y) 
eq (a,b)$ then $x \op (x \op y)$ was already defined in the original partial magma, and the claim follows from Equation 46155; hence we may assume $(x, x \op y) = (a,b)$, and we have $(x \op y) \op (x \op (x \op y)) = b \op c = b = x \op y$, giving the claim.
  \item Equation 378:  We can assume $x \op y 
eq x$, since the claim is trivial otherwise.  This rules out the $y=c$ and $x=c$ cases.  The only new case is then if $x \op y = c$, but forces $(x,y) = (a,b)$, and then $(x \op y) \op y = c \op b = c = x \op y$, giving the claim.
  \item Auxiliary law: if $x=c$, then the only possible value for $x \op y$ is $c$, and $c \op c$ is undefined, contradiction; thus $x 
eq c$.  If $y = c$, then the only possible value for $x \op y$ is $x$, and then $x \op (x \op y)$ cannot equal $x$ by the no idempotence law.  Thus $y 
eq c$.  Since $x \op (x \op y) = x$ is not equal to $c$, $(x,x \op y)$ is not equal to $(a,b)$.  If $(x,y) 
eq (a,b)$, then both $x \op y$ and $x \op (x \op y)$ were already defined in the original partial magma, and the claim follows from the auxiliary law for that magma.  Thus we may assume $(x,y) = (a,b)$, in which case $a \op c = a$, hence by construction either $a=b$ or $a=b_1$.  If $a=b$ then we are done.  If $a = b_1$, then $b_1$ cannot be relevant, and then $a \op c = b_1 \op c$ remains undefined, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Monotonicity
nodes.statement: Monotonicity: Observe that all the new values $x \diamond y$ of the multiplication table introduced are either equal to $x$, or larger than both $x$ and $y$, so the monotonicity property is preserved.

nodes.name: Unique factorization
nodes.statement: Unique factorization: the only way unique factorization breaks is if there is an element $z$ that has two distinct factorizations $z = x \op y = x' \op y'$ with neither $x \op y$ nor $x' \op y'$ a left absorptive product.  Since the only non-left-absorptive product introduced is $a \op b = c$, and $c$ has no prior representation as a product, we see that the unique factorization property is preserved.

nodes.name: No idempotence
nodes.statement: No idempotence: The only possible product $x \op x$ that could be introduced here is $a \op b$ if $x=a=b$, but in that case $x \op x = a \op b = c$ is clearly not equal to $x$, so the no idempotence property is preserved.

nodes.name: Equation 8
nodes.statement: Equation 8: If $x \op x$ were already defined in the previous magma, the claim would already be established, so $x \op x$ must be one of the new products $a \op b$, $b \diamond c$, $c \diamond b$, $b_1 \diamond c$, or $c \diamond b_1$.  As $c \neq a,b,b_1$, the only option is $x = a = b$, but then $x \op (x \op x) = b \op c = b = x$, as required.

nodes.name: Equation 101
nodes.statement:
Equation 101: By Equation 8, we may assume $x \op y 
eq x$, which implies $y 
eq c$ since $x \op c = x$ whenever the left-hand side is defined.  We can also assume $x 
eq c$, since we have $c \op z = c$ whenever the left-hand side is defined.  If $x \op y = c$, then $(x,y) = (a,b)$; as $(x \op y) \op x = c \op x$ is well-defined, $x=a$ is then either equal to $b$, or equal to $b_1$ if the latter exists and is relevant.  But the second case cannot occur since $a 
eq b_1$, so we have $x = b$, and then $x \op ((x \op y) \op x) = b \op (c \op b) = b = x$, giving the claim.  So we may assume $x \op y 
eq c$.  If $(x \op y, x) 
eq (a,b)$, then $(x \op y) \op x$ was already defined in the original partial magma, and the claim follows from Equation 101; hence we may assume $(x \op y, x) = (a,b)$, then $x \op ((x \op y) \op x) = b \op c = b = x$, giving the claim.

nodes.name: Equation 46155
nodes.statement:
Equation 46155: By Equation 8, we may assume $x \op y 
eq x$ and hence $y 
eq c$ as before.  The case $x=c$ is not possible, as this forces $x \op y = c$ and then $x \op (x \op y)$ is undefined.  If $x \op y = c$, then $(x,y) = (a,b)$; in order for $x \op (x \op y) = a \op c$ to be defined, either $a=b$ or $a=b_1$ with $b_1$ relevant, but the latter is impossible since $a 
eq b_1$; thus $x=y=a=b$ and $(x \op y) \op (x \op (x \op y)) = c \op (b \op c) = c = (x \op y)$, giving the claim.  Thus we may assume $x \op y 
eq c$.  If $(x, x \op y) 
eq (a,b)$ then $x \op (x \op y)$ was already defined in the original partial magma, and the claim follows from Equation 46155; hence we may assume $(x, x \op y) = (a,b)$, and we have $(x \op y) \op (x \op (x \op y)) = b \op c = b = x \op y$, giving the claim.

nodes.name: Equation 378
nodes.statement: Equation 378:  We can assume $x \op y \neq x$, since the claim is trivial otherwise.  This rules out the $y=c$ and $x=c$ cases.  The only new case is then if $x \op y = c$, but forces $(x,y) = (a,b)$, and then $(x \op y) \op y = c \op b = c = x \op y$, giving the claim.

nodes.name: Auxiliary law
nodes.statement:
Auxiliary law: if $x=c$, then the only possible value for $x \op y$ is $c$, and $c \op c$ is undefined, contradiction; thus $x 
eq c$.  If $y = c$, then the only possible value for $x \op y$ is $x$, and then $x \op (x \op y)$ cannot equal $x$ by the no idempotence law.  Thus $y 
eq c$.  Since $x \op (x \op y) = x$ is not equal to $c$, $(x,x \op y)$ is not equal to $(a,b)$.  If $(x,y) 
eq (a,b)$, then both $x \op y$ and $x \op (x \op y)$ were already defined in the original partial magma, and the claim follows from the auxiliary law for that magma.  Thus we may assume $(x,y) = (a,b)$, in which case $a \op c = a$, hence by construction either $a=b$ or $a=b_1$.  If $a=b$ then we are done.  If $a = b_1$, then $b_1$ cannot be relevant, and then $a \op c = b_1 \op c$ remains undefined, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Verify 854 by cases
nodes.statement:
Now we tackle the most difficult verification, which is 854.  This splits into a large number of cases.
 egin{itemize}
  \item Case 1: $x=c$.  Then $x \op z$ can only equal $c$, hence $z$ equals $b$ or $b_1$; and $y \op z$ can also only equal $b$ or $b_1$, and $(y \op z) \op (x \op z)$ is equal to $y \op z$.  If $y \op z = b$, then we are done since $c \op b = c$.  If $y \op z = b_1$, then $b_1 \op c$ needs to be defined, so $b_1$ is relevant.  Furthermore, from equation 378 we have $b_1 \op z = b_1$, hence by the no idempotence property $z$ must equal $b$, so $b 	o b_1$, and hence $c \op b_1 = c$, giving the claim.
  \item Case 2: $x 
eq c$, $z = c$.  This forces $x,y=b,b_1$ with $y \op z = y$ and $x \op z = x$, thus $y \op x$ is well-defined and we need $x \op (y \op x)$ well-defined and equal to $x$.  If $x=y$, this follows from Equation 8; otherwise, either $x = b_1 \op b_2$ and $y = b_1$ or $x = b_1$ and $y = b_1 \op b_2$, and the claim follows from Equation 101 or Equation 46155 respectively.
  \item Case 3: $x, z 
eq c$, $y = c$.  Then $z$ must equal $b$ or $b_1$, $y \op z$ must equal $c$, and $x \op z$ must equal $b$ or $b_1$, and $(y \op z) \op (x \op z)$ must equal $c$, with the $b_1$ options only available if $b_1$ is relevant.  If $x \op z = z$ then by equation 378, $z \op z = z$, contradicting the no idempotence law.  Thus we either have $z=b_1, x \op z = b$ or $z = b, x \op z = b_1$, and in either case $b_1$ must be relevant.  If $z 	o x$, then either have $x=b$, or $x = b_1$ and $b_1$ is relevant, and in either case we have $x \op c = x$ as required.  So we may assume $z 
ot 	o x$.  In the case $z = b_1, x \op z = b = b_1 \op b_2$ we may then apply unique factorization to conclude that $z = b_2$ and $x = b_1$, thus $x \op c = x$ as required.  In the opposite case $z = b$, $x \op z = b_1$ with $z 
ot 	o x$, we see from monotonicity that $b_1 = x \op z > z = b$; but from monotonicity again $b = b_1 \op b_2 > b_1$, a contradiction.
  \item Case 4: $x,y,z 
eq c$, $(y,z) = (a,b)$.  Here, $y \op z$ and $(y \op z) \op (x \op z)$ must equal $c$, and $x \op z$ must then equal $b$ or $b_1$, with the latter an option only if $b_1$ is relevant.  If $x \op z = b$, then by Equation 378, $b \op b = b$, contradicting idempotence, thus $x \op z = b_1$ and $b_1$ is relevant, and then $b 	o b_1$ by Equation 378 again.  If $z 	o x$, then $x = b_1$, and the claim follows since $b_1 \op c = c$, so we may assume $z 
ot 	o x$.  By monotonicity, this forces $b_1 = x \op z > z = b$ and $b = b_1 \op b_2 > b_1$, a contradiction.
  \item Case 5: $x,y,z 
eq c$, $(y,z) 
eq (a,b)$, $(x,z) = (a,b)$.  Now $x \op z = c$, and $y \op z$ must equal $b$ or $b_1$.  If $y \op z = b$, then by Equation 378, $b \op b = b$, contradicting idempotence, thus $y \op z = b_1$ and $b_1$ is relevant, and then $b 	o b_1$ by Equation 378 again, so $b_1 \op (b_1 \op b_2) = b_1$.  By the auxiliary law, this forces $b_1 = b_2$, so $x = b_1$, and then we are done since $b_1 \op c = b_1$.
  \item Case 6: $x,y,z 
eq c$, $(y,z), (x,z) 
eq (a,b)$, $(y \op z, x \op z) = (a,b)$.  Here $x \op z = b$ and $(y \op z) \op (x \op z) = c$.  If $z 	o x$, then $x=b$ and we are done since $b \op c = b$.  If $z 
ot 	o x$, then by unique factorization applied to $x \op z = b_1 \op b_2$ we have $(x,z) = (b_1,b_2)$.  By Equation 378, we have $z 	o y \op z$, hence $b_2 	o a$, so $b_1$ is relevant.  We are now done since $b_1 \op c = b_1$.
  \item Case 7: $x,y,z 
eq c$, $(y,z), (x,z) 
eq (a,b), (y \op z, x \op z) 
eq (a,b)$.  In this case $x \op ((y \op z) \op (x \op z))$ would already have been defined and equal to $x$ in the previous partial magma, thanks to Equation 854.

nodes.name: Case $x=c$
nodes.statement: Case 1: $x=c$.  Then $x \op z$ can only equal $c$, hence $z$ equals $b$ or $b_1$; and $y \op z$ can also only equal $b$ or $b_1$, and $(y \op z) \op (x \op z)$ is equal to $y \op z$.
