If $y \op z = b$, then we are done since $c \op b = c$.  If $y \op z = b_1$, then $b_1 \op c$ needs to be defined, so $b_1$ is relevant.  Furthermore, from equation 378 we have $b_1 \op z = b_1$, hence by the no idempotence property $z$ must equal $b$, so $b \to b_1$, and hence $c \op b_1 = c$, giving the claim.

nodes.name: Case $z=c$
nodes.statement: Case 2: $x \neq c$, $z = c$.  This forces $x,y=b,b_1$ with $y \op z = y$ and $x \op z = x$, thus $y \op x$ is well-defined and we need $x \op (y \op x)$ well-defined and equal to $x$.  If $x=y$, this follows from Equation 8; otherwise, either $x = b_1 \op b_2$ and $y = b_1$ or $x = b_1$ and $y = b_1 \op b_2$, and the claim follows from Equation 101 or Equation 46155 respectively.

nodes.name: Case $y=c$
nodes.statement:
Case 3: $x, z 
eq c$, $y = c$.  Then $z$ must equal $b$ or $b_1$, $y \op z$ must equal $c$, and $x \op z$ must equal $b$ or $b_1$, and $(y \op z) \op (x \op z)$ must equal $c$, with the $b_1$ options only available if $b_1$ is relevant.  If $x \op z = z$ then by equation 378, $z \op z = z$, contradicting the no idempotence law.  Thus we either have $z=b_1, x \op z = b$ or $z = b, x \op z = b_1$, and in either case $b_1$ must be relevant.  If $z 	o x$, then either have $x=b$, or $x = b_1$ and $b_1$ is relevant, and in either case we have $x \op c = x$ as required.  So we may assume $z 
ot 	o x$.  In the case $z = b_1, x \op z = b = b_1 \op b_2$ we may then apply unique factorization to conclude that $z = b_2$ and $x = b_1$, thus $x \op c = x$ as required.  In the opposite case $z = b$, $x \op z = b_1$ with $z 
ot 	o x$, we see from monotonicity that $b_1 = x \op z > z = b$; but from monotonicity again $b = b_1 \op b_2 > b_1$, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Case $(y,z)=(a,b)$
nodes.statement: Case 4: $x,y,z \neq c$, $(y,z) = (a,b)$.  Here, $y \op z$ and $(y \op z) \op (x \op z)$ must equal $c$, and $x \op z$ must then equal $b$ or $b_1$, with the latter an option only if $b_1$ is relevant.  If $x \op z = b$, then by Equation 378, $b \op b = b$, contradicting idempotence, thus $x \op z = b_1$ and $b_1$ is relevant, and then $b \to b_1$ by Equation 378 again.  If $z \to x$, then $x = b_1$, and the claim follows since $b_1 \op c = c$, so we may assume $z \not \to x$.  By monotonicity, this forces $b_1 = x \op z > z = b$ and $b = b_1 \op b_2 > b_1$, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Case $(x,z)=(a,b)$
nodes.statement: Case 5: $x,y,z \neq c$, $(y,z) \neq (a,b)$, $(x,z) = (a,b)$.  Now $x \op z = c$, and $y \op z$ must equal $b$ or $b_1$.  If $y \op z = b$, then by Equation 378, $b \op b = b$, contradicting idempotence, thus $y \op z = b_1$ and $b_1$ is relevant, and then $b \to b_1$ by Equation 378 again, so $b_1 \op (b_1 \op b_2) = b_1$.  By the auxiliary law, this forces $b_1 = b_2$, so $x = b_1$, and then we are done since $b_1 \op c = b_1$.

nodes.name: Case $(y\op z,x\op z)=(a,b)$
nodes.statement:
Case 6: $x,y,z 
eq c$, $(y,z), (x,z) 
eq (a,b)$, $(y \op z, x \op z) = (a,b)$.  Here $x \op z = b$ and $(y \op z) \op (x \op z) = c$.  If $z 	o x$, then $x=b$ and we are done since $b \op c = b$.  If $z 
ot 	o x$, then by unique factorization applied to $x \op z = b_1 \op b_2$ we have $(x,z) = (b_1,b_2)$.  By Equation 378, we have $z 	o y \op z$, hence $b_2 	o a$, so $b_1$ is relevant.  We are now done since $b_1 \op c = b_1$.

nodes.name: Case: old entries
nodes.statement:
Case 7: $x,y,z 
eq c$, $(y,z), (x,z) 
eq (a,b), (y \op z, x \op z) 
eq (a,b)$.  In this case $x \op ((y \op z) \op (x \op z))$ would already have been defined and equal to $x$ in the previous partial magma, thanks to Equation 854.

nodes.name: Seed partial magma
nodes.statement: Create a partial magma by imposing the laws $1 \op 0 = 2$, $0 \op 2 = 3$, $2 \op 0 = 2$, $3 \op 2 = 3$.  One can check that this is a partial magma.

nodes.name: Complete via the 854 extension
nodes.statement: We then extend it to a global magma using \Cref{extend-854}.

nodes.name: Auxiliary law gives the violation
nodes.statement:
We claim that we have the 413 violation
  $$ 0 \op (0 \op (0 \op (1 \op 0))) = 0$$
  or equivalently
  $$ 0 \op (0 \op 3) = 0.$$
Indeed this is immediate from the auxiliary law.

nodes.name: Case (i)
nodes.statement: Case (i) follows from \Cref{378}.

nodes.name: Case (ii)
nodes.statement:
For (ii), we observe
$$ y \op x = y \op ((a \op b) \op (y \op b)) = y$$
as required.

nodes.name: Case (iii)
nodes.statement:
For (iii), we see from (ii) that $y \to x$, and from (i) we have $x \op b \to y$, and then
$$ y \op x = y \op ((x \op (x \op b)) \op (y \op (x \op b))) = y$$
as required.

nodes.name: Case (iv)
nodes.statement:
For (iv), we have
$$ y \op x = y \op ((a \op z) \op (y \op z)) = y$$
as required.

nodes.name: Case (v)
nodes.statement:
Finally, for (v), in the $a=y$ case we have from \Cref{8} that
$$ y \op x = y \op ((y \op y^2) \op (y \op y^2)) = y,$$
in the $a = y \op z$ case we have from \Cref{8} that
$$ y \op x = y \op (((y \op z) \op (y \op z)^2) \op (y \op (y \op z)^2)) = y,$$
and finally in the $y = a \op z$ case we have from \Cref{8} that
$$ y \op x = y \op ( (a \op (a \op z)^2) \op ((a \op z) \op (a \op z)^2)) = y,$$
so the claim follows in all cases.

nodes.name: Free homomorphism
nodes.statement: Let  $f: X \to M$ be a function from $X$ to an $854$ magma $M$, then $\varphi_f$ is a homomorphism from $M_X$ (with the operation $*$) to $M$.

nodes.name: Restriction is a homomorphism
nodes.statement: We claim that the restriction of $\varphi_f$ to $M_{X,854}$ is a homomorphism from $M_{X,854}$ (with operation $\diamond$) to $M$.  Since $\varphi_f$ was already a homomorphism for $*$, it suffices to show that $\varphi_f$ preserves $\to$: that is to say, for any $x,y \in M_{X,854}$, that $x \to y$ implies $\varphi_f(x) \to \varphi_f(y)$.  By definition, one of the five scenarios (i)-(v) in \Cref{free-relate} holds, and in each case one can establish the claim from the corresponding claim of \Cref{854-relation} and an induction on the max-length of the claim $x \to y$.

nodes.name: Reduce to preserving $\to$
nodes.statement: Since $\varphi_f$ was already a homomorphism for $*$, it suffices to show that $\varphi_f$ preserves $\to$: that is to say, for any $x,y \in M_{X,854}$, that $x \to y$ implies $\varphi_f(x) \to \varphi_f(y)$.

nodes.name: Induction on max-length via the 854 relation lemma
nodes.statement: By definition, one of the five scenarios (i)-(v) in \Cref{free-relate} holds, and in each case one can establish the claim from the corresponding claim of \Cref{854-relation} and an induction on the max-length of the claim $x \to y$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on max-length via the 854 relation lemma

nodes.name: Remains to verify 854
nodes.statement:
It remains to show that $M_{854}$ actually satisfies 854, that is to say that
$$ (y \op z) \op (x \op z) \to x$$
for all $x,y,z \in M_{854}$.

nodes.name: Set $w=y\op z$; four cases
nodes.statement: Writing $w = y \op z$, we have $z \to w$ by \Cref{free-relate}(i), and we need to show that $w \op (x \op z) \to x$.  We divide into four cases.

nodes.name: Case 1
Reduce to $w\to x$
nodes.statement: Here we have $x \op z = x$ and $w \op (x \op z) = w$.  We now have $z \to x,w$ and $x \to w$, and we need to show that $w \to x$.

nodes.name: Subterm options
Subcases
nodes.statement: We split into subcases using \Cref{one-3}.

nodes.name: $x=w_R$
nodes.statement: If $x = w_R$ then the claim follows from \Cref{free-relate}(i).

nodes.name: $w=x_{RL}$
nodes.statement: If $w = x_{RL}$ then from \Cref{free-relate}(iii) we have $x_{RR} \to x_L$, and then the claim follows from \Cref{free-relate}(ii).

nodes.name: $x=w_{RL}$
nodes.statement: If $x = w_{RL}$, then $w_{RR} \to w_L$ by \Cref{free-relate}(ii) and from \Cref{free-relate}(iii) we will be done if we can show that $w_R \to w_{RL}$.  If $z = w_R$ then this follows from $z \to x$.  The claim $z = w_{RL}$ is not compatible with \Cref{one-1}, since $z=x$ in that case. If $w = z_R$ then $x = z_{RRL}$, and this is only compatible with \Cref{one-1} if $x = z_{RL}$, thus $z = a * (x * (x * b))$ and $w = x  * (x * b)$ for some $a,b$.  In order to have $x = w_{RL}$ in \Cref{one-3}, we must have $b \to x$ by \Cref{free-relate}(iii), but then $x*b$ would not lie in $M_{854}$, a contradiction.

nodes.name: $w=x_R$
nodes.statement: If $w = x_R$, then we cannot then have $z = x_R$ as then $z=w$ which is incompatible with \Cref{one-2}.  If $z = x_{RL} = w_L$ then $x_{RR} \to x_L$ by \Cref{free-relate}(ii), and the only available options from \Cref{one-2} are $z = w_R$ and $z = w_{RL}$.  For $z=w_R$ we have $w = z * z$ and $x = a * (z * z)$ for some $a$ with $z \to a = x_L$.  Since $z \to z*z = x_R$ as well by \Cref{free-relate}(i), and $z = x_{RR}$, we obtain $w \to x$ as required from \Cref{free-relate}(iv).

nodes.name: Case 2
Reduce to $w\to x$
nodes.statement: We now have $x * z, z \to w$, and we need to show that $w \to x$.

nodes.name: Subterm options
Subcases
nodes.statement: We split into cases depending on \Cref{wz-1}.

nodes.name: $w=(x*z)_R$
nodes.statement: If $w = (x*z)_R$ then $w=z$, which is incompatible with \Cref{wz}.

nodes.name: $w=(x*z)_{RL}$
nodes.statement: If $w = (x*z)_{RL}$ then $w = z_L$ and $z_R \to x$ by \Cref{free-relate}(ii). Only the first two possibilities of \Cref{wz} are compatible with $w=z_L$.  In the first case we are done since $z_R \to x$ and $w = z_R$.  In the second case, we have $z = w * (w * a)$ for some $a$ with $a \to w$ (from \Cref{free-relate}(ii) and $z \to w$), but then $w * a$ will not lie in $M_{854}$, contradiction.

nodes.name: $x*z=w_R$
nodes.statement: If $x*z = w_R$  then $w$ is longer than $z$ and $z \neq w_R$.  Comparing this with \Cref{wz} we see that the only compatible option is $z = w_{RL}$, thus $x=z$, and then $w = a * (x * x)$ and $x \to a$ by \Cref{free-relate}(iii), and the claim follows from \Cref{free-relate}(ii).

nodes.name: $x*z=w_{RL}$
nodes.statement: If $x * z = w_{RL}$, then $w = a * ((x *z) * b)$ for some $a,b$.  Then $w$, $w_R$, and $w_{RL}$ are all longer than $z$ and none of the options in \Cref{wz} can hold, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Case 3
nodes.statement:
Case 3: $x \op z \not \to w$, $z \to x$.  We now have $z \to x, w$, and we need to show that $w * x \to x$.

If $z \in \{ w_R, w_{RL}, x_R, x_{RL} \}$, then the claim follows from \Cref{free-relate}(iv), so we may assume that this is not the case.
By \Cref{one}, we then know that one of
$$ x = z_R, x = z_{RL}$$
holds, and also one of
$$
 w =  z_R, w = z_{RL}$$
 holds. Thus, we either have one of
$$ w = x, w = x_L, x = w_L.$$
But in any of these three cases the claim follows from \Cref{free-relate}(v).

nodes.name: Reduce to $w*x\to x$
nodes.statement: We now have $z \to x, w$, and we need to show that $w * x \to x$.

nodes.name: Subcase via (iv)
nodes.statement: If $z \in \{ w_R, w_{RL}, x_R, x_{RL} \}$, then the claim follows from \Cref{free-relate}(iv), so we may assume that this is not the case.

nodes.name: Remaining options
nodes.statement:
By \Cref{one}, we then know that one of
$$ x = z_R, x = z_{RL}$$
holds, and also one of
$$
 w =  z_R, w = z_{RL}$$
 holds. Thus, we either have one of
$$ w = x, w = x_L, x = w_L.$$

nodes.name: Conclude via (v)
nodes.statement: But in any of these three cases the claim follows from \Cref{free-relate}(v).

nodes.name: Case 4
nodes.statement: Case 4: $x \op z \not \to w$, $z \not \to x$.  Then $x = (w \op (x \op z))_{RL}$ and $z \to w$, so the claim follows from \Cref{free-relate}(ii).

nodes.name: Base cases
nodes.statement: This is trivial for $n=0,1$, and $n=-1$ follows from \Cref{906-b}.

nodes.name: Downward induction
nodes.statement: Observe that if the claim holds for $n=0,-1,\dots,-m$ for any $m \geq 1$ then it also holds for $n=-m-1$.

nodes.name: Periodicity gives all $n$
nodes.statement: Finally, since there is a common period to all the $L_y$ by finiteness (or Legendre's theorem), the set of $n$ for which the claim holds is periodic.  The claim follows.

nodes.name: Squares lie in $G$
nodes.statement: With these rules, $0$ is a unit, and the squaring operator is given by $Sa = 0$ and $S(x,a) = a$, so the set of squares is $G$.

nodes.name: Verify (16.2)
nodes.statement:
If $a \in G$ is a square number, we have
  $$ L_a b = R_a b = a+b$$
  and
  $$ L_a (x,b) = (x/\phi_b(a), b); \quad R_a (x,b) = (x \phi_b(a), b)$$
  so \Cref{lr} is satisfied.

nodes.name: Verify (16.3)
nodes.statement: Now we verify \Cref{lr-simp}.

nodes.name: Case $y$ a square
nodes.statement: If $y$ is a square, then the claim already follows from \Cref{lr} since $Sy=0$ is a unit.

nodes.name: Case $y\in N$: two subgoals
nodes.statement:
Otherwise, for $y \in \Q^\times$ and $b \in G \backslash \{0\}$, we have to show that
$$ L_{(y,b)} R_{(y,b)} a = R_b a = a+b$$
for $a \in G$ and
$$ L_{(y,b)} R_{(y,b)} (x,a) = R_b (x,a) = (\phi_a(b) x, a) $$
for $x \in \Q^\times$ and $a \in G \backslash \{0\}$.

nodes.name: First subgoal
nodes.statement:
In the first case, we have from \Cref{op-2} that
$$ R_{(y,b)} a = (y/\phi_a(b), b)$$
and then from \Cref{op-3} we have
$$L_{(y,b)} R_{(y,b)} a = a+b$$
as required.

nodes.name: Second subgoal, $a=b$
nodes.statement:
In the second case, if $a=b$, then by the bijective nature of $\phi_a$, we can write $x = \phi_a(c) y$ for some $c \in G$, then from \Cref{op-3} we have
$$ R_{(y,b)} (x,a) = a+c$$
and then by \Cref{op-1}
$$ L_{(y,b)} R_{(y,b)} (x,a) = (\phi_a(a+c) y, a)$$
but from construction we have $\phi_a(a+c)=-\phi_a(c) = \phi_a(b)\phi_a(c)$ and hence $\phi_a(a+c) y = \phi_a(b) x$ as required.

nodes.name: Distinct $a,b$ by (iii)
nodes.statement: It remains to handle the case when $a,b$ are distinct elements of $G \backslash \{0\}$.  But this follows from (iii).

nodes.name: Add a new tuple
nodes.statement:
We select a $c \in G \backslash \{0\}$ that has not previously been used by the partial solution, let $z \in \Q^\times$ be arbitrary, (e.g., one could take $z=1$ if desired), and add $(x,y,z,a,b,c)$ to ${\mathcal F}$, thus we now also assign
$$ (\phi_a(b)^n x,a) \op (\phi_b(c)^n y,b) = (\phi_c(a)^n z,c)$$
$$ (\phi_b(c)^n y,b) \op (\phi_c(a)^n z,c) = (\phi_a(b)^{n+1} x, a)$$
$$ (\phi_c(a)^n z,c) \op (\phi_a(b)^{n+1} x, a) = (\phi_b(c)^{n+1} y,b)$$
for all natural numbers $n$.

nodes.name: No self-collisions
nodes.statement: As the $a,b,c$ are distinct, the $\phi_a(b), \phi_b(c), \phi_c(a)$ are not equal to $\pm 1$, and the members of this infinite sequence do not collide with each other.

nodes.name: Novel $c$ avoids collisions
nodes.statement: The second and third equations in this family cannot collide with previous assignments because $c$ is novel.

nodes.name: Fresh primes avoid remaining collisions
nodes.statement: If we arrange matters so that $\phi_b(c)$ involves primes in the numerator or denominator that do not appear in any previous $\phi_a(b), \phi_b(c), \phi_c(a), x, y, z$ used by the greedy algorithm, or the current $x,y,z$, then we also see that the first infinite sequence does not collide with any previously assigned value of $\op$ either.

nodes.name: Reduce to non-injective $L_y$
nodes.statement: It suffices to produce a partial solution in which $L_y$ is not injective.

nodes.name: Choose parameters
nodes.statement: Pick distinct $a, b, b', c$ with $\phi_a(b)$, $\phi_a(b')$ having no prime factors in common in the numerator or denominator.

nodes.name: Seed partial solution
nodes.statement:
We take the partial solution consisting of $(1,1,1,a,b,c)$ and $(1,1,1,a,b',c)$, that is to say we impose the conditions
$$ (\phi_a(b)^n,a) \op (\phi_b(c)^n,b) = (\phi_c(a)^n,c)$$
$$ (\phi_b(c)^n,b) \op (\phi_c(a)^n,c) = (\phi_a(b)^{n+1}, a)$$
$$ (\phi_c(a)^n,c) \op (\phi_a(b)^{n+1}, a) = (\phi_b(c)^{n+1},b)$$
and
$$ (\phi_a(b)^n,a) \op (\phi_{b'}(c)^n,b') = (\phi_c(a)^n,c)$$
$$ (\phi_{b'}(c)^n,b') \op (\phi_c(a)^n,c) = (\phi_a(b')^{n+1}, a)$$
$$ (\phi_c(a)^n,c) \op (\phi_{a}(b')^{n+1}, a) = (\phi_b(c)^{n+1},b').$$

nodes.name: Left injectivity fails
nodes.statement: One can check that no collisions occur; on the other hand, as $L_{(1,a)} (1,b) = L_{(1,a)} (1,b') = (1,c)$, we already have a violation of left injectivity.

nodes.name: Complete greedily
nodes.statement: Completing this seed to a full magma using \Cref{greedy-iterate}, we obtain the claim.

nodes.name: WLOG $a_0$ new and non-zero
nodes.statement: We may assume that $E$ does not already contain any pair of the form $(a_0,c)$, since we are done otherwise.  By Axiom 1 implies that $a_0 \neq 0$.

nodes.name: Collect predecessors $b_i$
nodes.statement: Let $b_1,\dots,b_n$ denote all the integers $b_i$ such that $(b_i,a) \in E$, then $n \geq 0$ is finite, and by Axiom 2 all the $b_i$ are non-zero and not equal to $-a$.

nodes.name: Add the new pairs
nodes.statement: Let $c_0$ be a sufficiently large integer to be chosen later.  We then add the pairs $(a_0,c_0)$ and $(c-b_i,-b_i)$ to $E$ for all $i$.  Furthermore, if $i$ is such that $(-b_i,d_i) \in E$ for some (necessarily unique and non-zero) $d_i$, we also add $(d_i+b+i-c_0, b_i-c_0)$ to $E$.  Let $E'$ be the resulting set of pairs.

nodes.name: Axioms 1-3 preserved
nodes.statement: Axioms 4, 5 for $E$ ensure that (for $c_0$ large enough) the addition of these pairs do not cause a violation of Axioms 2 or 3 for $E'$, and of course Axiom 1 for $E'$ will also be retained.

nodes.name: Axiom 4 preserved
nodes.statement: As for Axiom 4, one can check that the only new pairs of pairs $(',b), (b,c)$ that would trigger these axioms either take the form $(b_i,a_0), (a_0,c_0)$ or $(c_0-b_i,-b_i), (-b_i,d_i)$, and in either case we see from construction that Axiom 4 remains in effect for $E'$.

nodes.name: Axiom 5 preserved
nodes.statement: Finally, the new quadruples of pairs $(b,a), (b',a), (-b, d), (-b',d') \in E'$ only arise when either $(-b,d)$, $(-b',d')$ is equal to $(a_0,c_0)$ and the other three pairs in the quadruple were already in $E$, and for $c_0$ large enough we see that Axiom 5 remains valid.

nodes.name: Greedy completion of the seed
nodes.statement: By \Cref{1516-ext}, \Cref{1516-ext-var} and the greedy algorithm starting with the seed consisting of $(0,0)$, $(-1,2)$, $(3,1)$, $(-10,20)$, $(30,10)$, we obtain a graph $\{ (a,f(a)): a \in \Z \}$ of a function $f:\Z \to \Z$ with $f(0)=0$, $f(-1)=2$, $f(3)=1$, $f(-10) = 20$, $f(30)=10$ and the property that if $f(a)=b$ and $f(b)=c$, then $f(c-a)=-a$, and also with the property that for every non-zero $h$ there are distinct $a_{h,1}, a_{h,2}, a_{h,3}, a_{h,4}$ with $f(a_{h,i})=a_{h,i}+h$ for $i=1, 2, 3, 4$.

nodes.name: 1516 holds and (i)
nodes.statement: We then have that \Cref{1516-f} holds.  If we then define the magma operation $\op$ by \Cref{xy-1516}, we obtain \Cref{1516}, and since $f(0)=0$ we have (i).

nodes.name: Property (ii)
nodes.statement: Also, from construction we see that $R_d (d - a_{h,i}) = d+h$ for any $d,h,i$, giving (ii).  Finally, from construction we have $R_a (a+1) = a+1+f(-1) = a+3$, so $L_a R_a (a+1) = a + f(3) = a+1$, and similarly $L_a R_a (a+10) = a+10$, giving (iii).

nodes.name: Choose $c_{y,a}$ via (iii)
nodes.statement: Let $y = (a,c,n)$.  By \Cref{1516-base} (iii), we can find $c_{y,a} \neq a,c$ such that $L_a R_a c_{y,a} = c_{y,a}$, or equivalently $L_a L_{c_{y,a}} a = c_{y,a}$.

nodes.name: Choose $c_{y,b}$ via (ii)
Verify the identity
nodes.statement: We now have $L_a L_{c_{y,b}} b = L_{Sa} L_{c_{y,b}} L_{c_{y,b}} a = c_{y,b}$ for such $b$, giving the claim.

nodes.name: Define by cases
nodes.statement: We define $L_{c'} y$ for $y = (a,c,n) \in G'$ as follows:

nodes.name: Case (i)
nodes.statement: (i) If $c' = a$ and $n=0$, then $L_{c'} y := a$.

nodes.name: Case (ii)
nodes.statement: (ii) If $c' = a$ and $n \neq 0$, then $L_{c'} y := (a,c,0)$.

nodes.name: Case (iii)
nodes.statement: (iii) If $c' = c_{y,b}$ for some $b$, then $L_{c'} y := b$.

nodes.name: Case (iv)
nodes.statement: (iv) In all other cases, $L_{c'} y$ is undefined.

nodes.name: On $\Z$ use the base magma
nodes.statement: We of course also define $L_{c'} y$ for $y \in \Z$ using \Cref{1516-base}.

nodes.name: Well-defined; properties hold
nodes.statement: From Lemma \ref{aux} we see that this is a well-defined operation, with $L_c y$ undefined for any $y = (a,c,n) \in G'$.  So properties (a)-(e) and (g) are clear from construction.  Property (e) is also clear from construction in each of the three cases (i), (ii), (iii) (for (i), (ii) we also use the fact that $L_a a = a$).

nodes.name: Find $b$ by surjectivity
nodes.statement: Write $y = (a,c,n)$. Because $L_a: \Z \to \Z$ and $L_{c'}: \Z \to \Z$ are surjective, we can find $b \in \Z$ such that $L_a L_{c'} b = c'$.

nodes.name: $b\ne c'$
nodes.statement: If we had $b=c'$, then $L_a c' = c'$, which from \eqref{1516} (and $Sc' = c'$) implies that $a = c'$, which contradicts the undefined nature of $L_{c'} y$ thanks to properties (b), (c) of a partial solution.  Hence, $b \neq c'$.

nodes.name: Define and check
nodes.statement: We then set $L_{c'} y := b$.  It is then clear that all the properties (a)-(g) of a partial solution are maintained.

nodes.name: Case analysis
nodes.statement: Write $y = (a,c,n)$. There are several cases.

nodes.name: Case $L_{c'}y\in G'$
nodes.statement: Case 1: $L_{c'} y = w$ for some $w \in G'$.  By Lemma \ref{aux}, $c_{w,c'}$ is distinct from $c'$, and from property (d) of a partial solution, $L_{c_{w,c'}} w = c'$.  By property (e) of a partial solution, we can find $z = (c_{w,c'}, c', n')$ such that $L_{c'} z$ is currently undefined.  Then set $L_{c'} z := y$, so that we have $L_{c_{w,c'}} L_{c'} L_{c'} z = c'$.  One then verifies that all the axioms (a)-(g) of a partial solution are valid in this case.

nodes.name: Case $L_{c'}y\in\Z$
nodes.statement:
Case 2: $c' 
eq a$ and $L_{c'} y = b$ for some $b \in \Z$. By property (g) of a partial solution, $c' 
eq b$.  By \Cref{1516-base}, we can find $a'$ such that $L_{a'} b = R_b a' = c'$ and $a' 
eq c'$.  By property (e) of a partial solution, we can find $z = (a', c', n')$ such that $L_{c'} z$ is currently undefined.  Then set $L_{c'} z = y$, so that we have $L_{a'} L_{c'} L_{c'} z = c'$. One then verifies that all the axioms (a)-(g) of a partial solution are valid in this case.

nodes.name: Case undefined
nodes.statement: Case 3: $c' \neq a$ and $L_{c'} y$ is currently undefined.  Use Lemma \ref{first-ext} set $L_{c'} y$ equal to some $b \in \Z$, then apply the Case 2 analysis.

nodes.name: Case $c'=a$
nodes.statement: Case 4: $c' = a$.  Because we are excluding the case $n=0$, we are now in Case 1 thanks to property (c) of a partial solution.

nodes.name: Build a chain of partial solutions
nodes.statement: By iterating \Cref{first-ext} and \Cref{second-ext} in alternation, we can find an increasing chain of partial solutions with the property that for any $y = (a,c,n) \in G'$ and $c' \in \Z$ and any natural number $k$, excluding the case where $c'=a$ and $n=0$, that one can find a partial solution on this chain for which $L_{c'} y$ is defined, and such that $L_{c'} z = y$ for at least $k$ distinct choices of $z \in G'$.
nodes.statement_short: Build a chain of partial solutions

nodes.name: Limit operation with infinite surjectivity
nodes.statement:
Taking the limit of this chain, we can then find a fully defined operation $L_{c'} y$ for $c' \in \Z$ and $y \in G$ satisfying the properties (a)-(d), (f), (g) (but not (e)) of a partial solution, with the property that
$y = (a,c,n) \in G'$ and $c' \in \Z$, excluding the case $c'=a$ and $n=0$, that there are infinitely many $z \in G'$ such that $L_{c'} z = y$.

nodes.name: Excluded case by (b)
nodes.statement: The excluded case $c'=a, n=0$ is also covered by property (b) of a partial solution.  The claim follows.

nodes.name: Reduce to (17.4), (17.5) for one $x$
nodes.statement:
We can work with a single $x \in G'$.  Our task is to find a function $L_x$ for which
\begin{equation} L_x x = Sx
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation} L_{Sy} L_x L_x y = x
\end{equation}
for all $y \in G$ (note that $L_{Sy}$ is already fully constructed).

nodes.name: Define seeds
nodes.statement: Define a \emph{seed} to be an injective partial function $L_x$ defined on finitely many values and satisfying \Cref{axioma-again}, as well as \Cref{axiomb-again} whenever $L_x L_x y$ is defined.

nodes.name: At most one preimage
nodes.statement: If there is a $y \in G$ for which $L_x y$ is currently undefined, then by hypothesis $y$ is equal to $L_x z$ for at most one $z$.

nodes.name: Case preimage exists
nodes.statement: If such a $z$ exists, we set $L_x y$ to be an element of $\{ w: L_{Sz} w = x \}$ different from $y$ that is not already in the domain or range of $L_x$; we are able to do so thanks to the infinite surjectivity (\Cref{1516-base} (ii)) and the fact that the domain and the range of $L_x$ are finite.

nodes.name: Case no preimage
nodes.statement: If no such $z$ exists, we set $L_x y$ to be arbitrary element of $G$ not already in the domain or range.  In either case, we see that the seed property is preserved.

nodes.name: Iterate from the initial seed
nodes.statement: Starting from the seed in which $L_x$ is only defined on $x$ and maps it to $Sx$, we obtain the claim.

nodes.name: Choose $x_0$
nodes.statement: Let us define the element $x_0 := (0, 1, 0) \in G'$.

nodes.name: $0\op x_0 = 0$
nodes.statement: Since $S x_0 = 0$, we know that $0 \op x_0 = 0$ (see the first part of the proof of \Cref{axiom-b}).

nodes.name: 255 fails
nodes.statement:
Therefore, $x_0$ does not satisfy the 255 equation, as we have
  $$((x_0 \op x_0) \op x_0) \op x_0 = (0 \op x_0) \op x_0 = 0 \op x_0 = 0 \neq x_0.$$

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: We need to show that $\op''$ verifies the law \Cref{1729}.

nodes.name: Both in $SM$
nodes.statement: In the case when $x,y \in SM$, then the claim follows from the fact that $SM$ already satisfied this equation.

nodes.name: $x\in SM$, $y\in N$
nodes.statement: If $x$ was equal to an element $a \in SM$ and $y \in N$, then by construction the law is equivalent to $L'_{Sa} R'_a L'_a y = y$, which follows from axiom (i).

nodes.name: $x\in N$, $y\in SM$
nodes.statement:
Now suppose that $x \in N$ and $y$ is equal to some element $a$ of $SM$.  From axiom (v) we have $x \op'' x = S'x$, and then this case of \Cref{1729} becomes
$$L_{S'x} ( R'_a x \op' x ) = a$$
which follows from axiom (vi).

nodes.name: Both in $N$: divide by axiom (ii)
nodes.statement: So the only remaining case is when $x,y \in N$.  Using axiom (ii), we can divide into cases:

nodes.name: Case $x=y$
nodes.statement: Case 1: $x=y$.  Then by (v) we need to show that $L'_{S'x} L'_{S'x} x = x$, which follows from axiom (iv).

nodes.name: Case $y=R'_ax$
nodes.statement: Case 2: $y = R'_a x$ for some $a \in SM$.  Then by axiom (vi), we need to show that $L'_{S'y} L'_{L_{S'x}^{-1} a} y = x$, which follows from axiom (iii).

nodes.name: Remaining case via (vii)
nodes.statement: Case 3: We are not in case 1 or case 2.  Then by axiom (vii), we have $y \op'' x = z$ for some $z \in N$ with $z \op'' y = (L'_{S'y})^{-1} x$.  But this implies $L'_{S'y} (z \op'' y) = x$, which is \Cref{1729}.

nodes.name: 817 fails by axiom (ii)
nodes.statement: We have now verified that $\op''$ satisfies 1729.  For any $x \in N$, we have $x \op'' SS' x = R'_{SS' x} x$, and so the final claim follows from axiom (ii).

nodes.name: Direct limit
nodes.statement: Take the direct limit of the chain to obtain total functions $L'_0, \op', S'$.  The axioms (i'), (iii'), (iv''), (v''), (vi''), (vii'') of the partial solutions then easily imply that the direct limit satisfies the axioms (i'), (iii'), (iv'), (v), (vi'), (vii') (one also uses axiom (P) to note that all pending identities disappear in the direct limit).

nodes.name: Apply the reduction lemma
nodes.statement: The claim now follows from \Cref{axiom-reduce}.

nodes.name: Whole coset is undefined
nodes.statement: By axiom (i''), $L'_0 (R'_0)^n x$ is undefined for every integer $n$.

nodes.name: Choose a fresh generator
nodes.statement:
Let $d = E_m$ be a generator of $SM$ that does not appear as a component of any index of any of the generators $e_a$ appearing anywhere in the partial solution; such a $d$ exists due to the finiteness hypotheses.  We set $L'_0 x := e_d$, and then extend by \Cref{itero}, \Cref{itero-2}, thus
$$L'_0 (R'_0)^n x := (R'_0)^n e_d$$
and
$$L'_0 (R'_0)^n e_d := (R'_0)^{n-1} x.$$

nodes.name: No collisions; axioms preserved
nodes.statement: Because of the new nature of $d$, no collisions in the partial function $L_0$ are created by this operation.  It is then easy to check that axiom (i'') is preserved by this operation, whereas none of the other axioms (S), (iii''), (iv''), (v''), (vi''), (vii''), (P), (P'), (P'') are affected by this extension.

nodes.name: Axiom (L)
nodes.statement: With some effort, axiom (L) can also be verified.

nodes.name: Fresh generators; define $S'x$
nodes.statement: Let $d_0, d_1 \in SM$ be generators $E_{n_0}$ of $SM$ that do not appear in the index $a$ of any $e_a$ that currently appears in the partial solution (of which there are only finitely many).  We also set some further distinct generators $d'_{y,z} \in SM$ for $y,z \in SM$ that are distinct from each other and all previous generators (this is possible as we have infinitely many generators).  We set $S'x,  x \op' x := d_0$; this preserves axiom (S) and (v'').

nodes.name: New $L'_0$ values
nodes.statement:
We set
$$ L'_0 R'_{2d_0} x := e_{d_1}$$
$$ L'_0 R'_{2d_0} (R'_{d_0})^{-1} e_{d_1} := R'_{d_0} x$$
and then extend these choices using \Cref{itero}, \Cref{itero-2} to recover axiom (i'), thus for instance
$$ L'_0 (R'_0)^n R'_{2d_0} x := (R'_0)^n e_{d_1}$$
and
$$ L'_0 (R'_0)^n e_{d_1}  := (R'_0)^{n-1} R'_{2d_0} x$$
for all $n \in \Z$.

nodes.name: Repair axiom (iii'')
nodes.statement:
To retain axiom (iii''), we perform the following actions:
\begin{itemize}
\item If $y_0$ is undefined, do nothing.
\item If $R'_a x = y_0$ for some $a \in SM$ (so that $L'_0 R'_{S'y_0} x$ is defined, by hypothesis (A)), set $L'_0 R'_{2(a-d_0)} y_0 := R'_{a-d_0} (R'_{2S'y_0})^{-1} R'_0 L'_0 R'_{S'y_0} x$. Then extend using \Cref{itero}, \Cref{itero-2}.
\item If $x = R'_a y_0$ for some $a \in SM$ (so that $L'_0 R'_{2(a-Sy_0)} x$ is already defined, by hypothesis (B)), set $L'_0 R'_{2d_0} (R'_{a-S'y_0})^{-1} L'_0 R'_{2(a-Sy_0)} x :=R'_{d_0} y_0$, and extend using \Cref{itero}, \Cref{itero-2}.

nodes.name: No parent
nodes.statement: If $y_0$ is undefined, do nothing.

nodes.name: Parent below
nodes.statement: If $R'_a x = y_0$ for some $a \in SM$ (so that $L'_0 R'_{S'y_0} x$ is defined, by hypothesis (A)), set $L'_0 R'_{2(a-d_0)} y_0 := R'_{a-d_0} (R'_{2S'y_0})^{-1} R'_0 L'_0 R'_{S'y_0} x$. Then extend using \Cref{itero}, \Cref{itero-2}.

nodes.name: Parent above
nodes.statement: If $x = R'_a y_0$ for some $a \in SM$ (so that $L'_0 R'_{2(a-Sy_0)} x$ is already defined, by hypothesis (B)), set $L'_0 R'_{2d_0} (R'_{a-S'y_0})^{-1} L'_0 R'_{2(a-Sy_0)} x :=R'_{d_0} y_0$, and extend using \Cref{itero}, \Cref{itero-2}.

nodes.name: Process pending identities
nodes.statement:
To retain axiom (P), we perform the following actions for each pending identity of the form $I[x,y,z]$ for some $y,z$, executed in some arbitrary order.
\begin{itemize}
\item Remove this identity $I[x,y,z]$ from the list of pending identities.
\item Set $L'_0 R'_0 R'_{d_0} y := e_{d'_{y,z}}$, and $x' \op y' := z'$, where $(x',y',z') := (z, x, (R'_{2d_0})^{-1} e_{d'_{y,z}})$. Extend all the new definitions of $L'_0$ using \Cref{itero}, \Cref{itero-2}.
\item If $S'x'$ is undefined, add $I[x',y',z']$ as a pending identity.
\item If instead $S'x'$ is defined (which makes $L'_0 R'_0 R'_{S'x'} y'$ defined, by axiom (C)), set $x'' \op y'' = z''$, where $(x'',y'',z'') := (z', x', (R'_{2S'x'})^{-1} L'_0 R'_0 R'_{S'x'} y')$.  Then add $I[x'',y'',z'']$ as a pending identity.

nodes.name: Remove
nodes.statement: Remove this identity $I[x,y,z]$ from the list of pending identities.

nodes.name: Define new entries
nodes.statement: Set $L'_0 R'_0 R'_{d_0} y := e_{d'_{y,z}}$, and $x' \op y' := z'$, where $(x',y',z') := (z, x, (R'_{2d_0})^{-1} e_{d'_{y,z}})$. Extend all the new definitions of $L'_0$ using \Cref{itero}, \Cref{itero-2}.

nodes.name: Add pending identity
nodes.statement: If $S'x'$ is undefined, add $I[x',y',z']$ as a pending identity.

nodes.name: Define and add pending identity
nodes.statement: If instead $S'x'$ is defined (which makes $L'_0 R'_0 R'_{S'x'} y'$ defined, by axiom (C)), set $x'' \op y'' = z''$, where $(x'',y'',z'') := (z', x', (R'_{2S'x'})^{-1} L'_0 R'_0 R'_{S'x'} y')$.  Then add $I[x'',y'',z'']$ as a pending identity.

nodes.name: Axioms preserved
nodes.statement: One can check that these definitions do not cause any collisions in the partial function $L'_0$, and that axioms (i'), (iii'), (iv''), (v''), (vii''), (P), (P'), (P'') are preserved; the remaining axiom (vi'') is unaffected by this extension.  Axiom (L) can also be shown to be preserved after a tedious calculation.

nodes.name: The parent $y_0$
nodes.statement: Let $y_0$ be the parent of $x$, that is to say the unique neighbor of $x$ in the path to $1$ (this is only defined for $x \neq 1$), then by axiom (i'') $y_0$ is the unique neighbor for which $S'y_0$ is defined, and we either have $x = R'_a y_0$ or $R'_a x = y_0$ for some unique $a \in SM$.

nodes.name: Impose (A)-(C) and apply
nodes.statement: By using \Cref{enlarge-l0-many}, we may impose axioms (A), (B), (C) without loss of generality, as this only imposes a finite set of conditions.  The claim now follows from \Cref{enlarge-S-induct-axioms}.

nodes.name: WLOG $S'x,S'y$ defined
nodes.statement: By applying \Cref{enlarge-S} as needed, we may assume without loss of generality that $S'x$ and $S'y$ are already defined (among other things, this removes the possibility that $x \op' y$ is part of a pending identity).  If this makes $x \op' y$ defined, then we are done, so we may assume that this is not the case.

nodes.name: WLOG $L'_0$ value defined
nodes.statement: Similarly, by using \Cref{enlarge-l0}, we may assume without loss of generality that  $L'_0 R'_0 R'_{S'x} y$ is defined.

nodes.name: Case analysis
nodes.statement: We now divide into cases:

nodes.name: Case $x=y$
nodes.statement: Case 1: $x=y$.  In this case we set $x \op' y := S'x$.  It is clear that this preserves axiom (v''), and no other axiom is impacted.

nodes.name: Case $x=R'_ay$
nodes.statement: Case 2: If $x = R'_a y$ for some $a \in SM$, then we set $x \op' y := a - S'y$.  This preserves axiom (vi''), and no other axiom is impacted.

nodes.name: Generic case
nodes.statement: Case 3: If $x$ is not equal to $y$ or $R'_a y$ for any $a \in SM$.  Let $d_0 \in SM$ be a generator that does not appear as a component of any index of any of the generators $e_a$ appearing anywhere in the partial solution.  We set $x \op' y := z$ with $z := e^2_{d_0}$.

nodes.name: Repair (vii'') with a pending identity
nodes.statement:
This temporarily disrupts axiom (vii'').  To recover it, we perform the following actions.
\begin{itemize}
  \item Set $x' \op' y' = z'$, where $(x',y',z') := (z, x, (R'_{2S'x})^{-1} L_0 R'_0 R'_{Sx} y)$.
  \item Add $I[x',y',z']$ as a pending identity.

nodes.name: Add pending identity
nodes.statement: Add $I[x',y',z']$ as a pending identity.

nodes.name: Axioms preserved
nodes.statement: One can check that these definitions do not cause any collisions in the partial function $L'_0$, and that axioms (i'), (vii'), (P), (P') are preserved; the remaining axioms (S), (iii''), (iv''), (v''), (vi'') are unaffected by this extension.

nodes.name: Normalize both terms
nodes.statement: Repeatedly apply $R$ to $a$ and $b$ until normal forms $a'$ and $b'$ are found for them (this is possible because $R$ is strongly normalizing).

nodes.name: Syntactic comparison
nodes.statement: Compare $a'$ and $b'$ for exact equality (sometimes called ``syntactic equality'').

nodes.name: Equivalent
nodes.statement: If $a' = b'$, we can conclude $a\leftrightarrow^* b$.

nodes.name: Not equivalent
nodes.statement: If $a' \neq b'$ can can conclude that they are \emph{not} equivalent due to the lemma.

nodes.name: Find unjoinable critical pairs
nodes.statement: identify such pairs, and

nodes.name: Add as equations, oriented if possible
nodes.statement: add them as an unoriented equation, to be oriented if possible, and
nodes.statement_short: Add as equations, oriented if possible

nodes.name: Repeat until all pairs join
nodes.statement: repeating until no un-joinable pairs exist.

nodes.name: Find equivalence classes and goals
nodes.statement: Using the graph of implications and refutations, it identifies equivalence classes/strongly-connected components in the implication graph and possible goals by subtracting out the refutation graph.

nodes.name: Bidirectional substitution search
nodes.statement: Iterating through all equivalence classes, it can perform a meet-in-the-middle graph search where it searches outwards from both hypotheses and goals by performing equation substitutions.

nodes.name: Adjust search depth
nodes.statement: Depending on the number of hypotheses versus goals, it dynamically adjusts the search depth on both sides based on a configured branching factor.
